questions.learningObjective: Apply Amdahl's Law to bound the maximum speedup of a workload with a non-parallel fraction, and identify the asymptotic ceiling.
questions.stem: A workload spends 5% of its serial time in a sequential preprocessing step that cannot be parallelized; the remaining 95% is embarrassingly parallel. By Amdahl's Law, what is the maximum achievable speedup as the number of workers p → ∞?

options.text: 20×. Amdahl's Law says S(∞) = 1 / f_serial = 1 / 0.05 = 20.
Unbounded: with an embarrassingly parallel 95% region, adding workers keeps reducing wall time without limit, since only the parallel portion dominates asymptotically.
5×, because only the serial 5% survives, so the maximum improvement is a factor equal to the serial fraction expressed as a multiplier.
19×. S(∞) = (1 − f_serial) / f_serial = 0.95 / 0.05 = 19; the serial region does not itself contribute to speedup.

questions.explanation: Amdahl's Law: S(p) = 1 / (f_s + (1 − f_s)/p). As p → ∞, S(p) → 1 / f_s. Here f_s = 0.05, so S(∞) = 1 / 0.05 = 20. The parallel portion vanishes asymptotically; only the serial fraction sets the ceiling.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: the asymptotic Amdahl ceiling is 1 / f_serial = 20×.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: any non-zero serial fraction bounds the speedup; this is the classic Amdahl insight.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: 5× is a misreading of the ratio; the ceiling is 1/f_serial, not 100×f_serial.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: 19× uses (1 − f_s)/f_s, which gives the ratio of parallel-to-serial work but not the total speedup relative to the original wall time.

assumptions: The serial fraction 5% is measured on the original single-worker execution and remains serial at all p.
Communication, synchronization, and scheduling overheads are ignored (idealized Amdahl model).
nonImplications: Does not imply that increasing workers is worthless past some threshold; diminishing returns matter but useful speedup often remains.
Does not imply that Gustafson's Law gives the same ceiling — Gustafson considers scaled workloads, which relax Amdahl's bound in weak-scaling settings.

distractorRationales.D: Confuses parallel/serial ratio with total speedup formula.

sourceRefs.locator: Amdahl and Gustafson in the introduction chapter

performanceClaim.scope: generic parallel speedup analysis, asymptotic p

questions.learningObjective: Apply the Roofline model to classify a batch-1 GEMV as compute- or memory-bound on a specific GPU and derive the achievable throughput ceiling from arithmetic intensity times HBM bandwidth.
questions.stem: On A100 SXM (peak FP16 Tensor-Core throughput ≈ 312 TFLOP/s, HBM2e bandwidth ≈ 2.0 TB/s), consider a batch-1 GEMV y = W x with W ∈ ℝ^{4096×4096} FP16, x ∈ ℝ^{4096} FP16, y ∈ ℝ^{4096} FP16 (all resident in HBM, weights streamed once, negligible reuse). Assuming steady state and ignoring launch overhead, which Roofline characterization is correct?

options.text: Memory-bound; AI ≈ 1 FLOP/byte is far below A100's FP16 ridge point (~ 153 FLOP/byte), so the ceiling is HBM × AI ≈ 2 TFLOP/s.
Compute-bound; the operational intensity for this GEMV is ≈ 2 FLOP/byte, comfortably above the A100 FP32 ridge point (~ 9.75 FLOP/byte), so the SMs saturate at the FP32 peak of 19.5 TFLOP/s.
Compute-bound; the achievable ceiling is approximately the FP16 Tensor-Core peak of about 312 TFLOP/s, since Tensor Cores are the dispatched math path for FP16 GEMV kernels on A100.
Memory-bound, but the binding ceiling is set by on-chip shared-memory (SRAM) bandwidth rather than HBM, because Tensor-Core GEMV routes each weight through SMEM staging before consumption.

questions.explanation: GEMV traffic is dominated by streaming the weight matrix: bytes ≈ 4096·4096·2 (W) + 4096·2 (x) + 4096·2 (y) ≈ 33.6 MB; FLOPs ≈ 2·4096·4096 ≈ 33.6 M. Arithmetic intensity ≈ 1 FLOP/byte. Ridge point for FP16 Tensor Cores on A100 is 312e12 / 2.0e12 ≈ 153 FLOP/byte. Since AI (1) << ridge (153), the operation is deeply memory-bound and the ceiling is AI × HBM BW ≈ 2 TFLOP/s.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: operational intensity is well below the FP16 ridge point; the HBM bandwidth × AI product gives the correct ceiling.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: the AI is ≈ 1, not 2, FLOP/byte; comparing against the FP32 ridge point is also inconsistent with FP16 Tensor-Core execution.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: batch-1 GEMV cannot approach the compute peak; the weight matrix must be streamed once from HBM and offers essentially no data reuse.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: shared-memory bandwidth is not the constraint here because each weight is loaded from HBM exactly once and does not linger in SRAM long enough to matter for the bandwidth ceiling.

assumptions: Weights resident in HBM, no persistent-kernel weight caching.
Launch and kernel-overhead time excluded from steady-state analysis.
nonImplications: The result does not imply that a batched GEMM with the same K would be memory-bound.
The result does not imply that lowering weight precision to INT8 always maintains bandwidth-boundedness (it depends on the ratio to the new ridge point).

distractorRationales.B: Miscomputes arithmetic intensity and mixes precision regimes.
distractorRationales.C: Confuses compute peak with achievable throughput for a bandwidth-limited op.
distractorRationales.D: Confuses on-chip and off-chip memory tiers.

sourceRefs.locator: Ch. 5 & Ch. 6, Roofline and Arithmetic Intensity

performanceClaim.scope: A100 SXM, FP16 GEMV, batch=1, K=N=4096

questions.learningObjective: Given an elementwise kernel's per-element FLOP and byte cost, compute the arithmetic intensity and classify the kernel against a specific GPU's FP32 ridge point.
questions.stem: On A100 SXM (peak FP32 ≈ 19.5 TFLOP/s, HBM ≈ 2.0 TB/s), a kernel reads an FP32 tensor A of shape [32M] and writes B[i] = softplus(A[i]) (≈ 10 FLOPs per element). Which Roofline analysis is correct?

options.text: Compute-bound; the 10 FLOPs per element push arithmetic intensity above the FP32 ridge point, so the achievable ceiling is close to the A100 FP32 peak of 19.5 TFLOP/s.
Memory-bound; AI = 10/8 = 1.25 FLOP/byte < A100 FP32 ridge (~ 9.75); ceiling ≈ 2.5 TFLOP/s.
Memory-bound; arithmetic intensity ≈ 2.5 FLOP/byte, obtained by counting only the input reads and ignoring the output writes since writes are asynchronous on the memory bus.
Compute-bound; achievable throughput ≈ 19.5 TFLOP/s because element-wise kernels always saturate the SM math pipelines once occupancy exceeds 50%.

questions.explanation: Per element: 10 FLOPs; 4 bytes read + 4 bytes written = 8 bytes. Arithmetic intensity = 10/8 = 1.25 FLOP/byte. A100 FP32 ridge point = 19.5 TFLOP/s / 2.0 TB/s = 9.75 FLOP/byte. AI (1.25) < ridge (9.75) → memory-bound. Ceiling = AI × BW = 1.25 × 2.0 = 2.5 TFLOP/s.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: 10 FLOPs per element only yields AI ≈ 1.25 FLOP/byte, still far below the ridge point; the kernel remains memory-bound.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: AI = FLOPs / (read+write bytes) = 10/8 = 1.25 FLOP/byte; ceiling = AI × HBM BW.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: correct classification (memory-bound) but the AI is miscomputed by omitting output-write bytes; proper streaming AI counts read + write traffic.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: element-wise kernels do not automatically saturate math pipelines; without high AI they saturate HBM instead.

assumptions: No cache reuse: each byte of A is read from HBM exactly once, each byte of B is written to HBM exactly once.
Softplus operates on a single tensor and does not fuse with adjacent ops in this measurement.
nonImplications: Does not imply that fusing softplus with a neighboring elementwise op has no benefit; fusion can reduce bytes moved and lift throughput.
Does not imply that FP16 softplus would be compute-bound; it would still be memory-bound, just with different AI.

distractorRationales.A: Overestimates the effect of adding math to an elementwise kernel.
distractorRationales.C: Common AI arithmetic error: counting only reads.

performanceClaim.scope: A100 SXM, FP32 elementwise softplus over 32 M elements, streaming

questions.learningObjective: Determine the degree of shared-memory bank conflict for a stride access pattern and its throughput impact.
questions.stem: A CUDA kernel declares `__shared__ float smem[32][32]` (32 banks × 4-byte bank width on Ampere). After a `__syncthreads()`, the block reads `smem[threadIdx.x][threadIdx.y]` with a 32×32 thread block. What is the resulting bank-conflict behavior for a warp with a single value of threadIdx.y (threads share y, differ in x)?

options.text: No conflict: threads in a warp read column `y` from rows `0..31`; each row starts on a different bank, so all 32 threads target distinct banks in one cycle.
The compiler automatically pads the shared-memory declaration to avoid conflicts, so this access pattern is transparently conflict-free.
16-way conflict: half-warp granularity limits shared-memory conflicts to at most 16-way on Ampere.

32-way conflict: threads in the warp read a single column `y`, i.e., addresses smem[0][y], smem[1][y], ..., smem[31][y]. Each of these lies in the same bank because 32 × 4 B row stride is a multiple of the bank stride (32×4 B), serializing to 32 accesses.

questions.explanation: Option D is correct; options A, B, C are incorrect. A (Wrong): with a 32-wide row of 4-byte elements, the row stride matches the bank period (128 B = 32 banks × 4 B), so column-major access hits the same bank across rows. B (Wrong): shared-memory padding must be programmer-written (e.g., declare [32][33]). C (Wrong): half-warp granularity applied to legacy architectures (Fermi and earlier); Ampere uses warp-wide conflict analysis. D (Correct): the access serializes to 32 cycles due to same-bank targeting. General context: Ampere shared memory has 32 banks with 4-byte width; bank = (address / 4) mod 32. For smem[i][y] with row size 32 floats (128 B), the byte address is i·128 + y·4. The bank index (i·128 + y·4)/4 mod 32 = (i·32 + y) mod 32 = y (since i·32 mod 32 = 0). All 32 threads in the warp map to the same bank y → 32-way conflict; access serializes into 32 cycles. Padding to [32][33] (or transposing the access) restores conflict-free behavior.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: with a 32-wide row of 4-byte elements, the row stride matches the bank period (128 B = 32 banks × 4 B), so column-major access hits the same bank across rows.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: shared-memory padding must be programmer-written (e.g., declare [32][33]).
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: half-warp granularity applied to legacy architectures (Fermi and earlier); Ampere uses warp-wide conflict analysis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: the access serializes to 32 cycles due to same-bank targeting.

assumptions: 32 banks × 4 B bank width (default on modern NVIDIA compute capabilities).
Warp is 32 threads with threadIdx.x varying and threadIdx.y constant.
No compiler transformation altering the declared layout.
nonImplications: Does not imply the kernel is unusable at 32-way conflict; the impact is on throughput, not correctness.
Does not imply that padding to [32][33] is universally the right fix; some kernels prefer swizzled addressing or transposed staging.

sourceRefs.locator: Shared memory bank organization; bank conflicts
Shared memory and bank conflict chapter

performanceClaim.scope: Ampere shared memory bank-conflict pattern for a 32×32 float array with transposed access

questions.subtopic: Batch size to cross ridge point
questions.learningObjective: Compute the batch size needed to move an LLM decode's linear layer from memory-bound into compute-bound regime on a specific GPU.
questions.stem: For a transformer linear layer Y = X · W with W ∈ ℝ^{4096×4096} FP16 (weight streamed once), on A100 SXM (FP16 Tensor-Core peak ≈ 312 TFLOP/s, HBM ≈ 2.0 TB/s, ridge point ≈ 156 FLOP/byte). Approximately what batch/token dimension B is needed for the layer's arithmetic intensity to reach the ridge point (assuming AI ≈ B in the weight-dominated small-B regime)?

options.text: B ≈ 4096: the batch must match the hidden dimension for arithmetic intensity to saturate.
B ≈ 16 tokens: because the FP16 Tensor Core is 16× faster than FP32, the required B is FLOP-peak / (16 × HBM) ≈ 16.
B = 1: LLM decode is always compute-bound because Tensor Cores parallelize FLOPs faster than HBM streams weights.
B ≈ 156 tokens: since AI ≈ B in the weight-dominated regime, B must equal the ridge point (~156 FLOP/byte) to cross into compute-bound territory.

questions.explanation: In the weight-dominated small-B regime (bytes ≈ K·N·2 for W, activations negligible), AI = (2·B·K·N) / (2·K·N + small) ≈ B FLOP/byte. Crossing the ridge point ≈ 156 FLOP/byte thus requires B ≈ 156 tokens. This matches empirical observations that LLM decode is memory-bound until continuous batching aggregates roughly this many concurrent requests. Options B, C, D contradict the analysis.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: batch does not need to equal K for ridge crossing; the arithmetic depends on ridge value and AI-in-B linearity.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: the 16× ratio is Tensor-Core vs CUDA-core density, not related to the ridge crossing arithmetic.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: LLM decode with B = 1 is a classic memory-bound GEMV; not compute-bound.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: AI ≈ B in the weight-dominated regime; crossing ridge ≈ 156 requires B ≈ 156.

assumptions: AI ≈ B in the small-B, weight-dominated regime (activations negligible).
Ridge point ≈ 156 FLOP/byte for A100 SXM FP16 (312 TFLOP/s / 2.0 TB/s).
Kernel implementation can realize the theoretical AI (e.g., cuBLAS or hand-tuned).
nonImplications: Does not imply that B ≥ 156 guarantees achieved peak throughput; the compute regime is a necessary but not sufficient condition.
Does not imply the same B threshold applies on H100; H100's higher FP16 peak (~989 TFLOP/s) roughly doubles the required B to stay compute-bound.

distractorRationales.B: Uses Tensor Core density ratio incorrectly.

sourceRefs.locator: Motivation section: LLM decode is memory-bound at low batch

performanceClaim.scope: A100 SXM FP16, LLM linear layer weight-dominated regime

questions.learningObjective: Compute the arithmetic intensity of a batched matrix multiplication and compare it against a GPU's ridge point to determine bind regime.
questions.stem: Consider a single-tile FP16 GEMM C = A · B with A ∈ ℝ^{M×K}, B ∈ ℝ^{K×N}, C ∈ ℝ^{M×N}, M=N=K=1024, all tensors streamed once from HBM (no persistence). On A100 SXM (FP16 Tensor Core peak ≈ 312 TFLOP/s, HBM ≈ 2.0 TB/s, ridge point ≈ 156 FLOP/byte), which classification is correct?

options.text: Compute-bound only for FP32 accumulation, but memory-bound for FP16 accumulation because the accumulator halves the effective register file and forces spilling to HBM.
Memory-bound: even at K=1024, streaming the operands limits performance; AI ≈ 1 FLOP/byte because each element of A and B is loaded once and reused only during the tile computation.
Compute-bound: FLOPs = 2·M·N·K ≈ 2.15 G; bytes moved ≈ (M·K + K·N + M·N)·2 ≈ 6.29 MB; AI ≈ 342 FLOP/byte, above the FP16 ridge of ~156, so the ceiling is the FP16 Tensor Core peak of ~312 TFLOP/s.
Undetermined without knowing the launch grid; the same math on the same GPU can flip compute/memory regimes depending on how many blocks are launched.

questions.explanation: GEMM FLOPs = 2·M·N·K = 2·1024^3 ≈ 2.147 × 10^9. Bytes for reading A, B and writing C = (1024·1024 + 1024·1024 + 1024·1024) · 2 B = 6.29 MB. Arithmetic intensity = 2.147e9 / 6.29e6 ≈ 341 FLOP/byte. This is above the A100 FP16 Tensor Core ridge point (~156 FLOP/byte), so the operation is compute-bound and the achievable ceiling is the FP16 Tensor Core peak (~312 TFLOP/s). Reaching that ceiling requires efficient tiling; the classification itself is bounded by the AI vs ridge comparison.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: FP16 vs FP32 accumulation affects Tensor Core selection and accuracy, not the Roofline classification via HBM traffic. Register file spilling to HBM is not what defines the compute/memory regime here.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: AI ≈ 1 FLOP/byte is characteristic of GEMV (batch=1), not GEMM with K=1024. GEMM has strong on-tile reuse.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: AI = 2·M·N·K / ((M·K+K·N+M·N)·2) ≈ 341 FLOP/byte, which exceeds the FP16 ridge point; ceiling is FP16 Tensor Core peak.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: Roofline classification for a well-formed GEMM is a function of AI vs ridge point; launch grid affects achieved efficiency, not the compute/memory-bound category.

assumptions: Operands are loaded from HBM exactly once through a tiled schedule; the arithmetic intensity is measured against HBM traffic.
No exotic streaming (e.g., persistent kernels reusing weights across steps) that would change effective bytes moved.
nonImplications: Does not imply the kernel will reach the ~312 TFLOP/s ceiling; achieving that requires good tiling, occupancy, and MMA scheduling.
Does not imply that reducing K further (e.g., K=1) would remain compute-bound: shrinking K reduces AI proportionally.

distractorRationales.A: Introduces an accumulation-precision fiction unrelated to Roofline classification.
distractorRationales.B: Confuses GEMV traffic pattern with GEMM tile reuse.
distractorRationales.D: Vacuous 'undetermined' claim contradicted by well-defined AI vs ridge comparison.

sourceRefs.locator: GEMM chapter, arithmetic intensity of tiled matmul
Ch. 4, arithmetic intensity for dense linear algebra

performanceClaim.scope: A100 SXM, FP16 GEMM 1024×1024×1024, single-shot streaming from HBM

questions.learningObjective: Compute the effective cache-line utilization of a strided CPU access pattern and connect it to the arithmetic intensity seen by the memory system.

hardwareContext.architecture: modern x86-64 with 64 B cache lines

questions.stem: A CPU loop reads a[i * S] for i = 0 .. N−1 where a is a contiguous FP32 array and S = 16 (stride 16 elements = 64 B). Cache lines are 64 B. Assuming N is large so warm-up effects are negligible and no prefetch reuse across iterations, what fraction of each transferred cache line is useful to the loop?

options.text: 1/16 (~6.25%): each 64 B cache line delivers only the 4 B accessed element; the remaining 60 B are transferred but unused.
1: hardware prefetchers combine adjacent strided loads into a single wide access, so effective utilization approaches 100% once the prefetcher locks on.
1/4: 4 B out of 16 B per element, computed against the SIMD lane width rather than the cache line width.
1/2: modern out-of-order cores double the effective utilization by reading two elements per cache line through speculative execution.

questions.explanation: Stride 16 × 4 B = 64 B means each iteration accesses one FP32 element that lives in a different 64 B cache line. Each line delivers 64 B; only 4 B are used. Utilization = 4 / 64 = 1/16 ≈ 6.25%. Hardware prefetchers may still fetch the correct next line, but they do not reduce per-line waste; speculative execution and SIMD width also do not change bytes moved per line.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: only 4 B out of every 64 B cache line are consumed.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: prefetching improves latency hiding, not per-line utilization; wasted bytes still traverse the memory system.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: SIMD lane width does not divide cache line bytes into 'useful vs wasted'; the cache line is the transfer granularity.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: out-of-order execution reorders memory ops but does not deliver more of a cache line as useful.

assumptions: Each accessed element lies in a distinct 64 B cache line (stride 16 × 4 B = 64 B).
No temporal reuse within the loop; each iteration touches a fresh line.
Cache pressure is high enough that prefetched but unused bytes cannot be later re-used.
nonImplications: Does not imply reordering the loop cannot help; a stride-1 access pattern would achieve 100% utilization.
Does not imply hardware prefetchers are useless; they still reduce miss latency even when per-line waste is high.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses latency hiding with bandwidth utilization.
distractorRationales.C: Applies SIMD arithmetic to a cache-line question.

sourceRefs.locator: Memory hierarchy chapter; cache-line utilization and spatial locality

performanceClaim.scope: generic x86-64 CPU, 64 B cache lines, stride-16 FP32 access

questions.learningObjective: Estimate effective HBM bandwidth achieved by a strided access pattern compared to the ideal coalesced case and identify the underlying mechanism.
questions.profileData: Kernel A (coalesced 4B stride-1 load, warp of 32 threads): 128 B per transaction, 1 transaction per warp. Kernel B (stride-32 4B load with 128 B sectors): 32 sectors, 32 B each = 1024 B moved per warp.
questions.stem: Two kernels each read 32 × 4 B = 128 useful bytes per warp. Kernel A reads contiguous 4 B elements (stride 1) and issues one 128 B coalesced transaction. Kernel B reads with stride 32 (4 B elements 128 B apart), touching 32 distinct 32 B sectors, so the memory system transfers 32 × 32 B = 1024 B per warp. Assuming HBM bandwidth is the bottleneck, what is the ratio of effective useful-bytes throughput of Kernel B to Kernel A?

options.text: 1/4: coalesced transactions are 128 B while strided transactions are 32 B; the ratio 128/32 = 4 gives the throughput penalty.
1/32: because Kernel B touches 32 sectors, its effective bandwidth is 1/32 of Kernel A's; the number of distinct sectors touched is the direct multiplier.
1: the L2 cache absorbs the extra transactions transparently and delivers the same useful bandwidth for both patterns on A100.
1/8: Kernel B moves 8× the bytes per warp for the same useful payload, so at HBM saturation it delivers 1/8 the useful throughput.

questions.explanation: Effective useful bandwidth = useful bytes / bytes transferred. Kernel A: 128/128 = 1.0. Kernel B: 128/1024 = 0.125. Ratio = 0.125/1.0 = 1/8. The waste factor equals bytes moved divided by useful bytes: 1024/128 = 8. It is not 1/32 because a 32 B sector still carries 32 B (only one of which is used, but the sector itself is the minimum granularity). L2 cannot rescue a first-access pattern that pulls fresh sectors from HBM.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: 128 vs 32 is transaction size, but Kernel B issues 32 transactions and moves 32×32 = 1024 B.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: the number of sectors is not the throughput divisor by itself; each sector still carries 32 B, so waste is bytes_moved / useful_bytes = 8.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: L2 can help on repeated access but cannot reduce first-touch HBM traffic; here each warp fetches fresh sectors.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: the waste factor is 1024 / 128 = 8×, so useful throughput is 1/8 of the coalesced case.

assumptions: Sector size at L2 is 32 B (typical for recent NVIDIA GPUs) and there is no cache line coalescing across the 32 accesses in Kernel B.
HBM is the bottleneck; kernels are wide enough to saturate it if traffic were coalesced.
One-shot access, no reuse from L2.
nonImplications: Does not imply the actual observed slowdown will be exactly 8×; latency hiding, launch overhead, and other kernels may modulate the observed number.
Does not imply Kernel B always wastes 8×; if consecutive warps happen to touch the same sectors, L2 reuse reduces effective waste.

distractorRationales.A: Uses transaction-size ratio without counting number of transactions.
distractorRationales.B: Confuses number of sectors with the throughput divisor.
distractorRationales.C: Overestimates L2's ability to hide bandwidth waste.

sourceRefs.locator: Global memory access patterns; coalesced accesses and sector transactions

performanceClaim.scope: A100, single-warp effective HBM bandwidth for stride-1 vs stride-32 4 B loads

questions.subtopic: CPU vs GPU execution model contrasts
questions.learningObjective: Compare CPU and GPU execution models on branch prediction, out-of-order execution, register file, and cache hierarchy design.
questions.stem: Which statements correctly contrast the CPU and GPU execution models? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: CPUs devote substantial die area to branch prediction, out-of-order scheduling and large caches per core; GPUs devote proportionally more area to compute units and register files, using massive thread-level parallelism to hide memory latency instead.

GPUs typically have a much larger register file per SM than a CPU core has per core, because switching between many warps requires their register state to remain resident for zero-cost context switching.
CPU L1 caches are typically per-core and larger per thread than GPU L1/shared memory per thread, reflecting the CPU's reliance on temporal locality within a single thread.
GPUs do not use caches at all; latency hiding via warp switching removes any need for a cache hierarchy.

questions.explanation: A: This is the canonical CPU-throughput vs GPU-throughput design philosophy, articulated in HP6/PMPP4. B: GPU register files (e.g., 65 K × 4 B per SM on A100 ≈ 256 KB) are much larger than CPU per-core register files (~2 KB architectural), enabling zero-cost warp switching. C: CPU L1D is ~32-48 KB per core with a small resident thread count; GPU L1/shared is up to 192 KB per SM but is shared across many threads, giving less per-thread capacity. D is wrong: modern GPUs have L1 (per SM) and L2 (per GPU) caches; latency hiding via warp switching complements, not replaces, caching.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: canonical design-philosophy contrast.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: large register file enables zero-cost warp switching in SIMT.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: CPU L1 per-thread capacity is typically larger than GPU L1/shared per-thread capacity.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: GPUs have L1 and L2 caches; latency hiding complements rather than replaces caching.

assumptions: Standard modern CPU (Intel/AMD OoO) vs data-center GPU (NVIDIA Ampere/Hopper) comparison.
Rough die-area allocations and per-thread capacities as documented in whitepapers and PMPP4.
nonImplications: Does not imply CPUs cannot exploit DLP; SIMD ISAs like AVX-512 provide substantial DLP.
Does not imply GPUs never benefit from data locality; kernels still use shared memory and L1 for reuse.

distractorRationales.D: Fabricated 'no cache' claim contradicting decades of GPU architecture.

sourceRefs.locator: Ch. 4 DLP, CPU vs GPU design philosophy
Compute Capability tables, register file per SM

questions.learningObjective: Estimate the throughput impact of warp divergence and identify when divergence does not degrade throughput.
questions.stem: A CUDA kernel executes an if/else branch that produces two disjoint code paths of similar cost (T_A ≈ T_B ≈ T). Which of the following statements about divergence within a warp are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Post-Volta independent thread scheduling changes the SIMT semantics so that both branches now truly execute in parallel within a warp with no serialization cost, eliminating warp divergence entirely.
If all 32 threads in a warp take the same side of the branch, no divergence penalty is incurred; the branch behaves like a single-path warp.
If the warp splits (some threads take path A, others path B), the two subsets execute serially and total warp time is approximately T_A + T_B (both paths are covered under mask), not max(T_A, T_B).
Divergence is per-block, not per-warp; as long as the block executes both branches somewhere, the compiler predicates the whole block uniformly.

questions.explanation: A: SIMT divergence is only an issue when threads in the same warp take different branch sides; a uniform branch has no divergence cost. B: Under divergence, the hardware masks off threads not taking a side and executes each side in turn, so warp wall time ≈ sum of side durations under mask; only threads on each side make progress at a time. C is wrong: divergence is a warp-level property, not block-level. D is wrong: independent thread scheduling improves correctness (deadlock-freedom, reconvergence flexibility) but does not eliminate serialization of divergent paths within a warp.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: Volta+ independent thread scheduling changed reconvergence semantics but did not remove per-warp serialization of divergent branches.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: uniform warps skip the divergence penalty entirely.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: divergent warps serialize the taken/not-taken sides using lane masking.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: divergence is per-warp; different warps in the same block can independently take different sides without penalizing each other.

assumptions: Both branch paths have similar cost T_A ≈ T_B and neither is trivially compiled to predicated math.
Compiler does not automatically predicate the branch away (i.e., real control divergence occurs).
nonImplications: Does not imply that eliminating all branches always helps; small predicated branches may be cheaper than restructuring.
Does not imply divergent warps waste all their bandwidth; masked-off threads still occupy warp slots but do not perform useful work during their masked-off cycles.

distractorRationales.A: Version-leak misinterpretation of independent thread scheduling.

sourceRefs.locator: SIMT architecture, branch divergence, independent thread scheduling

performanceClaim.scope: warp-level divergence performance model

questions.learningObjective: Reason about the relative energy costs of on-chip compute vs off-chip memory access and their implications for DNN accelerator design.
questions.stem: Survey figures (Sze et al., cited widely from Horowitz's ISSCC 2014 numbers) place DRAM access energy roughly 2–3 orders of magnitude above an on-chip multiply-add. Which of the following implications are correct for accelerator/DNN energy analysis? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Reducing DRAM accesses (via on-chip data reuse, tiling, buffer sharing) is often the largest lever for energy efficiency in DNN inference, even when compute FLOPs stay constant.
Quantization can reduce energy per operation on hardware that supports the lower-precision path, both by reducing bytes moved from DRAM and by reducing compute energy per MAC.
Because logic is 'free', minimizing FLOPs is the primary energy lever regardless of memory access patterns.
Since on-chip SRAM energy is orders of magnitude lower than DRAM, using more shared memory always reduces total energy without further conditions.

questions.explanation: A: DRAM access dominates energy in DNN workloads; increasing on-chip reuse (weight stationary, output stationary etc.) is the primary energy optimization. B: Quantization reduces both DRAM traffic and per-MAC compute energy on hardware with matched low-precision paths (INT8, FP8 Tensor Cores). C is wrong because FLOP minimization ignores the dominant memory-energy term. D is wrong because SRAM helps only when it enables reuse; a larger on-chip buffer with poor reuse can still lose to DRAM if data is fetched fresh each time.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: memory access energy dominates; reuse and tiling are the primary levers.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: lower precision reduces bytes moved and compute energy per operation when hardware supports it.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: FLOP-only optimization misses the memory-energy dominance well documented in accelerator surveys.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: SRAM is only cheaper than DRAM per access; benefit requires reuse. Increasing SRAM without reuse is not a general energy win.

assumptions: Standard survey-scale relative energy figures (DRAM access ≫ SRAM access ≫ MAC).
Kernel-level accounting: energy per op includes both compute and data movement.
nonImplications: Does not imply that DRAM energy dominates in every kernel; small tensors that fit in cache may be compute-energy-dominated.
Does not imply that quantization always saves energy; if hardware lacks the low-precision datapath, dequantization overhead can erase gains.

distractorRationales.D: Misses the reuse condition for SRAM benefit.

sourceRefs.locator: Ch. 1-2, relative energy per operation and DNN accelerator design

performanceClaim.scope: DNN accelerator energy accounting, survey-scale relative costs

questions.learningObjective: Order the tiers of a modern GPU memory hierarchy by latency, bandwidth and capacity, and identify design consequences.
questions.stem: Which statements about the NVIDIA GPU memory hierarchy (Ampere/Hopper) are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because L2 has higher bandwidth than HBM, an inference kernel that fits in L2 sees roughly HBM-tier throughput; L2 acts only as a latency shield, not a bandwidth multiplier.
Latency ordering (fastest to slowest): registers → shared memory / L1 → L2 → HBM. Latency grows by roughly an order of magnitude across the last two boundaries.
Capacity ordering (largest to smallest): HBM → L2 → shared memory (per SM) → register file (per SM). HBM dwarfs on-chip storage by several orders of magnitude.
Aggregate bandwidth ordering, summed across all SMs, is: register file ≫ shared memory ≫ L2 ≫ HBM. On-chip tiers close to compute are the widest.

questions.explanation: A: standard latency ordering; each on-chip step is faster than off-chip. B: HBM is orders of magnitude larger than on-chip caches (tens of GB vs KB-MB). C: aggregate on-chip bandwidths scale with number of SMs, greatly exceeding HBM's bandwidth (~2 TB/s A100). D is wrong: L2 acts as both a latency shield and a bandwidth multiplier when data fits and is reused — L2 aggregate bandwidth is well above HBM.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: L2 provides substantial bandwidth uplift over HBM when data is reused; it is not merely a latency shield.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: register < shared/L1 < L2 < HBM in latency; on-chip tiers dominate for locality.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: capacity increases moving away from compute.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: on-chip aggregate bandwidth greatly exceeds HBM; this is why kernels use shared memory and register-file reuse.

assumptions: Modern NVIDIA GPU (Ampere/Hopper) with the standard R/S/L2/HBM hierarchy.
Aggregate bandwidth is measured summed across all SMs where applicable.
nonImplications: Does not imply every kernel benefits from L2 residency; write-back patterns and capacity misses can reduce L2 effectiveness.
Does not imply register-file size is negligible per SM; it is comparable to shared memory in capacity but with per-thread lifetime.

distractorRationales.A: Reduces L2's role to latency reduction only, ignoring bandwidth aspect.

sourceRefs.locator: Memory hierarchy tables per compute capability

performanceClaim.scope: NVIDIA GPU memory hierarchy latency/bandwidth/capacity ordering

questions.subtopic: Little's Law / ILP + MLP requirements for latency hiding
questions.learningObjective: Apply Little's Law at the instruction/memory level to reason about the concurrency required to fully hide arithmetic and memory latency.
questions.profileData: Kernel X (memory-bound, single outstanding load per warp): occupancy 100%, HBM throughput 40% of peak. Kernel Y (memory-bound, 8 outstanding loads per warp): occupancy 25%, HBM throughput 90% of peak. Both target A100, N=32M elements.
questions.stem: Consider a memory-bound GPU kernel. Which of the following statements correctly apply Little's Law to reasoning about latency hiding? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Low occupancy can still saturate HBM if each active warp issues many in-flight loads simultaneously (high memory-level parallelism per warp), because Little's Law counts total outstanding requests, not warp count.
Once occupancy reaches 100%, latency hiding is guaranteed regardless of per-thread memory-level parallelism.

For compute latency (arithmetic pipeline), Little's Law analogously requires enough independent instructions in flight per warp scheduler; ILP within a warp complements TLP across warps to hide compute-pipeline latency.

To fully hide DRAM latency, the SM must maintain enough outstanding memory requests such that Little's Law (concurrency = bandwidth × latency) is satisfied; this is why kernels need many warps and each warp needs multiple outstanding loads.

questions.explanation: A: This is the standard application of Little's Law to memory-level parallelism (MLP) on GPUs. B: Volkov and others show that low-occupancy kernels can saturate HBM if each warp has enough outstanding loads; occupancy is one way to achieve concurrency, not the only way. C is wrong: 100% occupancy without per-warp MLP still cannot saturate DRAM if each warp issues at most one outstanding load. D: ILP hides arithmetic pipeline latency analogously — a compute pipeline with L cycles of latency needs L independent instructions in flight to be fully utilized.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: low-occupancy high-MLP kernels can saturate memory (Volkov's classic result).
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: occupancy alone does not guarantee latency hiding; per-warp MLP matters.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: ILP + TLP combine to hide compute-pipeline latency.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: Little's Law for MLP; total outstanding requests = BW × latency.

assumptions: Kernel is bandwidth or latency limited on either memory or arithmetic pipelines.
Warp scheduler can issue independent instructions from a warp when ready.
nonImplications: Does not imply low-occupancy kernels are always fine; when per-warp MLP is limited (e.g., data-dependent loads), occupancy is the fallback.
Does not imply that any technique alone (ILP, TLP, MLP) suffices; realistic kernels mix all three.

distractorRationales.B: Overgeneralizes occupancy as a sufficient condition for latency hiding.

sourceRefs.locator: Latency hiding via MLP and occupancy

performanceClaim.scope: GPU latency hiding via combined MLP/ILP/TLP; Little's Law application

questions.learningObjective: Quantify how batch size increases arithmetic intensity from GEMV to GEMM regime for weight-shared linear layers.
questions.stem: A transformer linear layer Y = X · W with W ∈ ℝ^{4096×4096} FP16 has an effective batch dimension B (e.g., #tokens in a step). Weight W is streamed once from HBM per launch; X and Y are proportional to B. Ignoring caching outside of W's single-pass streaming, how does arithmetic intensity (FLOP / bytes) scale with B?

options.text: AI is inversely proportional to B because larger batches move more X/Y data through HBM, diluting the FLOP density.

AI is approximately linear in B: at B=1 (decode step) AI ≈ 1 FLOP/byte (GEMV regime); at B ≈ 128 (prefill), AI is roughly 100+ FLOP/byte and typically enters compute-bound territory on FP16 Tensor-Core GPUs.
AI is independent of B because the number of FLOPs and bytes both grow linearly with B, so the ratio is invariant.
AI grows quadratically with B because each token performs B multiplications with each weight.

questions.explanation: FLOPs = 2·B·K·N with K = N = 4096. Bytes moved = W (K·N·2, one time) + X (B·K·2) + Y (B·N·2) = 2·K·N + 2·B·(K+N)·2/2 bytes for FP16. Simplifying: Bytes ≈ 2·K·N + 4·B·K (for K=N). AI = FLOPs / Bytes = (2·B·K·N) / (2·K·N + 4·B·K). For small B, the K·N (weight) term dominates → AI ≈ B (linear in B). At B ≈ 128 and K = N = 4096, AI ≈ (2·128·4096·4096) / (2·4096·4096 + 4·128·4096) ≈ 100+ FLOP/byte, entering compute-bound regime on FP16 Tensor-Core GPUs. Option A captures this.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: AI increases with B, not decreases; larger B amortizes the weight-load bytes over more FLOPs.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: AI scales approximately linearly with B while weight streaming dominates the bytes moved; B~128 typically crosses the ridge on FP16 Tensor-Core GPUs.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: FLOPs scale with B but bytes are dominated by W (constant in B) for small B, so AI grows with B.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: FLOPs scale linearly in B (not quadratically); AI ~ B for the small-B, weight-dominated regime, saturating for large B.

assumptions: Weight is streamed once from HBM per kernel launch (no persistence).
AI is measured against HBM bytes moved, not L2/SMEM.
nonImplications: Does not imply AI grows without bound; for B ≫ (K·N)/(2·K) = N/2, the activation term dominates and AI saturates.
Does not imply crossing the ridge point makes any GEMM achieve peak; achieved throughput depends on kernel implementation.

distractorRationales.A: Reverses the direction of AI with respect to B.
distractorRationales.C: Ignores that the weight-load bytes are B-independent while FLOPs are B-linear.

sourceRefs.locator: DNN dataflow, batching effect on data movement

performanceClaim.scope: generic FP16 linear layer, weight streamed once, batch B

questions.learningObjective: Reason about when kernel launch overhead dominates and what mitigations exist.

requiredFeatures: CUDA driver launch cost ~ 5–10 μs per kernel

questions.stem: Kernel launch overhead is typically ~5–10 μs on NVIDIA GPUs. Consider a training/inference loop dispatching many small kernels. Which of the following statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Kernel launch overhead is fully hidden by cudaStreamSynchronize because the CPU launch API is asynchronous; therefore small kernels do not suffer from launch overhead in practice.
Kernel fusion reduces per-op launch cost by combining multiple element-wise kernels into a single kernel, trading potential register pressure for a lower total launch count.
If a kernel executes for 2 μs and launch overhead is 5 μs, launch overhead dominates the wall time even at 100% GPU utilization; the effective GPU throughput is well below the kernel's peak.
CUDA Graphs capture a sequence of kernel launches once and replay them with a single API call, amortizing launch overhead across many small kernels.

questions.explanation: A: When kernel duration < launch overhead, wall time is dominated by the CPU-side launch cost. This is the classic small-kernel regime. B: CUDA Graphs is precisely the mitigation: capture once, replay with a single graph-launch call, amortizing per-kernel overhead across the whole graph. D: Kernel fusion reduces the count of launches (also reduces HBM traffic when fused ops share operands). C is wrong: asynchronous launch does not eliminate the CPU cost of issuing a launch; every kernel still costs ~5–10 μs of CPU time. The GPU cannot begin work until the launch has been submitted.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: asynchronous launch means the CPU does not wait for kernel completion, but the launch itself still consumes CPU time and imposes a lower bound on inter-kernel spacing.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: kernel fusion cuts launch counts as one of its benefits, alongside reducing HBM traffic via operand reuse.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: when launch overhead > kernel time, the loop is CPU-bound on launches; the GPU sits idle much of the time.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: CUDA Graphs is the documented mechanism for amortizing per-launch overhead.

assumptions: Launch overhead ~5–10 μs per kernel is representative of recent CUDA driver stacks; small variations occur across versions.
The workload has a large number of short kernels (typical of decode-time transformer inference).
nonImplications: Does not imply CUDA Graphs is free; graph construction has one-time overhead and may not fit every dynamic control-flow pattern.
Does not imply fusion always improves performance; over-fusion can increase register pressure and reduce occupancy.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses asynchronous launch semantics with elimination of launch cost.

sourceRefs.locator: Streams, asynchronous launches, CUDA Graphs chapter
Kernel launch overhead and graph capture guidance

performanceClaim.scope: CUDA runtime, short-kernel launch overhead regime

questions.learningObjective: Apply Little's Law to compute the number of in-flight memory loads required to saturate a GPU's HBM bandwidth given a target latency.
questions.stem: Little's Law states Concurrency = Bandwidth × Latency. Suppose an A100 has peak HBM bandwidth ≈ 2 TB/s and average DRAM load latency ≈ 400 ns, and each in-flight load fetches a 128-byte sector. Approximately how many 128-byte loads must be simultaneously in flight (aggregated across all SMs) to saturate HBM bandwidth?

options.text: ≈ 32 concurrent loads — one per warp scheduler on a single SM — because Little's Law counts per-scheduler concurrency, not aggregate outstanding requests across all SMs.
≈ 400 loads (roughly one per SM times four schedulers, since A100 has ~ 108 SMs and each SM has four warp schedulers dispatching one load at a time in steady state).
The number is independent of latency; only bandwidth determines the required concurrency, since bandwidth by itself already characterizes the memory system's throughput ceiling.

questions.explanation: Little's Law in byte units: bytes-in-flight = BW × latency = 2×10¹² B/s × 400×10⁻⁹ s = 8×10⁵ = 800,000 bytes. Each request is 128 bytes, so required outstanding requests = 800,000 / 128 = 6,250. This is why GPUs need many warps × loads-per-warp to saturate HBM.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: 32 requests is orders of magnitude too small; a warp scheduler dispatches many outstanding loads over the latency period.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: applies Little's Law and divides by request size.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: even 400 outstanding 128-byte loads only covers 51,200 bytes-in-flight, far below the 800 KB needed.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: latency is central to Little's Law; concurrency scales linearly with latency for fixed bandwidth.

assumptions: DRAM latency and bandwidth are steady-state, aggregate figures for the GPU.
Each load request completes in ~ 400 ns on average.
Requests are for 128-byte sectors (typical L2 sector granularity for coalesced accesses).
nonImplications: Does not imply that a single warp can issue 6,250 outstanding loads; the concurrency is provided by many warps × many outstanding loads per warp.
Does not imply latency-hiding is achievable on all kernels; kernels with low memory-level parallelism can bottleneck at DRAM latency.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses schedulers on one SM with aggregate concurrency.
distractorRationales.C: Uses SM count as concurrency proxy, ignoring in-flight requests per SM.
distractorRationales.D: Removes latency from Little's Law altogether.

sourceRefs.locator: Memory bandwidth and latency hiding via MLP

performanceClaim.scope: A100 HBM saturation via Little's Law, order-of-magnitude estimate

questions.subtopic: GPU memory hierarchy / bandwidth / access rules
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish structural and access-pattern properties of NVIDIA GPU memory tiers (register file, shared memory, constant memory, global memory).
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the A100 (sm_80) memory hierarchy are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Aggregate global-memory (HBM2e) bandwidth on the A100 board is higher than the aggregate on-chip shared-memory bandwidth summed across all SMs, since HBM stacks scale linearly with pin count and channels.

Shared memory is bank-organized: warp threads accessing distinct addresses in the same bank serialize (bank conflict); global memory has no banks but obeys coalescing rules on 32/64/128 B transactions.
Constant memory accesses in which all threads of a warp read the same address are broadcast, avoiding a per-thread memory transaction and delivering the value in one cycle to the whole warp.
The per-SM register file (65,536 × 32-bit ≈ 256 KB) is larger than the per-SM configurable L1/shared-memory partition (up to 192 KB total on A100).

questions.explanation: A: The A100 register file is 65,536 × 4 B = 256 KB per SM, whereas L1/SMEM is at most 192 KB per SM (configurable). C: Shared memory is bank-organized and conflicts serialize; global memory uses coalescing (bytes-per-transaction rules), not banks. D: Constant memory is optimized for broadcast when all threads in a warp read the same address. B is false: aggregate shared-memory bandwidth across all SMs is much higher than aggregate HBM bandwidth (SRAM ≫ HBM per-byte throughput).

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect: HBM bandwidth (~ 2 TB/s aggregate) is lower than the sum of per-SM shared-memory bandwidth over all 108 SMs (each SMEM partition supplies many TB/s effective).
optionExplanations.B: Correct: bank conflicts affect shared memory; coalescing affects global memory.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: constant-memory broadcast is a documented CUDA optimization.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: 256 KB (registers) > 192 KB (L1/SMEM).

assumptions: sm_80 (A100) compute capability configuration.
Shared-memory bank width = 32-bit (4 bytes) per bank.
nonImplications: Does not imply that programmers should always favor shared memory; small kernels may perform better with only register/L1 usage.
Does not imply that constant-memory broadcast is used automatically for uniform accesses to global memory.

distractorRationales.A: Reverses the ranking of on-chip vs. off-chip aggregate bandwidth.

sourceRefs.locator: Compute Capability 8.0 tables; memory hierarchy chapter
GPU memory hierarchy and bank conflicts chapters

performanceClaim.scope: sm_80 architectural properties

questions.learningObjective: Compare NVLink and PCIe bandwidth for inter-GPU communication and reason about ring-AllReduce throughput.
questions.profileData: Ring-AllReduce of a 1 GiB FP16 tensor across 8 H100 SXM5 nodes fully connected by NVLink 4.0. Same experiment across 8 H100 PCIe cards on PCIe Gen4 x16.
questions.stem: You have two 8-GPU setups: (i) H100 SXM5 with NVLink 4.0 (per-GPU aggregate ≈ 900 GB/s bidirectional) and (ii) H100 PCIe cards on PCIe Gen4 x16 (≈ 25 GB/s per-direction between neighbors, no NVLink). You run ring-AllReduce on a 1 GiB FP16 tensor. Which comparison is closest to correct in the bandwidth-bound regime?

options.text: NVLink is roughly 1–2 orders of magnitude faster than PCIe here because ring-AllReduce is limited by the slowest inter-GPU link; NVLink's ~900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU vs PCIe's ~25 GB/s per direction dominates the collective time.
Both complete in the same time because ring-AllReduce total bytes are dominated by the sum, independent of link technology.
PCIe is faster because CPU-mediated routing bypasses the NVLink handshake overhead, giving lower latency for tensors above 512 MiB.
NVLink and PCIe give the same throughput per direction; only bidirectional aggregate differs and AllReduce uses one direction at a time.

questions.explanation: Ring-AllReduce sends 2(P−1)/P × N bytes per link at bandwidth-limited steady state, where N is tensor size and P is number of GPUs. The runtime is roughly N / effective_link_BW. With NVLink 4.0's ~900 GB/s bidirectional aggregate per GPU vs PCIe Gen4 x16's ~25 GB/s per direction, the effective inter-GPU bandwidth differs by more than an order of magnitude. So NVLink completes the collective substantially faster. Options A, C, D contain factual or reasoning errors.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: for a bandwidth-bound ring, NVLink's link BW is roughly 10–30× PCIe's, giving a corresponding wall-time advantage.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: bandwidth-bound collective time is proportional to bytes / link BW; identical time would require identical BW.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: PCIe with CPU-mediated routing is slower, not faster, and NVLink does not require a per-transfer handshake that would offset its bandwidth advantage.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: NVLink's per-direction bandwidth already exceeds PCIe's by an order of magnitude; the bidirectional aggregate is not the only difference.

assumptions: Ring-AllReduce in the bandwidth-bound regime (tensor large enough that latency terms are negligible).
PCIe topology has no NVLink or NVSwitch fabric between GPUs.
NVLink 4.0 per-GPU aggregate ~ 900 GB/s bidirectional (H100 SXM5 typical published number).
nonImplications: Does not imply NVLink is always 10–30× faster; small message sizes are latency-bound, where the gap may narrow.
Does not imply the exact speedup ratio; effective BW is affected by NCCL algorithm, topology, and buffer chunking.

distractorRationales.B: Ignores link bandwidth in bandwidth-bound analysis.

performanceClaim.scope: 8-GPU H100 ring-AllReduce, 1 GiB FP16 tensor, bandwidth-bound regime

questions.learningObjective: From ptxas register report and launch configuration, derive the register-file-limited theoretical occupancy on a given GPU architecture.
questions.stem: A CUDA kernel targeting sm_80 is compiled with `nvcc -arch=sm_80 --ptxas-options=-v` and prints `ptxas info : Used 96 registers, 384 bytes cmem[0]`. The launch config is `<<<gridDim, 256>>>`. A100 provides 65,536 32-bit registers per SM, a max of 2,048 threads (64 warps) per SM, and up to 32 concurrent blocks per SM. Ignoring shared-memory and block-count limits, what is the register-limited theoretical occupancy?
questions.profileData: Used 96 registers, 384 bytes cmem[0]; block size = 256; per-SM: 65536 regs, max 2048 threads (64 warps), max 32 blocks

options.text: 50% (32 of 64 warps active per SM); 96 registers per thread and 256 threads per block allow 4 concurrent blocks per SM under the register-file budget.
12.5%; the effective limit is 8 concurrent blocks per SM regardless of register usage, since Ampere caps blocks-per-SM at 8 rather than 32 in practice.
100%; A100's register file is large enough to accommodate 8 concurrent blocks of 256 threads at 96 registers per thread, so occupancy hits the SM's maximum of 64 warps.

questions.explanation: Registers per block = 96 × 256 = 24,576. Blocks limited by register file = ⌊65,536 / 24,576⌋ = 2. Threads per SM = 2 × 256 = 512. Warps per SM = 512 / 32 = 16. Occupancy = 16 / 64 = 25%.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: 4 blocks × 24,576 registers/block = 98,304 registers, exceeding the 65,536 register file per SM.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: the register file caps blocks at 2, yielding 512 active threads = 16 warps = 25% occupancy on sm_80.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: 8 blocks/SM is not a hard limit on sm_80 (max is 32); and register pressure — not block count — is what constrains this kernel.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: 8 blocks would require 196,608 registers, three times the available register file.

assumptions: Shared memory usage per block is small enough to not further limit occupancy.
Grid dimension is large enough to fully populate the SMs (not launch-limited).
nonImplications: Does not imply that 25% occupancy is 'bad'; many memory-bound kernels achieve near-peak throughput at low occupancy.
Does not imply that lowering register usage always improves performance; register spills to local memory can be worse.

distractorRationales.A: Occupancy math without checking register file capacity.
distractorRationales.C: Confuses block-count limit with register limit.
distractorRationales.D: Misreads the register file size relative to per-block demand.

sourceRefs.locator: Compute Capability 8.0 table; register file and warp/thread limits per SM

performanceClaim.scope: sm_80 A100, register-limited occupancy calculation

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish instruction-level, data-level and thread-level parallelism, and identify architectural mechanisms exposing each form.
questions.stem: Which of the following statements correctly connect a parallelism level (ILP / DLP / TLP) to an architectural mechanism? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: DLP (data-level parallelism) is exposed by SIMD/SIMT execution: the same operation is applied across many data elements simultaneously by vector lanes or warp threads.
TLP (thread-level parallelism) is exposed by multi-core CPUs, SMT/hyperthreading, and GPU warps: multiple independent control streams run in parallel.
ILP, DLP and TLP are mutually exclusive: a program can exhibit only one of the three at a time, so architectures must choose which one to exploit at compile time.
ILP (instruction-level parallelism) is exposed by out-of-order execution, register renaming, and superscalar issue: independent instructions overlap in the pipeline of one core.

questions.explanation: A: OoO cores exploit independent instructions in a single thread's dynamic stream. B: SIMD lanes and SIMT warps apply the same operation across elements. C: multi-core CPUs, SMT (e.g., Intel HT), and GPU warp-level parallelism are all TLP mechanisms. D is false: modern systems routinely combine all three (e.g., a GPU: SIMT DLP within warp + TLP across warps/blocks + ILP within each thread via pipeline).

optionExplanations.A: Correct: SIMD lanes and SIMT warps are canonical DLP.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: multi-core, SMT, and GPU threads all instantiate TLP.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: modern architectures combine all three simultaneously.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: ILP mechanisms include OoO, renaming, superscalar issue.

assumptions: Comparison of general-purpose parallel architectures (CPU OoO cores, GPUs).
nonImplications: Does not imply the amount of each is unlimited; each has architectural budgets (issue width, SIMD width, thread count).
Does not imply exploiting one form always benefits another; ILP can degrade TLP if per-thread resources rise.

distractorRationales.C: Falsely assumes mutual exclusion of parallelism forms.

sourceRefs.locator: Introduction: GPU parallelism combining DLP and TLP

questions.learningObjective: Estimate host-to-device PCIe transfer time and reason about overlap with kernel execution.

requiredFeatures: PCIe Gen4 x16 ~ 32 GB/s unidirectional practical

questions.stem: A host-to-device H2D transfer of a pinned 4 GiB buffer is issued to a GPU connected via PCIe Gen4 x16 (practical unidirectional ≈ 25 GB/s in production, 32 GB/s theoretical). Ignoring driver setup overheads, roughly how long is the H2D transfer alone, and what is the implication for overlapping with a kernel that runs 40 ms on the same buffer?

options.text: H2D ≈ 170 ms at 25 GB/s. Because the transfer is ~4× longer than the kernel, even perfect overlap using cudaMemcpyAsync + separate streams cannot hide the H2D behind the kernel; end-to-end time is dominated by PCIe.

H2D ≈ 170 ms at 25 GB/s, but overlapping cudaMemcpyAsync with the kernel in separate streams reduces the end-to-end time to the maximum of transfer and kernel (40 ms) since the two operations execute in parallel.
H2D ≈ 40 ms because PCIe Gen4 x16 practical bandwidth is ~ 100 GB/s; the kernel and transfer can each finish in 40 ms.
H2D ≈ 1.7 s because PCIe transfers of pinned memory are throttled to ~ 2.5 GB/s by the OS DMA engine on typical systems.

questions.explanation: Time = size / bandwidth. Size = 4 GiB ≈ 4.29 × 10^9 B; at 25 GB/s that is 4.29e9 / 25e9 ≈ 0.172 s ≈ 170 ms. The kernel takes 40 ms. Even with perfect stream overlap, the maximum-throughput streaming pipeline is bounded by the slower operation (PCIe here), so PCIe dominates. Overlap turns the sum into max only when the two operations are on independent resources and durations, which does not shrink either duration.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: at 25 GB/s the 4 GiB transfer is ~170 ms, dominating the kernel's 40 ms; overlap turns the sum into the max (still ~170 ms), so PCIe is the wall-time bottleneck.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong reasoning: overlap gives max(H2D, kernel) = 170 ms in this case, not 40 ms; the option incorrectly picks the kernel time.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: PCIe Gen4 x16 practical is ~25 GB/s, not 100 GB/s (that is roughly NVLink territory).
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: 2.5 GB/s is roughly USB 3 territory or pageable-memory pathological rates; pinned PCIe Gen4 x16 achieves ~25 GB/s in production.

assumptions: Pinned host memory so DMA runs at PCIe-limited rate.
Practical PCIe Gen4 x16 unidirectional bandwidth ~ 25 GB/s (below the 32 GB/s theoretical due to protocol overhead).
Transfer size 4 GiB = 4.294 × 10^9 bytes.
nonImplications: Does not imply the transfer is unfixable; strategies include chunked pipelining, keeping weights resident, or NVLink for multi-GPU replication.
Does not imply cudaMemcpyAsync is useless; overlap still saves time whenever there is other work to run during the transfer.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses max(a,b) with min(a,b) in overlap accounting.
distractorRationales.C: Overestimates PCIe Gen4 x16 practical bandwidth by 4×.

sourceRefs.locator: Host-device data transfers, pinned memory and PCIe considerations

performanceClaim.scope: PCIe Gen4 x16 pinned H2D, 4 GiB payload

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose why a measured GEMM throughput falls significantly below the theoretical peak and identify the most plausible cause.
questions.profileData: cuBLAS FP16 GEMM (M=N=K=8192): measured throughput 220 TFLOP/s; theoretical peak 312 TFLOP/s (dense FP16 Tensor Core, A100 SXM). Nsight Compute reports 78% Tensor Core utilization and no HBM saturation.
questions.stem: You measure 220 TFLOP/s on a cuBLAS FP16 GEMM (M=N=K=8192) on an A100 SXM, versus a theoretical peak of 312 TFLOP/s. Nsight Compute shows 78% Tensor Core utilization and HBM is not saturated. Which explanation is most consistent with the data?

options.text: cuBLAS is memory-bound on this size, so achieved throughput is HBM × AI; the ridge point is above the achieved value.

Tensor Cores are not fully occupied every cycle (78% Tensor Core utilization); typical causes include tile boundary effects, epilogue/prologue, imperfect scheduling, and warp scheduler stalls, producing the gap from the 312 TFLOP/s ceiling.
Kernel launch overhead dominates; the 30% gap is CPU-side launch overhead not overlapping with compute.
The A100 SXM ridge point is 78 FLOP/byte and this GEMM sits exactly on the ridge, so the measured value equals the ceiling.

questions.explanation: For M=N=K=8192 FP16, AI ≈ 8192/3 ≈ 2731 FLOP/byte, well above A100's FP16 ridge (~156 FLOP/byte), so the kernel is deeply compute-bound and HBM is not the bottleneck (consistent with the profile). The measured 220 TFLOP/s ≈ 78% × 312 TFLOP/s matches the reported Tensor Core utilization. Typical gaps come from prologue/epilogue, tile-boundary padding, warp-scheduler stalls and non-ideal MMA pipeline packing. Options A (memory-bound), C (launch overhead), and D (ridge alignment) contradict the profile or the AI.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: HBM is not saturated and AI is far above ridge; kernel is compute-bound.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: 78% Tensor Core utilization × 312 TFLOP/s ≈ 244 TFLOP/s (order-of-magnitude match with 220), and the classical causes of the gap fit the profile.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: launch overhead is microseconds; a single GEMM of this size runs many milliseconds. Launch overhead cannot explain a 30% shortfall.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: A100 FP16 ridge is ~156 FLOP/byte and the GEMM AI is ~2731 FLOP/byte; the operation is far above the ridge.

assumptions: Single-kernel steady-state GEMM measurement; not a batch-of-tiny-kernels regime.
cuBLAS handle, FP16 inputs and outputs, no exotic epilogue fusion.
nonImplications: Does not imply Tensor Core utilization percentage directly maps to achieved TFLOP/s at any ratio; the mapping is approximate and depends on how the metric is defined by Nsight Compute.
Does not imply moving to a larger K would necessarily hit peak; other factors (SM occupancy, MMA scheduling) still cap it.

distractorRationales.A: Ignores profile evidence (HBM not saturated) and AI computation.
distractorRationales.C: Wrong order of magnitude for launch overhead scope.

sourceRefs.locator: Tensor Core utilization / SM active metrics; interpretation guide

performanceClaim.scope: A100 SXM, cuBLAS FP16 GEMM 8192×8192×8192, diagnosis of ~70% of peak

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose sustained-vs-burst GPU throughput given TDP constraints and identify power capping as a mechanism.

hardwareContext.architecture: generic data-center GPU with TDP power cap

questions.profileData: Burst FP16 GEMM (first 100 ms): 300 TFLOP/s. Sustained FP16 GEMM (steady state after 30 s): 240 TFLOP/s. GPU reports Power Limit = 400 W and Perf State drop from P0 to P2 during the sustained run.
questions.stem: Nsight Systems shows a data-center GPU reaching 300 TFLOP/s in a short FP16 GEMM burst, but sustained throughput over 30 s stabilizes at 240 TFLOP/s. GPU telemetry reports a TDP cap of 400 W and a performance-state drop from P0 to P2. Which explanation best fits the data?

options.text: PCIe bandwidth reduction under thermal load caps GPU compute; sustained throughput drops because the PCIe link cannot deliver enough data.
HBM bandwidth increases during the burst and decreases at steady state, so the gap is memory-bandwidth-related rather than power-related.
Nsight Systems mismeasures the burst throughput by 20% due to profiler overhead; the sustained figure is the true value at both phases.

Sustained power/thermal constraints throttle SM clock frequency to keep total power at or below TDP; short bursts can exceed sustained power via thermal headroom, but the long-run steady state respects the cap, reducing achievable throughput.

questions.explanation: Data-center GPUs use dynamic voltage/frequency scaling (DVFS) to keep power within the TDP cap. Short bursts can exceed the sustained power draw thanks to thermal capacity, but as the die heats up and rolling averages approach the TDP cap, the driver reduces clocks (Perf State P0 → P2). The GEMM is compute-bound, so throughput drops proportionally. Options B, C, D contradict the profile or introduce fictional causes.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: PCIe bandwidth applies to host-device transfers; a resident GEMM does not need PCIe traffic to run.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: HBM bandwidth is set by the memory subsystem and does not fluctuate meaningfully across burst vs steady state in this way. The kernel is compute-bound, so HBM is not the bottleneck.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: profiler overhead does not systematically bias burst measurements by 20%; both phases are captured similarly.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: TDP-driven DVFS reduces sustained clocks, cutting compute throughput.

assumptions: Kernel is compute-bound (large square GEMM) so throughput tracks compute frequency.
GPU exposes DVFS-based power management to stay at or under TDP.
Ambient cooling is fixed; only the die/board thermal headroom changes over the run.
nonImplications: Does not imply that all GPUs behave identically; some SKUs allow higher sustained power via improved cooling or firmware.
Does not imply power capping is the only cause of sustained-vs-burst gaps; measurement noise, background jobs, and JIT compilation can also contribute.

distractorRationales.C: Attributes real physical effect to profiler noise.

sourceRefs.locator: Performance tuning under thermal/power constraints; DVFS discussion

performanceClaim.scope: data-center GPU sustained-vs-burst throughput under TDP cap

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the performance impact of register spilling on GPU kernels and identify why 'local memory' spills traverse HBM.

requiredFeatures: per-thread local memory backed by global memory

questions.profileData: ptxas info: Used 255 registers, 0 bytes cmem[0], 128 bytes stack frame, 128 bytes spill stores, 128 bytes spill loads.
questions.stem: You compile a CUDA kernel and ptxas reports `128 bytes spill stores, 128 bytes spill loads`. Which statement about GPU register spills is correct?

options.text: Spills go to shared memory automatically; the ptxas 'spill' counters report shared-memory bytes rather than HBM bytes.
Spills go to a dedicated on-chip spill buffer separate from HBM and L1/L2, so spill traffic does not consume DRAM bandwidth.

Spill loads/stores traverse per-thread 'local memory', which physically resides in HBM (cached in L1/L2). Each spilled access can add hundreds of cycles of latency and adds HBM bandwidth pressure, especially if L1/L2 do not absorb the traffic.
Spills are always harmless because L1 hits them; the compiler only spills if it has proven the access will hit cache on the next reload.

questions.explanation: CUDA per-thread 'local memory' is a logical name; physically it lives in HBM (global memory) with L1/L2 caching. Spill stores/loads therefore incur potentially hundreds of cycles of latency and consume HBM bandwidth when L1/L2 do not absorb the traffic. Options B, C, D contradict the CUDA memory model.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: shared memory is programmer-managed and finite per block; the compiler does not implicitly spill registers to shared memory.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: there is no separate on-chip spill buffer; spills go to logical local memory backed by HBM.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: local memory backs spills; physically resides in HBM with L1/L2 caching.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: the compiler does not have general proof of cache residency; spills are decided by register-pressure heuristics, and their runtime cost varies.

assumptions: ptxas reports spill counters when register pressure exceeds a threshold controlled by --maxrregcount or -Xptxas -O.
Local memory is caching per NVIDIA's memory model (L1/L2 involvement).
nonImplications: Does not imply that every spill costs a full HBM latency; L1/L2 can hit repeatedly-used spill slots.
Does not imply reducing register count via --maxrregcount always improves performance; forcing spills may be worse than accepting lower occupancy.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses shared memory with logical local memory.
distractorRationales.D: Overstates compiler's knowledge of cache behavior.

sourceRefs.locator: Local memory section; register file and spills

performanceClaim.scope: ptxas spill diagnosis on NVIDIA GPUs

questions.learningObjective: Compute a GPU's Roofline ridge point from published peak throughput and memory bandwidth, and reason about how the ridge shifts across precisions.
questions.stem: H100 SXM5 published peaks (dense, non-sparse): FP16 Tensor Core ≈ 989 TFLOP/s, FP8 Tensor Core ≈ 1979 TFLOP/s, HBM3 bandwidth ≈ 3.35 TB/s. Which statement about ridge points on this GPU is correct?

options.text: FP16 ridge ≈ 295 FLOP/byte; FP8 ridge ≈ 590 FLOP/byte; lowering precision reduces the compute peak and hence the ridge point.
FP16 ridge ≈ 295 FLOP/byte; FP8 ridge ≈ 590 FLOP/byte; halving the operand precision doubles the ridge point (bytes per operand halve while compute doubles).
Both ridges collapse to the same value because ridge point is a hardware invariant defined by HBM alone, independent of the math throughput reported for a specific precision.
FP8 ridge ≈ 148 FLOP/byte, half of FP16's, because FP8 operands only need 1 byte and thus each byte can serve twice as many FLOPs at the same bandwidth.

questions.explanation: Ridge point = peak compute / peak memory bandwidth. FP16: 989e12 / 3.35e12 ≈ 295 FLOP/byte. FP8: 1979e12 / 3.35e12 ≈ 590 FLOP/byte. As you move from FP16 to FP8, peak compute typically doubles (more MMA per cycle) while HBM bandwidth is unchanged, so the ridge point roughly doubles. This is why lower-precision kernels demand higher arithmetic intensity to stay compute-bound.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: the FP8 ridge point value is right but the causal claim is inverted; lowering precision raises the peak (in TFLOP/s counted) and thereby raises the ridge.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: ridges computed as compute/BW; FP8 ridge is approximately 2× the FP16 ridge because FP8 peak is ~2× FP16 peak while BW is unchanged.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: ridge point depends on the compute peak, which is a function of the precision path used.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: reasoning confuses operand byte width with the compute peak. Ridge point is FLOP-per-byte-of-HBM-traffic; the operand byte width affects AI (op-side numerator/denominator), not the hardware ridge.

assumptions: Dense (non-sparse) Tensor Core peaks are used.
HBM3 bandwidth is the memory-side reference for ridge, not L2 or SMEM.
nonImplications: Does not imply an FP8 kernel is faster than an FP16 kernel on any given workload; achievable throughput depends on AI, tile size, kernel implementation and whether the ops are supported natively.
Does not imply that lowering to FP4 continues to double the ridge; hardware support and effective FLOP counting rules govern real ridges.

distractorRationales.A: Reverses the direction of change with precision.
distractorRationales.D: Conflates numerator/denominator sides of the Roofline plot.

sourceRefs.locator: Compute Capability 9.0 tables; Tensor Core throughput per precision

performanceClaim.scope: H100 SXM5, published peak FP16/FP8 Tensor Core and HBM3 bandwidth

questions.learningObjective: Contrast CPU SIMD lane execution with GPU SIMT warp execution, identifying differences in divergence handling, thread identity and programming model.
questions.stem: Which of the following statements distinguishing CPU SIMD (e.g., AVX-512) from NVIDIA GPU SIMT (warp-based) execution are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: SIMT presents each warp lane as an independently addressable thread with its own program counter view (post-Volta), while SIMD lanes share one architectural instruction pointer and are handled explicitly by the programmer or compiler as vector data.

In SIMT, control-flow divergence within a warp is resolved by hardware serialization of taken/not-taken paths, whereas SIMD lanes rely on programmer-written masking (predication) to emulate divergent control.
SIMD guarantees higher peak throughput than SIMT on the same silicon area because SIMT wastes ~30% of area on per-thread state.
SIMT and SIMD are the same execution model with different names; the choice of terminology is purely marketing.

questions.explanation: A: Under SIMT, each thread of a warp has an independent logical program state; post-Volta CUDA GPUs support independent thread scheduling with per-thread PCs and reconvergence. SIMD lanes share a single instruction pointer and are packed into wide vector registers manipulated by explicit instructions. B: SIMT hardware handles branch divergence via masking + serialization of divergent sides; SIMD requires the compiler/programmer to write predicated code (e.g., mask registers on AVX-512). C is false — throughput comparisons depend on many factors (memory bandwidth, precision, occupancy); no such generic silicon-area rule applies. D is false — the models differ in programming abstraction, divergence handling and thread-identity semantics.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: SIMT exposes threads as first-class entities with independent state (especially post-Volta), while SIMD packs lanes into a single instruction.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: hardware-managed divergence in SIMT vs software-managed predication in SIMD is a canonical distinction.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: peak throughput comparisons are workload- and architecture-specific; there is no universal SIMD > SIMT silicon efficiency claim.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: the models differ meaningfully in abstraction (threads vs lanes), divergence handling and programming interface.

assumptions: GPU baseline is Volta+ NVIDIA SIMT with independent thread scheduling.
CPU SIMD baseline is AVX-512 or similar wide-vector ISA with mask registers.
nonImplications: Does not imply SIMT eliminates divergence cost; divergence still serializes taken paths on GPUs.
Does not imply SIMD lanes cannot benefit from hardware-managed masking (some ISAs offer masks natively, e.g., AVX-512 k-registers).

sourceRefs.locator: Ch. 4, DLP: SIMD vs SIMT execution
Programming model, warps, independent thread scheduling

questions.learningObjective: Estimate the ideal wall time of a 3-stage H2D → kernel → D2H pipeline using multi-stream chunking, and identify the resource limits.

requiredFeatures: separate H2D and D2H copy engines

questions.stem: You process N chunks of equal size. Each chunk requires 10 ms H2D, 20 ms kernel, and 10 ms D2H. The GPU has two DMA copy engines (one H2D, one D2H), one kernel engine, and you use N ≥ 3 CUDA streams so H2D of chunk i+1, kernel of chunk i, and D2H of chunk i−1 can overlap. What is the approximate steady-state wall time per chunk, and what limits it?

options.text: ≈ 30 ms per chunk: H2D and D2H must share a single copy engine, so their times add (10 + 10) and run in parallel with the kernel; max(20, 20) = 20 ms but plus a 10 ms merge overhead per stage.
≈ 40 ms per chunk: the three stages serialize into 10+20+10 ms because CUDA streams do not truly overlap H2D and D2H on the same GPU.
≈ 10 ms per chunk: overlapping N streams with N ≥ 3 divides the total time by 3, so the effective per-chunk cost drops below the kernel time.
≈ 20 ms per chunk: the kernel stage (longest) sets the pipeline period; H2D and D2H run in parallel on separate copy engines, and kernel throughput is the bottleneck.

questions.explanation: Standard pipeline analysis: per-chunk steady-state period = max(stage times) = max(10, 20, 10) = 20 ms, provided the three stages run on independent hardware engines (H2D copy engine, kernel engine, D2H copy engine). Modern NVIDIA GPUs typically have separate H2D and D2H engines, so this holds. Kernel is the bottleneck; halving kernel time would drop steady-state period to 10 ms (max of the remaining stages).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: modern data-center GPUs (Ampere, Hopper) have two independent copy engines (H2D and D2H); no merge overhead applies.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: CUDA streams do overlap H2D/kernel/D2H on modern GPUs with separate engines; serial 10+20+10 = 40 ms is the non-overlapped worst case for a single chunk, not steady state.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: pipelining does not shrink per-chunk period below the slowest stage; it hides fill/drain latency across chunks.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: pipeline steady-state period = max of stage times when stages use independent engines.

assumptions: Ampere+ data-center GPU with separate H2D and D2H copy engines.
Enough pinned memory and independent streams to keep the pipeline filled.
No dependencies between chunks other than pipeline ordering.
nonImplications: Does not imply pipeline start-up and drain are free; the first chunk still incurs 10+20+10 = 40 ms end-to-end.
Does not imply overlap is automatic; the programmer must issue kernels and copies on non-default streams to enable overlap.

distractorRationales.A: Wrong assumption about single copy engine on modern data-center GPUs.
distractorRationales.C: Confuses parallel workers with pipelined stages.

sourceRefs.locator: Streams, asynchronous concurrent execution, copy engines

performanceClaim.scope: 3-stage CUDA stream pipeline steady state

questions.subtopic: Tensor Core density vs FP32 SIMT
questions.learningObjective: Compare the arithmetic density (FLOP per cycle per SM) of NVIDIA Tensor Core FP16 vs FP32 SIMT paths, and reason about when each dominates.
questions.stem: A100 SXM published peaks: FP32 CUDA-core ≈ 19.5 TFLOP/s; FP16 Tensor Core ≈ 312 TFLOP/s (dense). A GEMM kernel with sufficient AI can, in principle, choose between the two paths. Which statement about the Tensor Core vs CUDA-core throughput ratio is correct?

options.text: The paths are equal in throughput; the 312 TFLOP/s figure counts sparse Tensor Core throughput, which reduces to ~19.5 TFLOP/s once sparsity is disabled.
The FP16 Tensor Core path is roughly 2× denser than FP32 CUDA cores because Tensor Cores process 2 operands per lane in one instruction; the ratio 312 / 19.5 must be a benchmark artifact.
The FP16 Tensor Core path halves throughput compared to FP32 CUDA cores because reduced precision requires additional accumulation steps.

The FP16 Tensor Core path is roughly 16× more FLOP-dense than the FP32 CUDA-core path on A100; using FP16 tensor cores (when the workload tolerates FP16 precision) yields up to a 16× ideal speedup for compute-bound kernels.
