questions.explanation: 312 / 19.5 ≈ 16. This is the documented dense-throughput ratio on A100 SXM between FP16 Tensor Cores and FP32 CUDA cores. Compute-bound kernels that can tolerate FP16 (with FP32 accumulation) can approach this speedup; memory-bound kernels benefit less because HBM bandwidth is unchanged. Options B, C, D contradict the documented peak numbers.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: the 312 TFLOP/s figure is dense (not sparse). Sparse throughput would be ~624 TFLOP/s under 2:4 structured sparsity.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: the ratio is ~16×, not ~2×; A100 dense Tensor Core figures are architectural, not benchmark artifacts.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: FP16 Tensor Core throughput exceeds FP32 CUDA-core throughput; extra accumulation does not net a slowdown at the kernel level.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: 312 / 19.5 ≈ 16× dense; the actual ideal speedup applies only to compute-bound workloads that can adopt the FP16 tensor core path.

assumptions: A100 SXM dense FP16 Tensor Core peak = 312 TFLOP/s; FP32 CUDA-core peak = 19.5 TFLOP/s (NVIDIA published).
Comparison is compute peak vs compute peak, not achievable throughput on any particular kernel.
nonImplications: Does not imply that any real kernel achieves 16× speedup; achievable speedup depends on precision tolerance, kernel implementation, and Roofline regime.
Does not imply that FP16 always improves accuracy-normalized performance; some workloads require careful mixed-precision recipes to preserve accuracy.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses sparse and dense peak values.
distractorRationales.C: Reverses the direction of Tensor Core benefit.

sourceRefs.locator: Compute Capability 8.0 tables; Tensor Core throughput per precision

performanceClaim.scope: A100 SXM published FP32 CUDA and FP16 Tensor Core peaks

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish latency from throughput and identify architectural strategies that optimize one at the expense of the other.
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly distinguish latency from throughput in an architectural context? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Latency and throughput are reciprocals of each other, so improving one automatically improves the other by the same factor.

A workload's latency floor is at least the longest sequential dependency chain; increasing parallelism reduces throughput bottlenecks but cannot shrink an unavoidable data dependency's contribution to latency.

Latency is the time to complete one unit of work end-to-end; throughput is the rate of completed work per unit time. On pipelined or heavily parallel systems, throughput can be high while individual latency remains long.
GPU architectures optimize primarily for throughput via massive parallelism and latency hiding through overlapping many warps, at the cost of higher per-op latency than a CPU on isolated operations.

questions.explanation: A: Textbook definition and the observation that pipelined systems trade single-item latency for aggregate throughput. B: GPUs use SIMT with many warps and latency-hiding memory pipelines; single-issue latency on a CPU is often lower for a lone dependent instruction stream. D: Sequential dependencies (critical path) bound latency; parallelism can widen the pipeline but cannot fold two dependent ops in half. C is wrong: latency and throughput are not reciprocals when pipelining or parallelism is involved; throughput can be N-way while per-item latency is still 1 unit of pipeline depth.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: they are not simple reciprocals; pipelining and parallelism decouple them.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: critical path (sequential dependencies) sets a latency floor even with unlimited workers.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard definitions with the pipeline caveat.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: canonical characterization of GPU throughput orientation vs CPU latency orientation.

assumptions: Comparison of GPUs and CPUs as throughput- vs latency-oriented, respectively, per architectural design goals.
The workload can be pipelined or parallelized; a purely sequential critical-path workload is not the general case.
nonImplications: Does not imply CPUs are always slower per-op than GPUs; per-thread latency on CPUs is often lower for scalar workloads.
Does not imply throughput and latency are unrelated; they are related by Little's Law, but not as simple reciprocals.

distractorRationales.A: Overly simple algebraic relation that ignores pipelining and parallelism.

sourceRefs.locator: Ch. 1, latency vs throughput and pipeline chapters

questions.learningObjective: Explain the semantics of warps, blocks and grids in CUDA and the resources they share.
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship among threads, warps, blocks and grids on NVIDIA GPUs (compute capability 8.0)?

options.text: A warp is a group of 32 threads that share a warp scheduler and are always drawn from the same block; a block is assigned to a single SM and its threads share shared memory and __syncthreads() barrier; a grid spans many blocks that may run on different SMs and cannot rely on cross-block barriers without cooperative-groups grid sync.
A warp of 32 threads is scheduled independently and may be composed of threads from different thread blocks to improve occupancy when a single block cannot fill an SM.
All blocks in a grid share a single shared-memory bank because shared memory is L1-cached across SMs, providing a form of grid-level synchronization.
Grid-level synchronization is implicit at every kernel launch boundary; __syncthreads() therefore synchronizes all threads across the entire grid.

questions.explanation: A: The CUDA execution model defines a warp as 32 threads from a single block, scheduled together on one SM warp scheduler. A block is assigned to exactly one SM; block-scope shared memory and __syncthreads() operate within that block. Cross-block synchronization within a grid requires cooperative groups (grid.sync()) with grid-launch support. B is false — warps are not composed across blocks. C is false — shared memory is per-SM and per-block; there is no cross-SM shared bank. D is false — __syncthreads() is a block-scope barrier, not grid-scope.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: warps are within a block, blocks run on one SM, grid spans SMs, cross-block sync needs cooperative groups.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: a warp cannot mix threads from different blocks.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: shared memory is per-block; there is no cross-SM shared-memory bank.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: __syncthreads() is block-scope; grid-level barriers require grid.sync() with cooperative launch.

assumptions: NVIDIA Ampere or later; warp size 32.
Standard (non-cooperative) kernel launch semantics for the __syncthreads() claim.
nonImplications: Does not imply blocks are always resident concurrently on an SM; some blocks queue and become resident as prior ones finish.
Does not imply cooperative launch is always possible — it requires all blocks to fit resident on the GPU simultaneously.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses per-block shared memory with global L2/L1 caches.

sourceRefs.locator: Programming model chapter: thread hierarchy, warps, blocks, grids

questions.learningObjective: Identify sound and unsound assumptions in alias analysis and their effect on downstream optimizations.
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about alias analysis in a compiler are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Any imprecise alias analysis can be safely replaced by 'always no-alias' because most optimizations conservatively re-verify the aliasing before applying.

A sound alias analysis is a may-analysis: when it says two pointers 'may alias', the compiler must assume they could point to the same location. A conservative may-alias answer never breaks correctness but may inhibit optimizations.

A must-alias answer is strictly stronger than may-alias: 'p and q must alias' means every execution has *p and *q referring to the same location, enabling optimizations like store-to-load forwarding across the pointers.
Reporting 'no-alias' when two pointers actually may alias is a soundness bug in alias analysis; downstream passes (e.g., CSE, LICM) can miscompile programs based on the false no-alias claim.

questions.explanation: A: sound alias analyses are may-analyses (over-approximation). B: must-alias is strictly stronger; it certifies aliasing in every execution and enables optimizations like store forwarding. C: false no-alias is a soundness bug; passes that depend on it may commute stores or eliminate loads incorrectly. D is wrong: downstream passes trust the analysis; they don't re-verify. 'Always no-alias' is unsound and will miscompile programs where pointers do alias.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: passes trust the analysis; unsound 'always no-alias' will miscompile programs.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: sound alias analysis is a may-analysis / over-approximation.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: must-alias is a stronger, useful certification.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: false no-alias is a soundness bug affecting many optimizations.

assumptions: Standard alias-analysis framework (may-alias / no-alias / must-alias).
nonImplications: Does not imply may-alias is useless; it correctly bounds behavior even when pointers actually don't alias.
Does not imply must-alias is common; must-alias is typically only proved for trivial cases (same SSA name, obvious constants).

distractorRationales.A: Fabricates a re-verification step that does not exist in practice.

questions.learningObjective: Precisely define a basic block and identify what constitutes a valid CFG edge.
questions.stem: Which statement correctly defines a basic block (BB) and the corresponding control-flow graph (CFG)?

options.text: A basic block is a loop body; the CFG has one node per loop and edges represent nesting.
A basic block is any sequence of instructions with no data dependency between them; the CFG is a data-flow graph over these blocks.
A basic block is a function body; the CFG has one node per function and edges represent calls.

A basic block is a maximal straight-line sequence of instructions with exactly one entry (the first instruction) and one exit (the last instruction, typically a branch or terminator); the CFG has an edge from BB_i to BB_j if control can flow from the terminator of BB_i to the entry of BB_j.

questions.explanation: Textbook definition: a basic block is a maximal straight-line code sequence with a single entry (first instruction) and single exit (last instruction). CFG edges represent possible control flow between blocks (via branches, fall-throughs, and terminators). The other options misidentify BBs as data-flow constructs, functions, or loop bodies.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: a loop body typically contains multiple BBs; loops are structural properties of the CFG.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: BBs are defined by control flow (single entry/exit), not by data dependency.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: a function typically contains many BBs; a call graph is a different structure.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: canonical BB and CFG definition.

assumptions: Standard textbook definition (EAC3, Dragon Book).
nonImplications: Does not imply that BBs cannot contain calls (they can, unless calls are treated as terminators for exception-safety analysis).
Does not imply the CFG is unique for a given program; different partitions may exist, but the maximal one is standard.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses control-flow with data-flow analysis units.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish constant folding from constant propagation and identify when folding is legal.
questions.irSnippet:
; Before folding
%a = add i32 3, 4
%b = mul i32 %a, 2
%c = add i32 %b, 5

; After constant folding
%c = i32 19
questions.stem: Constant folding transforms the IR shown above by evaluating arithmetic on compile-time constants. Which statement about constant folding is correct?

options.text: Constant folding requires SSA form; a non-SSA IR cannot support folding because reaching definitions are ambiguous.

Constant folding evaluates operations whose operands are all compile-time constants at compile time, producing a new constant. It must respect the source semantics for overflow, rounding, and floating-point edge cases (NaN, infinity) — otherwise it can change program behavior.
Constant folding is identical to constant propagation; both refer to substituting known values into use sites.
Constant folding may reorder floating-point operations freely because IEEE-754 arithmetic is associative.

questions.explanation: Constant folding computes constant expressions at compile time but must preserve semantics — integer overflow behavior, floating-point rounding, NaN/Inf handling. Constant propagation is a distinct (but related) optimization: it replaces variable uses with their known constant values. Non-SSA IRs can also fold; SSA simplifies but is not required. IEEE-754 floating-point is NOT associative, so reordering is not always safe.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: constant folding is applicable in both SSA and non-SSA IRs.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: standard definition with the important semantic-preservation caveats.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: folding evaluates operations; propagation replaces uses. They are related but distinct.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: IEEE-754 addition/multiplication are NOT associative; naive reordering may change results (see -ffast-math implications).

assumptions: IR represents integer and/or floating-point operations with well-defined semantics.
nonImplications: Does not imply all constant expressions are folded; e.g., division by zero may need to be preserved as a trap.
Does not imply folding is 'free' compile-time work; large expressions may increase compile time.

sourceRefs.locator: Optimization chapter, constant folding vs propagation

questions.learningObjective: Explain how SCCP achieves greater precision than plain constant propagation by combining constant propagation with reachability analysis.
questions.irSnippet:
; Original SSA CFG snippet
bb_entry:
  %x = i32 5
  %cond = icmp slt i32 %x, 10
  br i1 %cond, label %bb_then, label %bb_else
bb_then:
  %y1 = add i32 %x, 1     ; reachable
  br label %bb_merge
bb_else:
  %y2 = mul i32 %x, %unknown ; NOT reachable per SCCP
  br label %bb_merge
bb_merge:
  %y = phi i32 [%y1, %bb_then], [%y2, %bb_else]
questions.stem: Sparse Conditional Constant Propagation (SCCP) achieves better precision than plain constant propagation by tracking both constant lattice values and edge reachability. Which statement about SCCP's advantage over plain constant propagation on the code above is correct?

options.text: SCCP is identical to plain constant propagation in this example; the difference only appears in loops.

SCCP infers %cond = true (since 5 < 10), marks the bb_else edge as unreachable, and treats the φ as effectively %y = %y1 = 6; plain constant propagation, unaware of reachability, must merge %y1 and %y2 into a non-constant top.
Plain constant propagation would already conclude %y = 6 by ignoring the else branch heuristically; SCCP is unnecessary for this pattern.
SCCP marks bb_then as unreachable because plain propagation cannot decide which branch runs, and the algorithm defaults to the else path.

questions.explanation: SCCP (Wegman & Zadeck 1991) maintains two lattices: variable values and edge reachability. It propagates constants only along edges proven reachable. In the example, %cond folds to true (5 < 10), so the bb_else edge is unreachable and does not contribute to the φ. This makes %y = %y1 = 6. Plain constant propagation without reachability tracking must merge %y1 and %y2 (with %y2 unknown due to %unknown), yielding non-constant top for %y. SCCP is more precise. Options B, C, D contain factual errors about the algorithm.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: SCCP is strictly more precise than plain propagation on branchy code, not only in loops.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: SCCP's edge-reachability tracking makes the difference.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: plain constant propagation does not have a heuristic to skip a branch; it merges all reaching values.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: SCCP does not default to a branch; it proves reachability from the constant condition.

assumptions: SSA form; canonical SCCP algorithm (Wegman & Zadeck).
nonImplications: Does not imply SCCP always beats plain propagation; when no conditional branches involve constants, the two coincide.
Does not imply SCCP is free; it operates on both lattices to fixpoint.

questions.learningObjective: Identify when CSE is legal given side effects and availability.
questions.irSnippet:
; Before CSE
%a = load i32, i32* %p    ; Load L1
call void @sink(i32 %a)   ; may write memory
%b = load i32, i32* %p    ; Load L2

; Naive CSE would replace %b with %a; is this legal?
questions.stem: The IR performs two loads from the same pointer %p, with a `call @sink` between them that may write to memory. A naive CSE would replace the second load with the first. Which statement is correct?

options.text: CSE is legal here because compilers assume by default that function calls are pure unless explicitly marked otherwise.
CSE is always legal for loads from the same pointer in SSA form because SSA ensures the pointer value is unchanged.

CSE cannot legally replace L2 with %a unless the compiler proves that @sink does not write to the memory pointed to by %p (via alias analysis or a nomemory/readonly attribute). Otherwise the two loads may observe different values and CSE would change semantics.
CSE is illegal in principle because loads are side-effecting operations that can never be eliminated.

questions.explanation: Option C is correct; options A, B, D are incorrect. A (Wrong): compilers default to conservative 'may-write' semantics for calls; purity/readonly must be proven or annotated. B (Wrong): SSA operates on virtual registers, not memory; a load's value can change if memory is modified between loads. C (Correct): CSE for loads requires proving no intervening memory clobber via alias analysis or function attributes. D (Wrong): loads can be eliminated when availability is proven; they are only side-effecting when volatile or atomic. General context: CSE requires the availability property: the earlier computation's result must still be valid at the later use point. For memory loads, this requires proving that no intervening operation writes to the same location. A call whose memory effects are unknown pessimistically kills all availability.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: compilers default to conservative 'may-write' semantics for calls; purity/readonly must be proven or annotated.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: SSA operates on virtual registers, not memory; a load's value can change if memory is modified between loads.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: CSE for loads requires proving no intervening memory clobber via alias analysis or function attributes.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: loads can be eliminated when availability is proven; they are only side-effecting when volatile or atomic.

assumptions: IR represents loads and calls with distinguishable memory effects.
Standard SSA semantics for register values, non-SSA memory model.
nonImplications: Does not imply CSE is always beneficial; sometimes rematerializing a value costs less than saving it in a register (increased register pressure).
Does not imply availability is easy to compute for loads; alias analysis precision is often the limiting factor.

distractorRationales.A: Falsely assumes calls are pure by default.

sourceRefs.locator: Function attributes: readonly, readnone, memory effects

questions.learningObjective: Explain the meet operator and lattice ordering choice for a canonical data-flow analysis.
questions.stem: In classical data-flow analysis, the meet operator combines information at a join point (multiple predecessor paths). Which pairing of analysis and meet operator is correct?

options.text: Both liveness and available expressions use union; the direction (forward/backward) is what distinguishes them.
Liveness uses intersection because a variable must be live on all paths to be considered live; available expressions use union to be sound.

Liveness (may-analysis, backward): meet = union — a variable is live-in at a block if it is live-in on some successor. Available expressions (must-analysis, forward): meet = intersection — an expression is available at a block only if it is available on every predecessor path.
Neither analysis uses a meet operator; both are point-to-point dataflow computations without merging.

questions.explanation: Standard textbook pairing: liveness (may-analysis, backward, union) — some path uses the variable in the future. Available expressions (must-analysis, forward, intersection) — every path has computed the expression. The direction (forward/backward) and the may/must nature (union/intersection) are independent and combine into the four-quadrant classification of classical dataflow analyses.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: available expressions use intersection, not union.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: reverses the operators for both analyses.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: liveness = may/backward/union; available expressions = must/forward/intersection.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: both use meet operators at join points.

assumptions: Standard textbook dataflow framework (Dragon Book, EAC3).
nonImplications: Does not imply all meet operators are union or intersection; more elaborate lattices (constant propagation, range analysis) have richer meets.
Does not imply meet direction of forward/backward is arbitrary; each analysis has a natural direction driven by its semantics.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish dead code elimination from unreachable code elimination and identify soundness conditions.
questions.stem: Which statements about Dead Code Elimination (DCE) and its relationship to unreachable code elimination are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: DCE can safely remove any pure computation whose result is unused, even if the computation may throw a floating-point exception, because unused values are always safe to elide.
DCE requires SSA to be applicable; non-SSA IRs cannot support DCE because reaching definitions are ambiguous.

DCE removes instructions whose results are not used and that have no observable side effects (no memory writes, no I/O, no exceptions). An instruction that writes to memory or calls a function that may have side effects cannot be removed by DCE, even if its return value is unused.
Unreachable code elimination removes basic blocks that no execution path can reach from the entry; this is distinct from DCE, which operates on live/dead value analysis within reachable code.

questions.explanation: A: DCE requires (unused value) AND (no observable side effects). Stores, I/O, and possibly-throwing calls remain. B: Unreachable-code elimination is control-flow based; DCE is data-flow based. They can be composed. C is wrong: FP exceptions are observable side effects (if the target environment traps or the language enforces exception semantics); removing a computation that may trap can change observable behavior. D is wrong: DCE works on non-SSA IRs with reaching-definition analysis; SSA simplifies it.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: FP exceptions can be observable; naive removal can change semantics under strict FP.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: DCE is applicable in non-SSA IRs, though SSA simplifies the analysis.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: dead value + side-effect-free are the twin conditions.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: DCE and unreachable code elimination are distinct passes.

assumptions: Program semantics may include observable side effects such as FP exceptions and I/O.
Standard IR with distinguishable pure vs side-effecting operations.
nonImplications: Does not imply that all unused loads can be removed; volatile loads are side-effecting.
Does not imply DCE eliminates all dead code in one pass; iterating with other optimizations often reveals more dead code.

sourceRefs.locator: Optimization: DCE and unreachable code chapter

questions.learningObjective: Explain why def-use chains are trivial to compute in SSA compared to non-SSA IR.
questions.stem: In SSA form, why are def-use chains typically simpler and cheaper to compute than in a non-SSA IR?

options.text: Because SSA prohibits loops, def-use chains cannot cross backedges.
Because SSA merges phi values at runtime into a single memory slot, the def-use graph collapses to a linear list.
Because each SSA name has exactly one textual definition, every use points unambiguously to that unique def; there is no reaching-definitions problem to solve to associate uses with their defs.
Because SSA form guarantees that any use is reachable from every def, making the chains trivially total.

questions.explanation: SSA guarantees a unique textual definition per name, so each use has a single unambiguous def. In non-SSA IR, reaching-definitions analysis is needed to determine which of possibly many textual definitions of a variable can reach a use. Options B, C, D contain incorrect claims about SSA semantics.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: SSA supports loops (via loop-header phis).
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: SSA does not merge phi values into single memory slots; phi is an IR construct.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: unique-definition property makes def-use chains direct.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: SSA doesn't guarantee every use is reachable from every def; each use has one unique reaching def.

assumptions: Standard SSA form (Cytron et al.).
nonImplications: Does not imply def-use chains are free to build in SSA; they still require a linear scan.
Does not imply non-SSA def-use analysis is infeasible; it just requires a dataflow analysis pass.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish dominance and post-dominance relations and identify implications for SSA construction and code motion.
questions.stem: Which statements about dominance and post-dominance in a CFG with a distinguished entry are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Dominance and post-dominance are the same relation; the two are equivalent for any well-formed CFG.
Dominance implies reachability from the entry, so unreachable code is not part of any dominator subtree and is typically removed before SSA construction.
Block D dominates block N (written D dom N) iff every path from the entry to N passes through D; the dominance relation forms a tree rooted at the entry block.

Block P post-dominates block N iff every path from N to the exit passes through P; post-dominance uses a reverse CFG and requires a distinguished exit (which may need to be synthesized for functions with multiple returns).

questions.explanation: A: standard dominance definition; the dominance relation forms a tree (dominator tree). B: post-dominance is the dual on the reverse CFG; a distinguished exit node is required for a well-defined post-dominance tree (synthesized when multiple returns exist). C is false: dominance and post-dominance are duals but not identical; e.g., a block may dominate itself trivially, but post-dominance depends on the exit structure. D is correct: unreachable code has no path from entry to it, so it is outside the dominator tree; DCE typically eliminates it first.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: they are duals, not identities; they coincide only in trivial CFGs.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: unreachable code is excluded from the dominator tree and typically pruned first.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: dominance definition and tree property.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: post-dominance is the dual over reverse CFG requiring an exit.

assumptions: CFG has a distinguished entry; for post-dominance, an exit (possibly synthesized) is added.
Standard textbook definitions from EAC3, Appel.
nonImplications: Does not imply that dominance is easy to compute; efficient algorithms (Lengauer-Tarjan) require some care.
Does not imply post-dominance is only useful for reverse analyses; sink-based optimizations and control dependence use it heavily.

questions.learningObjective: Identify structural properties of the dominator tree and its use in SSA construction.
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the dominator tree of a CFG and its use in SSA construction?

options.text: The dominator tree is identical to the loop nest tree; both express nested control-flow structures.
The dominator tree is the transpose of the CFG; edges are reversed and used for backward analysis such as liveness.
The dominator tree contains one node per phi function; edges represent phi operand relationships.

The dominator tree has the CFG entry as its root; the immediate dominator of each block is its parent. SSA construction places phi functions at the dominance frontier of each definition, which is the set of blocks that are just outside the region strictly dominated by the definition's block but reachable from it.

questions.explanation: Standard definition: the dominator tree is rooted at entry; each block's parent is its immediate dominator (idom). SSA construction (Cytron et al.) places phi functions at the dominance frontier of each definition — informally, at the 'edge' where the definition's dominance stops applying and multiple reaching definitions could merge. Options B, C, D describe unrelated structures (reverse CFG, phi graph, loop nest tree).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: loop nest tree captures loop containment, distinct from dominance.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: dominator tree is not a transpose of the CFG; it is a distinct tree derived from the dominance relation.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: dominator tree nodes are CFG blocks, not phi functions.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: rooted at entry, parent = immediate dominator; SSA uses dominance frontier for phi placement.

assumptions: CFG has a single entry block; dominance is defined with respect to it.
SSA construction follows the Cytron et al. algorithm.
nonImplications: Does not imply computing the dominator tree is expensive; Lengauer-Tarjan is nearly linear.
Does not imply the dominator tree fully captures control dependence; control dependence uses post-dominance.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses dominator tree with loop nest tree.
distractorRationales.B: Confuses dominator tree with reverse CFG.

sourceRefs.locator: Dominator tree and SSA construction chapter
Dominator tree and dominance frontier chapter

questions.learningObjective: Precisely define escape analysis and identify what optimizations it enables.
questions.stem: Which statement most precisely describes escape analysis and the optimizations it enables?

options.text: Escape analysis identifies variables that need to be stored in registers rather than memory; it drives register allocation.
Escape analysis proves that a variable is used outside a loop; the compiler then hoists its computation via LICM.
Escape analysis proves that a function does not throw exceptions; the compiler then removes exception-handling code paths.

Escape analysis proves that a heap-allocated object's lifetime is bounded by its allocating function (does not escape via return, thread, or stored reference); the compiler can then stack-allocate it, scalarize its fields, or eliminate it entirely (scalar replacement of aggregates).

questions.explanation: Escape analysis is a program analysis that determines whether an allocated object's reference can 'escape' the scope of its allocation (via return value, thread visibility, or a store into an escaping location). Non-escaping objects can be stack-allocated (avoiding heap GC pressure), scalarized (SROA), or eliminated. Options B, C, D refer to unrelated analyses.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: register allocation is a downstream pass; escape analysis operates at higher-level memory semantics.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: this describes loop-invariant analysis, not escape analysis.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: exception-throwing analysis is a distinct effect analysis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: standard escape analysis definition and its enabled optimizations.

assumptions: Language supports heap-allocated objects (e.g., Java, Go, or C++ with new/delete).
Standard escape-analysis definitions (Choi et al., Blanchet).
nonImplications: Does not imply escape analysis eliminates all heap allocations; only proven non-escaping ones.
Does not imply escape analysis is precise; imprecise conservative results simply prevent optimization without introducing bugs.

sourceRefs.locator: Heap analysis and stack allocation optimization chapter

questions.learningObjective: Identify the benefits and costs of function inlining and the conditions when it may be inhibited.
questions.stem: Which statements about function inlining as a compiler optimization are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Recursive functions cannot be inlined at all; the compiler always emits them as separate call sites.
Indirect / virtual calls typically require devirtualization (via type information or profiling) before they can be inlined, since the target is not statically known.
Inlining eliminates the call/return overhead and enables intraprocedural optimizations (constant propagation, CSE, LICM) to see across the previous call boundary.

Aggressive inlining can hurt performance by inflating instruction cache footprint (icache misses), increasing register pressure, and slowing compile time; heuristics balance size and estimated benefit.

questions.explanation: A: canonical benefit of inlining. B: canonical cost — icache pressure, register pressure, compile-time bloat. D: indirect calls need devirtualization (or PGO-guided speculative inlining) before they can be inlined. C is wrong: recursive functions CAN be inlined up to a bound (e.g., partial recursion unrolling for tail-recursive or bounded-depth cases); however, unbounded recursion prevents full inlining.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: bounded inlining of recursion is possible; unbounded is not.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: indirect calls need devirtualization first.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard benefit.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: canonical costs; heuristics balance them.

assumptions: Standard compiler with an inlining heuristic (size/benefit model).
nonImplications: Does not imply -O3 always inlines aggressively; heuristics may limit inlining based on caller/callee size.
Does not imply all indirect calls are irrecoverable; profiling and type-based devirtualization can convert many into direct calls.

questions.learningObjective: Explain instruction selection as pattern-tiling of an IR tree against target-instruction templates.

requiredFeatures: target ISA with multi-operation instructions (e.g., LEA, FMA)

questions.stem: Which statement most precisely describes instruction selection via tree/DAG pattern matching?

options.text: Instruction selection assigns virtual registers to physical registers using a greedy algorithm; it precedes register allocation.

The IR (or its expression trees) is tiled with patterns matching target instructions; each tile carries a cost, and the selector finds a minimum-cost covering. Multi-operation instructions (e.g., LEA, FMA) match larger tiles and typically win over sequences of simpler tiles.
Instruction selection is the process of choosing which functions to inline; it operates at the call graph level.
Instruction selection linearizes basic blocks into a schedule that minimizes pipeline stalls.

questions.explanation: Instruction selection matches IR patterns against target-instruction templates (tiles), each with a cost. Dynamic programming (Aho-Ganapathi-Tjiang, BURS, LLVM SelectionDAG) finds a minimum-cost cover of the IR. Multi-op instructions like x86 LEA (base + index*scale + disp) or FMA can cover multiple IR ops in one machine instruction, typically with lower total cost. Options B, C, D confuse instruction selection with register allocation, inlining, and scheduling respectively.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: describes register allocation.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: tree/DAG pattern tiling with cost model.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: describes inlining.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: describes instruction scheduling.

assumptions: Target ISA is expressible via a set of instruction patterns with costs.
IR is in a form amenable to tiling (typically DAG or tree).
nonImplications: Does not imply DP-based selectors always find globally optimal code; local optimality is common but interacts with scheduling.
Does not imply pattern selectors are the only technique; LLVM also has GlobalISel and TableGen-driven approaches.

questions.learningObjective: Compare JIT and AOT compilation on optimization opportunities, deployment characteristics, and cold-start behavior.
questions.stem: Which statements correctly compare Just-in-Time (JIT) and Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compilation? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: JIT and AOT are mutually exclusive: a compilation pipeline can be either JIT or AOT but not combine both.

JIT compilation can exploit runtime information (observed types, hot call sites, actual input shapes) to specialize code adaptively; AOT lacks this dynamic profile unless PGO or similar techniques feed profiles back before deployment.
AOT produces deployable artifacts with no compilation cost at runtime, avoiding warm-up latency; JIT amortizes compile time across program execution and thus has a warm-up phase.
JIT is inherently less optimized than AOT because it must be fast to compile; AOT compilers can spend arbitrary time on optimization.

questions.explanation: A: JIT sees runtime information (observed types, hot paths); AOT lacks this unless profile-guided. B: AOT avoids runtime compilation and its warm-up latency; JIT has a warm-up phase. C is wrong: JITs (V8, HotSpot) can spend significant compile budget on hot code, and can specialize adaptively; JITs are not inherently less optimized. D is wrong: modern systems mix both — HotSpot has AOT tiers (AppCDS, native-image), PyTorch has torch.compile (JIT) alongside torch.export (AOT), and V8's Sparkplug/TurboFan use tiered JIT with AOT-ish caches.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: modern systems mix JIT and AOT tiers.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: JIT's key advantage is runtime information; AOT lacks it without PGO.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: AOT has no runtime compile cost; JIT has warm-up.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: JITs can and do apply expensive optimizations to hot code; they are not inherently less optimized.

assumptions: Standard definitions of JIT and AOT in modern language runtimes and ML frameworks.
nonImplications: Does not imply JIT is always slower for cold-start; simple JITs can outperform AOT with poor profile.
Does not imply AOT always produces the same code as JIT; AOT lacks runtime specialization opportunities.

distractorRationales.A: Falsely treats JIT and AOT as mutually exclusive.

questions.subtopic: Loop Invariant Code Motion safety conditions
questions.learningObjective: State the safety conditions under which a loop-invariant computation can be hoisted out of a loop.
questions.irSnippet:
; Original loop (SSA CFG)
; Loop header: bb_header
; Loop body: bb_body containing:
;   %inv = sdiv i32 %a, %b     ; loop-invariant in %a, %b
;   %use = add i32 %inv, %i
; Loop preheader: bb_preheader (dominates the loop; single predecessor of header)
; Loop backedge closes bb_body -> bb_header.
questions.stem: The expression `%inv = sdiv i32 %a, %b` is loop-invariant. Under LICM, which conditions must hold for it to be safe to hoist `%inv` to the loop preheader?

options.text: Hoisting requires unrolling the loop first to prove the operation executes at least once.
The instruction just needs to be loop-invariant; hoisting is always safe because the value would have been computed inside the loop anyway.
Only pure instructions with side-effect-free operations (add, sub, mul) can be hoisted; divisions must remain in the loop regardless of invariance.

(1) The instruction is loop-invariant (operands defined outside the loop or themselves loop-invariant). (2) It dominates every use inside the loop, or has no side effects when speculated. (3) Its execution is safe in the preheader (no fault, no observable side effect) — for `sdiv`, this typically means %b is provably non-zero, otherwise hoisting can introduce a divide-by-zero that never occurred in the original loop body.

questions.explanation: Option D is correct; options A, B, C are incorrect. A (Wrong): unrolling is a separate transformation; LICM does not require it. B (Wrong): overlooks that the loop might not execute; hoisting introduces new side effects if the loop body was never entered. C (Wrong): divisions can be hoisted when non-zero divisor is proven; not category-blocked. D (Correct): all three conditions (invariance, dominance, speculative-safety) apply. General context: LICM safety requires: (1) loop-invariance; (2) dominance of exits so the hoisted value is used correctly; (3) speculative-safety — hoisting must not introduce faults or side effects that would not have occurred originally. For sdiv, the divisor must be provably non-zero (otherwise the original loop might never execute the body, e.g., a zero-trip loop, and hoisting would introduce a spurious trap).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: unrolling is a separate transformation; LICM does not require it.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: overlooks that the loop might not execute; hoisting introduces new side effects if the loop body was never entered.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: divisions can be hoisted when non-zero divisor is proven; not category-blocked.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: all three conditions (invariance, dominance, speculative-safety) apply.

assumptions: Standard LICM as described in EAC3 and LLVM's implementation.
SSA-based analysis of loop structure with a well-defined preheader.
nonImplications: Does not imply LICM always helps performance; hoisting can increase register pressure and force spills.
Does not imply LICM only applies to arithmetic; loads with proven no-alias to intervening stores can also be hoisted.

distractorRationales.B: Ignores the speculative-safety condition (loop may not execute).

questions.learningObjective: Compute liveness at a program point given standard live-in / live-out equations.
questions.irSnippet:
; Consider block B with the following instructions in order:
B:
  I1:  a := x + y      ; def a; use x, y
  I2:  b := a * 2      ; def b; use a
  I3:  c := b + z      ; def c; use b, z
  I4:  return c        ; use c
; Live-out at end of B: {} (this is a function's return block, no successor).
questions.stem: Using standard liveness data-flow equations (live_in[I] = (live_out[I] − def[I]) ∪ use[I]), which variables are live immediately BEFORE instruction I1?

options.text: {x, y, z, a, b, c}
{a, b, c}
{x, y}
{x, y, z}

questions.explanation: Backward liveness. Live-out of I4 = {}. live_in[I4] = ({} − {}) ∪ {c} = {c}. live_out[I3] = {c}; live_in[I3] = ({c} − {c}) ∪ {b, z} = {b, z}. live_out[I2] = {b, z}; live_in[I2] = ({b, z} − {b}) ∪ {a} = {a, z}. live_out[I1] = {a, z}; live_in[I1] = ({a, z} − {a}) ∪ {x, y} = {x, y, z}. So live-in of I1 = {x, y, z}.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: it includes definitions (a, b, c) that are killed before I1 (they don't exist yet at that program point).
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: {a, b, c} are defined values, not live-in variables before I1.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: this omits z, which is used by I3 and must be live before I1 since it is not defined between I1 and I3.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: applying backward equations yields {x, y, z}.

assumptions: Standard live variables analysis with use/def sets per instruction.
No aliasing complications (each variable is a distinct SSA-like name).
nonImplications: Does not imply liveness alone drives register allocation; interference graph construction combines liveness with allocation heuristics.
Does not imply liveness is unique across analyses; may-live vs must-live variants differ in precision.

distractorRationales.C: Fails to propagate liveness of z back through blocks.

questions.subtopic: Loop invariance under redefinition / edge cases
questions.learningObjective: Determine loop-invariance of an expression when its operands are themselves defined inside the loop via phi.
questions.irSnippet:
; Loop in SSA
bb_preheader:
  br label %bb_header
bb_header:
  %i    = phi i32 [0, %bb_preheader], [%i_next, %bb_body]
  %s    = phi i32 [1, %bb_preheader], [%s_next, %bb_body]
  %cond = icmp slt i32 %i, %N
  br i1 %cond, label %bb_body, label %bb_exit
bb_body:
  %e     = mul i32 %s, 2       ; candidate loop-invariant?
  %s_next = add i32 %s, %e     ; s_next uses e
  %i_next = add i32 %i, 1
  br label %bb_header
bb_exit:
  ret i32 %s
questions.stem: Is `%e = mul i32 %s, 2` loop-invariant in the loop shown, and can it be hoisted to bb_preheader?

options.text: Yes — LICM can hoist any expression whose operator (mul) is pure, regardless of the operands' definitions.
Yes — since %e uses only %s and a constant, and constants are invariant, %e is trivially loop-invariant regardless of %s's definition.
No — `%e` depends on `%s`, which is defined by a loop-header phi with a different value each iteration (`%s_next` from bb_body). `%s` is not loop-invariant, so `%e` is not loop-invariant either.
No — LICM never applies inside a loop that uses phi nodes to carry loop-carried state.

questions.explanation: Loop-invariance requires that all operands of the expression be themselves loop-invariant (or constants). `%s` is defined by a loop-header phi with `[1, %bb_preheader]` and `[%s_next, %bb_body]` — it takes different values each iteration, so it is loop-variant. `%e = %s * 2` is therefore also loop-variant and cannot be hoisted. Options B, C, D contain reasoning errors: constants + loop-variant operand ≠ invariant; operator purity is necessary but not sufficient; LICM does apply in the presence of phi nodes but only to genuinely invariant computations.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: purity of the operator is a necessary but not sufficient condition for hoisting.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: an expression is invariant only if all operands are invariant; a constant operand does not save an invariant-defined operand.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: %s varies across iterations (via phi + %s_next), so %e = %s * 2 also varies.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: LICM operates on SSA IR with phi nodes; loop-carried state is normal, and the test for invariance considers operand-by-operand invariance.

assumptions: SSA-form IR with phi at loop header carrying loop-carried state.
Standard LICM analysis rules.
nonImplications: Does not imply nothing in this loop can be hoisted; for instance, the constant `2` is trivially in the preheader and needs no hoisting; other invariant expressions might exist if we added them.
Does not imply loop-carried recurrences can never be optimized; strength reduction and IV optimizations exist.

distractorRationales.D: Falsely claims LICM cannot see through phi.

questions.learningObjective: Precisely characterize partial evaluation and identify a canonical use case.
questions.stem: Which statement most precisely defines partial evaluation as a compilation technique?

options.text: Partial evaluation specializes a program with respect to some subset of its inputs known at specialization time (static inputs); the residual program takes only the remaining (dynamic) inputs and behaves equivalently to the original on any completion of the static inputs. Constant folding, template specialization, and shape specialization in ML compilers are instances.
Partial evaluation is a fault-tolerance mechanism that recovers from partial execution failures by re-running only the incomplete portion.
Partial evaluation is a name for lazy evaluation in functional programming; expressions are evaluated only when their values are needed.
Partial evaluation is a synonym for peephole optimization; both simplify local subexpressions.

questions.explanation: Partial evaluation, introduced by Yoshihiko Futamura and refined by Neil Jones et al., specializes a program with respect to static input values, producing a residual program that depends only on the dynamic (unknown) inputs. Constant folding is a limited instance; more powerful cases include compiler generation (Futamura projections), template specialization in C++, and shape specialization in ML compilers (recompiling for a fixed input shape). Options B, C, D confuse partial evaluation with unrelated concepts.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: standard definition with canonical instances.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: fault-tolerance is unrelated to partial evaluation.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: lazy evaluation is a runtime strategy, not a compilation-time specialization.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: peephole is a local optimization; partial evaluation is a program specialization technique.

assumptions: Standard definition per Jones, Gomard, Sestoft (Partial Evaluation and Automatic Program Generation).
nonImplications: Does not imply partial evaluation always produces faster code; specialization may increase code size and compile time.
Does not imply partial evaluation is only for constant inputs; more sophisticated variants (online, offline PE) handle richer static structure.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish rewrite-based (declarative) pattern matching from ad-hoc peephole optimization.
questions.stem: Which statements about pattern rewriting vs peephole optimization are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Peephole optimization is guaranteed to terminate; pattern rewriting is inherently divergent unless a cost model bounds it.

Rewrite frameworks and peephole optimizers are conceptually related — both match a pattern and replace with an equivalent alternative — but differ in scope, expressiveness, and typical position in the compilation pipeline.

Peephole optimization inspects a small local window of instructions (e.g., 2–3 adjacent instructions) and applies rewrites without global information; it operates late in the backend and is largely target-specific.

Pattern rewriting frameworks (e.g., LLVM InstCombine, MLIR PDL/Rewrite, TVM Relax rewrite) apply declarative rewrite rules to IR patterns; the framework handles matching, termination, and cost-driven ordering, and the rules can be target-independent or target-specific.

questions.explanation: A: peephole is local, low-level, target-specific. B: rewrite frameworks provide declarative rule descriptions with framework-managed matching (e.g., LLVM InstCombine, MLIR's rewriter). D: they are conceptually similar (pattern → replacement) but differ in expressiveness (peephole is limited to small windows) and pipeline position (peephole late, rewriting throughout). C is wrong: neither is guaranteed to terminate without care; peephole can loop if rules produce a cycle. Both require attention to termination (e.g., decreasing complexity metric).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: peephole is not guaranteed to terminate either; termination requires care in rule design.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: both share the pattern-replace model but differ in scope and pipeline position.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: canonical peephole characterization.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: rewrite frameworks provide declarative matching.

assumptions: Standard compiler pipeline with distinct optimization phases (front-end, mid-end, backend).
nonImplications: Does not imply rewriting subsumes peephole; targets may still benefit from ad-hoc peephole on machine instructions late in codegen.
Does not imply LLVM InstCombine is 'just' peephole; it operates on LLVM IR (mid-level) with cross-instruction knowledge.

questions.subtopic: Phi node placement at CFG merges
questions.learningObjective: Determine correct phi placement and semantics at a control-flow merge involving multiple predecessors.
questions.irSnippet:
; Non-SSA source (pseudo)
; if (cond) { x = a; } else { x = b; }
; return x;

; Candidate SSA lowerings:
bb_entry:
  br i1 %cond, label %bb_then, label %bb_else
bb_then:
  %x1 = ... %a
  br label %bb_merge
bb_else:
  %x2 = ... %b
  br label %bb_merge
bb_merge:
  ; ??? phi placement
  ret i32 %x_merged
questions.stem: In the CFG shown, block bb_merge has two predecessors bb_then and bb_else, each defining a version of x (%x1 in bb_then, %x2 in bb_else). Which is the correct SSA representation of the merged value used in bb_merge?

options.text: Insert `%x_merged = select i1 %cond, i32 %x1, i32 %x2` at the top of bb_merge; select instructions replace φ nodes and are the canonical SSA construct for merging values.

Emit both %x1 and %x2 in bb_merge and let the register allocator pick which physical register holds the merged value at runtime; no φ is needed because SSA is only about textual assignments in the source block.
Duplicate bb_merge into two copies (one for each predecessor) so no merge exists; SSA cannot represent a value that has different definitions along different paths without CFG duplication.
Insert `%x_merged = phi i32 [%x1, %bb_then], [%x2, %bb_else]` at the beginning of bb_merge; the φ selects %x1 when control flow arrives from bb_then and %x2 when it arrives from bb_else.

questions.explanation: SSA φ-functions at a merge point select the appropriate reaching definition based on the predecessor block from which control arrived. The correct LLVM syntax is `%x_merged = phi i32 [%x1, %bb_then], [%x2, %bb_else]` at the top of bb_merge. B is wrong (SSA requires the merge to be encoded in IR, not deferred to the register allocator). C is wrong (SSA does not require CFG duplication to represent joins). D is wrong at the SSA level: `select` requires both operands to be defined and both branches to have executed — it is a data-flow operation, not a control-flow merge; using select here would force evaluating both sides. E is wrong (OR is not a merge semantic).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: `select` evaluates both operands and is a pure-data operation, not a control-flow merge. It is only equivalent when both branches can be safely evaluated (no side effects, no exceptions).
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: SSA requires the merge to be textually represented via φ; deferring to register allocation defeats the point of SSA.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: SSA handles joins with φ; duplication is neither required nor idiomatic.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: canonical SSA φ-placement at the merge with predecessor annotations.

assumptions: Both bb_then and bb_else complete and reach bb_merge; no exceptions or aborts.
LLVM IR conventions (phi at block top, block-annotated incoming values).
nonImplications: Does not imply select can never replace a φ; it can when the merged expressions are pure and side-effect-free and both branches are always safe to evaluate.
Does not imply φ has runtime cost; it lowers to copies during out-of-SSA.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses select data-flow with control-flow merge.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the graph-coloring formulation of register allocation, including the meaning of interference and spilling.

hardwareContext.architecture: generic scalar target with K physical registers

questions.stem: In the classical graph-coloring formulation of register allocation, what do the nodes, edges, K colors, and 'spill' correspond to?

options.text: Nodes = instructions. Edges = data dependencies. K colors = pipeline stages. Spill = pipeline stall.
Nodes = basic blocks. Edges = CFG edges. K colors = number of basic blocks the register allocator can process in parallel. Spill = block-level rearrangement.
Nodes = phi nodes. Edges = phi operands. K colors = SSA versions of a variable. Spill = eliminate a phi.

Nodes = live ranges (virtual registers). Edges = interference (two live ranges are live simultaneously and therefore cannot share a physical register). K colors = number of physical registers. Spill = assign a live range to memory because coloring with K colors is impossible; spilled uses/defs become loads/stores.

questions.explanation: The standard graph-coloring formulation: build the interference graph where nodes are live ranges (virtual registers), edges connect live ranges that are simultaneously live (must not share a physical register). K colors correspond to physical registers. If the graph is not K-colorable, one or more live ranges are spilled to memory (their uses/defs replaced by loads/stores), then the process repeats until success. Options B, C, D describe unrelated formulations.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: describes instruction scheduling, not register allocation.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: describes CFG partitioning, not register allocation.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: SSA and phi nodes are input to the allocator, not the coloring model.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: canonical Chaitin/Briggs graph-coloring formulation.

assumptions: Non-SSA IR at register-allocation time (SSA is typically destructed first, though SSA-based allocation variants exist).
Fixed K physical registers on the target.
nonImplications: Does not imply graph coloring is always used; linear-scan and PBQP are alternative modern algorithms.
Does not imply spilling to memory means all uses require memory access; live-range splitting can localize spills.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses register allocation with CFG partitioning.
distractorRationales.C: Confuses SSA constructs with allocation model.

sourceRefs.locator: Register allocation via graph coloring chapter

questions.learningObjective: Identify what semantic preservation guarantees a compiler optimization must uphold and where common flags relax it.
questions.stem: Which statements about semantic preservation in compiler optimization are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: For undefined behavior (UB) in the source language (e.g., signed overflow in C, out-of-bounds access), the compiler is free to assume UB does not occur; optimizations may exploit this to eliminate branches or code paths, which can produce surprising behavior when UB does occur.
Semantic preservation is always trivially satisfied by any optimization that reduces the number of instructions; fewer instructions cannot possibly change behavior.

An optimization is semantics-preserving if the optimized program has an observable-behavior set that is a subset of the source program's observable-behavior set (under the source language's semantics), typically allowing implementation-defined behaviors and some nondeterminism.

Flags like `-ffast-math` explicitly relax IEEE-754 semantics (associativity, NaN/Inf handling), allowing reassociation and other transformations that are not strictly semantics-preserving; using them may change numerical results.

questions.explanation: A: standard framing of semantic preservation as behavior refinement. B: canonical example of an intentional soundness relaxation for FP arithmetic. C: UB-based optimization is a known pattern in C/C++ that can surprise users. D is wrong: reducing instructions does not guarantee behavior preservation (removing a store can change observed memory; removing a call can skip side effects).

optionExplanations.A: Correct: UB assumptions enable aggressive optimizations that can surprise developers.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: fewer instructions can absolutely change behavior (dropping stores, calls, exceptions).
optionExplanations.C: Correct: canonical definition of semantics-preserving optimization.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: -ffast-math and similar flags explicitly relax FP semantics.

assumptions: Standard C/C++ semantics with defined observable behavior; language variants with different semantic models may allow different optimizations.
nonImplications: Does not imply -ffast-math is unsafe in all contexts; deep-learning training routinely uses it or its GPU equivalents.
Does not imply the compiler always warns when UB is assumed; it typically does not.

distractorRationales.B: Falsely claims instruction reduction implies behavior preservation.

sourceRefs.locator: Fast-math flags, UB semantics, poison values

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish sound and precise analyses and identify the direction of over-/under-approximation.
questions.stem: Which statements about soundness and precision in static compiler analyses are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A sound analysis in a bug-finding context can be an under-approximation: it may miss some bugs (false negatives) but reports only true bugs (no false positives). The direction of soundness depends on the analysis's intent.
Precision measures how close the analysis result is to the ideal answer; a maximally precise analysis is not always tractable, so most analyses trade precision for scalability.
Soundness and precision are equivalent: a sound analysis is always precise, and vice versa.

A sound analysis over-approximates behavior for compiler optimizations: it never claims 'safe to transform' unless the transformation is truly safe. Its errors are conservative — foregoing legal optimizations, not enabling illegal ones.

questions.explanation: A: For compiler optimizations, sound = over-approximation of possible behaviors (may-analysis); this ensures no illegal optimizations. B: In bug-finding, soundness typically means no false positives (only true bugs reported); the direction depends on the intent. C: precision is orthogonal to soundness; scalability often forces trading precision. D is wrong: soundness and precision are distinct dimensions — a maximally conservative analysis (e.g., 'everything may alias') is sound but has zero precision.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: soundness direction depends on intent (optimization vs bug-finding).
optionExplanations.B: Correct: precision is a scalability-precision tradeoff.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: soundness and precision are orthogonal dimensions.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: sound = over-approximation for optimization contexts.

assumptions: Standard abstract-interpretation framing (Cousot & Cousot lattices).
nonImplications: Does not imply that unsound analyses are useless; unsound bug-finders (e.g., some heuristic linters) are common and valuable in practice.
Does not imply that soundness comes for free; proving soundness of complex analyses is nontrivial.

questions.learningObjective: Precisely characterize the defining property of SSA (Static Single Assignment) form and distinguish it from related notions.
questions.stem: Which statement correctly defines Static Single Assignment (SSA) form?

options.text: Each variable is stored in a distinct memory location; SSA is a memory-layout property enforced by the register allocator.
Every variable is written exactly once at runtime along every execution path; loops therefore cannot be represented in SSA without unrolling.

Every variable in the intermediate representation is textually assigned in exactly one program statement, and phi (φ) functions are inserted at control-flow join points to merge different reaching definitions from predecessor blocks.
SSA requires all variables to be constants, since 'single assignment' means a value is fixed at compile time.

questions.explanation: SSA is a syntactic property of the IR: each name has exactly one textual definition; φ-functions reconcile values that reach a join from different predecessors. Loops are representable in SSA — the loop-header uses a φ-function to merge the initial value with the value flowing back from the backedge. SSA is not about runtime write counts, storage locations, or compile-time constancy.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: SSA is an IR-level concept independent of memory allocation; register allocation happens later (often after out-of-SSA).
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: SSA is a syntactic (textual) property, not a runtime-execution constraint; loops are naturally expressed.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard SSA definition (textual single assignment + φ at joins).
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: SSA variables can take runtime values; single assignment means single textual definition, not compile-time constancy.

assumptions: Standard SSA as defined in Cytron et al. and canonical compiler textbooks.
nonImplications: Does not imply that φ-functions have a runtime cost; they are pseudo-instructions eliminated by out-of-SSA copy insertion.
Does not imply SSA is only useful for optimization; it also simplifies dataflow analysis reasoning.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses syntactic single-assignment with runtime execution behavior.
distractorRationales.D: Confuses single assignment with compile-time constant.

sourceRefs.locator: Ch. on SSA (§9 in EAC3): definition and construction

questions.learningObjective: Explain how out-of-SSA translation lowers phi functions into copies at predecessor blocks and identify the swap/lost-copy problem.
questions.irSnippet:
; SSA before out-of-SSA:
bb_merge:
  %a = phi i32 [%x, %P1], [%y, %P2]
  %b = phi i32 [%y, %P1], [%x, %P2]

; Naive lowering inserts at end of each predecessor:
; In %P1: a := x; b := y
; In %P2: a := y; b := x
; but if we later assign both phis to the same physical register class, sequential copies may lose values.
questions.stem: During out-of-SSA translation, a compiler lowers phi functions into copies at predecessor block ends. Which statement about this lowering is correct, particularly regarding the swap / lost-copy issue?

options.text: Modern optimizers avoid out-of-SSA lowering entirely by preserving phi nodes into machine code emission.
Out-of-SSA lowering trivially inserts one move per phi at the merge block; no predecessor-side changes are needed.
Out-of-SSA lowering requires all phi functions to be first converted to `select` instructions; only then can the code generator produce copies.

Naive sequential copy insertion at predecessor ends can be incorrect when multiple phis form a cycle (e.g., swap: %a and %b exchange values). Correct lowering must schedule copies to respect the parallel-copy semantics of phi (all phis fire simultaneously), typically using a temporary register or scheduling algorithms like Sreedhar's or Boissinot's.

questions.explanation: Phi functions have parallel-copy semantics — all phis at a block are conceptually assigned simultaneously. Naively serializing them into predecessor-block copies can miscompile swap-like patterns. Correct out-of-SSA algorithms (Sreedhar, Boissinot) either schedule copies with temporaries or use permutation-decomposition to preserve semantics. Options B, C, D contain factual errors: B ignores that phis fire from predecessor edges; C describes an unrelated substitution; D is wrong because machine code cannot express phi natively.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: machine code has no phi instruction; SSA must be lowered before or during instruction selection.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: phi lowering happens at predecessor edges, not at the merge block, because each incoming value corresponds to a specific predecessor.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: converting phi to select requires speculating both branches; not applicable to control-flow merges with side effects.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: parallel-copy semantics plus swap problem require careful scheduling.

assumptions: Standard SSA and out-of-SSA algorithms (Sreedhar, Boissinot).
Target machine code lacks a native phi instruction.
nonImplications: Does not imply out-of-SSA is the only way; SSA-based register allocation can operate directly on SSA form.
Does not imply the swap problem always occurs; simple non-cyclic phi patterns lower without temporaries.

distractorRationales.A: Falsely claims machine code supports phi.

questions.learningObjective: Contrast tensor-typed IR (value semantics) with buffer-/memref-typed IR (reference semantics) and explain what bufferization does.
questions.stem: The IR is transformed from a linalg-on-tensor form to a linalg-on-memref form by MLIR's bufferization. Which pair of properties best describes the tensor-form and memref-form semantics, respectively?
questions.irSnippet:
// BEFORE (linalg on tensor — value semantics)
%y0 = linalg.generic { ... } ins(%x : tensor<Nxf32>)
                            outs(%init : tensor<Nxf32>) -> tensor<Nxf32>
%y1 = linalg.generic { ... } ins(%y0 : tensor<Nxf32>)
                            outs(%init : tensor<Nxf32>) -> tensor<Nxf32>

// AFTER (linalg on memref — reference semantics, after bufferization)
linalg.generic { ... } ins(%X : memref<Nxf32>)
                       outs(%Y0 : memref<Nxf32>)
linalg.generic { ... } ins(%Y0 : memref<Nxf32>)
                       outs(%Y1 : memref<Nxf32>)

options.text: Tensor and memref forms are semantically identical; the only difference is textual. Bufferization is a printing pass that renames tensors to memrefs without altering the IR's data model. Under this interpretation, the pass could be safely dropped from any production pipeline without affecting correctness or code quality of the emitted kernels, since both forms would be equivalent to the codegen backend.
Tensor form has reference semantics (ops mutate a shared buffer); memref form has value semantics (each op returns a new immutable buffer). Bufferization enforces immutability at the memref level.

Tensor form has value semantics (immutable SSA values; each op produces a fresh tensor); memref form has reference semantics (ops write into named buffers). Bufferization assigns buffers and inserts allocations/copies as needed to preserve semantics.

Tensor form is only used for GPU codegen; memref form is only used for CPU codegen. Bufferization is a device-selection pass that chooses which form to use based on the target. In this framing, tensor-form IR is exclusively a front-end concern that stops before device-specific lowering, while memref-form IR is an implementation detail of the GPU codegen path that CPU pipelines simply skip.

questions.explanation: In MLIR, `tensor<...>` is an SSA value with value semantics: each producing op yields a fresh, immutable tensor and no in-place update is expressible at that level. `memref<...>` has reference semantics: ops write into named memory locations. Bufferization is the pass that lowers tensor-form IR to memref-form IR, assigning buffers, inserting allocations, and inserting copies where required to preserve the tensor-level dataflow (e.g., when two consumers observe different versions of a value).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: the difference is semantic (value vs. reference), not textual.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: swaps the two semantics.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard MLIR terminology.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: both forms exist for all targets; the choice is about optimization stage.

assumptions: The MLIR pipeline uses the standard tensor + memref + bufferization dialects.
nonImplications: Does not imply bufferization removes all copies; when tensor-level SSA implies aliasing that cannot be proven safe, copies are inserted.
Does not imply memref form is always closer to codegen; some pipelines lower tensor-form IR directly to Triton or LLVM.

sourceRefs.locator: Tensor and MemRef types; bufferization semantics
Type system: value vs. reference semantics

questions.learningObjective: Explain what canonicalization does in an IR framework such as MLIR and distinguish it from lowering and legalization.
questions.stem: The MLIR canonicalization pass rewrites the fragment BEFORE into the fragment AFTER. Which statement best characterizes what canonicalization is doing here?
questions.irSnippet:
// BEFORE
%c0 = arith.constant 0 : i32
%c1 = arith.constant 1 : i32
%a  = arith.addi %x, %c0 : i32   // x + 0
%b  = arith.muli %a, %c1 : i32   // (x+0) * 1
%c  = arith.addi %b, %b : i32    // 2*b
return %c : i32

// AFTER (canonicalized)
%two = arith.constant 2 : i32
%c   = arith.muli %x, %two : i32  // 2*x
return %c : i32

options.text: Canonicalization is MLIR's dialect-conversion mechanism; it uses a Conversion Target and Type Converter to legalize illegal operations by replacing them with legal ones from a different dialect. Under this description, canonicalization essentially reuses the same machinery as `applyPartialConversion`: it walks the IR, applies the target's legality rules, and calls the type converter's materialization hooks to resolve any inserted casts.

Canonicalization is a synonym for lowering; the transformation shown is a lowering step from arith to a lower-level dialect such as LLVM, motivated by making the IR closer to backend instructions. In this reading, the pass renames operations from `arith` to a lower-level LLVM dialect at the boundary and is invoked as part of the standard lowering pipeline after all optimization passes have converged.

Canonicalization performs algebraic simplifications and constant folding within a dialect to bring semantically equivalent IR into a preferred normal form; it operates within a dialect and does not change the operations' dialects.

Canonicalization performs alias analysis and functionalization of in-place operations; the transformation shown is the SSA rename pass invoked as part of canonicalization. In this account, canonicalization runs SROA / mem2reg-style promotions on the IR by first performing alias analysis over memref reads and writes, then rewriting the affected sequences into single-assignment temporaries.

questions.explanation: Canonicalization in MLIR (driven by op-local `getCanonicalizationPatterns` / fold hooks) simplifies IR into a preferred normal form: constant folding, identity elimination (`x+0`, `x*1`), and small algebraic rewrites, all within the same dialect. It is distinct from Lowering (moving to a lower-level dialect) and from Dialect Conversion / Legalization (which uses a ConversionTarget and TypeConverter to move between dialects). Functionalization is a separate concern.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: describes dialect conversion / legalization, which is a separate mechanism.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: lowering moves to a lower-level dialect. Canonicalization stays in-dialect.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: describes canonicalization's role (fold + identity + normal form) and its scope (within-dialect).
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: functionalization is unrelated to arith canonicalization.

assumptions: MLIR uses op-registered canonicalization patterns and folders.
nonImplications: Does not imply canonicalization always improves runtime; it targets IR quality, not necessarily peak performance.
Does not imply canonicalization removes all redundancy; CSE and DCE are separate passes.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses in-dialect canonicalization with cross-dialect lowering.

sourceRefs.locator: MLIR CGO paper: canonicalization vs. lowering vs. dialect conversion

questions.subtopic: Dead code elimination on ops with side effects
questions.learningObjective: Explain why dead code elimination (DCE) in a tensor IR must respect ops that have side effects, and how the IR encodes this.
questions.stem: A tensor-IR pass tries to run DCE and removes both `linalg.copy` (writes to %B) and `linalg.matmul` (returns a used %C) below. Which statement most accurately describes what DCE is allowed to remove in this snippet?

options.text: DCE may remove `linalg.copy` (its result appears unused inside the function) and the pure `arith.addf` (unused); `linalg.matmul` must stay because its result escapes.

DCE may remove only the pure `arith.addf` because it has no observable side effects and its result is dead. Neither `linalg.copy` nor `linalg.matmul` can be removed: both have write side effects, and the copy's write to %B is externally observable through the function's memref argument.

DCE may remove all three operations because pass-by-memref semantics let the caller re-execute the code path; the callee is free to elide any write it does not itself observe internally. In this reading, pass-by-memref is equivalent to pure-value semantics because the compiler owns the buffer and only surfaces the writes through an explicit return value; thus stores to it are private to the callee.

DCE may remove `linalg.copy` and `linalg.matmul` but must keep `arith.addf` because SSA values are always considered live regardless of use, whereas memref stores are always dead absent an explicit `sync` op. Under this framing, MLIR's default DCE ignores memory-effect annotations entirely and treats any op whose SSA result is unused as removable, on the assumption that side effects are already tracked by a separate `sync` pass.

questions.explanation: DCE removes computations whose results are dead and that have no side effects. In an IR with memref writes, a store to a memref is a side effect: if the memref is a function argument or otherwise reachable outside the pass's SSA horizon, removing the store is unsound. `linalg.copy` writes to %B (a caller-owned memref) — externally observable — so it must stay. `linalg.matmul` writes to %C and %C is returned — clearly live. Only the pure `arith.addf` with a dead SSA result can be safely removed.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: it treats `linalg.copy` as dead. But the copy writes to a function-argument memref, which is externally observable.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: DCE respects memory side effects and only removes the pure, dead SSA op.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: elides observable writes; violates program semantics.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: reverses the rule about SSA-value liveness and memory-store elimination.

assumptions: The IR distinguishes ops with memory side effects from pure ops (as MLIR's MemoryEffects interface does).
The caller retains a reference to the memrefs `%A`, `%B`, `%C` after the call.
nonImplications: Does not imply DCE cannot remove any memref write; if analysis proves the write is unobservable (fully-local buffer, no escape), the write can be removed.
Does not imply DCE and CSE are the same; CSE deduplicates equivalent computations.

distractorRationales.A: Ignores that the copy's write is observable.

sourceRefs.locator: Dead code elimination; observable side effects

questions.subtopic: MLIR: Operation / Region / Block / Value / Type
questions.learningObjective: Recall the core structural concepts of MLIR (Operation, Region, Block, Value, Type, Attribute) and how they relate.
questions.stem: Consider MLIR's core structural vocabulary. Which statement most accurately describes the relationship among Operation, Region, Block, and Value?

options.text: An Operation may contain zero or more Regions; each Region contains a list of Blocks; each Block contains a list of Operations and defines Values (its arguments and results produced by operations within it).

Operations exist only at the top level of an MLIR module; nesting is achieved via a separate side-table mapping op ids to child operations rather than via Region containment. Under this account, ops carry Values as internal fields serialized into their attribute dictionary, and any cross-op edge is emulated by copying the value into a downstream op's operand slot rather than sharing an SSA reference.
Regions and Blocks are the same concept under different names; each Value is stored as an Operation's private state and cannot be referenced across operations.

Values in MLIR are Python objects owned by the parser; they are not modeled in the C++ IR and are attached to operations only for pretty-printing. Under this framing, Values are opaque handles injected by the parser to carry file and line info for diagnostics; the C++ IR routes them purely through the printer and does not consult them during pass execution.
