    y = e / s
    tl.store(y_ptr + row * stride_m + cols * stride_n, y, mask=mask)

# Launch: grid=(M,), BLOCK >= N (single-block-per-row)
# x, y: FP32 row-major [M, N]

options.text: Using `other=-float('inf')` for masked lanes causes the max computation to include -inf and biases `x_max` downward, so real softmax kernels must use `other=0.0` and add a separate `_valid_count` normalization step.
Subtracting `x_max` speeds up the kernel by ~2x on Ampere because Triton uses a fast-path `exp` that only runs on inputs in [-1, 0]; without the subtraction, the slow-path is invoked.

Subtracting `x_max` from every element is a mathematical identity for softmax (numerator and denominator both scale by e^{-x_max}); the transform prevents `tl.exp(x)` from overflowing when `x` contains large values (FP32 `exp` overflows around x ≈ 88.7).
The subtraction is required for correctness because `tl.exp` returns undefined values for any input greater than 0; softmax's mathematical definition assumes all inputs are non-positive.

questions.explanation: Option C is correct; options A, B, D are incorrect. A (Wrong): -inf is the correct identity for the max reduction. B (Wrong): no such fast-path/slow-path split in Triton exp. C (Correct): standard numerically stable softmax formulation. D (Wrong): exp accepts any float; overflow is the concern. General context: The numerically stable softmax uses the identity `softmax(x)_i = exp(x_i - c) / sum_j exp(x_j - c)` for any constant `c`; taking `c = max(x)` guarantees the largest exponent is 0 and all others are ≤ 0, so `exp` cannot overflow (FP32 `exp` overflows near x ≈ 88.7 → ~1e38). Choice B fabricates a fast-path story.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: -inf is the correct identity for the max reduction.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no such fast-path/slow-path split in Triton exp.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard numerically stable softmax formulation.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: exp accepts any float; overflow is the concern.

assumptions: FP32 arithmetic on IEEE-754 hardware.
`tl.exp` is the standard IEEE-consistent expf approximation.
nonImplications: Does not imply subtracting max is the only stabilization technique; log-sum-exp and online softmax are alternatives.
Does not imply BLOCK ≥ N is required in production; large-N kernels use online (two-pass or tree) softmax.

distractorRationales.A: Wrong claim about -inf's effect on max.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Stream, Event, and asynchronous ordering
questions.learningObjective: Understand CUDA stream ordering semantics and how events synchronize across streams.
questions.stem: Which statements about CUDA streams and events are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: All non-default streams block each other by default; concurrent execution across streams requires an explicit `cudaSetStreamPriority(concurrent=true)` call before use.
`cudaEventRecord` is a synchronous host operation that returns only after the event has been observed by the device; it blocks the calling CPU thread.
Kernels launched on the same non-default stream execute in program order; kernels on different streams may execute concurrently subject to resource availability.

`cudaEventRecord(e, s1)` followed by `cudaStreamWaitEvent(s2, e, 0)` makes any subsequent work on `s2` wait until the event fires (i.e., until all work enqueued on `s1` before the record has completed), enabling cross-stream dependencies without blocking the host thread.

questions.explanation: Options C, D are correct; options A, B are incorrect. A (Wrong): streams are concurrent by default. B (Wrong): `cudaEventRecord` is asynchronous. C (Correct): intra-stream ordered, inter-stream may overlap. D (Correct): canonical event-based cross-stream sync. General context: Neither operation blocks the host.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: streams are concurrent by default.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: `cudaEventRecord` is asynchronous.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: intra-stream ordered, inter-stream may overlap.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: canonical event-based cross-stream sync.

assumptions: Standard CUDA runtime semantics as documented.
Default stream = 0 behavior is per-thread or legacy depending on compile flag; question focuses on non-default streams.
nonImplications: Does not imply that any two streams always overlap; hardware resources (copy engines, SM count) still constrain concurrency.
Does not imply `cudaStreamWaitEvent` blocks the host.

distractorRationales.A: Wrong claim about default stream blocking.

questions.subtopic: Tensor Core / dtypes and per-architecture support
questions.learningObjective: Understand which Tensor Core dtypes are supported on which NVIDIA architectures and how throughput scales.
questions.stem: Which statement about Tensor Core dtype support across NVIDIA architectures is correct?

options.text: Tensor Cores support only FP16; other 'Tensor Core dtypes' (BF16, TF32, INT8, FP8) are software emulations built on the FP16 hardware path.
All Tensor Core dtypes (FP16, BF16, TF32, INT8, FP8) have been supported since Volta; the throughput is identical across all NVIDIA architectures for a given dtype.

Tensor Cores were introduced with Volta (sm_70) supporting FP16 with FP16/FP32 accumulate; Turing (sm_75) added INT8/INT4; Ampere (sm_80) added TF32, BF16, and FP64 Tensor Cores; Hopper (sm_90) added FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) and improved throughput. Not every dtype is on every architecture; kernels must be conditionalized on `__CUDA_ARCH__`.
FP8 Tensor Cores exist on every Ampere GPU; Hopper only added higher clock speeds without introducing new numeric formats to the Tensor Core.

questions.explanation: Tensor Core dtype support has expanded generation-by-generation: Volta (sm_70) — FP16; Turing (sm_75) added INT8 (also INT4/INT1 for research); Ampere (sm_80) added TF32, BF16, and FP64 Tensor Cores; Ada (sm_89) added FP8 for inference; Hopper (sm_90) formalized FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) with new throughput levels; Blackwell adds further dtypes. Because support is version-sensitive, portable kernels must dispatch on `__CUDA_ARCH__` or use CUTLASS-style dispatch. There is no software emulation of BF16/TF32/FP8 on the FP16 path — these are distinct hardware datapaths.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: BF16/TF32/FP8 have their own hardware paths.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: BF16/TF32 arrived with Ampere; FP8 with Ada/Hopper.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: generation-by-generation expansion of TC dtypes.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: FP8 is not on Ampere; Hopper added new formats.

assumptions: NVIDIA architecture history through 2025 as documented in whitepapers.
nonImplications: Does not imply FP4 or other exotic formats are absent; new formats continue to be added.
Does not imply throughput ratios are stable across generations.

distractorRationales.A: Wrong claim about emulation on FP16.
distractorRationales.B: Fabricates uniform dtype support across generations.
distractorRationales.D: Wrong claim about FP8 on Ampere.

sourceRefs.locator: Compute capability tables; Tensor Core dtype support per architecture

questions.learningObjective: Understand what the texture / read-only cache path provides and when it is beneficial.

hardwareContext.architecture: Kepler and newer (Kepler introduced read-only path; texture cache older)
requiredFeatures: read-only cache / __ldg intrinsic; texture object API

questions.stem: Which statement about the CUDA texture / read-only cache path (accessed via `__ldg`, texture objects, or `__restrict__` const pointers) is correct?

options.text: The texture cache is faster than shared memory for all access patterns; users should therefore always convert `__shared__` allocations to texture-bound arrays for peak performance.

The read-only path routes global-memory loads through a separate cache (historically the texture cache) that is optimized for read-only, spatially-local data; it can improve L1 pressure and bandwidth for read-only inputs (e.g., weight matrices), and is triggered by `__ldg` or by loading through `const T* __restrict__` pointers on Kepler and later.
`__ldg` is a synchronous host-side intrinsic that pre-copies data from device global memory to host DRAM; using it inside a kernel produces undefined behavior.
The read-only path bypasses coherence; using it on data that another kernel wrote in the same stream will always return stale values, so it should only be used for compile-time-constant arrays.

questions.explanation: The read-only data path routes loads through a cache designed for read-only access (historically shared with the texture unit; on modern GPUs unified with L1 to varying degrees). It reduces pressure on the main L1 for read-only inputs and is triggered explicitly by `__ldg(ptr)` or implicitly when the compiler proves a pointer is read-only (e.g., `const T* __restrict__`). It is beneficial for weights and other broadcast/spatially-local reads. Choice B overstates: the texture cache is not universally faster than SMEM. Choice C confuses `__ldg` with a host API. Choice D wrongly claims coherence problems within the standard CUDA memory model.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: SMEM is a distinct, generally faster on-chip memory.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: read-only path via `__ldg` / `const __restrict__` on Kepler+.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: `__ldg` is a device intrinsic.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: no stale-value coherence issue within a stream.

assumptions: Kepler+ architectures where `__ldg` is available.
nonImplications: Does not imply the read-only path is always faster; for write-heavy or streaming data, L1/L2 paths are appropriate.
Does not imply texture objects and __ldg are equivalent; texture objects also offer addressing modes and normalization.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses device intrinsic with host API.

sourceRefs.locator: Read-Only Data Cache; __ldg; texture object API

questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a 2D Triton launch grid maps to `tl.program_id(axis=0)` and `axis=1` and how to compute per-program tile bases.
questions.stem: The 2D Triton kernel below copies a row-major FP32 tensor of shape [M, N] with M=2048, N=1024. Launch: `grid = (triton.cdiv(M, BM), triton.cdiv(N, BN))`, `BM=32`, `BN=128`. Which statement about program (pid_m=17, pid_n=3) is correct?
questions.codeSnippet:
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def copy2d(in_ptr, out_ptr, M, N,
           stride_m, stride_n,
           BM: tl.constexpr, BN: tl.constexpr):
    pid_m = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    pid_n = tl.program_id(axis=1)
    offs_m = pid_m * BM + tl.arange(0, BM)
    offs_n = pid_n * BN + tl.arange(0, BN)
    mask_m = offs_m < M
    mask_n = offs_n < N
    # Row-major addressing: element (i,j) at stride_m*i + stride_n*j
    ptrs_in  = in_ptr  + offs_m[:, None] * stride_m + offs_n[None, :] * stride_n
    ptrs_out = out_ptr + offs_m[:, None] * stride_m + offs_n[None, :] * stride_n
    mask = mask_m[:, None] & mask_n[None, :]
    x = tl.load(ptrs_in, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    tl.store(ptrs_out, x, mask=mask)

# Launch: grid = (cdiv(M, BM), cdiv(N, BN)), BM=32, BN=128
# M=2048, N=1024, row-major FP32, stride_m=N=1024, stride_n=1

options.text: Program (17, 3) copies the tile rows `[17*32 .. 17*32+31]` and columns `[3*128 .. 3*128+127]`, i.e., rows 544..575 and columns 384..511; all lanes are in-bounds (since M=2048>575 and N=1024>511), so the mask is uniformly True and no lanes are skipped.
Program (17, 3) copies rows 17..48 and columns 3..130 because `pid_m * BM + arange(0, BM)` is interpreted as `(pid_m + arange)` due to Python operator precedence in the Triton JIT frontend.
Because `stride_n=1`, the pointer expression `offs_n[None, :] * stride_n` degenerates to a scalar; only column 0 is copied for each row in program (17, 3).
The `mask_m[:, None] & mask_n[None, :]` combination produces a 1D mask of length `BM+BN`; Triton then broadcasts it back to 2D during `tl.load`, which is why passing a 2D mask is redundant.

questions.explanation: Standard 2D tiling in Triton: `pid_m = program_id(0)` and `pid_n = program_id(1)` return the coordinates of the program in the 2D launch grid. Per-program offsets are `pid * BLOCK + arange(0, BLOCK)`. For (17, 3) with BM=32, BN=128: row offsets are 544..575, column offsets are 384..511. With M=2048, N=1024 the tile is fully in-bounds. Row-major stride: `stride_m = N = 1024`, `stride_n = 1`; the pointer expression uses broadcasting on `[:, None]` / `[None, :]` to form a 2D `[BM, BN]` address grid. Options B/C/D fabricate incorrect behaviors.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: standard 2D tile addressing with correct in-bounds computation.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: `pid_m * BM + tl.arange(0, BM)` is standard elementwise arithmetic; there is no Python precedence issue.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: `stride_n=1` does not collapse the column dimension; the arange still spans BN.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: `mask_m[:, None] & mask_n[None, :]` produces a 2D `[BM, BN]` mask via broadcasting.

assumptions: Row-major FP32 layout with `stride_m = N`, `stride_n = 1`.
Triton indexing broadcast semantics as documented in the language reference.
nonImplications: Does not imply BM=32, BN=128 is optimal for A100; it is chosen for clarity.
Does not imply that a 2D grid is required for copy kernels; a 1D flattened variant would also work.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses stride value with dimension collapse.

sourceRefs.locator: Triton language: program_id, tl.arange, broadcasting semantics

questions.learningObjective: Reason about how Triton's tl.load/tl.store mask semantics handle out-of-bounds lanes at the tail of a block-tiled kernel.
questions.stem: Consider the Triton vector-add kernel below launched with grid = (triton.cdiv(N, BLOCK),), BLOCK=1024, N=1_000_000, and 1-D contiguous FP32 CUDA inputs `x`, `y`, `out` of length N. Which statement about the last program (pid = 976) is correct?
questions.codeSnippet:
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, N, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < N
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=mask)

# Launch: grid = (triton.cdiv(N, BLOCK),), BLOCK = 1024, N = 1_000_000
# For pid = 976: base = 976 * 1024 = 999_424; offsets = 999_424 .. 1_000_447
# Valid lanes: offsets 999_424 .. 999_999 (576 lanes); OOB: 1_000_000 .. 1_000_447 (448 lanes)

options.text: Because `BLOCK` is a `tl.constexpr`, the mask is fully constant-folded at compile time and lanes with `offsets >= N` still incur memory traffic identical to the non-tail programs, so tail masking provides no bandwidth savings.

The last program reads 448 out-of-bounds addresses which produce undefined values, but even without a mask `tl.load` would remain safe because Triton performs implicit bounds checking on every load operation before dereferencing.

The `mask` argument affects only the store; the load always performs 1024 contiguous global-memory transactions and will read past the end of the tensor whenever `pid * BLOCK + BLOCK > N` on the last program.
Tail lanes with `offsets >= N` (448 lanes here) skip the load (using `other=0.0`) and skip the store thanks to `mask`; no OOB access occurs and those lanes are no-ops.

questions.explanation: In Triton, `tl.load(ptr, mask=..., other=...)` skips masked-off lanes and substitutes `other` (default 0). `tl.store(ptr, val, mask=...)` similarly suppresses masked-off writes. In the last program, 448 tail lanes fail the `offsets < N` predicate; they neither read nor write, and their contribution to `x + y` is defined by `other=0.0` (which is anyway not stored). No OOB access happens.

optionExplanations.D: Correct: matches Triton's documented `mask`/`other` semantics for both load and store.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: Triton has no implicit bounds checking; without a mask, `tl.load` on an OOB address is undefined behavior.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: `mask` applies to both loads and stores.
optionExplanations.A: Wrong: even if `BLOCK` is constexpr, `mask` is a runtime value dependent on `N` and `offsets`; masked lanes are suppressed at the hardware predication level.

assumptions: The pointers `x_ptr`, `y_ptr`, `out_ptr` correspond to tensors of length exactly N (no padding beyond).
Triton version implements `mask`/`other` as documented in the language reference.
nonImplications: Does not imply that masked lanes have zero cost; they still participate in warp execution but with predicated off memory ops.
Does not imply that masking eliminates all boundary logic; complex 2-D tiling still requires per-dim masks.

distractorRationales.A: Misunderstands the difference between compile-time BLOCK and runtime mask value.

sourceRefs.locator: tl.load / tl.store mask and other semantics

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Warp size, warp scheduling, and SIMT execution
questions.learningObjective: Reason about warp granularity: how threads are grouped into warps and how a warp is scheduled as a single instruction issue unit.
questions.stem: Which statement about NVIDIA warp execution is correct?

options.text: A warp is a group of 32 threads (`warpSize == 32`) that the SM schedules as a single instruction issue unit; all 32 lanes execute the same instruction on their respective data (SIMT), with per-lane predication used when a branch would otherwise diverge.

Warp size is architecture-dependent and has ranged from 16 to 128 across NVIDIA generations; portable kernels should query `blockDim.x % warpSize == 0` at runtime and adapt block dimensions accordingly.

Warps are software-only abstractions imposed by nvcc for readability; the underlying hardware schedules individual threads independently, and warp-level primitives (shuffles, votes) are software emulations.
Threads in a warp are scheduled in a round-robin order at instruction granularity; even for non-divergent code, each thread of the warp takes 32 cycles to complete one instruction.

questions.explanation: A warp is 32 threads on all current NVIDIA architectures; the SM's warp scheduler issues one instruction per warp per cycle (per scheduler; modern SMs have multiple schedulers). SIMT means every lane executes the same instruction; when a branch would diverge, lanes are predicated off, resulting in serialization of the divergent paths. The 32-thread size is a fixed hardware property (`warpSize == 32`). Warp-level primitives (`__shfl_*_sync`, `__any_sync`, etc.) map to actual hardware operations. Choice B is fabricated; warp size has been 32 for the entirety of NVIDIA's CUDA lineup.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: warp = 32 threads; SIMT + predication for divergence.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: warpSize has been 32 on all NVIDIA CUDA GPUs.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: warps are a hardware concept; primitives use real HW ops.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: SIMT executes 32 lanes in parallel; not round-robin.

assumptions: NVIDIA CUDA GPUs (as opposed to hypothetical wave-64 architectures like AMD).
nonImplications: Does not imply divergent code is always slow; divergence within a warp is where it hurts.
Does not imply lane scheduling is fully SIMT on Volta+; Independent Thread Scheduling allows lanes to make forward progress independently in specific cases.

distractorRationales.B: Fabricates variable warp size on NVIDIA.
distractorRationales.D: Confuses SIMT parallel issue with serial round-robin.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / WMMA C++ API vs mma.sync PTX
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the CUDA C++ WMMA API from raw mma.sync PTX and understand which layer each occupies.
questions.stem: Which statement about `nvcuda::wmma` (CUDA C++ API) vs raw `mma.sync` (PTX) is correct?

options.text: `wmma` is Volta-only; on Ampere+ users must switch to a completely different API called `cuda::mma`, which is unrelated to `nvcuda::wmma`.
`wmma` and `mma.sync` are mutually exclusive: a kernel using `wmma` cannot invoke `mma.sync`, and vice versa; the compiler will reject any mixture.

`nvcuda::wmma` is a higher-level C++ template API (fragment types, load/store/mma functions) that abstracts the fragment layout and typically compiles down to sequences of `mma.sync` and `ldmatrix` PTX; using raw `mma.sync` gives finer control over shape, layout, and fragment reuse, and is the path used by high-performance libraries like CUTLASS.
`mma.sync` PTX exists only for debugging; production kernels are required to use `wmma` because PTX is not guaranteed to be stable across CUDA versions.

questions.explanation: `nvcuda::wmma` (in `<mma.h>`) is a C++ template API providing `fragment<>` types, `load_matrix_sync`, `store_matrix_sync`, `mma_sync` free functions, and shape templates. It is a high-level abstraction that the compiler lowers to `mma.sync` + `ldmatrix` PTX. Raw `mma.sync` (via inline PTX or PTX intrinsics) gives more control — used by CUTLASS and other libraries for shape/layout combinations not directly exposed by wmma. Both are supported across Volta+; they can be mixed. PTX is a stable virtual ISA.

optionExplanations.C: Correct: two layers of the same abstraction; wmma → mma.sync at lowering.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: mixing is allowed.
optionExplanations.A: Wrong: wmma continues to work on Ampere and later; it lowers to newer mma shapes.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: PTX is a stable abstraction; production libraries use it heavily.

assumptions: CUDA 11+ toolchain.
nonImplications: Does not imply wmma exposes every mma shape; some shapes are only accessible via raw PTX.
Does not imply raw PTX is always faster; the compiler often generates equivalent code from wmma.

sourceRefs.locator: Warp Matrix Functions (wmma) and PTX mma.sync

questions.learningObjective: Explain Ansor's central design choice of subgraph-level schedule generation with a learned cost model, and what it replaces.
questions.stem: The Ansor paper (OSDI 2020) makes several design choices that distinguish it from prior work like AutoTVM and Halide autoscheduler. Which best describes Ansor's central design intent?

options.text: Ansor searches at the level of algorithmic sketches over multi-op subgraphs, uses a learned cost model to prune candidates, and prioritizes subgraphs by their contribution to end-to-end network runtime; this removes the need for per-operator manual templates while remaining tractable via the sketch abstraction.
Ansor is a compiler backend for CUDA that replaces cuBLAS and cuDNN with hand-written Tensor Core kernels; its main contribution is a superior tensor core code generator.
Ansor is a runtime autotuning framework that mutates kernel launch parameters between forward passes during model serving.
Ansor is a rewrite of AutoTVM's cost model in C++; the design intent is faster compile time at the cost of tuning quality.

questions.explanation: Ansor's contributions per the OSDI 2020 paper are (i) hierarchical sketch generation that composes algorithmic templates automatically, (ii) evolutionary search + learned cost model, and (iii) task scheduler that prioritizes subgraphs by their contribution to end-to-end network runtime. The result is a system that discovers schedules for new operators without per-op templates. Option B misrepresents Ansor as a Tensor Core code generator. Option C misrepresents it as a runtime autotuner. Option D is a straw-man reimplementation claim.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: matches the paper's abstract and design overview.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: Ansor is a scheduler generator, not a Tensor Core code generator.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: Ansor operates at compile time, not per-serving-request.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: Ansor is a new architecture, not a C++ port of AutoTVM.

assumptions: The reader has knowledge of the Ansor paper's abstract-level contributions.
nonImplications: Does not imply Ansor supplants library kernels — high-quality library GEMMs often remain preferable.
Does not imply the task scheduler solves all tuning-budget issues — resource allocation across many subgraphs is still an approximation.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses Ansor with a CUDA library.
distractorRationales.C: Confuses Ansor with a runtime autotuner.
distractorRationales.D: Reduces Ansor to an implementation port.

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose why an autotuner's best-config picks differ across runs and identify the primary contributor.

hardwareContext.architecture: generic sm_80 / sm_90 with default clock governor

questions.profileData:
Run A of autotuner (100 trials): best config = C1 at 0.42 ms; C2 comes second at 0.44 ms.
Run B (same code, same GPU, immediately after Run A): best config = C2 at 0.42 ms; C1 second at 0.45 ms.
Single-config replay: each of C1 and C2 individually measures at 0.42 ± 0.03 ms across 20 replays.
questions.stem: An autotuner picks different 'best' configs across two consecutive runs. Single-config replay shows both configs measure at 0.42 ± 0.03 ms. Which is the most likely root cause and appropriate fix?

options.text: The autotuner is using a broken random seed; setting the seed to a fixed value will make C1 and C2 report identical runtimes.
The GPU driver has a memory leak; upgrading the driver will fix the non-determinism.
The kernels have a genuine algorithmic difference that only manifests every other launch; C1 and C2 are actually different optima at odd- and even-numbered invocations.

Measurement noise is on the same order as the runtime gap between C1 and C2. Any winner-take-all comparison is dominated by variance; the fix is to increase repetitions per trial and use a robust statistic (e.g., median of medians) or an equivalence band.

questions.explanation: When measurement noise (±0.03 ms) is on the same order as the gap between candidates (0.02 ms), a winner-take-all comparison is essentially coin-flipping. This is the canonical problem for autotuners on real hardware: OS scheduling, GPU clock jitter, memory allocator state, and background processes contribute variance. Robust remedies include (a) increasing repetitions per trial, (b) using a statistical band and declaring a tie inside it, and (c) using median/geomean instead of mean. Options B (driver leak) and C (alternating optima) are unsupported. Option D confuses seed determinism with measurement noise — a seed affects the tuner's exploration path, not the underlying kernel runtime.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: seeds affect tuner exploration, not kernel runtime.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no evidence for a driver leak, and driver leaks would show as monotonic slowdown.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: physically implausible.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: standard measurement-noise vs. gap analysis; the fix aligns with Ansor / AutoTVM best practices.

assumptions: No background workload runs on the same GPU during measurement.
GPU clock governor is default (not locked).
nonImplications: Does not imply autotuning is unusable; robust methodology tames the problem.
Does not imply the gap will always be within noise; sometimes it exceeds noise and the winner is stable.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses seed determinism with kernel-runtime determinism.

performanceClaim.scope: Autotuner winner-take-all variance under real GPU noise

questions.learningObjective: Reason about the trade-off between compilation-time budget and end-to-end wall-clock savings across serving scenarios.
questions.stem: A compiler exposes a knob 'tuning budget' (compilation time spent tuning) that trades off against runtime speed. Which statements about the trade-off are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: For a one-off ad-hoc experiment (compile, run once, discard), tuning budget must be short; a slow compile that saves runtime only matters if runtime dominates.

Recompilation on shape changes (e.g., under `torch.compile` with recompiles enabled) can inflate the effective 'compile budget' well beyond the initial compile; the effective budget is per unique shape combination the runtime sees.
Tuning budget only affects the compiler and is orthogonal to serving latency; end-to-end latency is unaffected by tuning budget once the artifact is compiled.
For a model served millions of times per day, a longer tuning budget (hours) is easily amortized over serving lifetime; the wall-clock saving per request compounds.

questions.explanation: Options A, B, D are correct; option C is incorrect. A (Correct): short-lived usage inverts the trade-off. B (Correct): recompilation is a hidden compile-budget line item. C (Wrong): tuning budget determines the artifact's runtime performance. D (Correct): amortization over serving lifetime. General context: C captures an important practical concern: recompilation costs are hidden 'compile budget' spent per unique shape/config the runtime encounters.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: short-lived usage inverts the trade-off.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: recompilation is a hidden compile-budget line item.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: tuning budget determines the artifact's runtime performance.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: amortization over serving lifetime.

assumptions: The tuner and cost model behave as documented (convergent search).
nonImplications: Does not imply that longer budgets always improve runtime; measurement noise and cost-model plateaus can cap gains.
Does not imply short budgets are always sufficient — some workloads need substantial trials to leave a bad local optimum.

distractorRationales.C: Denies the causal path from tuning to runtime.

sourceRefs.locator: Section 6: tuning budget vs. speedup analysis

performanceClaim.scope: Tuning-budget-to-runtime-speedup relationship in autotuning

questions.subtopic: Constant folding / CSE / DCE / IR rewrite
questions.learningObjective: Given a small IR fragment, identify which classical optimization (constant folding, CSE, DCE) is applied and confirm semantic preservation.
questions.irSnippet:
// Before
%c1 = const 2
%c2 = const 3
%t1 = mul %c1, %c2       // = 6
%t2 = mul %c1, %c2       // = 6
%t3 = add %x, %t1
%t4 = add %x, %t2
%unused = mul %x, %x     // never used later
return %t3, %t4

// After
%c6  = const 6
%tsum = add %x, %c6
return %tsum, %tsum
questions.stem: Which sequence of classical optimizations transforms the 'Before' IR into the 'After' IR, and is the rewrite semantics-preserving?

options.text: Only constant folding is applied; the duplicate `add %x, %c6` values are not detected because CSE cannot fold across use points, and `%unused` is retained since DCE would violate side-effect ordering.

Constant folding fuses `%t1 = mul 2, 3` into `%c6 = const 6`; CSE identifies `%t3` and `%t4` as syntactically equivalent `add %x, %c6` and collapses them to one value; DCE removes `%unused`. All three preserve semantics.
The rewrite is illegal: returning `%tsum` twice from a function violates SSA form because a single value cannot flow to two return slots.
Loop-invariant code motion is applied to hoist `mul %c1, %c2` out of the loop; CSE and DCE are unrelated to this particular rewrite.

questions.explanation: Option B is correct; options A, C, D are incorrect. A (Wrong): mischaracterizes the reach of CSE and DCE. B (Correct): constant folding + CSE + DCE composition; all semantics-preserving. C (Wrong): SSA allows a value to have many uses. D (Wrong): no loop is present; LICM is irrelevant to this fragment. General context: The 'Before → After' rewrite is a canonical composition of three classical optimizations: constant folding (evaluate `mul 2, 3` at compile time), CSE (recognize `%t3` and `%t4` compute the same expression on the same operands, so they are one value), and DCE (remove `%unused` since it has no consumer and no side effect). All three are semantics-preserving on pure operations. Option D introduces an irrelevant loop context.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: mischaracterizes the reach of CSE and DCE.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: constant folding + CSE + DCE composition; all semantics-preserving.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: SSA allows a value to have many uses.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: no loop is present; LICM is irrelevant to this fragment.

assumptions: `mul` and `add` are pure operations without side effects.
The return signature is a tuple that can hold two references to the same SSA value.
nonImplications: Does not imply CSE can always eliminate `add %x, %c6` duplicates across function boundaries — it operates within a scope defined by the pass.
Does not imply DCE can always remove any unused op — ops with observable side effects are exempt.

distractorRationales.A: Underestimates CSE/DCE reach on pure ops.

sourceRefs.locator: Chapters on constant folding, CSE, DCE

questions.learningObjective: Enumerate factors that make a static analytical cost model differ from measured wall-clock runtime.
questions.stem: Modern autotuning frameworks (Ansor, MetaSchedule, AutoTVM) use cost models to prune the search space before actual measurement. Which of the following make a static analytical cost model DIVERGE from the measured wall-clock runtime? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The compiler's static model uses the same numerical precision as the target hardware; there is no divergence possible in principle.
Register spills that are hard to predict from source-level operation counts; the true register allocation is decided later by the backend (ptxas, LLVM).
Cache and TLB hit-rate variability caused by neighbour kernels, previous benchmark iterations, or OS scheduling that a purely analytical model cannot see.
Warmup effects such as JIT compilation, lazy kernel loading, and GPU clock ramp-up that dominate the first few measurements.

questions.explanation: Static analytical cost models operate on op counts, memory traffic estimates, and simple loop-bound arithmetic; they miss (B) register spill decisions made later by the backend (ptxas / LLVM), and (C) execution-context variability such as cache pollution and OS scheduling. Ansor's key contribution was to note that these gaps motivate learned or measurement-based rankings rather than pure analytical cost models. Option A asserts no divergence in principle, contradicting the entire motivation of learned cost models. Option D describes warmup effects, which are a *measurement-methodology* concern, not a source of divergence between the model and the true underlying runtime — one runs multiple warmed-up measurements to remove them.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: precision alone does not close the model-vs-measurement gap.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: register allocation and spill decisions are made post-source and affect real runtime.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: cache/TLB context effects are outside a static model.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong as a **cost-model vs runtime** discrepancy source: warmup, JIT compilation latency, lazy CUDA context initialization, and clock ramp-up are **measurement-methodology artifacts** eliminated by (i) a warmup phase, (ii) `torch.cuda.synchronize()`, and (iii) CUDA event timing. They inflate wall time on the *first* call but do not reflect a systematic under-estimate by the cost model of steady-state kernel behavior. The genuine cost-model gaps (options B and C) — undermodeled cache/coalescing effects and off-critical-path fixed costs (launch, alloc) — persist even after warmup and are the intended targets of this question.

assumptions: The analytical model is built on op counts, shape, and memory-traffic estimates only.
Measurements are taken after standard warmup and averaged/medianed.
nonImplications: Does not imply analytical cost models are useless — they are effective search-space filters.
Does not imply learned cost models close all gaps — they still approximate.

distractorRationales.A: Denies the well-documented gap that motivates learned cost models.
distractorRationales.D: Confuses measurement-hygiene concerns with model-vs-truth divergence.

performanceClaim.scope: Analytical vs. measured cost gap in tensor program autotuners

questions.subtopic: Operator fusion / Vertical vs. horizontal vs. epilogue
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish vertical (producer-consumer) fusion, horizontal fusion, and epilogue fusion by their data-flow patterns.
questions.stem: In deep-learning compilers, three commonly discussed fusion patterns are 'vertical', 'horizontal', and 'epilogue' fusion. Which description matches all three correctly?

options.text: All three refer to launching multiple CUDA kernels concurrently on separate streams; the names only differ by which kernel finishes first in the timeline.

Vertical fusion means merging operators executed on different devices; horizontal fusion means merging operators of the same type across the batch dimension; epilogue fusion means merging the backward pass into the forward pass.

Vertical fusion merges a producer with its consumer along the data-flow edge; horizontal fusion merges independent operators that share the same input or launch dimensions; epilogue fusion attaches a lightweight elementwise op onto the tail of a heavy compute op such as GEMM.
Vertical fusion is loop-level fusion of nested loops; horizontal fusion is basic-block CSE within a single operator; epilogue fusion is compile-time constant folding of the final output.

questions.explanation: Vertical (producer-consumer) fusion combines an op with its data-flow consumer so the intermediate tensor is kept in registers/shared memory instead of DRAM. Horizontal fusion combines independent ops sharing a launch dimension (e.g., three sibling elementwise ops on the same tensor) into one kernel to amortize launch overhead. Epilogue fusion fuses a small pointwise op (bias-add, activation, scaling) into the tail of a compute-heavy op like GEMM/Conv, reusing the accumulator without an extra DRAM round-trip.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: concurrent-stream launching is not fusion at all — fusion is a single-kernel construction.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: cross-device merge is not fusion; forward-backward merging is not epilogue fusion.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches the standard definitions used across TVM, TorchInductor, XLA, and cuBLAS epilogues.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: conflates fusion with unrelated optimizations (CSE, constant folding, loop nesting).

assumptions: The three names are used in their standard compiler-community sense.
nonImplications: Does not imply any of the three fusion kinds is always beneficial; each has legality and performance preconditions.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses fusion with placement / autograd concepts.
distractorRationales.D: Confuses fusion with CSE / constant folding.

questions.learningObjective: Identify when producer-consumer fusion of a pointwise op into a reduction is illegal or unprofitable due to reuse patterns.
questions.stem: A compiler considers fusing producer `T = f(A)` (pointwise) into consumer `Y = reduce_sum(T, axis=1)`. It observes that `T` is also consumed by a second, independent op `Z = g(T)` (pointwise). Which statement about this vertical fusion is correct?

options.text: Fusion is always legal and always beneficial because vertical fusion is semantics-preserving by construction; the compiler simply inlines `f` inside the reduction loop.
Fusion is legal only if `f` is bijective; otherwise the compiler cannot recover the original `T` for the second consumer.
Fusion is illegal because a reduction changes the shape of `T` and pointwise ops cannot be fused into shape-changing ops.

Fusion into the reduction is legal (semantics preserved), but if `T` remains materialized for the second consumer `Z`, the fused kernel will re-execute `f` for each element inside the reduction while `Z` still reads the original `T`; the compiler must either duplicate the compute or forgo the fusion.

questions.explanation: Vertical fusion inlines the producer computation inside the consumer's iteration space. If `T` has a second consumer that still needs the materialized tensor, three outcomes are possible: (1) recompute `f` inside the fused reduction while also computing `T` separately for `Z` (increases FLOPs); (2) keep `T` materialized and fuse only around it (defeats the memory-saving purpose); (3) fuse both consumers into the same kernel (only possible when their iteration spaces are compatible). Shape change is not a legality issue; bijectivity is irrelevant; SSA form is unrelated to reduction-axis position.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: fusion legality is preserved, but 'always beneficial' ignores the recompute-vs-materialize trade-off when producers have multiple consumers.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: bijectivity has no bearing; recompute or duplicate-consumer strategies solve the multi-consumer case.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: pointwise-into-reduction is a standard fusion pattern; shape change of the output does not block it.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: this is the canonical multi-consumer fusion dilemma discussed in TVM and Halide.

assumptions: Both `f` and `g` are pure (no side effects).
The tensor `T` is not marked as an explicit output.
nonImplications: Does not imply that re-computation is always worse than materialization; when `T` is large and `f` is cheap, recompute can win.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses shape-changing output with fusion legality.

questions.learningObjective: Enumerate boundary conditions that block or complicate operator fusion in a deep-learning compiler.
questions.stem: Which of the following are legitimate fusion-boundary conditions that a deep-learning compiler must respect? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The producer and consumer are placed on different devices (e.g., CPU producer, GPU consumer); crossing the device boundary requires an explicit copy op and cannot be absorbed into a single kernel.
The producer performs an in-place mutation of a tensor that is aliased by another live consumer; fusing across such a mutation would violate the observed side-effect ordering.

The producer and consumer have iteration spaces of very different rank/extent (e.g., a 4D pointwise op followed by a scalar reduction to a 0-D tensor); the compiler must decide whether a common loop nest is expressible.
The producer's output tensor is explicitly marked as a graph output that the caller reads; fusing away its materialization would violate the API contract.
The producer and consumer both use FP32 accumulation; fusing FP32 ops is forbidden because register pressure always grows unboundedly.

The producer is a pointwise op and the consumer is a pointwise op with the same shape; sharing an iteration space and being pure, they must not be fused because pointwise-pointwise fusion is disallowed.

questions.explanation: A, B, D are canonical fusion boundaries. Device boundaries require a data-transfer op and cannot be absorbed into one kernel. In-place mutation with aliased live consumers must preserve the mutation ordering; fusing across it can reorder reads and writes. Explicit graph outputs are contractually observable and cannot be optimized away. C is not a hard boundary — different iteration extents (e.g., pointwise → reduction) are routinely fused when the compiler can express a common nest; it may complicate scheduling but is not a boundary in itself. E is incorrect because FP32 accumulation says nothing about legality; register pressure is a heuristic concern, not a legality one. F is the opposite of the truth: pointwise-pointwise fusion is the most common fusion pattern.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: device boundaries require explicit transfer ops.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: aliased in-place writes constrain reordering.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: differing extents complicate scheduling but do not form a hard boundary; pointwise→reduction is a common fused pattern.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: explicit outputs are observable and cannot be fused away.
optionExplanations.E: Wrong: FP32 usage is not a legality condition; register pressure is a heuristic.
optionExplanations.F: Wrong: pointwise-pointwise fusion is the canonical vertical/horizontal fusion pattern.

assumptions: The IR distinguishes device placement, mutation/aliasing, and graph outputs.
nonImplications: Does not imply that heuristics such as register-pressure limits are illegitimate; they exist but are performance concerns, not legality boundaries.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses scheduling difficulty with a hard legality boundary.
distractorRationales.F: Reverses reality — pointwise-pointwise is the most common fusion.

sourceRefs.locator: Section 3: fusion pattern rules and opacity
Relax fuse-ops pass; device and output constraints

questions.learningObjective: Given a GEMM followed by a pointwise chain, decide which fusion form (epilogue vs. separate kernel) is expressible and legal.
questions.stem: The IR above shows a GEMM followed by a bias-add and GELU, and a proposed rewrite that folds them into a matmul epilogue. Which condition is required for the rewrite to be legal AND to deliver the intended memory-traffic benefit?

options.text: The rewrite is always legal because bias-add and GELU are pointwise; the memory benefit is automatic and independent of how the compute op streams its output.

The GEMM implementation must expose an epilogue slot that writes each output tile only after applying the pointwise chain in registers; without this, the pointwise ops still read/write the full M×N output via DRAM and no traffic is saved.
The rewrite is legal only if `bias` has shape `[M, N]` (same as the GEMM output); a broadcast `[N]` bias cannot be fused into an epilogue.
The rewrite is legal only when M×N is a multiple of the warp size, otherwise the epilogue introduces a tail block that violates SSA form.

questions.explanation: Legality of the rewrite is a pattern match on pointwise-after-GEMM; the intended traffic benefit only materializes when the GEMM kernel actually applies the epilogue to each output tile in registers before writing back to DRAM (as in cuBLAS Lt / CUTLASS epilogues). If the compiler emits a standalone GEMM plus separate pointwise kernels, the pointwise ops re-read the M×N tensor from DRAM and the fusion is 'logical' but has no memory-traffic benefit. Broadcast bias `[N]` is a supported epilogue pattern in cuBLAS Lt and CUTLASS. Warp-size divisibility affects tile boundaries but not SSA legality.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: legality alone does not deliver the traffic saving; the compute op must expose an epilogue path.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: this is the essential precondition — the GEMM kernel must fuse the epilogue in-register at tile granularity.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: broadcast biases are a standard epilogue pattern in cuBLAS Lt / CUTLASS.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: tail-block handling is a scheduling concern, not an SSA violation.

assumptions: The GEMM is implemented by a library or generated kernel that supports epilogue fusion.
Bias and GELU are pure and side-effect free.
nonImplications: Does not imply epilogue fusion is always faster in wall-clock; small M×N or memory-bound follow-ups can flip the trade-off.
Does not imply cuBLAS Lt supports every arbitrary pointwise chain; supported epilogues are a fixed catalog.

distractorRationales.A: Ignores the difference between logical fusion at IR level and physical fusion at kernel level.
distractorRationales.D: Introduces a spurious SSA claim about tail blocks.

performanceClaim.scope: GEMM + bias + activation epilogue on Tensor-Core capable GPUs

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a scenario where operator fusion increases register pressure and causes spill-driven slowdown.
questions.profileData:
Before fusion (two kernels):
  kernel_A (pointwise chain, 4 ops)   : 32 regs/thread, occupancy 100%,  0.42 ms
  kernel_B (reduction)                : 40 regs/thread, occupancy  75%, 0.31 ms
  total: 0.73 ms + ~0 ms launch overhead per kernel

After vertical fusion (single kernel):
  fused_AB                            : 96 regs/thread, occupancy 25%, register spills reported by ptxas: 48 bytes/thread
  total: 1.15 ms
questions.stem: A compiler fuses a 4-op pointwise chain with a downstream reduction into a single kernel on sm_80. Nsight Compute and ptxas outputs are above. The fused kernel is slower. Which is the best-supported explanation?

options.text: Fusion is buggy: producing correct results but running slower is a code-generation bug that must be reported to the compiler backend.
The reduction kernel was already memory-bound before fusion; adding pointwise math strictly reduces its runtime because the pointwise ops are 'free' inside a memory-bound region.

The fused kernel's live-range union pushed register usage to 96 regs/thread and induced spills; occupancy dropped to 25% and the spill-driven local-memory traffic exceeds the DRAM traffic saved by not materializing the intermediate.
The two-kernel version benefited from asynchronous kernel launch overlap on the default stream; fusion serialized the ops on the CPU launch queue.

questions.explanation: Option C is correct; options A, B, D are incorrect. A (Wrong): correctness is preserved; slowdown is a heuristic mismatch, not a compiler bug. B (Wrong): 'pointwise math is free inside memory-bound' ignores that spills add memory traffic. C (Correct): canonical register-pressure regression from over-fusion. D (Wrong): two sequential same-stream kernels do not overlap with each other. General context: Fusion widens the live-range set: pointwise intermediates that would have been consumed and dropped in kernel A now coexist with the reduction accumulator in kernel B's registers. When the union exceeds the per-thread register budget, ptxas spills to local memory (backed by L1/L2/DRAM). Meanwhile, occupancy collapses (from ~100%/75% to 25% at 96 regs on sm_80 with typical block size). Spill traffic and reduced latency hiding overwhelm the saved intermediate materialization.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: correctness is preserved; slowdown is a heuristic mismatch, not a compiler bug.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: 'pointwise math is free inside memory-bound' ignores that spills add memory traffic.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: canonical register-pressure regression from over-fusion.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: two sequential same-stream kernels do not overlap with each other.

assumptions: Block size and grid size are held constant across the two configurations.
ptxas spill report reflects local-memory usage backed by the memory hierarchy.
nonImplications: Does not imply fusion should be disabled globally; it implies the scheduler should track register pressure and back off when spills are induced.
Does not imply the two-kernel version is optimal; a smarter fusion partition (e.g., fuse 2 of the 4 pointwise ops) may win.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses heuristic failure with correctness bug.
distractorRationales.B: Overgeneralizes 'free work inside memory-bound' without accounting for spills.
distractorRationales.D: Invents a nonexistent overlap between same-stream kernels.

performanceClaim.scope: Register-pressure-driven fusion regression on sm_80

questions.learningObjective: Explain Halide's separation of algorithm (compute) from schedule and why the design choice matters for performance portability.
questions.stem: The Halide paper (PLDI 2013) is famous for separating a program's algorithm (the pure functional description of what to compute) from its schedule (the description of how to compute it — loop order, tiling, storage granularity, parallelism). Which best captures the paper's design intent behind this separation?

options.text: The separation matches the mathematical distinction between compilable and interpretable programs; algorithms are compiled while schedules are interpreted at runtime.
The separation was introduced only to enable static type checking of the algorithm at compile time; performance was a secondary consideration.
The separation was designed to allow multiple algorithms to share the same schedule; the schedule is the reusable artifact.

Because a single algorithm admits many valid schedules with vastly different performance, and the best schedule depends on hardware and problem size, separating the two lets a programmer or autoscheduler explore schedules without changing the correctness-critical algorithm; the same algorithm becomes portable across CPUs, GPUs, and DSPs by rescheduling.

questions.explanation: The Halide paper's central contribution is exactly the observation that many valid schedules realize the same algorithm with dramatically different performance, and that the optimal schedule depends on target hardware, memory hierarchy, and image size. Coupling the algorithm and schedule (as in hand-written C code) makes portability and performance tuning painful. Separating them lets programmers write the algorithm once and iterate on schedules or use autoschedulers. Options B, C, D are inversions or unrelated framings.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: both are compiled together in Halide.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: type checking is not the motivation.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: schedules are algorithm-specific, not reusable across algorithms.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: matches the paper's abstract and introduction.

assumptions: The algorithm is expressible in Halide's pure functional style.
nonImplications: Does not imply that any schedule can be chosen for a given algorithm — schedule primitives have legality preconditions.
Does not imply Halide's autoscheduler always finds an optimal schedule.

sourceRefs.locator: Abstract, Sections 1-2: separation of algorithm and schedule

questions.learningObjective: Given a TorchInductor scheduler log, explain why two pointwise ops were not fused.
questions.profileData:
TORCH_LOGS=+inductor output (excerpt):
  scheduler: fusing pointwise_add and pointwise_mul into single kernel (ok)
  scheduler: NOT fusing (pointwise_mul_output) with (reduction_sum):
      reason = 'consumer produces different output shape and reduces over inner axis;
                fusing would force reduction to broadcast pointwise input,
                producing >2× the memory traffic'
  final kernel plan: 2 kernels (fused_pointwise, reduction_sum)
questions.stem: The TorchInductor scheduler log above shows a pointwise chain fused but the subsequent reduction not fused with it. Given only this log, what is the most accurate reading of the scheduler's decision?

options.text: TorchInductor considered fusing the reduction with the pointwise chain, but the analysis found that fusion would force the reduction inner loop to re-read the pointwise inputs (broadcast), inflating memory traffic; the scheduler applied a heuristic that treats added memory traffic as a fusion cost.
TorchInductor cannot fuse pointwise ops with reductions at all; this is a permanent limitation of the scheduler.
The scheduler always separates reductions from pointwise ops when the reduction is over the inner axis, because reduction-over-inner-axis is semantically illegal to fuse.
The scheduler is memory-optimal by construction; the log demonstrates that any fusion decision it makes must reduce memory traffic.

questions.explanation: The log explicitly states the reason: fusing the reduction with the pointwise chain would force the reduction's inner loop to re-consume the pointwise inputs (a broadcast pattern) and would increase memory traffic by more than 2×. TorchInductor's scheduler uses heuristics that consider memory traffic as a fusion cost; it declined this fusion accordingly. Option B is false: TorchInductor routinely fuses pointwise with reductions (e.g., LayerNorm). Option C is false: pointwise-into-reduction is legal; the scheduler's decision is a performance heuristic, not a legality issue. Option D over-claims optimality; heuristics are approximations, not proofs of optimality.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: correctly reads the log and characterizes the heuristic.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: pointwise+reduction fusion is well-supported.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: legality is not at issue; performance is.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: heuristics are approximate.

assumptions: The log is representative of the TorchInductor scheduler's decision process in the specified version range.
nonImplications: Does not imply the scheduler's decision is always the best choice; a different memory-traffic model could reach a different conclusion.
Does not imply the same decision would be made in a future PyTorch version — the scheduler's heuristics evolve.

distractorRationales.D: Claims optimality beyond what heuristics guarantee.

performanceClaim.scope: TorchInductor fusion heuristic behavior in PyTorch 2.3-2.5

questions.learningObjective: Precisely define compile-time kernel selection and identify its inputs.
questions.stem: In deep-learning compilers, 'kernel selection' typically refers to which activity?

options.text: Choosing the physical filename of the shared library that will provide the CUDA runtime; this happens at link time and is independent of the model.

Choosing, for each operator instance in the graph, a concrete implementation (library call, generated kernel, or fused template) based on operator type, shape, dtype, layout, and target hardware — with an optional cost model or measurement-based ranking.
Choosing whether to run each iteration of a loop on the CPU or GPU based on runtime input size, decided at every launch by the executor.
Choosing which weights of the model to prune before compilation; kernel selection is another name for structured pruning.

questions.explanation: Kernel selection is the compile-time (or ahead-of-inference) step that maps each op-instance (with its concrete shape, dtype, layout, and target attributes) to a specific implementation from a catalog. Choices commonly include: (i) a hand-tuned library call like cuBLAS/cuDNN, (ii) a generated kernel from Triton/TensorIR/TIR templates, and (iii) a fused template with pointwise epilogues. The selection may be driven by a static cost model, a learned cost model, or by direct measurement. Option B refers to link-time library resolution, unrelated. Option C describes runtime device dispatch. Option D describes pruning, unrelated.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: link-time confusion.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: matches the standard use of the term in TVM, TorchInductor, TensorRT.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: runtime dispatch confusion.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: pruning confusion.

assumptions: The compiler operates over a graph where op-instances are already assigned concrete shape/dtype/layout attributes.
A catalog of kernel candidates exists per op-type.
nonImplications: Does not imply kernel selection is trivial; the search space can be very large.
Does not imply the selected kernel is optimal — the cost model may be approximate.

sourceRefs.locator: Kernel selection between ATen, Triton, and CPU C++ templates

questions.subtopic: Layout transformation / NCHW vs. NHWC on GPU
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an NCHW → NHWC layout transformation can improve GPU convolution performance and identify the precondition for the transformation to pay off.
questions.profileData:
Kernel: FP16 Conv2D on ResNet block, N=32, C=256, H=W=56, K=256, R=S=3.
  Under NCHW: cuDNN chooses IMPLICIT_GEMM_PRECOMP, Tensor Core utilization ~40%.
  Under NHWC:  cuDNN chooses NHWC_TENSOR_OP,       Tensor Core utilization ~85%.
questions.stem: Switching the tensor layout from NCHW to NHWC for a Conv2D on Ampere doubles Tensor Core utilization in the profile above. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.text: NHWC changes the mathematical result of the convolution, but the difference is within FP16 tolerance; the higher utilization comes from doing less numerical work.
NHWC uses less memory than NCHW because it interleaves channels, so it fits better in shared memory.

NHWC places the channel dimension as the fastest-varying axis, matching Tensor Core / im2col-tile access patterns and enabling cuDNN's NHWC Tensor Core kernels; NCHW places channel as a strided outer axis, which those Tensor Core kernels do not support directly.
NCHW is a deprecated layout on Ampere and later; cuDNN silently converts NCHW to NHWC internally, adding a permutation kernel that costs the reported utilization gap.

questions.explanation: NHWC makes the channel axis contiguous. Tensor Core convolution kernels (both explicit im2col GEMM and implicit GEMM variants) load tiles along the channel dimension, so contiguous channels give coalesced loads and match the Tensor Core K-fragment layout (K = input channels for forward conv). Under NCHW, the channel is an outer strided axis, which the NHWC-native Tensor Core kernels do not accept directly; cuDNN falls back to less-optimal precomputed variants or issues an internal permutation. NHWC does not change the memory footprint (same tensor, different layout) and does not change the mathematical output. NCHW is not deprecated on Ampere; both are supported, with NHWC preferred for Tensor Core.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: layout is semantics-preserving; NHWC does not change the mathematical output.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: layout does not change tensor size in memory.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches cuDNN's documented layout-kernel selection rules for Tensor Core.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: NCHW is still supported, and any internal permutation would appear as a distinct kernel, not as reduced TC utilization within the conv.

assumptions: The workload uses FP16/BF16 Tensor Core-capable kernels.
cuDNN's algorithm chooser follows its documented layout preferences.
nonImplications: Does not imply NHWC is always faster; small-channel workloads (C < 32) often prefer NCHW due to Tensor Core K-alignment constraints.
Does not imply the whole model should be transposed to NHWC; a permutation cost is incurred at layout boundaries.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses layout transformation with numerical change.
distractorRationales.D: Fabricates a deprecation and an internal-permutation cost model.

sourceRefs.locator: cuDNN conv layout preferences; Tensor Core alignment

performanceClaim.scope: cuDNN Tensor Core Conv2D layout preference on Ampere/Hopper

questions.learningObjective: Identify legitimate motivations for loop fission and cases where fission is counter-productive.
questions.stem: Loop fission (loop distribution) splits one loop body into two loops with the same iteration space. Which of the following are legitimate motivations for loop fission in a numerical / tensor pipeline? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: To improve cache behavior in a producer-consumer chain where a single loop body already fits in L1 cache and the intermediate values are reused within the same iteration.
To relieve register pressure when a single loop body has too many simultaneously live scalars, at the cost of touching some intermediate arrays twice.
To allow vectorization or parallelization of a subset of statements whose dependence structure permits it, while leaving unvectorizable statements in a separate loop.
To enable different tile sizes or schedules for the two halves, e.g., a compute-bound half and a memory-bound half.

questions.explanation: Loop fission is the inverse of fusion. Legitimate uses: (A) split a register-heavy body so each half fits in the register budget without spills; (B) isolate vectorizable statements from unvectorizable ones so the vectorizer can act on one half; (C) allow independent scheduling / tiling for the two halves. (D) is the opposite of the fission use case: if a single body already fits in cache and reuses intermediates, fusion is preferred; fission would force materialization of the intermediates. (E) is wrong: fission is a semantics-preserving transformation only when the dependence graph permits it — it cannot fix bugs, only preserve behavior.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: describes a case where fusion is preferred; fission would hurt cache behavior.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: canonical register-pressure motivation for fission.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: canonical vectorization motivation.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: canonical schedule-flexibility motivation.

assumptions: Both halves of the fission preserve the dependence graph (no forward-crossing dependences created).
nonImplications: Does not imply that any of these motivations always yield a net speedup; each is a candidate transformation that must be validated.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether two adjacent loops with a producer-consumer dependence can be legally fused into a single loop nest.
questions.stem: The proposed fusion above tries to combine a producer loop and a consumer loop into one. Is the fused loop semantically equivalent to the original, and why?

options.text: No — inside iteration `i`, the fused body reads `B[i+1]`, which has not been produced yet by iteration `i+1`; the fusion violates the flow dependence from producer to consumer.
Yes — because both loops have the same trip count `N`, fusion is always legal regardless of the access pattern.
Yes — because the two original loops iterate in the same order, fusion preserves semantics as long as all reads and writes touch the same array.
No — fusion is illegal because the two loops write to different arrays (`B` and `C`); fusion requires the write target to be identical.

questions.explanation: The classic legality condition for loop fusion is that no fused iteration can require a value that would be produced by a later iteration of the fused loop (no forward-crossing flow dependence). Here, iteration `i` needs `B[i+1]`, which is only defined by iteration `i+1` in the producer loop. In the fused loop, iteration `i+1` has not yet run when iteration `i` executes, so `B[i+1]` is either stale or uninitialized. Same trip count is necessary but not sufficient. Writing to different arrays is a normal fusion case, not a blocker.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: forward-crossing flow dependence violates fusion legality.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: identical trip count is necessary but not sufficient — cross-iteration dependences can still be violated.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: same iteration order does not save fusion when a later iteration's value is needed.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: writing to different arrays is normal for fusion; it is the dependence structure that matters.

assumptions: Boundary conditions for `i=0` and `i=N-1` are handled or ignored for this analysis.
`f` and `g` are pure functions of their inputs.
nonImplications: Does not imply the fusion is unrecoverable; a shift/peel or 2-iteration lookahead buffer can restore legality.

sourceRefs.locator: Chapter on loop transformations; fusion legality via dependence graphs

questions.learningObjective: Precisely define compiler-driven memory planning and buffer reuse for tensor programs and distinguish it from runtime allocation.
questions.stem: In a static tensor-program compiler (e.g., XLA, TVM Relax, TensorRT), 'memory planning' with 'buffer reuse' refers to which activity?

options.text: The compiler renames tensor variables via SSA renaming; each rename triggers a distinct buffer, and 'reuse' means the code generator emits fewer distinct variable names.
The runtime allocator caches recently-freed GPU buffers and hands them out to subsequent allocations to avoid the cost of cudaMalloc; this is the entire scope of memory planning.
The compiler always allocates one buffer per unique tensor identity; 'buffer reuse' refers to sharing that buffer across multiple training iterations of the same model.

The compiler analyzes tensor lifetimes across the graph, groups tensors whose lifetimes do not overlap, and assigns them to the same underlying storage buffer, producing a static allocation plan that the runtime executes without per-op malloc/free.

questions.explanation: Static memory planning is a compile-time pass over the tensor program's data-flow graph: the compiler computes the live range of every intermediate tensor, then packs them into a small set of pre-allocated buffers such that concurrently-live tensors do not share. The output is a schedule that assigns tensor → offset into an arena, so the runtime avoids per-op allocation. Option B describes a runtime allocator (like PyTorch's CachingAllocator), a different and complementary mechanism. Option C confuses per-iteration reuse (runtime concept) with the compile-time plan. Option D confuses SSA renaming with buffer assignment.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: SSA renaming has nothing to do with physical buffer allocation.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: describes a caching allocator, which is a runtime mechanism.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: buffer reuse is intra-graph, not inter-iteration.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: matches the definition in XLA's HLO buffer-assignment pass, TVM's memory planner, and TensorRT engine planning.

assumptions: The compiler has global visibility over the tensor program's data-flow graph.
Tensor sizes and lifetimes are known at compile time (static shapes or bounded dynamic shapes).
nonImplications: Does not imply memory planning replaces runtime allocation entirely — dynamic shapes and side-effecting operations may still require dynamic buffers.
Does not imply the resulting plan is optimal in general; buffer-packing is NP-hard and compilers use heuristics.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses inter-iteration reuse with intra-graph reuse.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the design motivations behind MetaSchedule / Ansor's approach to schedule search.
questions.stem: The MetaSchedule / Ansor design line replaced hand-written schedule templates with an automatic pipeline. Which of the following are TRUE about the design motivations of that line? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Manual per-operator templates are labor-intensive and do not generalize across new operator variants (e.g., new attention patterns, fused kernels), motivating an automatic sketch-generation stage.

A learned cost model is more predictive of measured runtime than a purely analytical model built on op counts and shape features alone, especially for GPU kernels where spills and bank conflicts matter.

The search space must be broken into a small number of algorithmic 'sketches' followed by numerical parameter annotation, so evolutionary search operates in a well-structured space rather than an unconstrained sequence of schedule primitives.
The system should replace real-hardware measurement with pure static analysis to eliminate measurement noise.
MetaSchedule sacrifices tuning quality for compile time; on any workload, a compiler with a manual template achieves better final kernels than MetaSchedule.

questions.explanation: The Ansor / MetaSchedule design is motivated by three points: (A) hand-written templates are unsustainable as operators proliferate; (B) analytical cost models are inaccurate on modern GPUs — learned models trained on measured runtimes are more predictive; (C) the search proceeds in two phases (sketch generation for algorithmic structure, then annotation of numerical parameters) so evolutionary search operates over a well-typed space. D is directly contrary to Ansor's design — the authors explicitly retain real-hardware measurement while using the cost model for pruning. E overgeneralizes empirical results; MetaSchedule often matches or exceeds handwritten templates.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: manual-template scalability motivates automation.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: learned cost model is more predictive on real hardware.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: sketch + annotation is the core structural design.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: measurement is retained; cost model prunes candidates but real hardware ranks finalists.
optionExplanations.E: Wrong: empirical results show MetaSchedule often matches / beats hand-tuned templates.

assumptions: The comparison is made under equivalent tuning budgets.
nonImplications: Does not imply MetaSchedule eliminates all human input — sketch primitives and cost-model features are still designed.
Does not imply MetaSchedule is universally better; on some heavily-optimized templated cases, hand tuning can still win.

distractorRationales.D: Contradicts Ansor's explicit design choice to keep measurement.

sourceRefs.locator: Sections 3-5: sketch design, learned cost model, evolutionary search

performanceClaim.scope: Ansor / MetaSchedule design motivations and comparative results

questions.learningObjective: Enumerate the dependence conditions under which a loop can be parallelized across iterations.
questions.stem: Which of the following are TRUE preconditions for a compiler to legally parallelize a loop's iterations (e.g., `#pragma omp parallel for`, or emit them as independent CUDA threads/blocks)? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: For a reduction (e.g., `s += a[i]`), the reduction operator is treated as associative/commutative so that partial results can be combined in any order, or the language exposes an explicit `reduction(...)` clause.
The loop body must be entirely branch-free; any conditional inside the loop makes parallelization illegal.
No two distinct iterations write to the same memory location (no output dependence).
No iteration reads a location that a different iteration writes (no true / anti dependence across iterations).

questions.explanation: Parallelization requires the absence of cross-iteration dependences on the same memory location. A (output dependence: WAW), B (true/anti dependence: RAW/WAR across iterations), and C (reduction treated with an appropriate associative combiner) are the standard legality conditions. Branch-free bodies (D) and compile-time trip counts (E) are neither required — SIMT / OpenMP happily parallelize branchy bodies (with warp divergence penalties) and runtime trip counts (`omp parallel for` on a variable N is standard).

optionExplanations.A: Correct: reductions require an associative combiner or an explicit clause.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: branchy bodies are legal to parallelize; divergence is a performance concern, not legality.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: WAW dependence blocks parallelization.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: RAW/WAR across iterations blocks parallelization without reordering.

assumptions: Statements have no external I/O or non-reentrant side effects.
Reductions, when present, use an associative combiner or an explicit reduction clause.
nonImplications: Does not imply parallelization is beneficial; small trip counts or memory-bound bodies may under-utilize parallel hardware.
Does not imply FP-associativity concerns are ignored in every context; numerical libraries may require deterministic ordering.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses warp-divergence performance concerns with legality.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the correct scope of a 'performance portability' claim and the conditions under which it can fail.
questions.stem: A compiler team claims that its scheduler achieves 'performance portability' across CPU, NVIDIA GPU, and AMD GPU targets for a workload. Which of the following are TRUE about the scope and preconditions of such a claim? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The claim's fairness depends on baseline choice: comparing the compiler's output to a vendor-tuned library on each target is more informative than comparing to a naive baseline.

As long as the framework reports the same peak Tensor Core utilization percentage across all three targets, the claim holds regardless of whether the underlying algorithm (e.g., FP16 GEMM vs. FP32 GEMM) differs between targets.

The claim requires that a comparable per-target schedule search or tuning was performed; a single schedule string cannot be optimal across three targets without retuning or target-specific specializations.
'Portability' here refers to the framework's ability to *generate* good schedules across targets, not to a single artifact running on all three; retargeting the compiler is part of portability.

questions.explanation: Options A, C, D are correct; option B is incorrect. A (Correct): honest baseline is required for a meaningful claim. B (Wrong): silently swapping the algorithm across targets invalidates the comparison; matching a utilization number is not the same as running the same computation. C (Correct): per-target tuning is required. D (Correct): portability is a framework property, not an artifact property.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: honest baseline is required for a meaningful claim.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: silently swapping the algorithm across targets invalidates the comparison; matching a utilization number is not the same as running the same computation.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: per-target tuning is required.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: portability is a framework property, not an artifact property.

assumptions: The compared framework and baselines target the same numerical algorithm.
nonImplications: Does not imply portability is unattainable; it is achievable within a well-defined scope.
Does not imply retuning cost is negligible — it must be part of the reported effort.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses matching a utilization percentage with a like-for-like comparison; algorithm swap invalidates portability.

performanceClaim.scope: Definition and boundaries of a performance-portability claim

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the situations in which recomputation (activation checkpointing) is a net win from those where it is not.
questions.stem: Activation recomputation (a.k.a. gradient / activation checkpointing) trades extra forward FLOPs at backward time for reduced peak activation memory. Which of the following statements about the trade-off are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Recomputation is a net win when the peak activation memory (before checkpointing) exceeds the device budget and prevents a larger batch size or sequence length that would raise end-to-end throughput more than the recompute FLOPs cost.
Recomputing a cheap operator (e.g., elementwise activation) whose activation tensor is large is generally favorable, since the FLOPs added are small relative to the memory saved.
Recomputing an operator whose forward is compute-bound and whose activation is small (e.g., a heavy GEMM with a tiny output) is usually favorable, because the compiler gains ILP.
Recomputation changes the mathematical output of the forward and backward passes; users must accept a small accuracy drop.
Selective (per-op) recomputation policies can outperform whole-block checkpointing by choosing to recompute only the ops with the highest memory-per-FLOPs ratio.

questions.explanation: A is the fundamental rationale (memory pressure enabling more batching / longer context often more than offsets the recompute cost). B is the classic favorable case: cheap op with big activation (e.g., GELU, dropout) is a prime candidate to recompute. E captures the observation behind selective checkpointing schemes: not every op has the same memory-per-FLOPs ratio, so a targeted policy dominates uniform block checkpointing. C is the opposite of the favorable case — recomputing an expensive op with a small activation adds a lot of FLOPs for little memory saving. D is wrong: recomputation is semantics-preserving; it produces the same values that would have been cached.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: the standard motivation is unlocking larger batches / longer contexts that raise throughput.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: high memory-per-FLOPs ops are ideal to recompute.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: describes the anti-pattern (recompute an expensive op with a small activation).
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: recomputation is exact (modulo hardware nondeterminism); no accuracy change is expected.
