optionExplanations.E: Correct: selective recomputation is a well-known refinement over uniform checkpointing.

assumptions: Recomputation reruns the forward function deterministically enough to reproduce the cached value.
The end-to-end throughput metric accounts for both FLOPs and memory-limited batch/context growth.
nonImplications: Does not imply recomputation is always a net win; when the model already fits with headroom, it only adds compile complexity and FLOPs.
Does not imply the memory saved is exactly the sum of avoided activation sizes; buffer reuse interactions can dilute the benefit.

sourceRefs.locator: Activation-memory / recompute trade-off in DNN training

performanceClaim.scope: Activation recomputation vs. caching trade-off in DNN training

questions.subtopic: Loop reordering / GEMM ikj vs. ijk
questions.learningObjective: Compare two loop orderings of a naive GEMM for their locality behavior and identify which is legal and preferred on a row-major layout.
questions.stem: Two loop orderings of naive GEMM are shown. All matrices are row-major FP32. Compared to Order 1 (ijk), which correctly describes Order 2 (ikj)?

options.text: Order 2 is not semantically equivalent to Order 1 because it accumulates into `C[i,j]` in a different order; floating-point non-associativity makes the two answer matrices different.
Order 2 is semantically equivalent but has worse locality: unit-stride writes to `C` cost more than unit-stride reads from `B`, so Order 1 remains preferred on row-major.
Order 2 is illegal because it introduces a loop-carried dependence on `C[i,j]` that did not exist in Order 1; the reordering violates SSA form.

Order 2 is semantically equivalent (same +='s over the same triples) and has better spatial locality on row-major storage: the innermost loop reads `B[k,:]` and writes `C[i,:]` with unit stride, unlike Order 1 which strides through `B` by N.

questions.explanation: Both orders compute the same set of multiply-accumulates on the same triples (i,j,k); the reduction on `C[i,j]` is +='s over `k`, so any permutation over `(j,k)` is semantically equivalent modulo FP non-associativity (typically ignored for GEMM correctness testing). Order 2 (ikj) is preferred on row-major layouts: the innermost `j` loop walks `B[k, 0..N]` and `C[i, 0..N]` with unit stride (cache-friendly, vectorizable), while Order 1's innermost `k` loop walks `B[0..K, j]` with stride `N` (cache-unfriendly). Option A over-states FP non-associativity as a correctness issue; option C is wrong (the dependence is a reduction on `C[i,j]`, present in both orders); option D reverses the locality direction.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: while FP addition is non-associative, GEMM reductions are treated as commutative/associative in practice; the two orders are considered semantically equivalent for optimization.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: reverses the locality direction.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: the reduction dependence exists in both orders; SSA is preserved by both.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: standard textbook explanation of the ikj vs. ijk locality difference on row-major.

assumptions: Row-major storage for all three matrices.
FP non-associativity is treated as a numerical concern, not a correctness concern for GEMM.
nonImplications: Does not imply ikj is optimal — blocked / vectorized orderings dominate in practice.
Does not imply the same order is preferred on column-major layouts (Fortran / BLAS-style would prefer jki).

distractorRationales.A: Overstates FP-non-associativity impact on optimization equivalence.
distractorRationales.C: Confuses reduction dependence with SSA violation.

performanceClaim.scope: Row-major naive GEMM cache behavior across loop orderings

questions.learningObjective: Contrast template-based schedule search (AutoTVM) and template-free schedule search (Ansor / MetaSchedule).
questions.stem: AutoTVM (template-based) and Ansor (template-free) both search for a good schedule of a tensor program, but they differ in what constitutes the search space. Which contrast is correct?

options.text: Both approaches use the same search space; the only difference is the choice of measurement backend (simulator vs. real hardware).
Template-based search learns the template from data; template-free search enumerates all schedules exhaustively.

Template-based search requires the developer to write a schedule template with parameter placeholders (tile size, unroll factor, thread bindings); the search explores parameter combinations of a fixed template. Template-free search generates candidate schedules by combining schedule primitives directly from the tensor expression, requiring no manual template but enlarging the search space.
Template-free search always outperforms template-based search on every workload; the two are strictly dominated.

questions.explanation: Template-based schedule search (AutoTVM) relies on a developer-authored schedule template with tunable parameters; the search explores those parameters. This produces a small, focused search space but requires per-operator template engineering. Template-free search (Ansor, MetaSchedule) constructs candidate schedules automatically by composing schedule primitives (split, tile, bind, unroll, vectorize) directly from the compute definition; this eliminates manual template work at the cost of a much larger search space, which is why learned cost models and evolutionary search become important. B misattributes 'learned template' to template-based. C claims equal search spaces which is inaccurate. D over-generalizes; on templated workloads AutoTVM can be competitive or better within its narrow space.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: search spaces differ substantially.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: template-based does not learn templates; humans write them.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches the definitions in the TVM/AutoTVM and Ansor papers.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: template-based can win on well-templated workloads with less tuning budget.

assumptions: The two systems are compared with equivalent compilation and measurement budgets in principle.
The operators being tuned admit valid schedule templates.
nonImplications: Does not imply template-free search is always faster to converge; the larger space needs more measurements.
Does not imply template-free eliminates all human input — the compute definition and cost-model features are still designed.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses template authorship with template learning.

sourceRefs.locator: Ansor: template-free search from compute definitions

questions.learningObjective: Contrast fully shape-specialized compilation with dynamic-shape compilation and identify the trade-offs each incurs.
questions.stem: Consider a compiler that must handle both fully shape-specialized compilation (one compiled artifact per shape combination) and dynamic-shape compilation (one artifact valid across a shape range). Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Shape-specialized artifacts can apply optimizations that require known constants (e.g., loop-tripcount-dependent unrolling, tile sizes tuned to exact dimensions) that a dynamic-shape artifact cannot use for the same code path.

Dynamic-shape artifacts trade some per-shape performance for reduced compilation time and reduced storage of many specialized kernels; symbolic shapes let the compiler emit one kernel with runtime-dispatched tail handling.
Fully shape-specialized compilation is always faster at runtime because it avoids all runtime dispatch, even for shapes seen only once during serving.
Dynamic-shape compilation is semantically incorrect for models with shape-dependent numerics (e.g., a broadcast that depends on the runtime shape); shape specialization is required for correctness.
A hybrid strategy — bucket runtime shapes into a small number of buckets and specialize each — can capture much of the per-shape speed while bounding compile time and cache size.

questions.explanation: A captures the fundamental optimization advantage of shape specialization. B captures the fundamental cost/storage/compile-time advantage of dynamic shapes; symbolic-shape emitters (TorchInductor with `dynamic=True`, TVM Relax with symbolic shapes) do exactly this. E is a well-known engineering compromise. C is false: for shapes seen once, specialization pays the compile-time cost that dominates the runtime saving. D is false: dynamic-shape compilation is semantics-preserving; the compiler symbolically tracks broadcast, and correctness does not depend on shape being a compile-time constant.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: canonical advantage of shape specialization.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: canonical advantage of dynamic shape.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: single-use shapes make specialization a compile-time loss.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: dynamic-shape compilation is semantics-preserving.
optionExplanations.E: Correct: bucket-and-specialize is a common production strategy.

assumptions: The compiler supports both modes and can bucket if desired.
nonImplications: Does not imply dynamic-shape compilation is universally worse at runtime; on some backends symbolic tiling reaches within 5-10% of specialized.
Does not imply bucketing is free — extra buckets add compile time and code size.

distractorRationales.C: Ignores compile-time amortization for single-use shapes.

performanceClaim.scope: Shape-specialized vs. dynamic-shape compilation trade-off

questions.learningObjective: Compute the largest square tile size for a GEMM inner kernel so that the three FP32 tiles fit within a target L1/SMEM budget.
questions.stem: A GEMM inner kernel `C_tile += A_tile * B_tile` uses square tiles of size `T×T` (FP32) for all three matrices. The target on-chip buffer (L1 cache line budget or GPU shared memory partition) available for this kernel is 48 KB. What is the largest tile size `T` (integer) such that the three tiles fit simultaneously in the 48 KB budget?

options.text: T = 96. Three 96×96 FP32 tiles occupy 3 × 96² × 4 = 110,592 bytes; caches typically allow 2× overcommit so 96 fits.
T = 32. Three 32×32 FP32 tiles occupy 3 × 32² × 4 = 12,288 bytes; anything larger overflows 48 KB.
T = 128. Three 128×128 FP32 tiles occupy 3 × 128² × 4 = 196,608 bytes, which is the standard 48 KB × 4-way associativity assumption.
T = 64. Three 64×64 FP32 tiles occupy 3 × 64² × 4 = 49,152 bytes = 48 KB exactly.

questions.explanation: Bytes = 3 × T² × sizeof(FP32) = 12 × T². Set 12 × T² ≤ 48 × 1024 = 49,152 → T² ≤ 4,096 → T ≤ 64. T = 64 achieves exactly 49,152 bytes. T = 96 requires 110,592 bytes (2.25× budget); T = 128 requires 196,608 bytes (4× budget); caches do not tolerate overcommit. T = 32 fits with room to spare and is not the largest.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: caches do not permit 2.25× overcommit; performance would collapse from thrashing / spills.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: 32 fits but is not the largest; the question asks for the largest T.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: 4× overcommit is not how cache/SMEM budgets work.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: 3 × 64² × 4 = 49,152 bytes exactly fits 48 KB.

assumptions: The three tiles are the sole occupants of the 48 KB budget.
FP32 is 4 bytes.
Register-file spills and reuse patterns are ignored for this sizing exercise.
nonImplications: Does not imply T=64 is the optimal choice in wall-clock time; smaller tiles may better match warp/thread shapes.
Does not imply the answer generalizes to non-square tiles or to different dtypes (FP16 doubles the fit).

distractorRationales.B: Correct arithmetic but not the maximum T.

sourceRefs.locator: Tiled GEMM sizing for shared memory

performanceClaim.scope: Cache/SMEM footprint arithmetic for square FP32 GEMM tile

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose why an autotuner-chosen tile size regressed on a new shape and identify the trade-off that triggered it.
questions.profileData:
Original tuned config: block=128×128, warp=64×64. Peak on M=N=K=4096: 82% TC utilization.
Same config on M=N=K=1024 shape: 34% TC utilization, only 8 blocks in grid, ~ 24 SMs idle on A100 (108 SMs).
Test of block=64×64 config on M=N=K=1024: 71% TC utilization, 256 blocks, all SMs busy.
questions.stem: An autotuned GEMM tile of block=128×128 is optimal at M=N=K=4096 but regresses to 34% TC utilization at M=N=K=1024. Retuning with block=64×64 recovers to 71%. Which trade-off is the primary cause?

options.text: At the smaller shape, the 128×128 tile produces too few grid blocks to fill all 108 SMs on A100; parallelism, not per-tile arithmetic intensity, becomes the bottleneck.
The 128×128 tile causes register spills at smaller shapes; smaller tiles avoid the spill and recover throughput.
A100 Tensor Cores require tile sizes that are exact multiples of 128 in each dimension; 1024 is not a valid choice for 128 tiles.
The autotuner overfit to M=4096 hardware calibration; the same 128×128 tile is still optimal at 1024 but Nsight Compute misreports utilization on small grids.

questions.explanation: For a 1024×1024 GEMM with 128×128 tiles, the grid is (1024/128)² = 64 blocks in the M-N plane before splitK; assuming no split-K, only 64 blocks are launched. A100 has 108 SMs; without persistent-kernel or split-K strategies, roughly 44 SMs are idle. Halving the tile to 64×64 yields 256 blocks — 2.4× the SM count — which restores full SM occupancy and lifts effective throughput. This is the canonical 'tile-too-big for small shapes' regression. Register spills or Tensor-Core divisibility (1024 IS a multiple of 128) are not the issue; the autotuner did not misreport utilization, it simply chose parameters for a different workload.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: too-few grid blocks under-utilize SMs at the smaller shape.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no spill evidence is given; the profile shows idle SMs, not spill.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: 1024 IS a multiple of 128; TC does not require this level of divisibility.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: 34% TC utilization on an under-populated grid is a real signal, not a mis-report.

assumptions: No split-K is enabled in the original config.
Tensor Core M×N×K = 16×16×16 (or larger) is compatible with both 64×64 and 128×128 blocks.
nonImplications: Does not imply the fix must be 64×64; alternatives include enabling split-K, persistent kernels, or shape-specialized tuning.
Does not imply block=128×128 is always suboptimal — at M=N=K=4096 it was the winner.

distractorRationales.B: Invents a spill without profile support.
distractorRationales.D: Blames the profiler for a real workload mismatch.

sourceRefs.locator: Section on shape-specialized tuning and tile-size search

performanceClaim.scope: Tile-size / grid-count trade-off on A100 GEMM at small shape

questions.subtopic: Transfer tuning / When learned cost model transfers
questions.learningObjective: Identify preconditions under which a learned cost model or tuned schedule from one workload transfers to a new workload.
questions.profileData:
Tuning history:
  Model A tuned on A100 with 4,000 trials, achieves 0.85× cuBLAS on GEMM kernels.
  Transfer-tuning experiment:
    - Cost model from A applied to Model B (GEMM shapes shifted, same dtype, same A100) → 3.8× fewer trials to reach 0.80× cuBLAS.
    - Cost model from A applied to Model C (Conv shapes, same A100) → NO speed-up in trial count vs. from-scratch.
    - Cost model from A applied to Model D (GEMM shapes, different GPU H100) → NO speed-up in trial count.
questions.stem: The transfer-tuning experiment above shows that reusing a tuned cost model helps in some cases but not others. Which is the best-supported explanation?

options.text: Transfer tuning is guaranteed to help any workload on any hardware once the cost model has enough data; the failure cases indicate a bug in the cost model implementation.

The learned cost model transfers to workloads with similar features (same op class, same dtype, same hardware); when either the op class or the hardware changes, the learned features are less applicable, so transfer provides little benefit.
Transfer tuning requires the exact same tensor shapes; even minor shape differences invalidate the cost model.
Cost models transfer freely across hardware because GPU features (register file, SM count) are captured symbolically; the failure on H100 must be due to a driver issue.

questions.explanation: Learned cost models transfer within a family: same operator class, same dtype, same hardware. When features shift substantially (different op class or different hardware), the model has not seen relevant training data and its predictions degrade toward random ordering. This matches the Ansor / MetaSchedule reports on transfer tuning: intra-op-class, intra-hardware transfer works; cross-op-class and cross-hardware transfer generally does not, unless the model was specifically trained across those axes. B, C, D make untenable universal claims or blame drivers without evidence.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: transfer is not unconditional.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: matches published transfer-tuning results.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: exact shape identity is not required; shape features generalize within an op class.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: hardware features are baked into the training data, not symbolically captured.

assumptions: The cost model is trained on features that include shape and dtype but do not explicitly enumerate hardware.
nonImplications: Does not imply cross-hardware transfer is unattainable; specifically-designed multi-hardware training can achieve it.
Does not imply transfer tuning replaces from-scratch tuning — it accelerates convergence within its scope.

distractorRationales.D: Attributes transfer failure to a driver bug without evidence.

performanceClaim.scope: Transfer-tuning effectiveness within an operator class and hardware

questions.learningObjective: Identify the legality preconditions of common TensorIR / TVM schedule primitives.
questions.irSnippet:
# TensorIR schedule primitives (simplified)
i, j, k = sch.get_loops(block)
io, ii = sch.split(i, factors=[None, 32])       # split loop i into outer and inner
sch.reorder(io, k, ii, j)                        # reorder loops (must preserve dependences)
sch.vectorize(ii)                                # vectorize the inner-32 loop
sch.bind(io, 'blockIdx.x')                       # map to a GPU block dimension
sch.parallel(k)                                  # parallelize k across threads
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the TensorIR schedule primitives above are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: `bind` to `blockIdx.x` is legal for any loop; TVM will emit correct code even if the loop has cross-iteration writes into shared state.
`split` is always legal because it only relabels the iteration space; the composition `factors=[None, 32]` decomposes `i` into `i = io * 32 + ii` and does not require dependence analysis.
`reorder` is legal only when the new order does not violate any dependence in the loop nest; TVM's schedule primitive rejects reorderings that would reverse a true dependence.
`vectorize` requires that the target loop's iterations are independent (no cross-iteration write dependence) and that the loop's trip count is compatible with the target's vector width.

questions.explanation: Options B, C, D are correct; option A is incorrect. A (Wrong): bind to a thread axis has independence preconditions. B (Correct): split is a pure reindexing. C (Correct): reorder requires dependence preservation. D (Correct): vectorize requires independence. General context: the target axis; otherwise cross-thread races occur.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: bind to a thread axis has independence preconditions.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: split is a pure reindexing.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: reorder requires dependence preservation.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: vectorize requires independence.

assumptions: The TensorIR block metadata correctly describes reads and writes.
The scheduler enforces primitive preconditions.
nonImplications: Does not imply all splits produce correct code once combined with subsequent primitives; downstream primitives (like vectorize) still have their own preconditions.
Does not imply MetaSchedule's search never generates illegal candidates internally — it may, but the primitives reject them at application.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize scenarios where loop unrolling degrades rather than improves performance.
questions.stem: Loop unrolling is often described as a 'free' optimization that reduces loop-overhead instructions. Which situation most clearly illustrates when unrolling is counter-productive?

options.text: A loop with data-dependent memory accesses; unrolling never helps because the CPU cannot prefetch data-dependent addresses.
A tight inner loop with a very small trip count (e.g., 4); unrolling by the exact trip count is illegal because it duplicates side effects and violates SSA form.
A GPU kernel where the compiler cannot statically determine the trip count; unrolling is impossible in that case, so no performance question arises.

A tight inner loop over a large array where the loop-overhead instructions (increment, compare, branch) already fit within a single instruction issue slot per iteration; unrolling 8× triples the object-code size, evicts hot code from the L1 instruction cache, and materially slows the surrounding function.

questions.explanation: Option D is correct; options A, B, C are incorrect. A (Wrong): unrolling can expose ILP even under data-dependent accesses. B (Wrong): full unroll of small fixed trip counts is legal and standard. C (Wrong): statically-unknown trip counts prevent unrolling, but the question is about when it hurts, not when it's impossible. D (Correct): code-bloat and I-cache pressure are the classic anti-unrolling scenarios. General context: The canonical downside of unrolling is code bloat leading to instruction-cache pressure and, on GPUs, higher register pressure and spills. When the loop body is already small enough that overhead is negligible relative to the body's work, aggressive unrolling only inflates code size without a compensating throughput gain.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: unrolling can expose ILP even under data-dependent accesses.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: full unroll of small fixed trip counts is legal and standard.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: statically-unknown trip counts prevent unrolling, but the question is about when it hurts, not when it's impossible.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: code-bloat and I-cache pressure are the classic anti-unrolling scenarios.

assumptions: The 'unrolled 8×' body substantially increases the number of instructions in the outer function.
The I-cache and register file have finite capacity.
nonImplications: Does not imply unrolling is generally bad; a moderate unroll factor (2-4) often helps for reduction and pointer chase loops.
Does not imply the compiler cannot back off; production compilers use heuristics based on I-cache and register budgets.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses full-unroll (legal) with a fictitious SSA violation.

sourceRefs.locator: Loop unrolling: benefits and code-size trade-off

performanceClaim.scope: Instruction-cache pressure from aggressive unrolling

questions.learningObjective: Identify the precondition set that a compiler must satisfy to vectorize a loop safely and effectively.

requiredFeatures: 8-lane FP32 vector unit (e.g., AVX2 or GPU SIMT)

questions.stem: The loop above is a candidate for 8-lane FP32 SIMD vectorization on an AVX2-like unit. Which is the correct summary of its vectorizability?

options.text: The loop is trivially vectorizable: `A[i-1]` and `A[i]` reads are independent, so 8 consecutive iterations can execute in parallel with no data reorganization.

Vectorization is legal (no cross-iteration write dependence, only reads), but the compiler must handle two extras: an unaligned or shifted load for `A[i-1]` (vector-shift or unaligned move), and a tail block for iterations where `N mod 8 != 0`.

The loop cannot be vectorized because reading `A[i-1]` in iteration `i` creates a loop-carried dependence via the read of a value written in a hypothetical earlier iteration; the vectorizer must serialize the loop.
The loop cannot be vectorized because FP32 multiplication is not associative; vector reductions must always use FP64 to preserve precision.

questions.explanation: There is no cross-iteration write dependence — `C[i]` is written once per iteration, and `A` is only read. Reads of `A[i-1]` and `A[i]` are legal to vectorize; the vectorizer must produce a shifted vector load (or an unaligned move) for the `A[i-1]` operand relative to the `A[i]` operand. In addition, if `N` is not a multiple of 8, a scalar or masked epilogue loop handles the tail. Option A ignores the shift/tail; C fabricates a loop-carried write dependence (there is none — only a read); D confuses reduction associativity with per-element vectorization.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: not 'trivial' — a vector-shift or unaligned load is needed, and the tail block must be handled.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: identifies both the legality (read-only cross-iteration access) and the two practical implementation obligations.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: cross-iteration READ of an already-written value is not a legality blocker; only cross-iteration WRITES pose loop-carried dependences.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: this is a pointwise loop, not a reduction; associativity is not at issue.

assumptions: Boundary at `i=0` is handled elsewhere or `A[-1]` is defined.
Vector unit supports unaligned or shifted loads.
nonImplications: Does not imply vectorization always yields a speedup; memory-bound loops gain little.
Does not imply the shifted-load cost is negligible on every architecture.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses cross-iteration read with cross-iteration write dependence.
distractorRationales.D: Applies reduction-associativity concern to a pointwise loop.

questions.subtopic: Accumulation precision / Mixed precision Tensor Core
questions.learningObjective: Enumerate the correct properties of mixed-precision Tensor Core GEMM: FP16/BF16 inputs with FP32 accumulator.
questions.stem: Regarding mixed-precision GEMM on NVIDIA Tensor Cores (e.g., FP16 or BF16 inputs with an FP32 accumulator), which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Storing weights and activations in FP16/BF16 halves memory footprint and doubles memory bandwidth utilization relative to FP32 for the load path.
Because the accumulator is FP32, the compute throughput of mixed-precision GEMM matches pure FP32 GEMM on Tensor Cores.
The accumulator dtype (FP32) determines the effective precision of the running sum, mitigating overflow and catastrophic cancellation compared to FP16/BF16 accumulation.
Downcasting the FP32 accumulator to FP16/BF16 on write introduces a rounding error per output element that can affect training stability if not accounted for.

questions.explanation: Options A, C, D are correct; option B is incorrect. A (Correct): bandwidth halving is central to Tensor Core speed-up. B (Wrong): mixed-precision Tensor Core is 8-16× faster than FP32 GEMM. C (Correct): accumulator dtype drives numerical stability. D (Correct): downcast rounding is a real, per-element error source.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: bandwidth halving is central to Tensor Core speed-up.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: mixed-precision Tensor Core is 8-16× faster than FP32 GEMM.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: accumulator dtype drives numerical stability.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: downcast rounding is a real, per-element error source.

assumptions: The GEMM uses standard cuBLAS or CUTLASS Tensor Core kernels.
nonImplications: Does not imply FP32 accumulator eliminates all numerical concerns — subnormal handling and non-associative order still matter.
Does not imply switching output to FP32 always improves accuracy meaningfully — many workloads see negligible difference.

performanceClaim.scope: Mixed-precision Tensor Core GEMM numerical properties and bandwidth

questions.learningObjective: Explain the swamping / small-magnitude-loss phenomenon in low-precision accumulation and identify the standard mitigations.
questions.stem: The naive FP16 reduction can lose small-magnitude terms after the running sum grows large. Which explanation of the phenomenon and the rewrite is CORRECT?

options.text: The issue is overflow (INF), not swamping; the rewrite's FP32 partial sums prevent overflow but not precision loss.
The naive loop is fine; both implementations produce identical results because FP16 addition is associative.
The rewrite is a bug: converting `x[i]` to float changes the mathematical result of the reduction, so it should be avoided in numerical code.

Once the FP16 sum exceeds ~2^k, values with magnitude below ~2^(k-11) round to zero when added, because FP16's 10-bit mantissa cannot distinguish them; this is 'swamping'. The rewrite fixes it by accumulating small partial sums in FP32 and combining them at the end — most additions happen when the running total is still small.

questions.explanation: This is the classical swamping / small-magnitude-lost-to-large-running-sum problem. FP16 has 11 bits of precision (including implicit leading 1); once the running sum reaches magnitude 2^k, additions of magnitude < 2^(k-11) round to zero. Block-parallel FP32 combining reduces the running sum in each partial, keeping most additions numerically visible. Option B claims associativity, which FP addition does not have. Option C confuses precision-preserving upcast with a semantic bug. Option D confuses swamping with overflow — the reduction may not overflow but still lose precision.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: swamping is a precision issue that can occur without overflow.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: FP addition is not associative.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: upcasting to FP32 is a precision-preserving refinement, not a bug.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: standard analysis of swamping and its block-partial mitigation.

assumptions: N is large enough for the running sum to grow past the mantissa's precision threshold.
Input distribution has some small-magnitude entries.
nonImplications: Does not imply block partials always match a reference FP32 reduction; different block sizes yield different (but generally better) results.
Does not imply Kahan summation is unnecessary — it can further reduce accumulated error.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses valid precision refinement with a bug.

questions.learningObjective: Explain AWQ's central technique: identifying salient channels via activation magnitude and applying per-channel scaling to protect them.
questions.stem: AWQ (Lin et al., MLSys 2024) achieves state-of-the-art W4A16 accuracy on LLMs. Which statements about AWQ's design are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: AWQ identifies a small fraction (~1%) of 'salient' channels by activation magnitude on a calibration set, based on the observation that quantizing these channels causes disproportionately large output error.

AWQ applies a per-channel scaling `s` (searched, not derived) that shrinks weights of salient channels before quantization and correspondingly scales activations in the preceding op; the scaled salient weights round to more accurate INT4 values.
AWQ is weight-only quantization (W4A16): activations stay in FP16 and no activation calibration is needed at inference time; the scaling is fused into the preceding LayerNorm / previous op.
AWQ uses a Hessian-based second-order update identical to GPTQ; the two algorithms produce the same INT4 weights.
AWQ requires INT4 Tensor Core support on the deployment GPU; without it, no speed-up is possible.

questions.explanation: A, B, C match the AWQ paper's central design: identify salient channels by activation magnitude (weight magnitude alone is not the criterion), scale them up before quantization to give them more effective bits, and scale activations of the preceding op inversely for mathematical equivalence. AWQ is W4A16 (weight-only quant) and fuses the diagonal scaling into the preceding op. D is false: GPTQ uses Hessian-based updates; AWQ uses a search-based per-channel scale factor without Hessian inversion. E is false: AWQ deploys via kernels that dequant INT4 to FP16 in registers and use FP16 Tensor Cores; INT4 Tensor Cores are not required.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: activation-magnitude-based salience.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: search-based per-channel scaling.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: W4A16 deployment; scaling fused into preceding op.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: AWQ and GPTQ are distinct algorithms.
optionExplanations.E: Wrong: AWQ uses FP16 Tensor Cores with dequant-in-register.

assumptions: The target layer is a linear layer preceded by an op that can absorb the diagonal scaling (e.g., LayerNorm).
nonImplications: Does not imply AWQ dominates GPTQ on every workload; empirical results are close and depend on model and evaluation.
Does not imply activation calibration is entirely unused — it is used offline to identify salient channels, not at inference.

distractorRationales.E: Invents an INT4 Tensor Core requirement.

sourceRefs.locator: Sections 3-4: salient-channel identification and per-channel scaling

performanceClaim.scope: AWQ W4A16 LLM quantization technique

questions.subtopic: Calibration / MinMax vs Percentile vs KL
questions.learningObjective: Compare MinMax, Percentile, and KL-divergence calibration for PTQ activation scales.
questions.stem: For PTQ activation calibration to INT8, which of the following statements about MinMax, Percentile (e.g., 99.9%), and KL-divergence (entropy) calibration are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: MinMax is always the most accurate calibration because it never clips any true activation value.

MinMax uses the observed absolute maximum activation across the calibration set as the clipping threshold; it is simplest but very sensitive to outliers that inflate the range and waste INT8 levels on rare extremes.
Percentile calibration (e.g., 99.9%) discards the top 0.1% of activations, keeping the range tighter and dedicating INT8 levels to the bulk of the distribution at the cost of clipping true outliers.

KL-divergence (entropy) calibration searches for a threshold that minimizes the KL divergence between the FP activation distribution and the quantized distribution; TensorRT's default INT8 calibrator uses a variant of this.

questions.explanation: Options B, C, D are correct; option A is incorrect. A (Wrong): not clipping ≠ most accurate. B (Correct): MinMax definition and outlier sensitivity. C (Correct): percentile definition. D (Correct): KL calibration definition; TensorRT's default. General context: MinMax's outlier sensitivity is well-documented; percentile trades a bit of clipping for a tighter distribution fit; KL calibration is TensorRT's classical INT8 workflow.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: not clipping ≠ most accurate.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: MinMax definition and outlier sensitivity.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: percentile definition.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: KL calibration definition; TensorRT's default.

assumptions: Symmetric per-tensor quantization; scale determined by threshold.
The calibration set is representative of inference-time activations.
nonImplications: Does not imply KL is universally better than MinMax; for narrow distributions with no outliers, MinMax is fine.
Does not imply percentile is a fixed threshold; 99%, 99.9%, 99.99% are common tunable choices.

questions.learningObjective: Given a W4A16 kernel snippet, identify the correct dequantization sequence: unpack INT4 → convert → scale.
questions.stem: The W4A16 inner-loop pseudo-code above shows the standard 'dequant-in-register' sequence. Which is a correct description of what it does and why it works with FP16 Tensor Cores?

options.text: It uses INT4 Tensor Cores directly; the `__int2half_rn` cast is a no-op emitted by the compiler and is not executed on hardware.

It unpacks two 4-bit weights per byte (sign-extending each nibble to signed int), converts to FP16, then multiplies by the group's FP16 scale to reconstruct the FP16 weight vector; the resulting FP16 vector is fed to an FP16 Tensor Core matmul. HBM traffic is reduced by ~4× vs FP16 storage while compute stays on standard FP16 Tensor Cores.
It applies the scale before conversion to FP16, mixing integer arithmetic with FP16 without any explicit conversion; the final FP16 Tensor Core silently interprets the bit pattern as FP16.
It performs the entire GEMM in INT4 without any conversion; the scale is applied only at the end of the K-loop, once per output element.

questions.explanation: The snippet is the canonical W4A16 dequant-in-register pattern: (1) load packed INT4 bytes from HBM, (2) unpack via nibble sign-extension into signed int, (3) convert to FP16 (`__int2half_rn` is a real conversion instruction), (4) multiply by the group's FP16 scale to reconstruct the FP16 weight, (5) feed to an FP16 Tensor Core matmul. HBM traffic drops by ~4× because packed INT4 is stored, but compute uses standard FP16 Tensor Cores (no INT4 Tensor Core is required). Option B fabricates a no-op conversion. Option C misdescribes the numerical composition. Option D wrongly claims INT4 GEMM, which would require INT4 Tensor Core hardware.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: conversion is a real instruction, not a no-op.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: standard W4A16 dequant-in-register + FP16 TC.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: cannot compute with mixed integer / FP16 without explicit conversion.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: INT4 GEMM requires INT4 Tensor Core hardware not used here.

assumptions: Symmetric per-group quantization (z=0).
FP16 Tensor Core available (Ampere+).
Weights packed as two INT4 per byte.
nonImplications: Does not imply the dequant + scale is free — it adds a small number of ops per weight; in bandwidth-bound regimes this is negligible.
Does not imply the same sequence works for asymmetric per-group quantization — an extra zero-point subtraction is needed.

distractorRationales.C: Ignores the need for explicit dtype conversion.
distractorRationales.D: Confuses W4A16 storage with INT4 compute.

questions.learningObjective: Correctly report the exponent and mantissa widths of FP32, FP16, and BF16.
questions.stem: Which row correctly gives the (sign, exponent, mantissa) bit widths for FP32, FP16, and BF16 respectively?
questions.explanation: FP32 is IEEE 754 single: 1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 mantissa (24 bit precision with the implicit leading 1). FP16 is IEEE 754 half: 1 sign, 5 exponent, 10 mantissa. BF16 was designed with the same 8-bit exponent as FP32 (matching dynamic range) and a truncated mantissa: 1 sign, 8 exponent, 7 mantissa. BF16's rationale is dynamic-range preservation at the cost of mantissa precision.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: swaps FP16 and BF16 exponent widths.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: standard IEEE 754 and Google BF16 layouts.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: FP32 has 8 exponent bits, not 10.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: BF16 differs from FP16 in exponent/mantissa split.

assumptions: Standard IEEE 754 and Google BF16 conventions.
nonImplications: Does not imply BF16 is universally superior to FP16; BF16's larger dynamic range comes with reduced mantissa precision.
Does not describe FP8, TF32, or FP4 formats.

distractorRationales.A: Common confusion between FP16 and BF16 layouts.
distractorRationales.D: Treats BF16 as identical to FP16.

questions.subtopic: FP16 vs BF16 / Precision vs range trade-off
questions.learningObjective: Explain why FP16 and BF16 trade precision against dynamic range and identify a scenario that dictates the choice.

hardwareContext.architecture: generic accelerator supporting both FP16 and BF16

questions.stem: A team is training a large language model and hits gradient underflow at some layers when using FP16 with dynamic loss scaling barely keeping activations in range. Which statement about switching to BF16 is correct?

options.text: BF16 uses the same 5-bit exponent as FP16 with a different rounding rule; the choice is a numerical style issue with no dynamic-range effect.
BF16 uses more bits than FP16, so switching increases memory footprint but eliminates the underflow entirely.

BF16 uses FP32's 8-bit exponent, giving it FP32-like dynamic range and mostly removing underflow/overflow risk during training, at the cost of a coarser mantissa (7 bits vs. FP16's 10); most gradient-dynamic-range problems disappear, and loss scaling can often be simplified or removed.
BF16 is a fixed-point format optimized for training; underflow is impossible because there is no exponent.

questions.explanation: Option C is correct; options A, B, D are incorrect. A (Wrong): BF16's exponent width is 8, not 5. B (Wrong): BF16 and FP16 are both 16 bits. C (Correct): matches the widely-documented BF16 rationale. D (Wrong): BF16 is floating-point. General context: BF16 shares FP32's 8-bit exponent and thus its dynamic range, at the cost of a 7-bit (vs. FP16's 10-bit) mantissa. In deep learning training, gradients often have very small magnitudes that underflow FP16's ~[6e-5, 6.5e4] range; BF16's ~[1e-38, 3e38] range accommodates them without loss scaling. The trade-off is mantissa precision, which some pathological accumulations may notice; empirically most training runs prefer BF16 when hardware supports it.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: BF16's exponent width is 8, not 5.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: BF16 and FP16 are both 16 bits.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches the widely-documented BF16 rationale.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: BF16 is floating-point.

assumptions: The hardware supports BF16 with equivalent throughput to FP16 (true on Ampere/Hopper Tensor Cores).
The workload is a typical LLM training run with gradient scaling concerns.
nonImplications: Does not imply BF16 always achieves final accuracy identical to FP16 or FP32; edge cases with very small updates may be affected by reduced mantissa.
Does not imply loss scaling is never needed with BF16; it is much less common but not universally unnecessary.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses total bits with exponent design.
distractorRationales.D: Confuses BF16 with a fixed-point format.

performanceClaim.scope: BF16 vs. FP16 dynamic range in DNN training

questions.learningObjective: Correctly define TF32 and its relationship to FP32.
questions.stem: TF32 (TensorFloat-32) is a numerical format used by NVIDIA Tensor Cores starting with Ampere. Which best describes TF32?

options.text: TF32 is a 24-bit format used by CPU vector units for machine-learning workloads; it is unrelated to GPU Tensor Cores.
TF32 is a 32-bit format equivalent to FP32; the name is a marketing rebrand with no numerical difference.
TF32 is a 16-bit format identical to BF16; the '32' refers to the accumulator width.

TF32 is a 19-bit internal Tensor Core input format: 1 sign, 8 exponent (FP32 range), 10 mantissa (FP16 precision). Storage remains FP32; only the Tensor Core multiplier truncates mantissa on input. Accumulation is FP32.

questions.explanation: TF32 is a Tensor Core input format: 8-bit exponent (FP32 dynamic range) with 10-bit mantissa (FP16 precision), totaling 19 bits internally. Storage in memory remains FP32; the truncation happens as inputs enter the Tensor Core multiplier. The accumulator stays FP32. This gives roughly 8-16× the compute throughput of pure FP32 while preserving FP32 range for training. TF32 is the default matmul mode for FP32 tensors on Ampere+ when `torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True`. Options B, C, D misrepresent the format.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: TF32 is a GPU Tensor Core format.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: TF32 has different mantissa precision from FP32.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: TF32 is not identical to BF16 (different mantissa width).
optionExplanations.D: Correct: matches NVIDIA's TF32 documentation.

assumptions: The reader is on Ampere or newer NVIDIA GPUs.
nonImplications: Does not imply TF32 matches FP32 accuracy bit-for-bit — the mantissa truncation is observable in numerical tests.
Does not imply TF32 is used automatically for all FP32 tensors — a flag controls it in PyTorch and other frameworks.

sourceRefs.locator: Ampere Tensor Core TF32 format documentation

performanceClaim.scope: TF32 format definition; not a specific measured speedup

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish dynamic and static activation quantization by scale computation and runtime cost.
questions.stem: 'Dynamic quantization' and 'static quantization' of activations differ in a specific way. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Dynamic quantization uses a different integer format (INT4) than static quantization (INT8); the term refers to the format's dynamic range.
Dynamic quantization is a synonym for QAT; static quantization is a synonym for PTQ.

Dynamic quantization computes the activation scale (and zero-point) from the tensor's own statistics at each forward pass (per-tensor min/max or absmax); static quantization computes and freezes the scales offline via a calibration pass over representative inputs, so the scales are constants at runtime.
Static quantization computes scales from the tensor's own statistics at each forward pass; dynamic quantization freezes them offline.

questions.explanation: Dynamic quantization: at each forward pass, compute activation statistics (typically absmax or min/max) from the runtime tensor and derive the quant params on the fly. Static quantization: run a calibration pass on representative inputs offline, freeze the derived scales, and use those constants at runtime. Dynamic adds per-tensor reduction cost at inference; static needs a calibration corpus but avoids runtime scale calculation. Option B conflates orthogonal concepts (dynamic/static is about scale timing; PTQ/QAT is about training-time involvement). Option C invents a format-dependent meaning. Option D is the direct reverse.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: format has nothing to do with dynamic vs static.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: dynamic/static and PTQ/QAT are orthogonal.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard definition used across TensorRT, PyTorch, TF-Lite.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: reverses the definitions.

assumptions: Standard framework terminology (TensorRT / PyTorch / TF-Lite).
nonImplications: Does not imply dynamic quantization is always slower — for small per-tensor reductions the cost is negligible.
Does not imply static quantization always yields lower accuracy — often it is more stable because scales don't drift with input distribution.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a correct fake-quantization forward implementation (quantize → clamp → dequantize) used during QAT.
questions.codeSnippet:
def fake_quantize_symmetric(x: torch.Tensor,
                            scale: float,
                            qmin: int = -127,
                            qmax: int = 127) -> torch.Tensor:
    # Forward: simulate INT8 quantization but keep FP values so autograd flows.
    q = torch.round(x / scale)
    q = torch.clamp(q, qmin, qmax)
    x_hat = q * scale                # dequantize back to FP
    return x_hat
questions.stem: The function above is intended as a symmetric fake-quantization forward for QAT (values quantized to the INT8 grid, then dequantized to FP, so that downstream layers see the quantization noise while gradients can still flow). Is the implementation correct and, if so, what is the standard trick required to make its gradient useful during training?

options.text: The forward is wrong: multiplying by `scale` after rounding produces the original `x`, so no quantization noise is introduced. The correct forward must add explicit noise.
The forward is correct and no special backward trick is needed; PyTorch's autograd computes the mathematically-correct gradient of `round` (zero) and training proceeds normally.

The forward is correct. The gradient of `round` and `clamp` is zero almost everywhere, so during backward the standard trick is the 'straight-through estimator' (STE): treat `d(round(x))/dx ≈ 1` (with the clamp mask applied), so gradients pass through as if the fake-quant were identity on the interior of the clamp.
The forward is wrong because `torch.round` uses banker's rounding, which is incompatible with quantized inference kernels that use round-half-away-from-zero.

questions.explanation: Option C is correct; options A, B, D are incorrect. A (Wrong): round destroys precision; q*scale ≠ x. B (Wrong): without STE, gradient is zero. C (Correct): identifies fake-quant + STE. D (Wrong): RNE / round-half-even is standard and matches inference kernels. General context: The forward is the canonical fake-quant: quantize (round), clamp to the INT range, then dequantize by multiplying by scale. `x_hat` differs from `x` by the quantization error (up to 0.5 * scale in magnitude plus any clamp truncation). For backward, the gradient of `round` is zero almost everywhere, so a naive autograd would produce zero gradients and training would stall. The straight-through estimator (STE) treats the identity as the derivative on the interior of the clamp region (and zero outside). This is standard in QAT frameworks. Option D describes rounding-convention mismatches (a real concern) but the mismatch is minor and does not make the forward 'wrong'; RNE is the IEEE default and used by most inference kernels.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: round destroys precision; q*scale ≠ x.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: without STE, gradient is zero.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: identifies fake-quant + STE.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: RNE / round-half-even is standard and matches inference kernels.

assumptions: Symmetric quantization (z=0); scale > 0.
The training-time framework registers a custom backward or uses `torch.ops.aten.fake_quantize_per_tensor_affine`.
nonImplications: Does not imply the STE is unbiased; it is an approximation that can affect convergence.
Does not imply any specific `qmin`, `qmax` values; symmetric convention uses [-127, 127] but asymmetric uses [0, 255] etc.

distractorRationales.D: Elevates a minor rounding-convention issue to a correctness failure.

sourceRefs.locator: QAT fake quantization and straight-through estimator

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the intended uses of FP8 E4M3 and E5M2 formats and their trade-offs.
questions.stem: NVIDIA Hopper Tensor Cores support two FP8 formats: E4M3 (4-bit exponent, 3-bit mantissa) and E5M2 (5-bit exponent, 2-bit mantissa). Which of the following statements about their intended uses and trade-offs are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: E4M3 has narrower dynamic range but higher mantissa precision than E5M2; it is typically preferred for forward-pass activations and weights whose distribution is bounded and needs precision.
E5M2 has wider dynamic range (5-bit exponent) but lower precision; it is typically preferred for gradients during training, whose values span a large magnitude range.
Both formats have the same total bit width (8 bits including sign); the choice affects precision-vs-range, not memory footprint.
Using FP8 requires no scaling factors; the format itself handles the entire dynamic range needed in DNN training.
FP8 kernels are supported on Ampere Tensor Cores at the same throughput as FP16; the format was retroactively enabled on sm_80 via a driver update.

questions.explanation: A and B match the design intent as codified in the NVIDIA / Arm / Intel FP8 whitepaper and Transformer Engine: E4M3 for weights/activations (bounded distributions), E5M2 for gradients (wide dynamic range). C is a straightforward observation: both are 8 bits total. D is false: FP8's dynamic range is small enough that per-tensor or per-block scaling is essential; Transformer Engine automates this via `DelayedScaling`. E is false: FP8 Tensor Cores debuted on Hopper (sm_90); they are not supported on Ampere (sm_80).

optionExplanations.A: Correct: E4M3 use case per NVIDIA/Arm/Intel FP8 spec.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: E5M2 use case per FP8 spec.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: both are 8-bit total.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: FP8 workflows require per-tensor/block scale factors.
optionExplanations.E: Wrong: FP8 Tensor Cores are Hopper (sm_90) and later; not available on Ampere.

assumptions: The FP8 formats refer to the NVIDIA/Arm/Intel 2022 specification.
The workload is a DNN training or inference pipeline on Hopper or later.
nonImplications: Does not imply E4M3 and E5M2 always dominate FP16/BF16 in accuracy — they trade precision for compute throughput.
Does not imply all Hopper GEMMs use FP8 by default — frameworks require explicit opt-in.

distractorRationales.D: Understates the need for scaling factors.

sourceRefs.locator: FP8 Tensor Core and Transformer Engine documentation

performanceClaim.scope: FP8 format definitions and intended uses on Hopper

questions.subtopic: FP8 mul + FP32 accum on Hopper
questions.learningObjective: Explain FP8 matmul semantics on Hopper Tensor Cores including accumulator dtype and scaling requirements.
questions.stem: On Hopper Tensor Cores, FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) matmul is a common training precision. Which of the following statements about the FP8 GEMM numerical pipeline are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.profileData:
Hopper H100 Tensor Core peak throughput (dense, per NVIDIA whitepaper):
  BF16 / FP16      : ~ 989 TFLOPS
  FP8 (E4M3, E5M2) : ~1979 TFLOPS  (~ 2×)
  Accumulator dtype in FP8 QMMA/WGMMA: FP32.
  Transformer Engine 'DelayedScaling' recipe: per-tensor scale factors updated with a lag over recent statistics.

options.text: FP8 GEMM on H100 has approximately 2× the peak throughput of BF16 GEMM on the same hardware, but only when memory bandwidth is not the bottleneck.
The FP8 accumulator is itself FP8; the small dynamic range is deliberately preserved to force early saturation, which acts as an implicit regularizer.

FP8 Tensor Core matmuls use an FP32 accumulator; the per-tile accumulator is FP32 regardless of whether inputs are E4M3 or E5M2. This mitigates the very limited dynamic range of FP8 for the sum of products.

Because FP8's dynamic range is small, production FP8 pipelines apply per-tensor (or per-block) scale factors that keep the values within FP8's representable range; NVIDIA's Transformer Engine automates this via its `DelayedScaling` recipe.

questions.explanation: Options A, C, D are correct; option B is incorrect. A (Correct): peak-throughput advantage in compute-bound regimes. B (Wrong): no FP8 accumulator in production paths. C (Correct): FP32 accumulator is standard for FP8 Tensor Cores. D (Correct): Transformer Engine's DelayedScaling recipe.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: peak-throughput advantage in compute-bound regimes.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no FP8 accumulator in production paths.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: FP32 accumulator is standard for FP8 Tensor Cores.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: Transformer Engine's DelayedScaling recipe.

assumptions: The target GPU is Hopper (sm_90) with FP8 Tensor Core support.
The workload uses NVIDIA's Transformer Engine or equivalent FP8 pipeline.
nonImplications: Does not imply FP8 always matches BF16 accuracy — small residual differences are typical, and workload-dependent.
Does not imply the 2× peak is always realized — memory-bandwidth-bound kernels see much less benefit.

distractorRationales.B: Invents an FP8 accumulator that no production path uses.

sourceRefs.locator: H100 FP8 Tensor Core specification; QMMA / WGMMA

performanceClaim.scope: FP8 Tensor Core semantics on Hopper

questions.learningObjective: Identify scenarios where INT8 GEMM is NOT faster than FP16 GEMM on an Ampere-class GPU.
questions.profileData:
On A100 (Tensor Core INT8 peak ~ 2× FP16 peak):
  Case 1: M=4096, N=4096, K=4096, batched=1. INT8 GEMM ≈ 0.5× FP16 GEMM runtime (compute-bound; INT8 wins).
  Case 2: M=1, N=4096, K=4096 (GEMV / decode batch=1). INT8 kernel time ≈ FP16 kernel time (bandwidth-bound; weights dominate).
questions.stem: On A100, INT8 GEMM has ~2× the FP16 Tensor Core throughput, yet Case 2 (M=1) shows INT8 no faster than FP16. What is the correct explanation?

options.text: The M=1 case has such low arithmetic intensity that CUDA cannot launch a grid at all; the runtimes reflect kernel-launch overhead only.
INT8 Tensor Cores are disabled on A100 in cuBLAS; the observed times are FP16 in both cases.

At M=1 (batch-1 decode), the kernel is bandwidth-bound: the dominant cost is loading the K×N weight matrix, which is the same size regardless of activation dtype. INT8 activations barely affect memory traffic when they represent a tiny fraction of the total bytes moved; peak-TOPS advantage of INT8 Tensor Cores cannot be realized because there is not enough compute per byte.
INT8 GEMM at M=1 is slower than FP16 due to quantize/dequantize overhead in the kernel; the fix is to disable dequantization.

questions.explanation: At M=1 with FP16 weights (K*N = 4096*4096 = 16 MB), the kernel is bandwidth-bound; the FP16 activation vector is negligible. Replacing FP16 activations with INT8 activations saves at most K bytes; the weight matrix bytes dominate. Since both kernels move the same weight bytes (both FP16 weights in this case), the INT8 kernel's TC advantage cannot manifest — the compute path is idle waiting on weight loads. The proper solution is weight-only quantization (W4A16, W8A16) that reduces the weight bandwidth. Options B, C, D are inventions.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: CUDA can launch any grid; kernel-launch overhead is not the story here.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: INT8 Tensor Cores are enabled on A100 in cuBLAS.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: bandwidth-bound M=1 case where compute peak is irrelevant.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: quantize/dequantize overhead is minor; the primary issue is weight bandwidth.

assumptions: Both configurations use FP16 weight storage.
GPU has sufficient memory bandwidth headroom for FP16 weights but not compute-bound at M=1.
nonImplications: Does not imply INT8 GEMM is useless — for compute-bound (large M) cases it delivers.
Does not imply W4A16 solves all bandwidth issues — for very small K it may not.

sourceRefs.locator: Bandwidth vs. compute analysis for W4A16 vs W8A8

performanceClaim.scope: INT8 vs FP16 GEMM at M=1 (batch-1 decode) on A100

questions.learningObjective: Explain GPTQ's central technique: per-layer weight quantization via second-order (Hessian-inverse-based) error compensation.
questions.stem: GPTQ (Frantar et al., ICLR 2023) is a PTQ algorithm that quantizes LLM weights to INT4 with small accuracy loss. Which best captures its central technique?

options.text: GPTQ quantizes weights column-by-column, and after each column's quantization it updates the remaining unquantized columns using the Hessian of the per-layer reconstruction error (approximated as `H = 2 X^T X` from calibration activations); this compensates for the just-introduced quantization error and dramatically improves the fit versus naive round-to-nearest.
GPTQ retrains the entire model with a straight-through estimator on the quantized weights; it is essentially QAT with a specific initializer.
GPTQ uses reinforcement learning to search for optimal per-tensor scales; the 'GPT' in the name refers to a GPT-2 policy network.
GPTQ is a runtime dequantization technique that computes INT4 → FP16 dequants faster than standard kernels; it does not change how weights are quantized offline.

questions.explanation: GPTQ's core technique is a per-layer optimization: quantize one column of the weight matrix at a time, then use the (once-computed) Cholesky-inverse of the Hessian of the reconstruction error to update the still-unquantized columns to compensate for the introduced error. This is a second-order variant of OBS/OBQ adapted for LLM-scale weight matrices. It runs offline (no full model training) and produces INT4 weights with 1-4% perplexity increase on 175B-parameter models. Options B, C, D are unrelated inventions.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: matches GPTQ paper's algorithm description.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: GPTQ is PTQ, not QAT.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: 'GPT' refers to the target model class (GPT-family), not RL.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: GPTQ is an offline quantization algorithm.

assumptions: The layer is a linear layer with a computable per-layer Hessian.
A calibration set of activations is available.
nonImplications: Does not imply GPTQ handles activation outliers — it focuses purely on weight quantization; W4A16 is its typical deployment.
Does not imply GPTQ is the only choice; AWQ and RTN are alternatives with different trade-offs.

distractorRationales.D: Confuses offline algorithm with runtime kernel.

sourceRefs.locator: Sections 3-4: algorithm description and Hessian update rule

performanceClaim.scope: GPTQ INT4 weight-quantization technique for LLMs

questions.subtopic: Quantization granularity / Per-tensor vs per-channel vs per-group
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish per-tensor, per-channel, and per-group quantization by scale/zero-point count and hardware/kernel implications.
questions.stem: For quantizing an FP16 weight matrix `W` of shape `[out_channels, in_channels]` to INT8/INT4 for a subsequent quantized GEMM, which of the following statements about quantization granularity are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Per-tensor uses one (scale, zero-point) pair for the entire W; simplest to implement and cheapest in metadata storage but loses accuracy when different channels have very different value ranges.

Per-channel (also called per-output-channel or per-row here) uses one (scale, zero-point) per row of W; the GEMM epilogue applies a different scale to each output element, adding negligible extra work per output.

Per-group divides the `in_channels` axis into groups (e.g., 128 elements per group) and stores one scale per (row, group) pair; standard for W4A16 kernels where groups of 128 give a good accuracy/memory-metadata trade-off.
Per-tensor is strictly more accurate than per-channel because a single scale allows Tensor Cores to run at peak throughput without any metadata handling.
Per-group quantization is illegal in INT8 GEMM because the accumulator cannot mix multiple scales within one dot product.

questions.explanation: A, B, C are standard characterizations: per-tensor (single scale, low metadata, worst fit on heterogeneous channels), per-channel (one scale per output row, negligible extra epilogue cost), per-group (finer scales along the K axis, the standard for W4A16 GPTQ/AWQ kernels typically with group_size 128). D is false: per-tensor is generally LESS accurate than per-channel because it forces one scale to cover all channels. E is false: per-group INT/W4 GEMMs handle multiple scales along the K axis by partial-accumulating within a group, applying the group scale, then adding to the outer accumulator.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: per-tensor definition and trade-off.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: per-channel implementation and epilogue cost.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: per-group is standard for W4A16.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: per-tensor is generally LESS accurate.
optionExplanations.E: Wrong: per-group GEMM handles multiple scales via grouped accumulation.

assumptions: The GEMM kernel is designed for the chosen granularity.
The 'in_channels' axis in this discussion corresponds to the K axis of the matmul.
nonImplications: Does not imply per-group is always better than per-channel — smaller group sizes increase metadata and can offset accuracy gains.
Does not imply per-channel weight quantization always requires per-channel activation quantization; the two are chosen independently.

performanceClaim.scope: Granularity trade-off for quantized weight GEMMs

questions.learningObjective: Given a code snippet, identify the correct per-channel dequantization broadcast for a `[out, in]` weight quantized per-output-channel.
questions.codeSnippet:
# W_int8: shape (out_features, in_features), symmetric per-output-channel
# scale:  shape (out_features,), FP16, one per row
# Reconstruct W_fp:
W_fp = W_int8.to(torch.float16) * scale                # broadcast form
questions.stem: The intended semantics is: for each row `i` of `W_int8`, multiply the entire row by `scale[i]`. Given `W_int8.shape == (out, in)` and `scale.shape == (out,)`, does the expression `W_int8.to(torch.float16) * scale` produce the correct result under standard broadcasting rules?

options.text: Yes. Broadcasting aligns the first axis by default, so `scale` broadcasts across rows correctly.

No. Broadcasting aligns the last axis, so `scale` (shape `[out]`) would broadcast against the *last* axis of W (shape `[out, in]`), multiplying every column by `scale[j]` — this is per-input-channel, not per-output-channel. The fix is `W_int8.to(torch.float16) * scale.unsqueeze(1)` (or `.view(out, 1)`).
No. The `.to(torch.float16)` conversion is incorrect; INT8 must be dequantized via a dedicated op, not a cast.
Yes, but only when `out == in`; broadcasting fails silently when shapes are different, producing incorrect results without an error.

questions.explanation: Option B is correct; options A, C, D are incorrect. A (Wrong): broadcasting aligns from the last axis. B (Correct): identifies broadcasting rule and the correct fix. C (Wrong): cast + multiply is the standard symmetric-quant dequant. D (Wrong): even when out == in, the result is per-column, not per-row. General context: NumPy / PyTorch broadcasting aligns dimensions from the trailing (last) axis. `scale` with shape `[out]` broadcasts against `W`'s last axis (of size `in`), requiring `in == out`; otherwise a shape error is raised. Even when `in == out`, the intended semantics (one scale per row) is not what broadcasting does — it applies one scale per column. The fix is to reshape `scale` to `[out, 1]` via `.unsqueeze(1)` or `.view(out, 1)`, so it broadcasts across the trailing (in) axis. Option D partially recognizes the trailing-axis alignment but misdescribes the failure mode.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: broadcasting aligns from the last axis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: identifies broadcasting rule and the correct fix.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: cast + multiply is the standard symmetric-quant dequant.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: even when out == in, the result is per-column, not per-row.

assumptions: Symmetric per-output-channel quantization (z=0).
Standard NumPy / PyTorch broadcasting semantics.
nonImplications: Does not imply the fix `scale.unsqueeze(1)` is the only correct way — `scale.view(-1, 1)` or `scale[:, None]` are equivalent.
Does not imply the runtime always raises a shape error when broadcasting fails; when `out != in`, PyTorch raises, but when `out == in`, silent incorrect broadcast occurs.

distractorRationales.D: Partially correct but misdescribes silent-failure mode.

questions.learningObjective: Precisely state the representable value ranges of INT8 (signed) and INT4 (signed) for symmetric quantization.
questions.stem: For symmetric quantization to signed integers, which pair correctly gives the representable range of INT8 and INT4 (using the symmetric convention that restricts the value range to be symmetric around zero, i.e., [-127, 127] and [-7, 7])?

options.text: INT8 symmetric = [-128, 128]; INT4 symmetric = [-8, 8].
INT8 symmetric = [0, 255]; INT4 symmetric = [0, 15].
INT8 symmetric = [-127, 127]; INT4 symmetric = [-7, 7].
INT8 symmetric = [-128, 127]; INT4 symmetric = [-8, 7] (using the full two's-complement range).

questions.explanation: Symmetric quantization intentionally sacrifices the negative extreme (-128 for INT8, -8 for INT4) to keep the range symmetric around zero, mapping the symmetric quantization scale to [-(2^(N-1)-1), 2^(N-1)-1]. This avoids the asymmetry problem that would otherwise complicate GEMM implementations. Option B is the unsigned range (UINT8/UINT4). Option C invents ranges (there is no +128 in INT8, no +8 in INT4). Option D describes the full two's-complement range but is not the symmetric convention used in quantization frameworks (which prefer symmetry).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: +128 does not exist in signed INT8.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: unsigned range, not signed symmetric.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard symmetric quantization range definitions.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: describes full two's-complement, not the symmetric convention.

assumptions: Signed integer format with symmetric quantization convention.
The framework in question uses the standard TensorRT / PyTorch symmetric-range definition.
nonImplications: Does not imply the sacrificed value (-128 / -8) is never used; asymmetric quantization uses the full range but introduces a zero-point offset.
Does not imply symmetric is always preferred; asymmetric gives one more value at the cost of more complex GEMM.

distractorRationales.D: Describes full two's-complement, not symmetric convention.

questions.subtopic: INT4 KV cache / Aggressive KV quantization
questions.learningObjective: Identify the trade-offs of INT4 KV cache quantization vs INT8/FP8 for LLM serving.
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about aggressive INT4 KV cache quantization (relative to FP16 or INT8 KV) are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.profileData:
KV cache footprint (LLaMA-70B, 8K context, batch=1, per token):
  FP16 KV: ~2.5 MB per token → 20 GB per request
  INT8 KV: ~1.25 MB per token → 10 GB per request
  INT4 KV: ~0.65 MB per token (INT4 + per-token FP16 scales) → 5.2 GB per request

Long-context QA benchmark (Needle-in-a-Haystack, 32K context, LLaMA-13B):
  FP16 KV  : baseline accuracy
  INT8 KV  : ≈ FP16 - 0.4%
  INT4 KV  : ≈ FP16 - 2.1%

Kernel support:
  vLLM 0.5+: INT8/FP8 KV production; INT4 KV experimental (dequant-in-register to FP16).
  TensorRT-LLM 0.9+: INT8/FP8 KV production; INT4 KV in preview.

options.text: Kernel support for INT4 KV attention is less mature than for INT8/FP8; some production stacks support INT4 for KV storage only, dequantizing to FP16 in the attention kernel.
INT4 KV cache is always at least as accurate as INT8 KV cache because more scale factors are needed and are stored per-token.
INT4 KV halves the KV memory footprint again vs INT8 (4× vs FP16), enabling substantially longer contexts or higher batch sizes on the same GPU memory.

INT4 KV quantization accuracy is more sensitive to context length than INT8 KV because the coarser quantization step amplifies softmax's cumulative sensitivity; long-context QA / retrieval-heavy benchmarks show larger drops than at INT8.

questions.explanation: Options A, C, D are correct; option B is incorrect. A (Correct): kernel-support maturity. B (Wrong): fewer bits = less precision, regardless of scale count. C (Correct): footprint arithmetic. D (Correct): sensitivity to context length grows with quantization coarseness.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: kernel-support maturity.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: fewer bits = less precision, regardless of scale count.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: footprint arithmetic.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: sensitivity to context length grows with quantization coarseness.

assumptions: Per-token or per-head-per-token scaling for KV quantization.
Standard attention kernel with configurable KV dtype.
nonImplications: Does not imply INT4 KV is unusable — it works for many workloads at modest accuracy cost.
Does not imply INT4 KV always yields the theoretical 2× speedup over INT8; kernel overhead and metadata reduce the effective gain.

distractorRationales.B: Overestimates the effect of scale count.

sourceRefs.locator: KV cache quantization: INT8 and FP8 support; INT4 experimental notes

performanceClaim.scope: INT4 KV cache trade-offs vs INT8 / FP16

questions.subtopic: Kernel availability / INT4 across GPU generations
questions.learningObjective: Identify which GPU generations support which quantized Tensor Core precisions and what falls back to software-emulated kernels.
questions.stem: For quantized inference kernels, which of the following are TRUE about hardware / kernel availability across NVIDIA GPU generations? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: INT8 Tensor Cores are supported on Turing (sm_75), Ampere (sm_80/86), Ada (sm_89), and Hopper (sm_90); INT8 GEMM is broadly available via cuBLAS / CUTLASS on all these.
FP8 Tensor Cores debuted on Hopper (sm_90) and Ada (sm_89); Ampere (sm_80) does NOT support FP8 Tensor Cores, and W8A8-FP8 kernels on Ampere fall back to FP16 or software emulation.

For W4A16 kernels, the INT4 weights are typically dequantized to FP16/BF16 in registers and consumed by FP16/BF16 Tensor Cores; this means W4A16 works on any GPU with FP16/BF16 Tensor Cores (Ampere+), regardless of whether that GPU has 'INT4 Tensor Core' hardware.
Because INT4 was deprecated in Hopper's Tensor Cores, W4A16 kernels are slower on H100 than on A100.
Any quantized precision that lacks a native Tensor Core kernel can still deliver speedup as long as the compiler can generate a software-emulated INT/FP kernel on CUDA cores.

questions.explanation: A: INT8 Tensor Cores exist from Turing onward; supported by cuBLAS Lt and CUTLASS. B: FP8 debuted on Hopper (and Ada with the sm_89 subset); Ampere lacks FP8 Tensor Cores, so FP8-labeled kernels there are fallbacks. C: W4A16 kernels dequant INT4→FP16 in registers and use FP16 TCs; INT4 Tensor Core hardware is not required. D is misleading: while the H100 architecture does deprioritize dedicated INT4 Tensor Core paths that existed on Turing/Ampere, W4A16 kernels do not rely on INT4 TC and remain fast on H100 (through FP16/FP8 Tensor Cores). E is false: CUDA-core INT/FP emulation is often SLOWER than the FP16 baseline it tries to beat; 'as long as a kernel exists' is not the same as 'delivers speedup'.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: INT8 TC availability across generations.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: FP8 TC generational availability.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: W4A16 uses FP16 TCs via dequant-in-register.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: W4A16 does not rely on INT4 TC.
optionExplanations.E: Wrong: fallback kernels are often slower, not faster.

assumptions: Standard NVIDIA GPU generation naming (Turing sm_75, Ampere sm_80/86, Ada sm_89, Hopper sm_90).
nonImplications: Does not imply INT8 has the same peak throughput on every generation — Hopper INT8 is faster per SM than Turing INT8.
Does not imply all frameworks expose all precisions — some may require build flags or specific runtime versions.

distractorRationales.D: Ties W4A16 speed to nonexistent INT4 TC dependence.

sourceRefs.locator: Tensor Core precision support by compute capability

performanceClaim.scope: Tensor Core precision availability across NVIDIA GPU generations

questions.learningObjective: Precisely define the goal of KV cache quantization in LLM serving.
questions.stem: In LLM inference serving, 'KV cache quantization' primarily targets which resource?

options.text: Compressing the input token embeddings before they enter the transformer blocks.
Reducing the compute cost of attention by using INT8 Tensor Cores for the KV projections.
Reducing the size of the model weights loaded from HBM during decode.

Reducing the memory footprint of the per-request KV cache (Key and Value tensors stored across decode steps), thereby allowing longer contexts or larger batches on the same GPU memory; and, when the attention kernel reads quantized KVs, reducing attention memory bandwidth.

questions.explanation: In LLM inference, the KV cache is the per-request memory that stores K/V projections across all previously generated tokens; it grows linearly with sequence length. For long contexts and large batch sizes, KV cache dominates GPU memory (e.g., a 32K-context 70B model needs tens of GB per request for FP16 KV). Quantizing KV to INT8 or INT4 halves or quarters the footprint, enabling larger batches / longer contexts. If the attention kernel reads KVs at quantized precision, memory bandwidth also drops. Option B: KV compute is a small fraction of total attention work. Option C: model weights are separate. Option D: input embeddings are separate.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: input embeddings are separate.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: KV compute is not the target.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: model weights are separate.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: memory footprint and bandwidth of the KV cache.

assumptions: Standard Transformer decoder with per-token K/V caches stored across decode steps.
nonImplications: Does not imply KV quantization is free — some accuracy cost is typical.
Does not imply attention kernel automatically supports quantized KVs — kernel-side support is needed.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses KV cache with attention compute.
distractorRationales.C: Confuses KV cache with model weights.

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the accuracy trade-off of KV cache INT8 quantization in long-context LLM decoding.
questions.profileData:
Experiment on a 32K-context 13B LLM:
  Baseline FP16 KV: per-request KV = 4 GB; max concurrent requests = 2 (16 GB budget).
  INT8 KV: per-request KV = 2 GB; max concurrent requests = 4.
  Long-context QA benchmark: FP16 KV baseline exact-match = 42.1%; INT8 KV = 41.6%.
  Same benchmark at 4K context (short): FP16 = 74.3%; INT8 = 74.3%.
questions.stem: The experiment above shows a small accuracy drop for INT8 KV at 32K context but none at 4K. Which is the best-supported reading?

options.text: KV cache quantization error accumulates over the attention softmax as the context grows; at 4K the error is negligible, but at 32K the softmax's sensitivity to small logit changes (compounded over 32K attended positions) surfaces the loss. The trade-off is favorable if the accuracy drop is acceptable and the doubled batch capacity is valuable.
INT8 KV cache quantization is mathematically identical to FP16 for attention; the 0.5% drop is measurement noise.
The accuracy drop at 32K is because INT8 KVs cannot represent long contexts due to a dtype range issue; using UINT8 would eliminate it.
The doubled batch capacity is illusory: INT8 KV storage does not actually free GPU memory since the paged allocator still reserves FP16 slots.

questions.explanation: KV quantization introduces small errors in both K and V; attention amplifies these because softmax normalizes over the whole context length, and small logit perturbations at long contexts can shift attention distribution. The observation that the drop appears at 32K but not 4K is consistent with error accumulation. The trade-off (0.5% accuracy for 2× batch capacity) is often favorable in production. Option B is false: INT8 KV is not bit-exact with FP16. Option C invents a range issue (INT8 quantizes each K/V element with its own scale; range is handled per-element scale). Option D falsely claims the memory savings are illusory; PagedAttention allocators respect the actual element size.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: canonical error-accumulation explanation.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: INT8 KV introduces real quantization error.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: signed vs unsigned integer type is not the issue.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: memory savings are real; allocators honor element size.

assumptions: Per-token or per-head scaling for KV quantization.
PagedAttention or equivalent memory allocator respects the actual quantized element size.
nonImplications: Does not imply INT8 KV is always safe; models sensitive to attention distribution (e.g., in-context retrieval) may see larger drops.
