Does not imply FP8 KV always outperforms INT8 KV — depends on distribution and hardware kernel support.

sourceRefs.locator: KV cache quantization guide with accuracy notes

performanceClaim.scope: INT8 KV cache accuracy vs FP16 at long context

questions.subtopic: KV cache quantization / Attention kernel compatibility
questions.learningObjective: Identify the kernel-support requirements for KV cache quantization to be effective for both memory and bandwidth savings.
questions.stem: For KV cache quantization to deliver both memory-footprint and memory-bandwidth savings in attention, which of the following statements about kernel support are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If the attention kernel is written to consume quantized KVs natively (e.g., FP8 attention on Hopper, or INT8 attention kernels), both storage AND read bandwidth are reduced without dequant overhead.
Storing INT8 KVs but transposing them to FP16 in a separate kernel before attention (an eager dequant) eliminates the bandwidth savings — the same FP16 buffer is then read by the attention kernel.
KV cache quantization requires the model weights to also be quantized to the same precision; mixed-precision (FP16 weights + INT8 KV) is not supported by any framework.

If the attention kernel expects FP16 KVs and the storage is INT8, the kernel must dequantize INT8 → FP16 in registers on the fly; this saves KV storage but adds dequant instructions per attention step (still bandwidth-net-positive because HBM traffic drops).

questions.explanation: Options A, B, D are correct; option C is incorrect. A (Correct): native quantized attention benefits. B (Correct): eager dequant defeats bandwidth benefit. C (Wrong): mixed-precision KV+weight is common. D (Correct): dequant-in-register pattern.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: native quantized attention benefits.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: eager dequant defeats bandwidth benefit.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: mixed-precision KV+weight is common.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: dequant-in-register pattern.

assumptions: The attention kernel is FlashAttention-family (single-kernel over K and V) or paged-attention.
The framework supports per-token or per-block-per-token scaling.
nonImplications: Does not imply FP8 KV is always better than INT8 KV — depends on hardware and distribution.
Does not imply dequant-in-register is free — for very small heads it may become a noticeable fraction of the kernel.

distractorRationales.C: Fabricates a coupling between KV and weight precision.

sourceRefs.locator: INT8 / FP8 KV cache kernel implementation

performanceClaim.scope: KV cache quantization + attention kernel data-flow interactions

questions.learningObjective: Compute the approximate weight-loading bandwidth saving of W4A16 vs FP16 for LLM decode.
questions.profileData:
Model: 7B-parameter LLM.
  Decode step at batch=1: dominant cost = load all weights once, do FP16 matmuls.
  FP16 weights: 7 × 10^9 × 2 B = 14 GB per decode step.
  W4A16 weights: 7 × 10^9 × 0.5 B (INT4 packed) + per-group scales (group_size 128) ≈ 3.5 GB + ~0.11 GB scales.
questions.stem: Based on the memory-traffic estimate above, what is the primary reason W4A16 accelerates batch-1 LLM decode, and by roughly what factor is weight-load traffic reduced?

options.text: Weight-load traffic doubles because per-group scales double the metadata; W4A16 is slower than FP16 for decode.
Weight-load traffic is unchanged because INT4 weights are stored in FP16-sized buffers; the improvement comes purely from INT4 Tensor Core arithmetic.

Weight-load traffic drops by roughly 4× (14 GB → ~3.6 GB including scales); batch-1 decode is dominated by weight loading, so decode throughput improves by close to the same factor, minus overhead from dequantization in registers.
W4A16 accelerates decode by 8× because INT4 uses ¼ the bytes and per-channel scaling gives another 2×.

questions.explanation: Option C is correct; options A, B, D are incorrect. A (Wrong): per-group scales add ~3% not 100%. B (Wrong): INT4 storage is packed. C (Correct): 4× traffic reduction + accurate accounting of scales. D (Wrong): fabricated 8× argument. General context: INT4 weights use 0.5 bytes/param vs FP16's 2 bytes — a 4× reduction. Per-group scales at group_size 128 add ~1/32 of the FP16 weight size (one FP16 scale per 128 INT4 weights ≈ 0.5 bit per weight in scale metadata), so total is ~3.6 GB vs 14 GB. Batch-1 decode is bandwidth-bound (kernel time is roughly bytes_moved / bandwidth); the observed decode speedup is close to 4× minus dequant-in-register overhead. Option D fabricates an 8× that has no basis (per-channel scale saves no additional bandwidth in this context).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: per-group scales add ~3% not 100%.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: INT4 storage is packed.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: 4× traffic reduction + accurate accounting of scales.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: fabricated 8× argument.

assumptions: Batch-1 decode dominated by weight loading.
Group size 128 for W4A16 scales.
The dequant kernel achieves close to the theoretical bandwidth (real kernels reach 70-95%).
nonImplications: Does not imply the full 4× speedup is realized in wall-clock — dequant, scale broadcast, and kernel overhead reduce the effective gain to ~2.5-3× in practice.
Does not imply the same argument applies to prefill or large-batch cases — those are compute-bound and W4A16's gain shrinks.

questions.subtopic: Mixed precision / Master weights / Accumulation dtype
questions.learningObjective: Explain the master-weight pattern in mixed-precision DNN training and the roles of the various dtypes.
questions.stem: Standard mixed-precision (FP16 with FP32 master weights) DNN training on GPU has several dtype roles. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: For FP16 training, dynamic loss scaling multiplies the loss by a factor before backward and unscales the gradients before optimizer step; this shifts gradient magnitudes into FP16's representable range and avoids underflow.

Because BF16 has the same exponent range as FP32, BF16 mixed-precision training never needs FP32 master weights — production frameworks (Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed, NeMo) run the optimizer state in pure BF16 with no accuracy penalty.
The forward pass runs matmuls in FP16 on Tensor Cores; the accumulator inside each matmul is FP32; the output is cast to FP16 for the next op.

The optimizer maintains a FP32 copy of the weights ('master weights') and applies updates to them; the FP32 weights are then cast to FP16 for the forward pass. This preserves accumulated small-magnitude gradients that would round to zero in FP16.

questions.explanation: Options A, C, D are correct; option B is incorrect. A (Correct): loss scaling for FP16 underflow. B (Wrong): BF16 has FP32 exponent range so **loss scaling** is not required — that part is correct in the literature. But FP32 **master weights and FP32 optimizer state (moments)** are still standard practice in production BF16 training (Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed BF16 optimizer, NeMo) to prevent small weight-update underflow into BF16 mantissa noise. Running the optimizer purely in BF16 does incur measurable convergence degradation for LLM-scale training. C (Correct): matmul dtype roles. D (Correct): master-weight rationale.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: loss scaling for FP16 underflow.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: BF16 has FP32 exponent range so **loss scaling** is not required — that part is correct in the literature. But FP32 **master weights and FP32 optimizer state (moments)** are still standard practice in production BF16 training (Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed BF16 optimizer, NeMo) to prevent small weight-update underflow into BF16 mantissa noise. Running the optimizer purely in BF16 does incur measurable convergence degradation for LLM-scale training.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matmul dtype roles.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: master-weight rationale.

assumptions: Standard mixed-precision training as implemented in PyTorch autocast + GradScaler or Megatron / DeepSpeed.
nonImplications: Does not imply optimizer state (moments) are always FP32 — some methods (e.g., 8-bit optimizers, LAMB) use lower precision optimizer state.
Does not imply BF16 always achieves the same convergence as FP32 — very small learning-rate schedules may require FP32.

performanceClaim.scope: PyTorch mixed-precision training dtype roles

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose why per-tensor MinMax INT8 activation quantization collapses accuracy on a Transformer layer with heavy-tail activation outliers.
questions.profileData:
Per-tensor INT8 quantization of LLM linear layer input activations:
  Activation distribution: ~99% of values within [-2, 2]; ~1% of values in [-50, 50] (channel-localized outliers).
  MinMax calibration: threshold = 50 → scale s = 50 / 127 ≈ 0.394 → ~99% of values occupy only ~2 / 0.394 ≈ 5 out of 254 quantization levels.
  Observed effect: post-quantization perplexity increases 3-5×.
questions.stem: Per-tensor MinMax INT8 quantization on this LLM layer collapses accuracy. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.text: INT8 GEMM is mathematically incapable of representing LLM activations; only FP16 works.

Outliers force the per-tensor MinMax scale to be dominated by rare extremes, leaving only ~5 quantization levels for the 99% of activations in [-2, 2]; the resulting resolution is inadequate. Per-channel activation quantization or techniques like SmoothQuant that shift the outlier magnitude to the weights address this.
The issue is a bug in the calibration code; a correct MinMax implementation would automatically handle outliers.
Per-tensor MinMax is the recommended calibration for LLMs; the perplexity increase reflects an inherent property of LLM output distributions and is unrelated to outlier handling.

questions.explanation: The scenario captures the classical LLM outlier problem (documented in LLM.int8, SmoothQuant, AWQ): a small fraction of activation channels have magnitudes far exceeding the bulk distribution, driving the per-tensor MinMax scale up and wasting quantization levels. The fix is granularity refinement (per-channel activation quantization is often infeasible for post-attention activations, but per-token or per-channel-weight + activation-migration strategies work), or algorithmic techniques like SmoothQuant that migrate the outlier magnitude to weights (which can be per-channel-quantized). Options B, C, D are misdirection or misdiagnosis.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: INT8 GEMM works for LLMs with appropriate calibration.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: standard outlier-driven MinMax failure and standard mitigations.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: correct MinMax implementation still fails on outliers; the problem is the method, not the code.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: MinMax is not recommended for outlier-heavy activation distributions.

assumptions: The activation distribution matches the reported profile (99% narrow, 1% wide outliers in specific channels).
Symmetric per-tensor quantization with MinMax calibration.
nonImplications: Does not imply per-channel activation quantization is always feasible — some architectures make it hard to align activation channels across ops.
Does not imply SmoothQuant is the only remedy — AWQ, LLM.int8's mixed-precision fallback, and other methods exist.

distractorRationales.C: Blames implementation for a methodological limit.

sourceRefs.locator: Section on outlier characterization and migration

performanceClaim.scope: Per-tensor INT8 MinMax failure on outlier-heavy LLM activations

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose overflow in FP16 accumulation on a long reduction and explain why FP32 accumulation is required.
questions.profileData:
Kernel: FP16 GEMM with FP16 accumulation, K = 4096.
  Observed output: many INF values in the C matrix; ~5% of elements saturate.
  Rework: same kernel with FP32 accumulator, downcast to FP16 on write.
  Observed output: no INF; matches FP32 reference within 1e-3 tolerance.
questions.stem: An FP16 GEMM with K = 4096 and FP16 accumulation produces INF entries in the output. Switching to an FP32 accumulator fixes the issue. What is the correct explanation?

options.text: FP16's maximum representable magnitude is roughly 6.5×10⁴; accumulating 4096 partial products of moderate magnitude can exceed this range, producing INF. FP32's ~3.4×10³⁸ range comfortably holds the intermediate sum; downcasting to FP16 on the final write preserves the observable output precision without overflow.
FP16 GEMM cannot compute anything mathematically meaningful; the fix is unrelated to overflow and is simply due to numeric library differences.
The FP16 kernel had a bug in its indexing that produced random INF values; the accumulator dtype is irrelevant.
The FP32 accumulator provides higher precision (23-bit mantissa), which somehow prevents overflow because higher-precision numbers cannot overflow.

questions.explanation: FP16's max value is ~65504; a K=4096 reduction of moderate-magnitude partial products commonly grows beyond this range. FP32's much larger dynamic range (~3.4×10³⁸) prevents overflow of the running sum. This is precisely why Tensor Core matmul (HMMA) accumulates in FP32 by default: A and B are FP16, but the multiply-accumulate accumulator is FP32, and the output is downcast on write. Option B dismisses the numerical issue. Option C invents an indexing bug. Option D confuses precision with range (they are orthogonal properties of a floating-point format).

optionExplanations.A: Correct: standard FP16 accumulation overflow argument.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: dismisses the well-known accumulation-precision issue.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: unsupported bug hypothesis.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: conflates precision with range.

assumptions: Input magnitudes are typical for DNN GEMM (values in [-1, 10] range for both A and B).
K is large enough to allow the running sum to grow into the danger zone.
nonImplications: Does not imply FP16 accumulation is always dangerous — for small K or bounded-magnitude inputs it can be fine.
Does not imply BF16 is immune to overflow of downstream operations (e.g., squaring).

sourceRefs.locator: Tensor Core mixed-precision accumulation; HMMA FP32 accumulator

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish post-training quantization (PTQ) from quantization-aware training (QAT).
questions.stem: 'Post-training quantization' (PTQ) and 'quantization-aware training' (QAT) refer to which distinction?

options.text: PTQ is a runtime technique that quantizes model weights on-the-fly during serving; QAT precomputes quantization parameters offline.
PTQ and QAT differ only in the numerical format used (PTQ = INT8, QAT = INT4); the training process is identical.
PTQ quantizes only weights; QAT quantizes only activations.

PTQ quantizes a pre-trained FP model without retraining, using a calibration set to determine scales; QAT inserts fake-quantization ops during training so the model learns weights that are robust to the quantization noise, typically achieving higher accuracy at low bit widths.

questions.explanation: PTQ takes an already-trained FP model and produces a quantized model without further training, using a calibration set to determine quantization parameters (scales, zero-points, sometimes weight-optimization like GPTQ/AWQ). QAT inserts fake-quantization operators into the training graph so gradient descent finds weights that survive the eventual quantization; the model learns to cope with quantization noise. QAT typically wins at low bit widths (INT4 or below) or on sensitive layers, at the cost of a training run. Options B, C, D are unrelated or reversed.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: PTQ is offline (calibration + freeze); this option reverses the training/runtime axis.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: distinction is process, not format.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: both quantize weights (and often activations).
optionExplanations.D: Correct: standard PTQ/QAT distinction.

assumptions: Standard framework terminology (TensorRT, PyTorch, TF-Lite).
nonImplications: Does not imply QAT is always better — for INT8, PTQ often matches QAT accuracy.
Does not imply PTQ is training-free in all cases; GPTQ / AWQ do run per-layer optimization that is not full retraining.

sourceRefs.locator: PTQ context and comparison to QAT

questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the straight-through estimator (STE) in QAT and its limitations.
questions.stem: In quantization-aware training (QAT), the 'straight-through estimator' (STE) is used to backprop through fake-quant ops. Which best describes STE and its limitations?

options.text: STE is only used during inference to accelerate quantized kernels; it has no role during training.
STE is a mathematical identity, not an approximation; the derivative of `round` inside the clamp region actually equals 1.

STE approximates the derivative of `round` (which is zero almost everywhere) as identity on the interior of the clamp region, so gradients pass through the fake-quant op as if it were a no-op. This works well in practice for INT8 but becomes noisier at very low bit widths (INT2/INT3), motivating alternatives like PACT or LSQ that learn better step sizes.
STE requires the loss to be differentiable everywhere including at the quantization boundaries; if any input lands exactly on a boundary, the training run must be aborted.

questions.explanation: STE is an approximation: because `round` has zero derivative almost everywhere and undefined derivative at half-integer points, gradient descent needs a workable surrogate. The straight-through estimator treats round's derivative as identity inside the clamp region and zero outside, letting gradients flow to preceding layers. It works well for INT8 QAT and modestly for INT4; below that, methods like PACT (learned clip point) or LSQ (learned step size) reduce STE noise. Options B, C, D misdescribe STE or its scope.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: STE is a training-time construct.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: STE is an approximation, not identity.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: STE as an approximation and its bit-width sensitivity.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: half-integer inputs are handled by rounding; no training abort is required.

assumptions: Standard QAT pipeline with fake-quant ops in the training graph.
nonImplications: Does not imply STE converges to the same optima as full-precision training — some accuracy gap can remain.
Does not imply LSQ / PACT always beat STE — for INT8 they may be indistinguishable.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish round-half-to-even (RNE) from stochastic rounding and identify when each is used.
questions.stem: Two commonly discussed rounding modes for quantization are round-half-to-even (RNE) and stochastic rounding. Which pair correctly describes them?

options.text: RNE and stochastic rounding produce the same values; the only difference is that stochastic rounding uses a random seed.

RNE rounds to the nearest representable value, with exact half-way ties broken toward the even neighbor (IEEE 754 default; deterministic). Stochastic rounding rounds up or down probabilistically in proportion to distance to each neighbor, producing an unbiased estimator that is useful for training in very low precision (e.g., BF16 or FP8 gradient accumulation).
RNE always rounds down (floor); stochastic rounding always rounds up. Both are deterministic.
Stochastic rounding is illegal for quantization because it produces non-deterministic outputs that violate correctness testing.

questions.explanation: RNE (round-half-to-even, also called banker's rounding) is the IEEE 754 default: round to nearest and break ties toward the even neighbor. Stochastic rounding assigns a probability to each of the two neighbors proportional to distance: e.g., a value 0.7 rounds to 1 with probability 0.7 and to 0 with probability 0.3. Expectation matches the true value → unbiased. Stochastic rounding is used for low-precision training (BF16/FP8 gradient accumulation, INT-only training) to preserve small gradient updates that RNE would systematically round away. Options B, C, D misdescribe or forbid.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: they produce different values.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: standard definitions and use cases.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: neither rounds always up or always down.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: stochastic rounding is used in production for low-precision training.

assumptions: 'Nearest' means minimum absolute distance in the target representation.
Stochastic rounding uses a per-value random draw.
nonImplications: Does not imply stochastic rounding is uniformly superior — for inference, deterministic RNE is preferred.
Does not imply hardware always supports stochastic rounding; it is opt-in on some accelerators.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the difference between saturation and wrap-around handling of out-of-range values in integer quantization.
questions.stem: During INT8 quantization, a value exceeds the representable range (e.g., quantize(x/s) = 200 > 127). Which is the correct comparison of saturation vs. wrap-around handling?

options.text: Saturation and wrap-around are equivalent modulo a sign flip; both preserve the underlying signal.

Saturation clamps the out-of-range value to the boundary (200 → 127); this loses information about the extreme but preserves ordinal relationships and is the mathematically-desired behavior for neural-network quantization. Wrap-around uses modular arithmetic (200 → 200-256 = -56); it turns a large positive into a moderately-negative value, which is catastrophic for signal-carrying activations.
Wrap-around is the mathematically-desired behavior because it preserves the exact bit-count of the value.
Saturation is only used for weights; activations always use wrap-around because it is what CUDA integer instructions default to.

questions.explanation: Saturation clamps out-of-range results to the nearest representable extreme, preserving monotonicity of the mapping and avoiding catastrophic sign flips. Wrap-around (two's-complement modular arithmetic) is the default behavior of raw integer arithmetic on most hardware; if applied naively during quantization, it produces values that are semantically nonsensical (a large positive becomes a large negative). Quantization frameworks (TensorRT, PyTorch, ONNX Q/DQ, cuDNN) all use saturation. Options B, C, D are unrelated or wrong.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: they are qualitatively different.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: saturation preserves ordinal semantics; wrap-around is catastrophic.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: bit-count preservation is irrelevant to signal preservation.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: saturation is used for both weights and activations.

assumptions: Standard integer quantization for DNN inference; not a bit-level cryptographic use case.
nonImplications: Does not imply saturation is free — repeated saturation on many activations indicates a scale choice problem.
Does not imply wrap-around is never used — some cryptographic or checksum contexts require it.

questions.subtopic: Scale / Zero point / Basic quantization mapping
questions.learningObjective: Precisely define the scale and zero-point of an affine quantizer and the dequantization formula.
questions.stem: For an affine (asymmetric) quantizer with scale `s > 0` and zero-point `z` mapping real value `x` to integer `q`, which pair correctly gives the quantize and dequantize formulas?

options.text: quantize: `q = round(x * s) + z`; dequantize: `x_hat = (q - z) / s`.
quantize: `q = round(x / s) + z`; dequantize: `x_hat = (q - z) * s`.
quantize: `q = round(x / s) - z`; dequantize: `x_hat = (q + z) * s`.
quantize: `q = round(x + z) / s`; dequantize: `x_hat = q * s - z`.

questions.explanation: The standard affine quantizer maps `x` to `q = round(x / s) + z` where `s` is the scale (larger real range per integer step) and `z` is the integer value that represents real zero. Dequantization inverts: `x_hat = (q - z) * s`. This is the definition used across TensorRT, PyTorch's `torch.ao.quantization`, ONNX QuantizeLinear / DequantizeLinear, and academic literature. Options B, C, D swap operators (multiplication vs. division), swap sign of z, or reorder operations incorrectly.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: multiplication and division are swapped.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: canonical affine quantizer.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: sign of z is reversed.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: order of operations violates the affine structure.

assumptions: Standard affine quantization convention used by ONNX / PyTorch / TensorRT.
nonImplications: Does not imply `z = 0` (symmetric quantization) is always preferred; asymmetric is common for activations.
Does not imply `q` must always be clamped to the integer range; explicit clamping is a separate step.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the SmoothQuant technique: migrating activation outlier magnitude to weights via a per-channel diagonal scaling.
questions.stem: SmoothQuant enables W8A8 quantization for LLMs where naive per-tensor activation quantization fails due to outliers. Which best describes its central technique?

options.text: SmoothQuant applies a global smoothing filter to activation tensors before quantization, low-passing the outliers.
SmoothQuant identifies outlier channels and casts them to FP16 while quantizing the rest to INT8; the resulting kernel is mixed-precision.

SmoothQuant chooses a per-channel diagonal scaling vector `s` and rewrites `Y = XW` as `Y = (X · diag(1/s)) · (diag(s) · W)`; the activation channels are 'smoothed' (outlier magnitude reduced), while the weights absorb the migrated magnitude. Since weights are easy to per-channel-quantize but activations are usually per-tensor, this makes W8A8 tractable.
SmoothQuant retrains the model with regularization that penalizes outlier activations, producing a naturally quantization-friendly network.

questions.explanation: SmoothQuant's core observation: activation outliers concentrate in a small number of channels; per-tensor activation quantization suffers, but per-channel weight quantization is cheap. Multiplying activations by `diag(1/s)` (which requires `s` on their per-channel scale) and correspondingly multiplying weights by `diag(s)` is a mathematically-equivalent rewrite that pushes the outlier magnitude from activations into weights. The rewritten activations are 'smooth' (small dynamic range → good per-tensor INT8), while the rewritten weights have per-channel-magnitude variation that per-channel weight quantization already handles well. Option B describes LLM.int8, not SmoothQuant. Option C invents a filtering-based approach. Option D invents a training-based method.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: SmoothQuant is a mathematical rewrite, not signal smoothing.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: describes LLM.int8's mixed-precision fallback.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches the SmoothQuant paper's central technique.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: SmoothQuant is a PTQ method, not a training modification.

assumptions: The linear layer is `Y = XW` with per-channel activation outliers along X's feature dimension.
Weights are per-channel quantized (standard for INT8 W8A8).
nonImplications: Does not imply the diagonal scaling absorbs the entire outlier — the migration factor `s` is a tunable hyperparameter balancing activation smoothness vs. weight quantization difficulty.
Does not imply SmoothQuant matches every FP16 accuracy — some residual loss is typical, though small.

sourceRefs.locator: Sections 3-4: diagonal scaling and migration factor

performanceClaim.scope: SmoothQuant PTQ technique for W8A8 LLM quantization

questions.learningObjective: Compare symmetric and asymmetric quantization formulas, and identify why symmetric is preferred for weights but asymmetric can help for activations.
questions.codeSnippet:
# Symmetric per-tensor quantization to INT8
def quantize_sym(x: torch.Tensor) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, float]:
    s = x.abs().max().item() / 127.0     # z = 0
    q = torch.round(x / s).clamp(-127, 127).to(torch.int8)
    return q, s

# Asymmetric per-tensor quantization to UINT8
def quantize_asym(x: torch.Tensor) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, float, int]:
    x_min, x_max = x.min().item(), x.max().item()
    s = (x_max - x_min) / 255.0
    z = round(-x_min / s)                # zero-point pinned to represent x=0
    q = torch.round(x / s + z).clamp(0, 255).to(torch.uint8)
    return q, s, z
questions.stem: The two quantizers above map an FP32 tensor to INT8 (symmetric) or UINT8 (asymmetric). Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Symmetric and asymmetric quantization produce identical accuracy on all distributions; the choice is aesthetic.

Symmetric quantization has z=0, so the dequantized value is `q * s` — this simplifies INT8 GEMM because there is no zero-point cross-term to compute. Asymmetric quantization uses the full [0, 255] range and captures skewed distributions (e.g., post-ReLU activations) better, at the cost of an extra bias term in the GEMM.
Asymmetric quantization to UINT8 has a larger representable range than symmetric INT8, so it is always more accurate.
Symmetric quantization is illegal for negative values because unsigned integers cannot represent them; only asymmetric works for signed distributions.

questions.explanation: Option B is correct; options A, C, D are incorrect. A (Wrong): symmetric and asymmetric can differ substantially on skewed distributions. B (Correct): standard trade-off analysis between symmetric and asymmetric. C (Wrong): representable levels differ by 1; accuracy depends on distribution. D (Wrong): symmetric INT8 IS signed. General context: Symmetric quantization (z=0) simplifies the GEMM: `sum_k (a_q * s_a) * (b_q * s_b) = s_a * s_b * sum_k (a_q * b_q)` — no zero-point cross-terms. Asymmetric quantization gives a better fit to skewed distributions (e.g., post-ReLU activations that are always non-negative) but introduces cross-terms of the form `sum_k a_q * z_b` and `sum_k z_a * b_q`. signed 8-bit's 255 (symmetric convention) — this is a small quantization-level count difference, not a systematic accuracy edge.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: symmetric and asymmetric can differ substantially on skewed distributions.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: standard trade-off analysis between symmetric and asymmetric.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: representable levels differ by 1; accuracy depends on distribution.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: symmetric INT8 IS signed.

assumptions: Both quantizers target 8-bit integers with standard rounding.
The subsequent GEMM implementation matches the quantization convention.
nonImplications: Does not imply asymmetric is always more accurate — for symmetric weight distributions, symmetric is optimal.
Does not imply the extra bias term makes asymmetric GEMM prohibitively slow — cuBLAS supports asymmetric INT8 with a manageable overhead.

questions.subtopic: W4A16 group size / Metadata vs accuracy trade-off
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the trade-off between W4A16 group size, quantization accuracy, and metadata bandwidth.
questions.profileData:
W4A16 group-size sweep on LLaMA-7B (perplexity, WikiText-2; lower is better):
  group=32:   4.51   (metadata = ~0.5 bit/param equivalent)
  group=64:   4.55   (metadata = ~0.25 bit/param)
  group=128:  4.62   (metadata = ~0.125 bit/param)
  group=256:  4.85   (metadata = ~0.0625 bit/param)
questions.stem: The perplexity trend above shows finer group sizes yield better accuracy but with rising metadata cost. Which is the correct reading of the trade-off?

options.text: Smaller groups give more scale factors per weight matrix, letting each group's scale track a narrower value distribution — more accurate but with higher metadata bandwidth (still small relative to the weights). The right choice depends on the accuracy budget and bandwidth headroom; group=128 is a widely-used default because it captures most of the accuracy at ~3% metadata overhead.
Smaller groups are always better because more scales mean more information; the metadata cost is negligible and never affects wall-clock.
Larger groups are always better because they mean fewer scales to load; the accuracy differences are measurement noise.
The perplexity trend is unreliable because group size cannot affect model output; the differences must be caused by different random seeds during quantization.

questions.explanation: Finer groups (smaller group size) mean each scale factor covers fewer weight values, allowing tighter fit to local distribution — higher accuracy. But each scale adds metadata: at group=32 with FP16 scales, metadata is one FP16 per 32 INT4 values = 2/(32*0.5)=12.5% overhead on top of the INT4 storage; group=128 gives 2/(128*0.5)=3.125%; group=256 gives 1.5%. The observed perplexity curve captures this trade-off directly. Options B, C are absolutist; option D denies a well-established mechanism.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: standard accuracy/metadata trade-off analysis.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: metadata cost is real, not negligible at small groups.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: accuracy differences are systematic, not noise.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: group size is a fundamental quantization parameter.

assumptions: FP16 scale values (2 bytes each).
Symmetric per-group quantization; INT4 weights.
nonImplications: Does not imply group=32 is always preferable when accuracy is critical — kernel-side handling of many scales can add latency.
Does not imply group=128 is optimal for every model — larger or more sensitive models may benefit from smaller groups.

sourceRefs.locator: Group size ablations in AWQ paper

performanceClaim.scope: W4A16 group-size accuracy vs metadata trade-off

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish weight-only, W8A8, and W4A16 quantization schemes by their memory-traffic and kernel-support profiles.
questions.stem: Consider three inference quantization schemes: (i) weight-only INT4 with FP16 activations (W4A16), (ii) weight-only INT8 with FP16 activations (W8A16), (iii) full W8A8 (weights AND activations INT8). Which statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In W4A16, using an INT4 Tensor Core is required for the speedup; without INT4 Tensor Core support, the scheme cannot accelerate anything.
W8A16 is a compute-bound quantization scheme: it uses INT8 Tensor Cores for the matmul and therefore requires an activation calibration pass to determine INT8 activation scales.

W4A16 primarily targets memory-bandwidth-bound decode where the dominant cost is loading weights; the INT4 weights halve HBM traffic vs. INT8, and dequantization to FP16 in-register keeps the compute in FP16 Tensor Cores.
W8A8 targets compute-bound scenarios where an INT8 Tensor Core kernel is available and delivers higher TFLOPS than FP16; activations are quantized dynamically or with a calibrated static scale.

questions.explanation: C: W4A16's design intent is exactly memory-bandwidth-bound decode; INT4 halves weight traffic vs. INT8 while dequant-in-register keeps compute in FP16 Tensor Cores — INT4 Tensor Core hardware is NOT required (contradicting A). D: W8A8 targets compute-bound cases where INT8 Tensor Core throughput dominates and activations can be quantized cheaply. A is false: W4A16 GEMMs typically dequant INT4 to FP16 in registers and use FP16 Tensor Cores. B is false: W8A16 is weight-only quantization; activations stay in FP16, so no activation-calibration step is needed and the matmul uses FP16 Tensor Cores with dequantized weights, not INT8.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: W4A16 does not require INT4 Tensor Cores.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: W8A16 is weight-only — activations stay in FP16, no activation calibration needed, matmul uses FP16 TCs.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: W4A16 memory-bandwidth logic and dequant-in-register.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: W8A8 use case description.

assumptions: The GPU has FP16 Tensor Core support (Ampere or newer).
The kernel available for W4A16 performs dequant-in-register (typical of Marlin, ExLlama, gptq_gemm).
nonImplications: Does not imply W4A16 beats W8A8 for large-batch prefill (compute-bound); W8A8 can win there.
Does not imply weight-only quantization has zero accuracy cost; it depends on calibration method (RTN, GPTQ, AWQ).

distractorRationales.A: Fabricates a Tensor Core precision requirement.
distractorRationales.B: Confuses weight-only W8A16 with W8A8; the '16' in A16 means FP16 activations.

performanceClaim.scope: Comparative use cases of W4A16 vs W8A8 vs W8A16 on GPU

questions.subtopic: Attention backward / Memory footprint and recomputation
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the peak activation memory of standard attention backward and how FlashAttention-style recomputation changes it.
questions.stem: Consider the backward pass of standard attention O = softmax(Q @ K^T / sqrt(d)) @ V for shapes Q, K, V ∈ [B, H, N, d]. Select all correct statements about activation memory and recomputation. (Choose all that apply.)
questions.codeSnippet:
# Forward:
# S = Q @ K^T / sqrt(d)                # [B, H, N, N]
# P = softmax(S, dim=-1)               # [B, H, N, N]
# O = P @ V                             # [B, H, N, d]

# Backward (given dO):
# Need dQ, dK, dV. Naive requires materialized P (or S).

options.text: FlashAttention avoids storing P in HBM by re-tiling backward: it stores only per-row (m, l) statistics from forward (size O(B*H*N)) and recomputes P block-by-block from Q, K in backward, trading extra compute for a large HBM saving.

In FlashAttention backward, the extra recomputation makes total FLOPs strictly larger than the forward-only baseline; the wall-clock speedup comes entirely from reduced HBM traffic dominating the extra compute.

The naive backward stores the softmax output P (or S) of shape [B, H, N, N] from forward and re-uses it in backward; this dominates activation memory for long sequences (quadratic in N) and is the main reason non-flash attention runs out of memory at long context.

The backward gradient of softmax with respect to logits requires access to the full P matrix element-by-element; there is no way to avoid materializing P in HBM at some point in any correct algorithm.

questions.explanation: Options A, B, C are correct; option D is incorrect. A (Correct): FlashAttention backward recomputation strategy. B (Correct): FA backward is a compute-for-I/O trade. C (Correct): standard attention backward memory footprint. D (Wrong): block-wise recomputation avoids full P materialization.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: FlashAttention backward recomputation strategy.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: FA backward is a compute-for-I/O trade.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard attention backward memory footprint.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: block-wise recomputation avoids full P materialization.

assumptions: Discussion is training attention with standard cross-entropy loss upstream.
'Naive backward' means a straightforward autograd derivation without I/O-aware fusion.
nonImplications: Does not imply that all attention backward implementations recompute; some do checkpoint P.
Does not imply that recomputation is always the best trade; on short sequences, storing P may be preferable.

performanceClaim.scope: Attention backward activation memory and FlashAttention recomputation trade

questions.learningObjective: Compare direct convolution and im2col-based GEMM convolution in terms of memory and compute.
questions.stem: Compare two implementation strategies for a standard 2D convolution: (1) direct convolution kernel that computes each output pixel with its own R*S*C-tap sum; (2) im2col followed by cuBLAS/GEMM. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Both have the same FLOP count. im2col replicates each input pixel R*S times into a lowered matrix (extra memory and HBM traffic), then calls a highly-tuned GEMM; direct convolution avoids the replication cost but requires a custom kernel with careful data reuse. im2col is often faster in practice because the GEMM tail leverages tensor cores well.
im2col strictly reduces FLOPs compared to direct convolution because it removes the redundant multiplications along the receptive field, converting the convolution into an equivalent smaller matmul.
Direct convolution stores overlapping receptive fields once in HBM and streams them per output; im2col requires strictly less memory because the reshaped matrix reuses input storage in place.
Both strategies have the same FLOPs, memory traffic, and peak memory; the choice is purely about kernel implementation complexity and does not affect end-to-end performance.

questions.explanation: im2col does not change the FLOP count of convolution; it rearranges data so a standard GEMM can compute it. The rearrangement replicates each input pixel R*S times, inflating the intermediate tensor and its HBM traffic (a memory cost). Direct convolution avoids this replication but must be implemented carefully to reuse the input across overlapping outputs. In practice im2col + cuBLAS often wins because tuned GEMMs achieve near-peak tensor-core throughput on large matrices, whereas direct convolution kernels are harder to reach that peak on generic shapes. Implicit-GEMM convolution eliminates the explicit im2col materialization while keeping GEMM's tile structure.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: FLOP-equal, memory-different, GEMM-quality-driven choice.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: im2col does not reduce FLOPs; it reorders data for GEMM.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: reverses the memory relationship; im2col uses more memory, not less.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: memory traffic and peak memory differ significantly.

assumptions: Standard 2D convolution with stride >= 1 and non-trivial R, S.
im2col produces a [N*H_out*W_out, C*R*S] matrix multiplied by a [C*R*S, K] weight matrix.
nonImplications: Does not imply im2col is always faster; small tensor sizes or unusual strides may favor direct or FFT-based convolutions.
Does not imply Winograd convolution is equivalent to im2col; Winograd trades multiplications for additions via linear transforms and does change FLOP count.

sourceRefs.locator: Convolution kernels — direct and lowered variants

performanceClaim.scope: Direct convolution vs im2col-GEMM trade-off

questions.learningObjective: Characterize the embedding lookup as a gather kernel and identify its memory access pattern.
questions.stem: The input embedding layer takes an int64 index tensor [B, N] and gathers rows from a weight table [V, D] (vocabulary V, hidden dim D). Which characterization of this kernel is correct?

options.text: It is a random-access read of individual elements: for each output element out[b, n, d] the kernel reads a single scalar table[idx[b,n], d], so global memory transactions are uncoalesced by design and the kernel is latency-bound.

It is functionally equivalent to a GEMM between a one-hot [B, N, V] input and the [V, D] table; a good implementation actually forms this one-hot and calls a sparse-GEMM primitive, which is faster than a hand-written gather kernel.
It is a reduction kernel that sums the embedding rows selected by all B*N indices; the output is [D] per batch item, and the runtime is dominated by the reduction depth log2(B*N).

It is a gather kernel with irregular but coalesced-per-row access: each of the B*N indices induces one contiguous read of D floats from the [V, D] table. FLOPs are zero; runtime is bandwidth-bound on the D-element rows read from the embedding table.

questions.explanation: Input embedding = weight[indices[b, n]] gives a [B, N, D] output. Each of the B*N indices induces one contiguous read of D floats from the corresponding row of weight[V, D]. Within a warp, threads collaboratively load a single row (or a subset of rows) with coalesced accesses per row, but the row selection across warps is irregular. Zero FLOPs; strictly bandwidth-bound on the D bytes per index. The output side is also a coalesced write of D elements per token.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: within a row, threads read contiguous D floats — coalesced. Only the choice of row is data-dependent.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no framework materializes the one-hot; the gather primitive is far more efficient.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: embedding is a gather, not a reduction; the output has shape [B, N, D], not [D].
optionExplanations.D: Correct: gather with per-row coalesced access.

assumptions: Standard row-major embedding weight [V, D].
Warps cooperatively load a row rather than each thread choosing a different row.
nonImplications: Does not imply the backward is also just a gather; it is a scatter-add / segment-sum on the weight gradient.
Does not imply that embedding lookup is always the bottleneck; on modern LLMs it is typically a small fraction of runtime.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses row selection irregularity with per-element uncoalesced access.

performanceClaim.scope: Embedding lookup as a bandwidth-bound gather kernel

questions.subtopic: GEMM epilogue fusion / Bias + activation + norm
questions.learningObjective: Reason about which operations can be fused as a GEMM epilogue and what the HBM-traffic benefit is.
questions.stem: A GEMM Y = X @ W is followed by (i) bias add, (ii) elementwise activation (GELU), (iii) RMSNorm along the last axis. Select all statements about fusing these into a GEMM epilogue that are correct. (Choose all that apply.)
questions.codeSnippet:
# Sequence to fuse:
# Y0 = X @ W                              # GEMM
# Y1 = Y0 + bias                          # (i) bias add, per-row broadcast
# Y2 = gelu(Y1)                           # (ii) elementwise activation
# Y3 = rmsnorm(Y2, gamma)                 # (iii) reduction across last axis + normalize

options.text: Fusing the epilogue removes tensor-core benefit because tensor cores can only accumulate into registers, and any epilogue instruction moves the accumulator to shared memory first, forcing a synchronous barrier that undoes the tensor-core throughput advantage.

(i) bias add and (ii) elementwise activation fuse naturally as a GEMM epilogue because they are pure elementwise transforms on the accumulator tile before it is written to HBM; the fused kernel avoids the intermediate Y0 and Y1 HBM roundtrips.

(iii) RMSNorm fuses as a standard GEMM epilogue in the same way as bias-add and activation, because normalization is elementwise once the running variance is precomputed as a scalar constant of the workload.

(iii) RMSNorm requires a reduction along the last axis (i.e., across the D_out output columns of the GEMM tile), which typically cuts across CTAs unless the GEMM is designed with a full-row tile; in mainstream libraries, RMSNorm is left as a separate kernel or fused only with a specialized 'GEMM-with-row-reduction' epilogue.

questions.explanation: Options B, D are correct; options A, C are incorrect. A (Wrong): tensor-core epilogues are supported natively; they do not disable the tensor cores. B (Correct): standard bias/activation epilogue. C (Wrong): RMSNorm is per-row, not element-independent. D (Correct): RMSNorm needs row-reduction which conflicts with typical GEMM tile decomposition. General context: They act on the accumulator tile in registers before write-back, saving one HBM roundtrip per intermediate.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: tensor-core epilogues are supported natively; they do not disable the tensor cores.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: standard bias/activation epilogue.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: RMSNorm is per-row, not element-independent.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: RMSNorm needs row-reduction which conflicts with typical GEMM tile decomposition.

assumptions: Standard cuBLASLt / CUTLASS epilogue programming model applies.
GEMM tile size does not span the full D_out row of the output.
nonImplications: Does not imply RMSNorm can never be fused with GEMM; specialized implementations exist.
Does not imply that the bias-add saves compute; it only saves an HBM roundtrip.

performanceClaim.scope: GEMM epilogue fusion candidates on tensor-core GPUs

questions.learningObjective: Reason about the memory and compute characteristics of FFT and related transforms as custom operators inside ML models.
questions.stem: A model uses a 1D FFT of length N (with N a power of two) as a custom operator inside a layer. Select all correct statements about this operator on GPU. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: The Cooley-Tukey FFT has O(N log N) compute (versus O(N^2) for a naive DFT); on modern GPUs cuFFT organizes the computation into O(log N) rounds of butterfly operations, each round with a specific stride pattern that dominates its memory access.

FFT of length N reads/writes O(N) elements per round; the compute-to-byte ratio per round is essentially constant (small), which makes FFT of large N memory-bandwidth bound on GPU rather than compute bound.
Because FFT preserves L2 norms (Parseval), it introduces no numerical error and can therefore be treated as a bit-exact linear operator regardless of floating-point precision used.

In ML models, FFT is often used to accelerate long-range convolutions via the convolution theorem: conv(a, b) = IFFT(FFT(a) * FFT(b)); the crossover point where FFT-based convolution beats direct convolution grows with kernel size.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Cooley-Tukey achieves O(N log N) via log N butterfly stages. B is correct: each stage reads and writes O(N) elements with a small constant amount of compute per element, making the operator bandwidth-bound. D is correct: FFT-based convolution's cost is O((N+K) log(N+K)) vs O(N*K) for direct; large K makes FFT competitive (this is the basis of long-range convolutional layers like FlashFFT / SSMs). C is wrong: FFT is not bit-exact; it involves complex multiplications with irrational twiddle factors and accumulates rounding error; Parseval is a mathematical identity in exact arithmetic, not a numerical guarantee.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: O(N log N) with log N butterfly rounds.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: per-round constant flops/byte, hence memory-bound.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: convolution theorem gives FFT-based conv, competitive for large kernels.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: Parseval is an exact-arithmetic identity, not a numerical guarantee; twiddle factors introduce rounding.

assumptions: N is a power of two so radix-2 or radix-4 FFTs apply directly.
GPU has HBM and standard cuFFT-like optimized implementations available.
nonImplications: Does not imply FFT is always faster than direct methods for small N; direct is faster below the crossover.
Does not imply that FFT of a real input equals FFT of a complex input in cost; real FFT is roughly half the cost.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses exact-arithmetic identity with numerical guarantee.

sourceRefs.locator: Chapter on FFT and spectral operators on GPU

performanceClaim.scope: FFT compute and memory characteristics on GPU

questions.subtopic: FlashAttention / IO complexity and backward recomputation
questions.learningObjective: Explain FlashAttention's core algorithmic idea: block-tiled attention with online softmax and backward recomputation of the attention matrix.

requiredFeatures: large SMEM for K, V, S tiles

questions.stem: Which statement most accurately describes the algorithmic contribution of FlashAttention (as an exact attention algorithm)?

options.text: FlashAttention keeps the attention math exact but reorders the computation into K/V-block tiles with an online softmax so the full N x N attention matrix is never materialized in HBM; in the backward pass the attention weights are recomputed from stored (m, l) statistics and Q, K, V rather than reloaded from HBM.

FlashAttention replaces softmax with a low-rank approximation whose rank is chosen per tile, reducing attention from O(N^2) to O(N sqrt(N)) FLOPs while remaining within an epsilon-approximation of exact attention.

FlashAttention prunes tokens with attention weight below a learned threshold (sparse attention) and skips the corresponding tiles; correctness is preserved because the pruned weights are provably below numerical noise for typical language models.
FlashAttention rewrites attention in FP8 with per-row scale factors that let the softmax denominator be computed without dequantization; the FP8 arithmetic is the key to the wall-clock speedup.

questions.explanation: FlashAttention is an IO-aware but exact attention algorithm. It tiles Q, K, V into blocks and computes softmax(QK^T)V per tile using the online softmax recurrence, so the N x N attention matrix S is never stored in HBM. Only per-row statistics (m, l) and the running output O are kept. In the backward pass, S and the softmax probabilities P are recomputed from Q, K, V and the stored (m, l), avoiding an HBM-resident P. This trades a small amount of extra compute (backward recomputation) for a large reduction in HBM I/O.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: exact algorithm + IO-aware tiling + backward recomputation.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: FlashAttention is exact, not approximate; it does not change asymptotic FLOP count.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: FlashAttention is dense and exact; token pruning is a different (approximate) family.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: FlashAttention v1/v2 do not require FP8; the win is HBM I/O reduction, not lower precision.

assumptions: Discussion refers to FlashAttention v1/v2 exact attention (not FlashAttention-style approximate variants).
SMEM per SM is large enough to hold Q, K, V, and S tiles for the chosen block sizes.
nonImplications: Does not imply that FlashAttention is faster than a well-implemented naive attention on very short sequences.
Does not imply that the speedup is uniform across shapes; head dim, sequence length, and batch all matter.

questions.subtopic: FlashAttention / HBM traffic analysis of attention
questions.learningObjective: Compare HBM traffic patterns between naive attention (materialized S = QK^T) and FlashAttention (block-tiled, streamed).
questions.stem: Compare the HBM traffic of naive attention (which explicitly materializes S = QK^T in HBM before softmax and O = softmax(S)V) with FlashAttention over a single (B=1, H=1) head with sequence length N and head dim d = 64. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Naive: O(N*d) reads/writes; FlashAttention: O(N^2) reads/writes. FlashAttention pays more HBM traffic in exchange for constant SMEM usage and lower peak register pressure.
Both algorithms have HBM traffic dominated by loading Q, K, V (O(N*d)) and writing O (O(N*d)); FlashAttention's benefit is entirely from fusing softmax into the matmul, not from I/O.
Both have HBM traffic O(N^2); FlashAttention only saves compute by fusing softmax with the K, V matmul into a single kernel.

Naive attention has HBM traffic dominated by writing and re-reading S (O(N^2)), on top of loading Q, K, V, and writing O. FlashAttention keeps S entirely on-chip and its HBM traffic is O(N^2 * d / M) where M is on-chip memory per SM, reducing to roughly O(N*d) when a full K/V tile fits — much less than naive for large N.

questions.explanation: Naive attention materializes S = QK^T with shape [N, N] in HBM, so it incurs O(N^2) reads/writes for S (plus O(N*d) for Q, K, V, O). FlashAttention keeps S entirely on-chip: for a K/V tile of size B_c fitting in SMEM (size ~M), Q is streamed once per K/V tile, giving HBM I/O of O(N^2 * d / M). When M is large enough to hold K/V for the full computation, this collapses to O(N*d). The gap widens with N because the avoided O(N^2) S traffic scales quadratically.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: reverses the direction — naive is O(N^2), FA is much less.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: naive really does write/read S from HBM; that is the primary I/O cost.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: FLOP count is comparable; the win is I/O, not compute.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: FA's I/O is O(N^2 d / M), naive is Ω(N^2); FA wins as N grows.

assumptions: Standard (non-fused) baseline actually writes S to HBM (as in an unoptimized softmax-then-matmul kernel).
The on-chip memory M is at least large enough to hold one Q tile and one K/V tile.
nonImplications: Does not imply naive attention always materializes S; some implementations already fuse softmax with the S computation but still keep row-wise stats in HBM.
Does not imply that FLOP counts are equal in the backward pass; backward recomputation adds some FLOPs.

performanceClaim.scope: Asymptotic HBM traffic comparison of naive vs FlashAttention

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish claims about FlashAttention that are algorithm-level truths from common overgeneralizations about performance.
questions.stem: Select all statements about FlashAttention that are correct at the algorithm-and-analysis level (i.e., independent of any specific paper wall-clock number). (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: FlashAttention delivers a fixed wall-clock speedup (roughly 3-4x) uniformly across sequence lengths, batch sizes, and head dimensions on all modern GPUs, because it is designed to be independent of hardware configuration.

The backward pass of FlashAttention deliberately recomputes the softmax probabilities block-by-block from stored (m, l) statistics; this recomputation trades extra FLOPs for a much smaller HBM footprint.
FlashAttention is exact (bitwise up to summation-order rounding, not approximate) and does not change the FLOP count of forward attention.
FlashAttention's asymptotic HBM I/O scales as O(N^2 d / M), where M is on-chip memory per SM; the gap versus O(N^2) baselines grows with N.

questions.explanation: Options B, C, D are correct; option A is incorrect. A (Wrong): benchmark_leak — a specific measurement is treated as a universal fact. B (Correct): backward design. C (Correct): exactness and preserved FLOP count. D (Correct): paper's IO complexity result. General context: Speedup depends strongly on N, d, batch, and hardware SMEM.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: benchmark_leak — a specific measurement is treated as a universal fact.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: backward design.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: exactness and preserved FLOP count.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: paper's IO complexity result.

assumptions: 'FlashAttention' refers to the FA v1/v2 exact algorithms.
'Wall-clock speedup' is shape and hardware dependent.
nonImplications: Does not imply FA is beneficial on all attention shapes; very small N may not benefit.
Does not imply FA is the endpoint of attention optimization; ring/tree/sparse variants extend it.

distractorRationales.A: Turns a benchmark number into a universal claim.

sourceRefs.locator: Sec 3.2 IO complexity; Sec 4 experiments (scope of numbers)

performanceClaim.scope: Algorithm-level properties of FlashAttention

questions.learningObjective: Reason about which parts of an MLP block can be fused into a single GPU kernel and where the fusion boundary lies for a Fused-QKV/-MLP style optimization.
questions.stem: A standard MLP block computes y = down(activation(up(x))) with intermediate size F. For x shape [B, N, D] and F > D, which fusion strategy is most consistent with how modern LLM inference kernels are structured?

options.text: Fuse up + activation into one kernel (writing intermediate a of shape [B, N, F] to HBM) and keep down as a separate GEMM. The [B, N, F] tensor is written and read once, which is acceptable because the down GEMM is a big matmul that would not fuse with an elementwise activation without hurting its tile design.

Fuse up + activation + down into a single kernel that never materializes the [B, N, F] intermediate in HBM, using a K-block reduction over the intermediate dim to stream partial outputs directly into y. Because F is a reduction dim, this fusion is a producer-consumer along a shared iteration space.

Do not fuse anything: three separate kernel launches (up GEMM, activation, down GEMM) let each op run its optimal tile shape and give the profiler cleaner boundaries; fusion of any pair uniformly slows the block due to register pressure.

Fuse up + down into a single kernel by concatenating W_up and W_down^T into one weight matrix, then apply the activation last. This yields one GEMM with concatenated weights and one final elementwise activation.

questions.explanation: up + activation is a classic producer-consumer fusion: the activation is elementwise on the [B, N, F] intermediate a, so both share the same iteration space and combine cleanly into one kernel. down is a separate GEMM: fusing it with the elementwise activation would force down's tile design to also handle the elementwise transform, and — crucially — down accumulates over the F dimension, so it cannot avoid reading a. Skipping the a materialization to HBM would require a K-reduction fusion that changes down's tiling and is rarely a win for standard MLPs (it is used by more specialized techniques like producer-consumer fused MLP with persistent kernels). The standard, robust choice is: fuse up + activation, keep down separate.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: the mainstream production fusion boundary.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: attractive on paper but hard in practice — the K-reduction fusion changes down's tile design and rarely wins on standard MLP shapes.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: fusing up + activation is a well-known, robust win.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: cannot concatenate weights of different reduction axes into one GEMM (up reduces over D, down reduces over F).

assumptions: F > D so the intermediate [B, N, F] is larger than the input/output.
Standard elementwise activation (GELU/SiLU) that is cheap per element.
nonImplications: Does not imply that no framework fuses down; some specialized inference libraries do implement full-block fusion.
Does not imply that writing [B, N, F] to HBM is free; on very small B*N the fused up+act is memory-bound and might even benefit from further fusion.

distractorRationales.B: Overstates the feasibility of full-block MLP fusion.

performanceClaim.scope: Fusion boundary in an MLP block on modern GPUs

questions.subtopic: Fused kernels / Benefits and boundary conditions
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish real benefits and non-benefits of kernel fusion for transformer building blocks.
questions.stem: Select all correct statements about kernel fusion in transformer inference. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Kernel fusion always improves latency because it eliminates all HBM traffic between the fused ops; there is no configuration in which fusion hurts performance.
Aggressive fusion can hurt occupancy by inflating per-thread register footprint; when register pressure spills to local memory, the fused kernel may be slower than the un-fused version.
Fusion primarily reduces HBM roundtrips of intermediate tensors and amortizes kernel-launch overhead; the FLOP count of the fused operations is unchanged.

Producer-consumer fusion (e.g., pointwise ops on the output of a GEMM) is straightforward, but fusing across a reduction boundary (e.g., across softmax) requires restructuring the tiling and typically only pays off under specific tile-size constraints.

questions.explanation: Options B, C, D are correct; option A is incorrect. A (Wrong): fusion has real costs; not universally beneficial. B (Correct): register pressure can undo the gains. C (Correct): fusion reduces HBM traffic and launch overhead. D (Correct): reduction-boundary fusion is hard and conditional.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: fusion has real costs; not universally beneficial.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: register pressure can undo the gains.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: fusion reduces HBM traffic and launch overhead.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: reduction-boundary fusion is hard and conditional.

assumptions: 'Fusion' means combining multiple logical ops into a single kernel launch.
GPU with register file and SMEM as the on-chip staging levels.
nonImplications: Does not imply un-fused kernels are ever better on typical shapes; when register pressure is fine, fusion wins.
Does not imply fusion decisions are static; auto-tuners typically evaluate multiple fusion configurations.

performanceClaim.scope: Kernel fusion benefit/limit trade-offs on GPU

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the three Q, K, V linear projections are fused into a single GEMM and what the correctness and performance requirements are.
questions.stem: A transformer implementation replaces three separate linear projections (X@W_Q, X@W_K, X@W_V) with a single fused GEMM X @ [W_Q | W_K | W_V] whose output is sliced into Q, K, V. Which characterization is correct?

options.text: Fusing the three projections produces different Q, K, V values compared to separate projections because the shared reduction accumulator introduces cross-projection numerical coupling; the fusion must be disabled whenever bit-exact reproducibility of separate projections is required.
Fused QKV is only safe when H_kv = H (i.e., MHA); MQA and GQA break the fusion because Q has H heads while K, V have H_kv < H heads, so the concatenated weight matrix is no longer rectangular.

The fusion doubles compute FLOPs because the combined weight matrix is [D, 3D] rather than [D, D], turning the projection into a wider GEMM whose runtime is bounded by tensor-core issue rate rather than memory.

Numerically the fused and separate projections are equivalent (up to rounding order). The primary benefit is a single kernel launch and one HBM read of X instead of three; the concatenation of the weight matrices is done offline so W is fetched once for the combined GEMM.

questions.explanation: Concatenating [W_Q | W_K | W_V] into a single [D, 3D] weight matrix and computing X @ W in one GEMM produces the same numerical result as three separate GEMMs (up to summation order rounding). The wins are: one kernel launch (amortizes launch overhead), one HBM read of X (activation is reused across all three output slices), and better tensor-core utilization on a wider GEMM. FLOPs are unchanged. MQA/GQA are handled by concatenating a rectangular [D, D + 2*H_kv*d_head] matrix.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: no cross-projection coupling; each output column is an independent dot product.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: MQA/GQA just concatenate a differently-shaped rectangular matrix.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: FLOPs are 2 * B*N*D*3D total either way (sum of three separate GEMMs = one wide GEMM).
optionExplanations.D: Correct: standard fused-QKV rationale.

assumptions: Weights are stored contiguously as a single [D, 3D] (or [D, D + 2*H_kv*d]) tensor.
The output is contiguous and can be sliced without copies.
nonImplications: Does not imply the fused kernel is always faster; on very small B*N, launch overhead is not the bottleneck.
Does not imply that a fused kernel must also fuse the RoPE / bias-add / attention itself.

sourceRefs.locator: GEMM launch amortization and shared-input reuse

performanceClaim.scope: Fused vs separate QKV projections

questions.subtopic: GEMM / Tile size and shared-memory reuse
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the arithmetic intensity of a tiled GEMM kernel and why larger tiles increase compute-per-byte until register/SMEM pressure caps the design.

requiredFeatures: sufficient register file for M_TILE x N_TILE accumulators

questions.stem: A tiled GEMM kernel uses per-thread-block tiles M_TILE x N_TILE with a K-loop step of K_TILE, staging A and B fragments in shared memory. Which statement about arithmetic intensity is correct?

options.text: Arithmetic intensity is independent of M_TILE and N_TILE because each output element ultimately requires exactly 2K flops and 2K element reads regardless of tiling; tile sizing only affects launch grid dimensions, not HBM traffic per output.

Arithmetic intensity scales with K_TILE, not with M_TILE/N_TILE, because A and B are streamed along K; therefore choosing K_TILE = K (full K in one step) is always optimal for HBM traffic minimization.

Increasing M_TILE and N_TILE raises arithmetic intensity roughly as (M_TILE*N_TILE)/(M_TILE+N_TILE), so larger tiles amortize each fetched A/B row/column over more MACs; the ceiling is set by register/SMEM capacity per SM.

Because the C accumulator is written once at the end, HBM write traffic dominates and arithmetic intensity is determined by the M_TILE*N_TILE / (M_TILE*N_TILE*sizeof(C)) ratio, so increasing tile size reduces intensity.

questions.explanation: For a tiled GEMM, each K-step reads (M_TILE + N_TILE) * K_TILE elements from HBM into SMEM and performs 2 * M_TILE * N_TILE * K_TILE flops. Per-element arithmetic intensity therefore scales as (M_TILE * N_TILE) / (M_TILE + N_TILE). Bigger M_TILE/N_TILE means each fetched A row / B column is reused across more output positions, cutting per-flop HBM traffic. The upper bound is imposed by the register file (accumulator tile) and SMEM (staged A/B fragments) per SM.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: without tiling, each output would re-fetch A/B rows/columns from HBM; tiling raises reuse and cuts HBM traffic per output.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: intensity depends on the reuse of A and B rows/columns across the M and N dimensions; K_TILE = K is usually infeasible and irrelevant to HBM/output intensity.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: this is the textbook tile-blocking result; the reuse factor is bounded by on-chip storage.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: C write traffic is O(M*N), an order below the A*B fetch/compute cost for square-ish problems; larger tiles increase, not decrease, intensity.

assumptions: M, N, K are large enough that boundary effects are negligible.
A and B are fetched from HBM (no L2 residency guarantees).
nonImplications: Does not imply that arbitrarily large tiles are optimal; register spill or reduced occupancy dominates past a threshold.
Does not imply that tile shape M_TILE = N_TILE is always optimal; imbalanced tiles help skinny GEMMs.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses K-loop streaming with intensity source.

sourceRefs.locator: Ch. 5 — Tiled matrix multiplication and reuse

performanceClaim.scope: Analytical intensity formula for tiled GEMM

questions.learningObjective: Explain why GEMV is memory-bound on GPU and how per-row parallelism does not change its roofline classification.
questions.stem: For y = A @ x where A is [M, N] and x is [N], both FP16, what is the correct classification of a well-implemented GEMV on modern GPUs, and why?

options.text: Memory-bound: each output element reuses x lightly (N reads) but A is streamed with essentially no reuse, so intensity is ≈ 1 flop/byte for FP16, well below the ridge point of modern GPUs; runtime is dominated by HBM bandwidth of A.
Compute-bound when N is large: as N grows, the intensity per output row grows linearly with N, so long inner dimensions push GEMV into the compute-limited regime regardless of dtype or memory system.

Compute-bound: GEMV performs 2*M*N flops with M*N loads, giving arithmetic intensity of about 2 flops/byte for FP16, which sits comfortably above modern GPU ridge points and therefore saturates tensor-core throughput.

Latency-bound: the reduction across N introduces a long serial dependency chain on each output row, and this dependency, not memory or compute, determines runtime on modern out-of-order GPU pipelines.

questions.explanation: GEMV reads A (M*N elements) once with no reuse, x (N elements) with M reuses (trivially cached), and writes y (M elements). Total flops = 2*M*N; total bytes ≈ M*N*sizeof(dtype). For FP16 that is ~1 flop/byte — far below the ridge point (~50-100 flops/byte on modern GPUs). GEMV is therefore memory-bandwidth bound; the bottleneck is streaming A from HBM. Parallelism (one warp per row, warp-shuffle reductions) does not change this; it only realizes the memory-bound ceiling.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: matches roofline analysis for GEMV — bandwidth of A dominates.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: intensity does not grow with N; both flops and bytes scale linearly with N, so the ratio is constant.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: 1 flop/byte is well below the ridge point; GEMV cannot be compute-bound on modern GPUs.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: within a row the reduction is a short fixed-depth log(N) tree; runtime is dominated by streaming A, not by reduction latency.

assumptions: A is not cache-resident (M*N is much larger than L2).
The kernel uses efficient row-parallel decomposition with warp-shuffle reductions.
nonImplications: Does not imply that GEMV can never benefit from tensor cores; batched GEMV (GEMM with small N) can, but that changes the problem.
Does not imply that FP16 is always the best choice; INT8 GEMV cuts bandwidth further at the cost of quantization overhead.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses linear scaling with intensity growth.

performanceClaim.scope: Roofline classification of GEMV, FP16 on modern data-center GPUs

questions.learningObjective: Explain what a Grouped GEMM is and why it is preferred over per-expert independent GEMMs in sparse MoE serving.
questions.stem: In a sparse MoE layer with E experts, after routing each expert i receives n_i tokens (n_i variable, sum n_i = k * B * N). Which choice best describes Grouped GEMM and why it is used?

options.text: Grouped GEMM is a Winograd-like transform that combines groups of adjacent experts into a shared linear operator; only the transform + inverse-transform cost per group scales with n_i, so the algorithm reduces FLOPs by a factor of E.

Grouped GEMM sums the outputs of E GEMMs into a single [B*N, F] tensor as part of the same kernel; the 'grouping' refers to the reduction across experts, and the kernel is chosen because it fuses the final combination step of MoE.

Grouped GEMM pads all n_i to the same length n_max and runs a single batched GEMM [E, n_max, F]. It is preferred because a single batched GEMM primitive is always faster than a grouped kernel; the padding overhead is negligible.

Grouped GEMM executes E GEMMs of shapes [n_i, D] x [D, F] as a single kernel launch that dispatches per-group tile schedules across SMs. Compared to E independent GEMM launches, it amortizes launch overhead and lets small n_i groups share SMs with larger groups, avoiding SM under-utilization on skinny GEMMs.

questions.explanation: Grouped GEMM (as in CUTLASS/cuBLAS grouped-GEMM APIs) fuses many independent GEMMs of varying shapes into a single kernel launch. It computes a per-group tile schedule so that SMs can work on tiles from any group in parallel, avoiding the SM-underutilization problem that occurs if you dispatch each expert's small GEMM independently. This is critical for MoE where token counts per expert (n_i) are small and highly variable. Padding to n_max would waste flops proportional to expert imbalance; grouped GEMM avoids that waste.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: fabricates a Winograd-like decomposition; grouped GEMM does not reduce FLOPs.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: grouping is over independent GEMM problems, not over an output-summation reduction.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: padding wastes compute proportional to imbalance; grouped GEMM avoids padding.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: standard rationale for MoE grouped GEMM.

assumptions: Token distribution across experts is variable and often skewed.
Modern CUTLASS or cuBLAS grouped-GEMM APIs are available.
nonImplications: Does not imply grouped GEMM is faster than batched GEMM for uniformly-sized groups; batched is fine there.
Does not imply zero routing overhead; the permutation of tokens into per-expert input buffers still costs a scatter kernel.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses group over problem shapes with reduction across outputs.

sourceRefs.locator: CUTLASS grouped GEMM for irregular problem sizes

performanceClaim.scope: Grouped GEMM utility for MoE with variable per-expert token counts

questions.subtopic: GQA / Compute vs memory trade-off across variants
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish how MQA/GQA affect KV memory, decode compute, and quality relative to MHA.
questions.stem: Select all statements that are correct about GQA (Grouped Query Attention) relative to MHA and MQA. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: GQA is typically found to preserve model quality better than MQA, at the cost of using more KV memory than MQA but still much less than MHA.

GQA cannot be applied to a pretrained MHA model without full retraining, because the arrangement of KV heads is a topological property of the attention operator that is not amenable to post-hoc adaptation.
GQA reduces per-token KV cache to 2 * G * d per layer (G = number of KV groups), which for typical G = H/8 or H/4 gives 4-8x KV footprint reduction over MHA.
GQA reduces total attention FLOPs at inference by the same factor as it reduces KV heads, because each query head only needs to compute attention against a subset of KV heads.

questions.explanation: A is correct: GQA groups H query heads into G KV groups; per-token KV cache is 2*G*d per layer, and typical H/G ratios of 4-8 give the same factor of reduction over MHA. C is correct: this is the empirical motivation for GQA (better quality than MQA at slightly higher memory). B is wrong: total attention FLOPs per token do not shrink because each query head still computes a full Q@K^T against its shared K (the same total number of multiply-adds; only the memory reads are shared). D is wrong: GQA can be initialized from an MHA checkpoint by averaging or replicating KV projections and then finetuned briefly.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: empirical finding motivating GQA.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: 'uptraining' from MHA to GQA is a documented practice.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: canonical GQA footprint formula.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: FLOPs are unchanged; only KV bandwidth/storage shrinks.

assumptions: G divides H evenly; each group of H/G query heads shares one KV head.
Discussion is inference decode compute/memory, not training.
nonImplications: Does not imply GQA always matches MHA quality; it is a compromise.
Does not imply that any G value is optimal; the choice depends on model scale and data.

distractorRationales.D: Confuses memory reduction with FLOP reduction.

performanceClaim.scope: GQA memory reduction and quality trade-off vs MHA/MQA

questions.subtopic: KV Cache / Read-write pattern in prefill vs decode
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the KV cache read/write pattern in prefill vs decode and characterize the resulting HBM traffic per token.
questions.stem: Consider a decoder-only transformer running (a) prefill on an input of length P, then (b) autoregressive decode for T new tokens. For a single attention layer with H_kv KV heads and head dim d, which characterization of KV cache HBM traffic is correct?

options.text: Prefill writes P tokens' KV once (O(P * H_kv * d)) and reads nothing; decode reads the growing cache once per step but does not write, so total KV bandwidth is O(P * H_kv * d + T * (P+T) * H_kv * d / 2) roughly.

Prefill and decode both write and read the entire KV cache every step: prefill because each token attends to all previous tokens, and decode because each step re-verifies previously written entries. Total KV bandwidth is O((P+T)^2 * H_kv * d).

KV cache is never touched in decode; decode only recomputes K and V from the current token and multiplies by all previous Q vectors that are re-read from HBM. Total KV bandwidth is therefore O(T * H_kv * d).

Prefill writes each of the P tokens' KV once and reads the growing cache for the causal attention (roughly O(P^2 * H_kv * d) reads inside a FlashAttention-style kernel this collapses to O(P^2 d / M) HBM).
