Decode writes exactly 1 new KV entry per step and reads the entire current cache (P + t) each step, giving read traffic Σ_{t=1..T} (P+t) * H_kv * d ≈ O(T*(P+T) * H_kv * d).

questions.explanation: Prefill processes all P tokens in one attention call: it writes each token's K, V once (O(P*H_kv*d)) and computes causal attention which conceptually reads all pairs; with FlashAttention this HBM cost collapses. Decode is autoregressive: at step t (with cache length P + t − 1), the model writes one new K, V (O(H_kv * d)) and reads the entire cache (P + t) once. Summed over T steps, decode reads Σ_{t=1..T} (P + t) * H_kv * d ≈ T * (P + T/2) * H_kv * d.

optionExplanations.D: Correct: standard KV cache access pattern.
optionExplanations.A: Wrong: prefill also reads the growing cache internally (attention over previously written tokens), and decode does write one entry per step.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no rewrite; each cache entry is written exactly once when the token is processed.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: decode reads KV cache, not previous Q vectors; Q is recomputed each step from the current token.

assumptions: Standard causal decoder attention (each token attends to all earlier positions including itself).
KV cache is a monotonically growing tensor; entries are written once and never overwritten (except on preemption).
nonImplications: Does not imply that PagedAttention changes the total bytes read, only the memory layout.
Does not imply that MQA/GQA changes this pattern qualitatively — it only scales H_kv.

distractorRationales.A: Denies prefill reads and decode writes.

sourceRefs.locator: Sec 2 — attention memory access patterns in prefill vs decode

performanceClaim.scope: Prefill vs decode KV cache HBM traffic characterization

questions.subtopic: KV cache dataflow / Layout and bandwidth
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the KV cache dataflow during a single autoregressive decode step and its interaction with attention kernels.
questions.stem: Consider one decode step for a batch of B sequences, each of length seq_len (varying). Select all correct statements about KV-cache dataflow inside a single attention layer. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Because decode is memory-bandwidth bound on KV reads, KV cache quantization (e.g., FP8 or INT8 KV) is a direct lever on decode latency, subject to available dequant kernels and acceptable accuracy loss.

The step writes exactly one new K entry and one new V entry per sequence (each of size H_kv * d), then reads the full cache of length seq_len for each sequence to compute attention. Write traffic is small; read traffic is dominated by seq_len.

KV cache must be stored in one contiguous [B, H_kv, MAX_SEQ, d] tensor per layer to enable coalesced reads by the attention kernel; PagedAttention breaks this requirement and therefore has strictly higher HBM latency per attention step.

In MQA/GQA the same K, V pair is read by multiple query heads within a token; a well-designed attention kernel keeps the loaded K/V tile in SMEM and reuses it across query heads, avoiding redundant HBM reads.

questions.explanation: Options A, B, D are correct; option C is incorrect. A (Correct): KV quant is a direct bandwidth lever. B (Correct): standard decode-step KV pattern. C (Wrong): paged layout is not intrinsically slower per step; it addresses fragmentation. D (Correct): MQA/GQA KV reuse across Q heads.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: KV quant is a direct bandwidth lever.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: standard decode-step KV pattern.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: paged layout is not intrinsically slower per step; it addresses fragmentation.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: MQA/GQA KV reuse across Q heads.

assumptions: Sequences of varying length are handled either as a batched-with-mask kernel or via a paged attention kernel.
Standard decoder-only causal attention.
nonImplications: Does not imply PagedAttention has zero overhead; there is a small indirection cost.
Does not imply KV quantization is free; it needs kernels and adds accuracy risk.

distractorRationales.C: Overstates paged overhead; ignores fragmentation benefits.

sourceRefs.locator: Attention kernel KV reuse in SMEM

performanceClaim.scope: KV cache dataflow in decode

questions.subtopic: MHA vs MQA vs GQA / KV cache footprint
questions.learningObjective: Compare per-token KV-cache footprint of MHA, MQA, and GQA and its effect on decode-time HBM traffic.
questions.stem: A transformer has H query heads and head dim d. Which comparison of per-token KV-cache size and decode-time HBM traffic is correct? (K and V each contribute one head dim per KV head.)

options.text: MHA, MQA, and GQA all use H_kv = H; they only differ in how the QK^T scores are shared across heads at the software level and therefore have identical KV footprint per token. The performance difference is entirely due to different attention kernels.

MHA has H_kv = H, so per-token KV footprint (K+V) is 2*H*d elements per layer; MQA has H_kv = 1 (2*d per layer); GQA has 1 < H_kv < H (2*H_kv*d per layer). Decode-time HBM traffic is dominated by streaming KV each step, so MQA cuts KV bandwidth by a factor of H relative to MHA and GQA sits between MQA and MHA.

MHA has H_kv = 1 (one shared K, V), MQA has H_kv = H, and GQA has H_kv in between. The naming follows 'multi' for the multi-headed K/V design in MHA and 'multi-query' for the multi-headed Q design in MQA.
MQA halves KV cache versus MHA (H_kv = H/2) and GQA halves it again (H_kv = H/4); both are fixed ratios and independent of the number of query heads.

questions.explanation: Per-token KV cache is 2 * H_kv * d elements per layer (one entry each for K and V, per KV head). MHA has H_kv = H (each query head has its own KV). MQA has H_kv = 1 (all query heads share one KV). GQA groups query heads into G groups, H_kv = G with 1 < G < H. Decode is memory-bound on KV cache reads, so KV footprint per token is proportional to KV bandwidth per step. Cutting H_kv from H to 1 (MQA) cuts KV bandwidth per token by H×.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: MQA/GQA explicitly reduce KV heads, not just re-share scores.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: this is the canonical definition and consequence.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: swaps MHA and MQA definitions.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: fabricates fixed ratios; H_kv is a design choice, not a fixed fraction.

assumptions: Discussion is about the KV cache of a decoder-only transformer at inference; per-token cache excludes Q since Q is not cached.
GQA uses H_kv = G groups; each group of query heads shares one K and one V head.
nonImplications: Does not imply that MQA is always better; MQA typically loses some quality vs MHA (GQA is the common compromise).
Does not imply that per-token KV footprint alone determines wall-clock latency; batch size and paging efficiency also matter.

performanceClaim.scope: Per-token KV cache footprint under MHA / MQA / GQA

questions.subtopic: MoE / Compute, parameter, and imbalance properties
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish correct claims about MoE compute/parameter efficiency and imbalance from common misconceptions.
questions.stem: A top-2 MoE model with E=8 experts replaces a dense FFN block. Select all correct statements. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: MoE inference is always memory-bandwidth bound because every forward pass must load all E experts' weights from HBM; expert parallelism does not help because it only distributes the weight-loading cost, not the parameter footprint.

The total parameter count scales linearly with E (all E experts have their own weight matrices), and the compute per token scales with E as well because the router must compute a gating score against every expert.
Total parameter count scales linearly with E, but compute per token is roughly constant in E (top-k activated) plus a small O(E) gating cost. This is why MoE gives parameter-to-flop leverage.

In serving, load imbalance across experts is a real problem: with random routing the variance of tokens-per-expert scales as sqrt(B*N/E), which can cause hot experts to bottleneck the batched matmul. Capacity limits or expert-parallel load-balancing are needed.

questions.explanation: Options C, D are correct; options A, B are incorrect. A (Wrong): expert parallelism does help by distributing weights. B (Wrong): overstates compute cost. C (Correct): parameter scales with E, activated compute stays at O(k). D (Correct): routing skew is a real serving problem.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: expert parallelism does help by distributing weights.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: overstates compute cost.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: parameter scales with E, activated compute stays at O(k).
optionExplanations.D: Correct: routing skew is a real serving problem.

assumptions: Top-k MoE with k << E.
Routing is roughly balanced under normal training; imbalance is a corner case, not the norm.
nonImplications: Does not imply MoE is always faster than dense at equal parameter count; imbalance and communication overheads can eat the win.
Does not imply MoE quality equals dense at equal parameter count; it usually differs.

performanceClaim.scope: MoE compute/parameter/routing properties

questions.learningObjective: Describe the MoE routing pipeline: gating, top-k expert selection, and token dispatch to experts.
questions.stem: In a top-k MoE MLP layer with E experts, each token is routed to k experts based on a gating network. Which description of the dataflow is correct?

options.text: The gate produces scores over the E experts per token; top-k experts (typically k=2) are selected and each token contributes to those k experts' input batches with weights = softmax over the top-k scores. Only the k selected experts run their MLP on that token, and outputs are combined by the gate weights. Load balancing across experts is enforced by auxiliary losses / capacity limits.

The gating network selects a single expert per token; multi-expert (top-k > 1) MoE always requires k independent forward passes through the full MLP block, because token-to-expert routing is not amenable to batched execution.

The gate produces per-expert probabilities for each token; every token is routed to the expert with highest probability, and its output is scaled by that probability. The scaling is what preserves gradient flow through the routing decision.

Every token is sent to every expert; the gating scores are used only as a soft mask on the outputs so that experts with score 0 contribute nothing. The 'sparsity' of MoE is entirely about the sum of gating weights, not about avoided compute.

questions.explanation: Top-k MoE (as in Switch Transformer, Mixtral) computes gating scores g = x @ W_gate of shape [B*N, E], selects the top-k experts per token, and normalizes the k selected scores (softmax over the k) to get combining weights. Each token is dispatched to k expert input batches; each expert runs a standard MLP over the tokens routed to it. Outputs from the k experts are combined by the normalized gate weights. Load balancing is a serious concern (some experts get too many tokens) and is addressed via auxiliary losses in training and capacity factors / dropping in serving.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: canonical top-k MoE routing.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: k > 1 does not force k passes; a single grouped dispatch handles all k slots.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: describes top-1 MoE only and mischaracterizes the scaling role.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: sparsity means skipped compute; not every expert runs on every token.

assumptions: Discussion is of top-k sparse MoE at inference or training, not dense mixture.
Capacity limits and drop policies are implementation details not affecting the routing definition.
nonImplications: Does not imply MoE always improves throughput; imbalance and communication (in TP/EP) can hurt.
Does not imply that all-to-all is the only dispatch method; token-shuffle and grouped-GEMM approaches exist.

performanceClaim.scope: Top-k MoE routing and dispatch dataflow

questions.learningObjective: State the online softmax update rules that let a single-pass streaming algorithm compute exact softmax over a partitioned row.
questions.stem: An online softmax algorithm streams over a row in tiles B_1, B_2, .... After processing tile B_t it maintains a running max m_t and a running denominator d_t such that d_t = sum_{i in B_1..t} exp(x_i - m_t). Which update rule is correct when a new tile B_{t+1} arrives with local max m' and local denominator d' = sum_{i in B_{t+1}} exp(x_i - m')?
questions.codeSnippet:
# State after tile t:  m_t (running max), d_t = sum_{i<=t} exp(x_i - m_t)
# New tile stats:      m' = max over B_{t+1};   d' = sum_{i in B_{t+1}} exp(x_i - m')
# We want:             m_{t+1} = max(m_t, m'),  d_{t+1} = sum_{i<=t+1} exp(x_i - m_{t+1})

options.text: m_{t+1} = max(m_t, m') ; d_{t+1} = d_t * exp(m_t - m_{t+1}) + d' * exp(m' - m_{t+1})  (both partial denominators are rescaled by the exponential of the difference between their old reference max and the new global max.)
m_{t+1} = max(m_t, m') ; d_{t+1} = d_t + d'  (the max is the elementwise maximum; the denominator combines by simple addition because both partial sums are already normalized.)

m_{t+1} = max(m_t, m') ; d_{t+1} = d_t + d' * exp(m' - m_{t+1})  (only the new tile's denominator needs a correction factor because the old running sum was already normalized to the true maximum seen so far.)
m_{t+1} = m_t + m' ; d_{t+1} = d_t + d'  (sum both running max and denominator to preserve the streaming invariant.)

questions.explanation: d_t was accumulated with reference max m_t. If m_{t+1} > m_t, every term in d_t must be re-referenced: exp(x_i - m_t) = exp(x_i - m_{t+1}) * exp(m_{t+1} - m_t)^{-1}, so d_t is rescaled by exp(m_t - m_{t+1}) (which is <= 1). Symmetrically d' is rescaled by exp(m' - m_{t+1}). Summing gives the correct d_{t+1} = sum_{i<=t+1} exp(x_i - m_{t+1}). This is the identity that lets FlashAttention (and any tiled softmax) work in a single pass with exact results.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: both partial denominators are rescaled to the new global max.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: without rescaling, the sums use different reference maxes and are incomparable.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: only rescaling the new tile leaves the old sum on a stale reference; the old d_t also needs a rescale unless m_t is already the new global max.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: max is not additive; adding running maxes yields nonsense.

assumptions: All exp arguments (x_i - m_{t+1}) are non-positive so no overflow.
Sufficient accumulation precision (typically FP32).
nonImplications: Does not imply that online softmax is faster than a two-pass safe softmax on all hardware; it is faster mainly when reloading the row would be expensive (attention).
Does not imply that the algorithm avoids all rounding differences from summation order.

questions.subtopic: Reduction / Warp shuffle vs shared-memory tree
questions.learningObjective: Compare warp-shuffle intra-warp reductions with shared-memory tree reductions for a per-block sum.
questions.stem: A CUDA kernel needs to sum an array of length N per thread block (block size 256, 8 warps of 32 threads). Which implementation strategy is standard and correct?

options.text: Strategy Y is preferred: shared-memory tree with __syncthreads() barriers is the most portable and typically fastest option because it avoids shuffle latency, and the cost of 8 barriers is amortized over N reads.

Strategy X is preferred: __shfl_down_sync reduces within a warp in log2(32) = 5 cycles without SMEM or barriers, then the 8 warp-level partial sums are written to SMEM and reduced by one warp with another shuffle. This is the standard 'warp-shuffle + shared' pattern and is faster than a pure SMEM tree.

Strategy Z (atomicAdd from every thread) is preferred: modern GPUs have hardware-level atomic aggregation that makes this the fastest path; it also avoids the need for shared memory and barriers entirely.
All three strategies produce bit-identical results in FP32 because the number of additions is the same; the choice is purely stylistic and has no measurable performance impact.

questions.explanation: The canonical CUDA block-reduce pattern is (1) each thread accumulates its partial sum, (2) reduce within a warp using __shfl_down_sync (log2(32) = 5 steps, no SMEM, no barrier), (3) lane 0 of each warp writes its partial to SMEM, (4) one __syncthreads(), (5) the first warp loads the 8 SMEM values and reduces again with __shfl_down_sync. This is faster than a pure SMEM tree because shuffles have lower latency than SMEM round-trips, and it uses far less SMEM. atomicAdd from every thread is contention-prone and much slower for dense reductions.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: pure SMEM tree needs multiple __syncthreads() and is slower than the shuffle-based pattern.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: the standard warp-shuffle + SMEM combo.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: high-contention block-wide atomicAdd is slow for dense reductions.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: FP addition is non-associative; different reduction orders produce different rounding.

assumptions: Reduction is over FP32 or integer values; the strategy generalizes to FP16 with FP32 accumulate.
Block size is a multiple of 32 (warpSize).
nonImplications: Does not imply that shuffles are always faster; a very large per-thread partial that is already in registers dominates whichever cross-thread strategy is chosen.
Does not imply that atomicAdd is always bad; for sparse or one-value-per-warp write-back, atomics are fine.

performanceClaim.scope: Block-wide sum reduction pattern on CUDA GPUs

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish correct claims about RMSNorm's compute pattern from common overgeneralizations.
questions.stem: Select all correct statements about RMSNorm y = x * rsqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * g. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: RMSNorm is memory-bandwidth bound in practice: for a row of length N, the kernel reads N x-values and 1 weight tensor once, writes N y-values once, and performs O(N) elementwise operations plus one reduction — the reduction and rsqrt are negligible relative to HBM traffic on modern hardware.
RMSNorm requires a single reduction (E[x^2]) over the normalization axis and no mean subtraction; per-element compute is fewer ops than LayerNorm.
RMSNorm is compute-bound on modern GPUs because the rsqrt and elementwise scaling per element are expensive relative to the memory bandwidth used.
RMSNorm is mathematically identical to LayerNorm applied to zero-mean inputs, so it can always be replaced by LayerNorm with the same weights without changing the trained model.

questions.explanation: Options A, B are correct; options C, D are incorrect. A (Correct): bandwidth-bound on GPU. B (Correct): single reduction; no mean subtraction. C (Wrong): intensity is O(1) flop/byte — memory bound. D (Wrong): RMS(x) != sigma(x) even when mean(x) = 0 unless x is zero-mean AND biases match.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: bandwidth-bound on GPU.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: single reduction; no mean subtraction.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: intensity is O(1) flop/byte — memory bound.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: RMS(x) != sigma(x) even when mean(x) = 0 unless x is zero-mean AND biases match.

assumptions: Standard implementations with FP32 accumulation.
Weight g is per-feature (one scalar per feature dim).
nonImplications: Does not imply RMSNorm is equivalent to LayerNorm in trained-model semantics.
Does not imply that RMSNorm and LayerNorm produce identical gradients.

performanceClaim.scope: RMSNorm compute/memory characterization

questions.subtopic: RMSNorm vs LayerNorm / Compute and memory pattern
questions.learningObjective: Compare compute and memory patterns of RMSNorm vs LayerNorm and identify which reduction operations each requires.
questions.stem: Compare a per-row RMSNorm — y = x * rsqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * g — with LayerNorm — y = (x - mean(x)) / sqrt(var(x) + eps) * g + b. Which comparison of reductions and memory is correct?

options.text: Both require exactly one reduction (over the row); RMSNorm reduces sum(x), LayerNorm reduces sum(x^2). Total HBM traffic is identical because both read the row once and write the row once.

LayerNorm requires two reductions over the row (mean and variance) that must be executed in two passes; RMSNorm requires two reductions as well (sum of x and sum of x^2) because rsqrt needs both statistics.

RMSNorm needs one reduction (sum of x^2); LayerNorm can be computed with one reduction (using E[x^2] - E[x]^2) but requires two moments (sum and sum of squares). HBM read of x is once per row in both; RMSNorm skips the mean subtraction and the bias b, giving fewer per-element ops.
RMSNorm requires two passes over x (one to compute mean(x^2), one to normalize); LayerNorm is single-pass because the numerator can subsume the mean in a running formula.

questions.explanation: RMSNorm needs only sum(x^2) to compute rsqrt(mean(x^2) + eps); it does not use the mean of x. LayerNorm needs both mean and variance, but variance can be computed as E[x^2] - E[x]^2, so the two moments can be gathered in a single reduction pass. HBM traffic per row is the same order — one read of x, one write of y — but per-element compute differs: RMSNorm skips the (x - mean) subtraction and does not use bias b. This makes RMSNorm slightly cheaper per element and is why many modern LLMs use it.

optionExplanations.C: Correct: RMSNorm needs one moment (E[x^2]); LayerNorm needs two but can be fused into one pass.
optionExplanations.A: Wrong: RMSNorm uses sum(x^2), not sum(x); mixes up the reductions.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: RMSNorm only needs sum(x^2), not both moments; and LayerNorm can be done in one reduction pass.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: both can be done in a single pass with an appropriate algorithm (Welford or two-moment reduction).

assumptions: The full row fits in one program's registers / SMEM for a single-pass implementation; if not, an online algorithm is needed.
eps is a positive scalar to avoid division by zero.
nonImplications: Does not imply RMSNorm is always faster; both are memory-bound and the difference is small in practice.
Does not imply that RMSNorm is a mathematically identical simplification of LayerNorm; they compute different values.

performanceClaim.scope: RMSNorm vs LayerNorm compute and reduction pattern

questions.learningObjective: Explain the elementwise rotation pattern of RoPE and where in the transformer stack it is applied.
questions.stem: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is applied to Q and K in an attention layer. Which characterization of RoPE's computation and dataflow is correct?

options.text: RoPE is applied to the attention scores QK^T by adding a bias matrix whose entry (i, j) is a function of the relative position i - j; the scores are then softmaxed. Q and K themselves are unchanged.

RoPE is added elementwise to Q, K, and V as a learned position embedding table indexed by position; the addition happens after the softmax so that the rotation applies to the attention weights themselves rather than to the projections.

RoPE rotates pairs of feature dimensions of Q and K by position-dependent angles theta_{pos, i}; it is applied elementwise to Q and K after the QKV projection but before the QK^T score computation. RoPE is not applied to V, and each token's rotation is independent of other tokens.

RoPE is a data-dependent low-rank correction applied to Q, K, V that requires a full reduction over the sequence dimension per token; this reduction is the reason RoPE is expensive to compute in decode.

questions.explanation: RoPE rotates pairs (q_{2i}, q_{2i+1}) and (k_{2i}, k_{2i+1}) by an angle theta_{pos, i} = pos * base^{-2i/d}, embedding position into Q and K such that <RoPE(q, m), RoPE(k, n)> depends only on m - n (relative position). It is applied after the linear projection to Q and K, before the QK^T dot product. V is not rotated. Each token's rotation is a pointwise operation that only depends on its own features and its position, so it fuses trivially with the QKV projection or the attention entry kernel.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: describes ALiBi-style additive bias, not RoPE.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: RoPE is a rotation, not an additive embedding, and is not applied to V or after softmax.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: canonical RoPE description.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: RoPE is pointwise per token; no cross-token reduction.

assumptions: Standard RoPE as in RoFormer / Llama; extensions (linear/NTK scaling) modify the frequency schedule but not the rotation structure.
d is even so features can be paired.
nonImplications: Does not imply RoPE incurs no memory cost; the rotation cos/sin tables must be loaded or precomputed.
Does not imply that RoPE cannot be interpreted as bias; the equivalence to a relative-position formulation is a derived property, not the primary implementation.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses with learned absolute position embedding.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what temperature and top-p sampling do at the logits/probability level.
questions.stem: Which description of temperature (T) and top-p (nucleus, p) sampling for LLM decoding is correct?

options.text: Temperature T scales the logits by exp(T) after softmax; top-p sorts the resulting probabilities in ascending order and keeps the first p fraction of the distribution, then renormalizes.

Temperature T divides the logits by T before the softmax (T > 1 flattens the distribution, T < 1 sharpens it); top-p, after softmax, sorts probabilities in descending order and keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability first exceeds p, then renormalizes over this set before sampling.
Temperature T divides the softmax output by T; top-p keeps exactly floor(p * V) tokens by count (not by cumulative probability) to give an upper bound on the sampling set size.
Temperature T is applied by clipping logits above the T-th percentile; top-p is a synonym for top-k with p = k / V, so the two are algebraically equivalent under this identification.

questions.explanation: Temperature scales logits: p_i = softmax(z / T)_i. T > 1 flattens, T < 1 sharpens, T -> 0 becomes greedy (argmax), T -> inf becomes uniform. Top-p (nucleus sampling) after computing probabilities sorts them descendingly, forms the smallest prefix whose cumulative sum first exceeds p, and samples from this set (renormalized). This lets the effective set size adapt to the distribution's peakedness at each step, unlike top-k which uses a fixed count.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: temperature is applied to logits before softmax, not to the softmax output; and top-p uses cumulative-descending, not ascending.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: canonical definitions of temperature and nucleus sampling.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: top-p is by cumulative probability, not by count.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: top-p is adaptive and not equivalent to top-k with a fixed fraction.

assumptions: T > 0 (strictly positive).
nonImplications: Does not imply top-p and top-k are mutually exclusive; they are commonly combined.
Does not imply that temperature preserves relative rank; T -> inf makes the distribution uniform, losing rank information numerically.

distractorRationales.A: Wrong ordering (T after softmax) and wrong top-p direction.

questions.subtopic: Softmax / Numerical stability via max subtraction
questions.learningObjective: Explain why row-max subtraction is required for a numerically stable softmax and what happens when it is omitted.
questions.stem: The 'safe softmax' formulation is softmax(x)_i = exp(x_i - m) / sum_j exp(x_j - m) where m = max_j x_j. Which statement about this formulation is correct?
questions.codeSnippet:
# Naive softmax
# y_i = exp(x_i) / sum_j exp(x_j)

# Safe softmax
# m   = max_j x_j
# e_i = exp(x_i - m)          # e_i in (0, 1]
# y_i = e_i / sum_j e_j

options.text: Subtracting m makes every exponent non-positive so exp(x_i - m) lies in (0, 1], preventing overflow when any x_i is large; the algebraic identity softmax(x) = softmax(x - c) for any constant c guarantees the result is unchanged in exact arithmetic.

The subtraction shifts the outputs by exp(-m) but this factor cancels in the ratio, so mathematically both forms are equivalent and safe softmax is only needed on integer hardware without native FP exponent range.

The main benefit of max subtraction is preventing underflow of the denominator; overflow of individual exp(x_i) is already handled by IEEE-754 saturation to inf which cancels in the division and yields the correct value.

Max subtraction changes softmax outputs by a constant additive offset; this offset is absorbed by the following LayerNorm in transformer stacks, so safe softmax and naive softmax produce identical logits at the final output only in the presence of a downstream normalization.

questions.explanation: For any constant c, softmax(x - c) = softmax(x) exactly: exp(x_i - c) / sum_j exp(x_j - c) = (exp(x_i)/exp(c)) / (sum_j exp(x_j)/exp(c)) = softmax(x). Choosing c = max_j x_j makes every argument to exp non-positive, so exp(x_i - m) is in (0, 1] and cannot overflow. Without the subtraction, if any x_i is large (e.g. > 88 for FP32, > 11 for FP16), exp(x_i) overflows to inf and the ratio becomes inf/inf = NaN.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: identity + non-positive exponents avoid overflow.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: the identity does hold, but overflow is a real hazard in finite precision; safe softmax is required on FP hardware too.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: inf / inf is NaN in IEEE-754, not the correct probability; overflow is the primary concern, not underflow.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: max subtraction produces identical softmax outputs in exact arithmetic; it does not shift the outputs.

assumptions: Inputs are finite floats; NaN inputs are not addressed by max subtraction.
The reduction uses appropriate precision (typically FP32 accumulate).
nonImplications: Does not imply that safe softmax is exact under all rounding modes; small differences from summation order still occur.
Does not imply that safe softmax removes the need for tiling on very long sequences (see online softmax).

sourceRefs.locator: Sec 3.1 — safe softmax as building block

questions.subtopic: Sparse vs dense kernel boundary / When sparsity pays
questions.learningObjective: Identify when unstructured or structured sparsity actually reduces wall-clock time on GPU, vs when it only reduces FLOP count.

hardwareContext.architecture: Ampere or newer for 2:4 sparse tensor cores

questions.stem: Select all statements that correctly characterize the boundary between sparse and dense GPU kernels. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Any percentage of sparsity greater than 50% in a weight matrix automatically gives a proportional wall-clock speedup on modern GPUs, since sparse tensor-cores dynamically skip zero tiles regardless of the sparsity pattern.

Unstructured sparsity (arbitrary zero pattern) rarely translates to wall-clock speedup on GPU unless density is well below ~10%, because indexing overhead and irregular memory access outweigh the FLOP reduction on tensor-core-driven dense hardware.
Structured 2:4 sparsity delivers a real ~2x speedup on any dtype and any GEMM shape, since the Sparse Tensor Core hardware is dtype- and shape-agnostic once the mask is applied.

For LLM inference, weight sparsity that reduces HBM traffic (e.g., N:M or block-sparse weight formats) is more impactful than FLOP reduction, because decode is bandwidth-bound. However, this only works if a compatible sparse kernel exists for the target dtype.

questions.explanation: Options B, D are correct; options A, C are incorrect. A (Wrong): hardware requires the 2:4 structure; arbitrary sparsity does not get hardware-native skipping. B (Correct): unstructured sparsity break-even point on GPU is very low density. C (Wrong): Wrong (as stated): 2:4 does provide speedup but only on supported dtypes and with dedicated kernels; the option's blanket 'yields real speedup' is unconditional and misleading. D (Correct): decode is bandwidth-bound; sparsity that reduces HBM traffic can help if a kernel exists.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: hardware requires the 2:4 structure; arbitrary sparsity does not get hardware-native skipping.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: unstructured sparsity break-even point on GPU is very low density.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong as stated: while structured 2:4 sparsity on Ampere+ Sparse Tensor Cores can deliver up to ~2x GEMM speedup, this is scoped to (a) supported dtypes (FP16 / BF16 / INT8 / TF32 on A100; FP8 added on H100), (b) sufficiently large M/N/K so the sparse path is dispatched, and (c) accuracy-preserving pruning of the weight to the 2:4 pattern. The blanket 'any dtype and any GEMM shape' claim is an overclaim.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: decode is bandwidth-bound; sparsity that reduces HBM traffic can help if a kernel exists.

assumptions: GPU refers to modern NVIDIA GPUs (Ampere and newer).
'Sparse kernel' means a specialized kernel that reads only nonzeros and their indices.
nonImplications: Does not imply that sparsity never helps; it does at extreme sparsity or with structured formats.
Does not imply block-sparse and 2:4 are equivalent; they trade regularity for compression differently.

performanceClaim.scope: Sparse vs dense wall-clock speedup on GPU

questions.subtopic: SwiGLU MLP / Parameter count and compute
questions.learningObjective: Characterize the SwiGLU MLP block: three linear layers with a gated activation and its parameter/compute compared to a standard two-linear MLP.
questions.stem: The SwiGLU MLP block used in Llama-style LLMs computes y = (silu(x @ W_gate) * (x @ W_up)) @ W_down where W_gate, W_up are [D, F] and W_down is [F, D]. Which characterization is correct?

options.text: SwiGLU has three linear layers (gate, up, down) — 3 * D * F parameters vs 2 * D * F for a standard two-linear MLP at intermediate dim F. To keep parameter/FLOP budget constant when moving from a GELU MLP with intermediate dim F to SwiGLU, implementations typically use SwiGLU with intermediate dim (2/3) * F.

SwiGLU is equivalent to a GELU MLP with intermediate dim F, but requires an extra elementwise multiplication that raises per-token FLOPs by 50% compared to a two-linear MLP with the same F; parameter count is the same.

SwiGLU uses three linear layers (gate, up, down), which triples both parameters and FLOPs relative to a standard two-linear MLP at the same intermediate dim F; to keep parameter budget constant, implementations must halve F when switching from GELU to SwiGLU.

SwiGLU is a bilinear activation between x @ W_gate and x @ W_up; the elementwise product of these two projections replaces the ReLU/GELU nonlinearity but does not increase parameter count over a standard MLP because the gate and up projections share weights via a symmetry constraint.

questions.explanation: SwiGLU introduces a third linear layer (the 'gate' projection) in addition to the up and down projections of a standard MLP, giving 3 * D * F parameters (and correspondingly 50% more compute) at the same intermediate dim F. To keep parameter/FLOP budget matched with a GELU MLP with dim F_std, SwiGLU is typically deployed with F_SwiGLU = (2/3) * F_std. This is the recipe in the original GLU-variants paper and used in Llama.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: three-linear-layer accounting and the (2/3) F rescale.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: SwiGLU has 50% more parameters, not just 50% more FLOPs at same F.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: the ratio is 3/2 (up/gate/down vs up/down), not 3, so F is scaled by 2/3, not 1/2.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: gate and up projections have distinct learnable weights, not tied.

assumptions: The comparison baseline is a two-linear GELU MLP: up [D, F] and down [F, D].
silu(x) = x * sigmoid(x) is the elementwise nonlinearity on the gate branch.
nonImplications: Does not imply SwiGLU is universally better; it is an empirical improvement in language modeling.
Does not imply that the (2/3) F recipe is the only sensible choice; some models pick different ratios.

performanceClaim.scope: SwiGLU parameter and compute compared to GELU MLP

questions.learningObjective: Explain the standard GPU strategy for computing top-k over a large vocabulary and why full sort is not required.
questions.stem: An LLM sampler needs to compute the top-k tokens per batch row over a [B, V] logits tensor, where V is typically 32K-200K and k is small (e.g. 50). Which GPU strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Use a two-stage approach: partition each row into blocks, keep a per-block top-k with a small in-register heap or bitonic-select, then merge the per-block candidates into a single top-k with a final reduction. Total work is O(V log k), well below full-sort.

Sort each row in full with a merge sort or radix sort of complexity O(V log V), then take the top k. This is essentially the only correct approach because partial-selection algorithms cannot guarantee stable order among ties.
Compute softmax over the entire row and then threshold at 1 / (k * V); this yields top-k without any sort because the probability of the k-th largest logit is bounded above by 1/k in expectation.
Top-k is inherently sequential across the V dimension because each selection depends on all previous ones; the only GPU-friendly path is to move top-k to the CPU on a small logits copy over PCIe.

questions.explanation: The standard GPU top-k algorithm partitions the row and keeps a small per-partition candidate set (top-k or top-K' with K' >= k) using a small heap/bitonic selection network in registers/SMEM; a final reduction merges these candidate sets into the global top-k. Total work per row is O(V log k) instead of O(V log V). No full sort is needed. Frameworks like cuDNN, cutlass, and inference engines (TRT-LLM, vLLM) use this pattern. Sampling then usually applies temperature/top-p on the resulting top-k set.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: the two-stage partitioned top-k is the canonical GPU approach.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: full sort is unnecessary and wasteful; log(V/k) work per element is enough.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: fabricates a mathematical relation; softmax thresholds do not give top-k.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: top-k is highly parallel; the partition+merge pattern is the standard.

assumptions: V is much larger than k so partitioning is beneficial.
Ties can be resolved with an arbitrary stable rule (e.g., lower index wins).
nonImplications: Does not imply that a fully sorted output is available; only the top-k values and indices.
Does not imply this is the only correct approach; approximate top-k, radix-based top-k, and heap-based top-k all exist.

sourceRefs.locator: Sort and selection primitives on GPU

performanceClaim.scope: GPU top-k for LLM sampling over large vocabulary

questions.learningObjective: Explain what continuous (iteration-level) batching is and why it improves throughput over static batching for LLM serving.
questions.stem: Continuous batching (also called iteration-level batching, as introduced by Orca and used by vLLM) is compared to static request-level batching. Which description of its main mechanism and benefit is correct?

options.text: Continuous batching runs each request on its own dedicated CUDA stream so that per-request scheduling decisions do not serialize across the batch; the throughput win comes from independent execution paths per request.

At every model-forward iteration the scheduler builds a batch from currently-active requests: new requests can join and finished requests can leave between iterations without waiting for the whole batch to complete. This keeps the GPU utilized despite variable-length outputs.

Continuous batching converts autoregressive decode into a single-pass generation by predicting all output tokens simultaneously with a non-autoregressive draft model; the primary win is bypassing the sequential decode dependency.

Continuous batching packs all decode requests together every step but forbids adding new requests until every existing request has produced the same number of tokens; this uniform-progress requirement preserves batching efficiency at the cost of latency.

questions.explanation: Continuous (iteration-level) batching, as introduced by Orca and implemented in vLLM, rebuilds the batch at the granularity of a single model-forward iteration. New requests can join mid-flight and finished ones leave immediately, avoiding the head-of-line blocking of static batching where the whole batch waits for the longest request. This dramatically improves GPU utilization for workloads with variable-length outputs.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: iteration-level batching runs one shared model forward per iteration; per-request streams are irrelevant.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: canonical continuous batching mechanism.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: describes non-autoregressive generation, not continuous batching.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: uniform progress is not required; that would defeat the whole point.

assumptions: Requests share the same model but can have different sequence lengths and prompt positions.
The scheduler operates at the model-forward-iteration granularity.
nonImplications: Does not imply per-token quality changes; the same math runs.
Does not imply zero overhead; batch composition and KV cache management have some cost.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses batching granularity with stream parallelism.

performanceClaim.scope: Continuous batching for variable-length LLM generation

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish real benefits and limits of continuous batching from common overclaims.
questions.stem: Select all correct statements about continuous (iteration-level) batching in LLM serving. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Continuous batching removes head-of-line blocking under variable-length outputs: short requests exit as soon as they finish rather than waiting for the longest request in the batch.
Continuous batching reduces per-token latency (TPOT) below the batch-1 baseline because sharing weight loads across requests amortizes HBM bandwidth per token.
Continuous batching is only meaningful for MoE models; dense transformers see no benefit because their batch dynamics are fully static.

Continuous batching improves aggregate throughput but does not improve (and may slightly worsen) per-token latency for a single request compared to running that request alone: joining a batch adds interference.

questions.explanation: A is correct: iteration-level batching's canonical benefit is removing HoL blocking. D is correct: continuous batching improves throughput and fairness but a solo request on a dedicated GPU actually has the fastest TPOT for that request; joining a shared batch adds contention. B is wrong: continuous batching does share weight loads across requests (which raises throughput), but TPOT for a single request is bounded below by the total per-token bandwidth cost — joining a batch does not shorten one request's own per-token latency. C is wrong: dense transformers benefit primarily.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: removes HoL blocking.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: throughput up, per-request TPOT slightly up.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: TPOT is per-request; batching cross-shares weights but does not reduce one request's per-step cost.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: dense models are the primary beneficiaries.

assumptions: 'Continuous batching' means iteration-level scheduling.
Standard dense transformer decode.
nonImplications: Does not imply continuous batching solves all throughput problems.
Does not imply continuous batching is beneficial with only one active request.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses throughput improvement with per-request latency reduction.

performanceClaim.scope: Continuous batching benefit/limit boundary

questions.learningObjective: Explain what chunked prefill is and why it improves multi-tenant serving under mixed prefill+decode load.
questions.stem: Chunked prefill in modern LLM serving systems addresses which problem, and how?

options.text: Long prefill requests block decode requests behind them, spiking TPOT for concurrent short-completion requests. Chunked prefill splits a prefill of length P into chunks (e.g., 512 tokens each) and lets each chunk share a model-forward iteration with ongoing decode requests, keeping per-token latency bounded while making forward progress on the long prefill.

Prefill sometimes exceeds available HBM for the intermediate activations of the whole prompt at once; chunked prefill processes the prompt in windows so that only one chunk of activations lives in memory at a time. This is the sole reason for chunked prefill.

Chunked prefill splits the prompt across multiple GPUs via tensor parallelism; each GPU handles one chunk of the prompt independently, and the chunks are recombined at the attention step. It is essentially a form of context parallelism.
Chunked prefill converts the prefill matmul into smaller matmuls that fit tensor-core tile sizes better; the primary benefit is arithmetic throughput improvement of the prefill phase itself.

questions.explanation: Chunked prefill (an SGLang / vLLM / TRT-LLM inflight-batching feature) is a scheduling policy: a long prefill is broken into chunks (typical 512-2048 tokens per chunk) and each chunk is packed into the same model-forward iteration as concurrent decode requests. This keeps TPOT bounded for other tenants while the long prefill makes forward progress. It is orthogonal to how the prefill kernel is written; it is a scheduling / batching decision.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: chunked prefill's role in preventing TPOT spikes under mixed workload.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: activation memory can motivate chunking, but it is not the primary motivation in modern serving stacks.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: describes context parallelism / sequence parallelism, not chunked prefill.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: prefill is already compute-bound and tile-friendly; chunking is about scheduling, not tiling.

assumptions: Serving system supports continuous / inflight batching so a chunk can be co-scheduled with decode requests.
Chunk size is a tunable parameter, typically 512-2048 tokens.
nonImplications: Does not imply that chunked prefill speeds up prefill in isolation; it may slow it slightly due to overhead.
Does not imply prefill activation memory is never a concern; it is, especially for very long prompts.

distractorRationales.B: Names a secondary motivation as primary.

performanceClaim.scope: Chunked prefill scheduling and its TPOT benefit under mixed workloads

questions.learningObjective: Explain when CUDA Graphs help LLM inference and what limitation they impose on batch composition.
questions.stem: Which characterization of CUDA Graphs in LLM inference is correct?

options.text: CUDA Graphs re-order kernels for better cache reuse across a captured region; the primary benefit is fusion of adjacent kernels into a single hardware unit that runs at higher SM utilization than the individual kernels combined.

CUDA Graphs automatically fuse kernels across their captured region into a smaller number of hardware kernels; the fusion is opaque to the user but is the source of the throughput improvement in inference workloads.

CUDA Graphs are only useful for compute-bound workloads; memory-bound kernels do not benefit because their runtime is dominated by HBM traffic, not launch overhead. LLM decode is memory-bound and thus CUDA Graphs provide no wall-clock benefit.

CUDA Graphs amortize per-kernel launch overhead by capturing a sequence of kernels once and replaying it many times. For LLM decode (many small kernels per step), replay eliminates most CPU-side dispatch cost. The limitation is that the shape and memory layout must match the captured version; batch composition changes require different graphs (or falling back to eager).

questions.explanation: CUDA Graphs let you record a sequence of kernel launches once and replay them repeatedly with a single CPU-side submit call. This amortizes launch overhead — critical for LLM decode where each step has many small kernels (attention, GEMV, norms, sampling), often 20-50 µs each with 5-20 µs of CPU dispatch between them. The limitation is capture-replay determinism: shapes, pointers, and control flow must match the captured version. In serving, this forces per-batch-shape graphs (e.g., one per common batch size) or fallback for uncommon shapes.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: CUDA Graphs do not fuse or reorder kernels; they replay them faster.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no automatic fusion; the graph is a fixed sequence of the same kernels.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: many small memory-bound kernels are exactly where CUDA Graphs pay off (launch gaps between them are eliminated).
optionExplanations.D: Correct: launch-overhead amortization + shape/layout constraint.

assumptions: Standard CUDA Graphs API (capture + replay).
Kernels have known static shapes at capture time.
nonImplications: Does not imply CUDA Graphs help every workload; large kernels dominated by their own compute see little benefit.
Does not imply Graphs are incompatible with continuous batching; frameworks typically capture graphs for a set of common batch sizes.

performanceClaim.scope: CUDA Graph benefit for LLM decode and its shape/layout limitation

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose memory-bandwidth-bound decode from profile data and identify effective vs ineffective mitigations.
questions.stem: The following profile is collected for a single decode step at batch size 1 on a Llama-2-13B model on A100 80GB. Which mitigations are consistent with the bottleneck and select those that would concretely reduce TPOT. (Choose all that apply.)
questions.profileData:
Model: Llama-2-13B, FP16 weights.
  Per decode step (batch=1):
    HBM read for weights: 26 GB / step, elapsed 13 ms → effective bandwidth ≈ 2000 GB/s (close to A100 peak ~2 TB/s)
    HBM read for KV cache: 200 MB / step, elapsed 0.1 ms
    SM compute utilization inside kernels: 22%
    Kernel launch gaps: ~10% of step time
    TPOT (this step): ~14.5 ms

options.text: Continuous batching that raises the effective batch size (multiple requests decoded together) would amortize the same weight read across all requests, cutting TPOT-per-request substantially when the amortized batch is large enough (moving the operator toward compute-bound).

Adding tensor-core-accelerated math kernels for the MLP GEMMs would raise SM utilization from 22% to near 100% and cut TPOT proportionally, because the low utilization directly indicates undersubscribed compute.
CUDA Graph capture of the decode step would eliminate most of the 10% launch-gap fraction, cutting TPOT by roughly that amount (a modest but real improvement).

Weight-only INT4 quantization would cut weight HBM reads by ~4x, reducing the weight-read time (dominant cost) by close to a factor of 4 and directly cutting TPOT — subject to available INT4 GEMM kernels and acceptable accuracy loss.

questions.explanation: The signature is memory-bandwidth-bound decode: weight reads dominate (13 ms of 14.5 ms), effective bandwidth is already near peak, and SM utilization is low because the kernels are bandwidth-bound. Real levers are (A) reducing weight bytes (quantization) — biggest lever; (B) sharing weight reads across a batch (continuous batching / batched decode); (D) reducing launch overhead (CUDA Graphs) — small but real. (C) is wrong: 22% utilization is a symptom of being memory-bound, not undersubscribed compute; adding math capability does not help a bandwidth-bound kernel.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: amortize weight reads across batch.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: reverses diagnosis; low utilization is expected for bandwidth-bound.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: launch overhead reduction.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: bandwidth-bound → cut bytes; INT4 is the standard lever.

assumptions: INT4 kernels are available and accuracy loss is acceptable.
Multiple concurrent requests are available for batching.
nonImplications: Does not imply INT4 is quality-neutral.
Does not imply CUDA Graphs are compatible with all shape configurations.

performanceClaim.scope: Decode bandwidth-bound diagnosis and effective mitigations

questions.subtopic: TTFT and TPOT diagnosis / Metric decomposition
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose per-metric bottlenecks (TTFT vs TPOT) from serving-side data.
questions.stem: A team observes the following per-request metrics under moderate load. Select all diagnoses that are consistent with the data. (Choose all that apply.)
questions.profileData:
Workload: 4K-token prompts on average, 200-token outputs. TP=1, batch scheduler = continuous batching.
  P50 TTFT: 800 ms
  P99 TTFT: 3.2 s
  P50 TPOT: 45 ms/token
  P99 TPOT: 60 ms/token
  GPU compute utilization during prefill windows: 92%
  GPU compute utilization during pure decode windows: 25%
  KV cache usage: ~85% of budget under steady load
  Preemption rate: 12% of requests are preempted at least once

options.text: P99 TTFT >> P50 TTFT combined with a 12% preemption rate is consistent with head-of-line blocking or queueing under load: new prefills wait for KV space, and preempted sequences pay extra prefill on resume. TTFT tail is largely a queueing / preemption problem.

P50 TPOT ~ 45 ms/token combined with decode-window utilization ~25% is consistent with decode being memory-bandwidth bound (low compute utilization, low SM occupancy per token, but bandwidth spent on weight and KV reads). Adding more compute density would not directly reduce TPOT.
Prefill compute utilization ~92% indicates prefill is memory-bound; the fix is to increase batch size for prefill to reduce arithmetic intensity, since bandwidth is the current bottleneck.

High KV cache usage (~85%) plus a nontrivial preemption rate is a symptom that batch size is constrained by KV memory; MQA/GQA if applicable, KV quantization, or shorter contexts are direct levers to raise effective batch and reduce preemption.

questions.explanation: A is correct: preemptions extend affected requests' TTFT dramatically, showing up as P99 tails. B is correct: decode is bandwidth-bound so low compute utilization is expected; TPOT is set by memory bandwidth, not SM occupancy. D is correct: high KV usage pushes preemption; the direct memory-side levers are MQA/GQA, KV quant, and shorter context. C is wrong: 92% compute utilization means prefill is compute-bound; increasing batch would improve arithmetic intensity if we were memory-bound, but we're already compute-saturated.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: HoL/queueing + preemption explains P99 TTFT tail.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: low decode utilization with bandwidth-bound TPOT is the standard signature.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: high KV usage → preemption → memory levers apply.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: reverses the direction — 92% utilization already indicates compute-saturated prefill.

assumptions: Compute utilization is measured as active-SM fraction inside kernels.
Baseline model is a dense transformer (non-MoE).
nonImplications: Does not imply KV quantization is always safe accuracy-wise.
Does not imply preemption is always fixable within a single GPU; sometimes throughput-preserving preemption is intrinsic.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses utilization direction — 92% = compute-bound, not memory-bound.

performanceClaim.scope: TTFT tail and TPOT bottleneck diagnosis

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish correct claims about disaggregated prefill/decode serving from common overclaims.
questions.stem: Select all correct statements about disaggregated prefill/decode serving. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Disaggregation adds a per-request KV cache transfer between prefill and decode pools; this transfer cost sets a floor on TTFT that co-located serving does not have. High-bandwidth interconnects (NVLink Switch, InfiniBand RDMA) are needed to keep this cost small.
Disaggregation eliminates the need for KV cache entirely because prefill's KV is only consumed by decode via the transfer, so both pools can operate stateless.
Disaggregation improves TPOT under mixed load compared to co-located serving because decode nodes are shielded from long prefills interrupting the decode-step cadence.
Disaggregation reduces total GPU count for a given SLA because each phase's pool can be sized smaller than the combined co-located pool needed to satisfy both metrics simultaneously.

questions.explanation: Options A, C are correct; options B, D are incorrect. A (Correct): transfer overhead is a real new cost. B (Wrong): KV still needed on decode side. C (Correct): TPOT protection. D (Wrong): disaggregation does not reduce total compute; may increase it slightly.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: transfer overhead is a real new cost.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: KV still needed on decode side.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: TPOT protection.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: disaggregation does not reduce total compute; may increase it slightly.

assumptions: Disaggregation refers to physically separate prefill and decode GPU pools.
KV transfer uses zero-copy RDMA over InfiniBand or NVLink.
nonImplications: Does not imply disaggregation is always the right architecture; small clusters may not benefit.
Does not imply that co-located serving cannot mitigate prefill-decode interference (chunked prefill helps too).

distractorRationales.B: Denies KV cache on decode side.

performanceClaim.scope: Disaggregated serving benefits and costs

questions.learningObjective: Explain the motivation and dataflow of disaggregated prefill/decode serving.
questions.stem: Disaggregated prefill/decode (as in DistServe / SplitWise / TRT-LLM disagg mode) serves prefill and decode on different physical GPU pools. What is the primary motivation?

options.text: Different LLMs are used for prefill and decode; disaggregation lets each pool run a model best suited to its phase, improving quality without doubling parameter memory.

Prefill is compute-bound and benefits from high compute density (large batches on high-flops GPUs); decode is memory-bandwidth bound and benefits from high HBM bandwidth per token. Serving them on separate pools lets each pool be provisioned and scheduled independently (avoiding mutual interference), at the cost of transferring KV cache from prefill pool to decode pool once per request.

The two phases have different numerical precision requirements; prefill is run in FP32 on CPUs while decode runs in FP16/BF16 on GPUs. Disaggregation is fundamentally a precision-partitioning technique.

Disaggregation is a security-driven design that isolates prefill (which handles user prompts) from decode (which produces model outputs) into different trust domains; the performance benefits are secondary.

questions.explanation: Disaggregated prefill/decode splits serving into two GPU pools because prefill and decode have opposing performance profiles: prefill is compute-bound (large-batch matmuls), decode is memory-bandwidth bound (batch-1 GEMV per weight matrix). Co-locating them on the same GPUs creates mutual interference (prefill's compute-heavy iterations spike TPOT for decode; decode's small kernels hurt prefill batching). Disaggregation trades a per-request KV cache transfer between pools for independent scheduling, provisioning, and hardware choice per phase.

optionExplanations.B: Correct: prefill/decode asymmetry motivates disaggregation.
optionExplanations.A: Wrong: same model on both pools; disaggregation is about phase-splitting, not model-splitting.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: no precision partitioning here.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: security is not the motivation.

assumptions: High-bandwidth interconnect (NVLink or InfiniBand) is available for KV transfer.
The extra KV transfer cost is small relative to gained scheduling flexibility.
nonImplications: Does not imply disaggregation is always a win; small clusters or short prompts may not benefit.
Does not imply that co-located serving is obsolete; many production deployments still co-locate.

performanceClaim.scope: Disaggregated prefill/decode architecture motivation

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish dynamic (request-level) batching from continuous (iteration-level) batching and diagnose a workload that suffers head-of-line blocking.
questions.stem: A serving stack uses dynamic batching (each 'batch' completes fully before the next batch starts). The following aggregated metrics are observed for a workload with heterogeneous output lengths. What is the correct diagnosis?
questions.profileData:
Server: 8 concurrent requests batched per iteration.
  Output length distribution across a batch: 15, 20, 22, 28, 30, 35, 800, 40 tokens.
  Observed metrics (per batch):
    - GPU utilization during first 40 decode steps: ~78%
    - GPU utilization during decode steps 41 through 800: ~13%
    - Wall time: 800 * ~20 ms = ~16 s
    - Requests 1-7 (short) block waiting for request 8 to complete before returning.
    - New arriving requests wait for the batch to finish before being scheduled.

options.text: This is head-of-line blocking under request-level (static) dynamic batching: the batch is dominated by the single long request, wasting SM cycles on almost-empty batches and delaying shorter requests. The right fix is to move to continuous (iteration-level) batching so shorter requests can leave the batch and new requests can join per iteration.
The workload is memory-bound during long decode; the correct fix is to enable KV cache quantization to speed up decode steps 41-800, which will bring GPU utilization back up.
The bottleneck is compute-bound decode; adding a smaller draft model for speculative decoding will improve utilization by generating multiple tokens per verification step.
This is a launch-overhead problem: 800 kernel launches per decode step create CPU-side dispatch gaps. The correct fix is CUDA Graph capture of the decode loop.

questions.explanation: The signature is textbook static-batching head-of-line blocking: after the first ~40 decode steps, only one request (the 800-token one) remains active, but the batched kernel still runs at effective batch size 1, wasting SM parallelism. All shorter requests are held in the batch until the longest finishes; new requests cannot enter until the whole batch completes. Continuous (iteration-level) batching — Orca's contribution and vLLM's core scheduler — fixes exactly this by allowing per-iteration join/leave.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: HoL blocking under static batching, fixed by continuous batching.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: KV quantization does not address the batch composition problem.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: decode is memory-bound at batch-1; spec decoding helps but does not solve the imbalance.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: launch overhead is not the primary cause; the batch is running one long generation.

assumptions: The reported utilization measure captures effective batch size after short requests are done.
The scheduler is truly static (no per-iteration rebatching).
nonImplications: Does not imply KV quantization or CUDA Graphs are never useful; they are orthogonal levers.
Does not imply continuous batching solves all imbalance; extreme variance still requires additional policies (preemption, chunked prefill).

performanceClaim.scope: Head-of-line blocking diagnosis under static batching

questions.subtopic: Expert parallelism and sequence parallelism / Purposes and dataflow
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish expert parallelism (EP) and sequence parallelism (SP) from TP/PP and identify their communication primitives.
questions.stem: Which comparison of Expert Parallelism (EP) and Sequence Parallelism (SP) is correct?

options.text: EP places different experts of a Mixture-of-Experts on different devices; token-to-expert routing requires all-to-all communication to shuffle tokens to their assigned expert. SP shards intermediate activations along the sequence dimension inside a TP region (e.g., after a norm) to reduce activation memory; SP requires AllGather/ReduceScatter around the sharded region.
EP shards attention heads across experts; SP shards the sequence length across attention groups. Both are Attention-only parallelism schemes and do not touch the MLP block.

Both EP and SP shard the MLP weights across devices. They differ only in whether the shard axis is aligned with expert index (EP) or with sequence position (SP); both require a single AllReduce per MLP block just like TP.
EP is used for training-time load balancing only and has no role in inference; SP is exclusively an inference-time trick that reduces KV cache footprint by sharding along the sequence axis.

questions.explanation: EP (Expert Parallelism, from GShard / DeepSpeed-MoE / vLLM MoE): experts of a MoE layer are placed on different devices; routing shuffles tokens to their assigned expert via all-to-all, and results are all-to-all'd back. SP (Sequence Parallelism, from Megatron): inside a TP region, some ops (norm, dropout) that don't need cross-hidden-dim communication are sharded along the sequence axis instead of being replicated; AllGather/ReduceScatter transitions between SP and TP regions save activation memory. They serve different purposes and have different communication patterns.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: EP = MoE expert placement + all-to-all; SP = sequence-axis sharding within TP region.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: EP is about experts (MLP), not attention heads; SP is not attention-only.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: both are collapsed into an incorrect single collective.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: EP is heavily used in inference; SP is not about KV cache.

assumptions: Standard EP as in GShard / DeepSpeed-MoE / vLLM MoE.
SP is defined as in Megatron-LM's sequence-parallel augmentation of TP.
nonImplications: Does not imply EP and TP cannot be combined; they often are (e.g., TP=8 within a node, EP across nodes).
Does not imply SP is universally beneficial; small models may not need it.

performanceClaim.scope: EP and SP definitions and communication patterns

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose fairness issues in multi-tenant LLM serving and identify levers that improve fairness without collapsing throughput.
questions.stem: Multi-tenant serving of an LLM shows the following per-user metrics under load. Which mitigations would reduce the unfairness without regressing aggregate throughput below the load's floor. (Choose all that apply.)
questions.profileData:
Two tenants share a serving pool:
  Tenant A (short prompts, ~200 tokens; short outputs, ~50 tokens): TPOT p50 = 55 ms, TTFT p50 = 200 ms
  Tenant B (long prompts, ~4K tokens; long outputs, ~500 tokens): TPOT p50 = 55 ms, TTFT p50 = 4.5 s
  Preemption rate on tenant A: 25%
  Preemption rate on tenant B: 8%
  When tenant B has a burst of arrivals, tenant A's TPOT spikes to 180 ms.
  KV usage: ~90% steady, ~99% during bursts.

options.text: Add a fairness-aware scheduler (e.g., token-level fair queueing across tenants): prevents one tenant's long-decoding requests from monopolizing decode iterations.
Enable chunked prefill so tenant B's long prefills are broken into chunks that interleave with tenant A's decode iterations; tenant A's TPOT during bursts drops back near the steady-state 55 ms.
Serialize the scheduler to only run one tenant at a time: this eliminates cross-tenant interference and guarantees fair TPOT to whichever tenant is running.
Enforce per-tenant KV budgets or admission quotas so tenant B's bursty long prompts cannot consume more than a bounded fraction of KV, preventing tenant A's preemption rate from spiking.

questions.explanation: Options A, B, D are correct; option C is incorrect. A (Correct): fair queueing. B (Correct): chunked prefill. C (Wrong): serializing kills aggregate throughput. D (Correct): per-tenant KV quotas.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: fair queueing.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: chunked prefill.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: serializing kills aggregate throughput.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: per-tenant KV quotas.

assumptions: Serving stack supports chunked prefill and per-tenant admission control.
Fair-queueing scheduler is available (or can be added).
nonImplications: Does not imply chunked prefill has zero overhead; there is a small per-chunk cost.
Does not imply admission quotas eliminate all bursts; they cap the worst case.

distractorRationales.C: Kills aggregate throughput to gain fairness.

performanceClaim.scope: Multi-tenant fairness diagnosis and mitigations

questions.subtopic: KV cache fragmentation / Paged vs contiguous allocator
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose external fragmentation in a contiguous per-sequence KV allocator vs paged allocation.
questions.stem: A serving stack allocates KV cache as contiguous per-sequence slabs sized to each request's max_new_tokens. Diagnose the memory behavior described below.
questions.profileData:
Setup: 40 GB total KV cache budget.
  Requests come and go with varying max_new_tokens = 512 to 8192.
  Steady-state observation:
    Sum of active sequences' allocated KV: 38 GB
    Sum of KV actually used by generated tokens: 12 GB
    Free KV memory: 2 GB
    New request (max_new_tokens=2048, requires 300 MB contiguous KV): FAILS to allocate despite 2 GB free.
    OOM error reported.

options.text: This is a bug in the KV cache accounting; free memory shows 2 GB but the allocator sees 0. Fix the accounting by including reserved slabs in the free counter, and the new request will succeed.
This is compute-bound behavior: the OOM is a symptom of decode being too slow to release KV blocks quickly enough. Increasing tensor parallelism will speed up decode and prevent OOM.
This is a data race between the scheduler and the allocator; the fix is to serialize KV cache allocation with a global mutex, which will resolve the OOM at the cost of some throughput.

This is textbook external fragmentation from contiguous per-sequence slab allocation: each slab is reserved up-front at max_new_tokens size, so 26 GB of allocated KV is actually unused (reserved for tokens not yet generated), and the 2 GB free area is scattered in non-contiguous pieces too small to fit any single slab. Paged KV cache (fixed-size blocks + indirection) directly addresses this.

questions.explanation: The signature is classic external fragmentation: allocated ≠ used, and the small remaining free memory is not contiguous enough to hold a new slab. The reserved-up-to-max_new_tokens policy causes internal waste (26 GB reserved but not yet used), and freed slabs of varying sizes create external fragmentation. PagedAttention's fixed-size block allocation with block-table indirection eliminates external fragmentation and only over-allocates by at most one block per sequence.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: not an accounting bug; the memory really is fragmented/reserved.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: OOM is a memory-management issue, unrelated to TP or decode speed.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: no data race; the problem is fragmentation.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: external + internal fragmentation from contiguous slab allocation.

assumptions: 'External fragmentation' is used in the OS memory-management sense: free space exists but not in a single contiguous block.
'Internal waste' is the reservation-up-to-max phenomenon.
nonImplications: Does not imply paged KV cache has zero waste; it does have small per-sequence internal waste bounded by block size.
Does not imply that all fragmentation problems are solved by paging alone; preemption policy still matters.

sourceRefs.locator: Sec 2 — motivation: fragmentation in prior systems

performanceClaim.scope: External + internal KV fragmentation from contiguous slab allocation

questions.subtopic: LLM kernel fusion / Serving stack fused kernels
questions.learningObjective: Identify which fusions are standard in production LLM inference stacks and what each fusion saves.
questions.stem: Which set of kernel fusions is typical in a production LLM inference stack such as vLLM or TensorRT-LLM?

options.text: No fusion is applied; each math op (matmul, add, softmax, silu, mul, norm) has its own kernel launched separately. This gives the profiler the cleanest boundary information and modern GPUs' launch overhead is negligible for LLM workloads.

Fused full transformer block into a single CUDA kernel per layer that computes attention + MLP + residuals together; this is the standard pattern because it collapses all HBM roundtrips of intermediates into a single kernel.
Fused entire model into one giant kernel per forward pass; because CUDA supports variable-shape launches, this scales to any model size without recompilation.

Fused QKV projection; fused RMSNorm (or RMSNorm as GEMM epilogue on the following linear); fused SwiGLU (silu on gate output * up output); fused attention using FlashAttention/PagedAttention that combines QK^T, softmax, and PV in one kernel; fused sampling (temperature + top-k/top-p) at the end of the head.

questions.explanation: Production LLM stacks use targeted fusion: (1) fused QKV projection (one wide GEMM); (2) fused RMSNorm (or fused as an epilogue on the next linear's input read); (3) fused SwiGLU gate*up (elementwise on the up/gate projection results); (4) fused attention (FlashAttention/PagedAttention combines QK^T, softmax, and PV in one kernel keeping S on-chip); (5) fused sampling. Full-block fusion into one kernel is not standard and would require different tile designs than the current tensor-core-friendly ones. No-fusion is a straw man.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: launch overhead is a real cost, and fusion is central to production stacks.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: full-block fusion is not the standard pattern (some research prototypes attempt it).
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: entire-model fusion is not practical or done.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: the actual fusion set in vLLM / TRT-LLM / SGLang.

assumptions: 'Production' means widely-deployed inference stacks like vLLM, TRT-LLM, SGLang.
Fusion decisions target both HBM traffic and launch overhead.
nonImplications: Does not imply every framework fuses identically; specific choices vary.
Does not imply fusion always yields wall-clock speedup on all shapes; some fusions are conditional.

performanceClaim.scope: Standard kernel fusion set in production LLM inference stacks

questions.subtopic: KV cache capacity / Memory budget arithmetic
questions.learningObjective: Compute the KV cache memory footprint of a specific model configuration and reason about capacity limits.
questions.stem: Model configuration: 32 layers, H_kv = 8 KV heads, head_dim = 128, FP16 KV. The model weights occupy 26 GB on an 80 GB GPU. Which computation of KV cache capacity and its implication is correct?
questions.profileData:
GPU: A100 80 GB (usable HBM ≈ 76 GB after runtime/allocator overhead)
Model weights (FP16): 26 GB
Activation + workspace budget: ~4 GB
Available for KV cache: ~46 GB
Model config: L=32 layers, H_kv=8, d=128, FP16 (2 bytes)
Per-token KV = 2 (K and V) * L * H_kv * d * 2 B = 2 * 32 * 8 * 128 * 2 = 131,072 B ≈ 128 KB

options.text: Per-token KV is ~256 KB; the cache holds ~180,000 tokens. If the average sequence length is 2000 tokens, that supports about 90 concurrent sequences before running out of KV cache.

Per-token KV is 8 * 128 * 2 = 2 KB (one KV entry across all layers). The cache holds ~23 million tokens. KV capacity is effectively unlimited for realistic workloads and cannot be a bottleneck on an 80 GB A100.

Per-token KV = 2 (K and V) * L * H_kv * d * 2 B = 128 KB. With 46 GB available for KV: 46 * 1024^3 / 131072 ≈ 376,832 tokens total. At 2000 tokens per sequence, that's ~188 concurrent sequences. Long-context (say 32K tokens/seq) drops this to ~11 concurrent sequences — a direct capacity constraint on batch size.

KV cache capacity is fixed by the model architecture alone (32 layers * 8 heads * 128 * 2 bytes = 65 KB) and does not scale with sequence length; capacity per GPU is therefore just ~700,000 sequences regardless of context length.

questions.explanation: Per-token KV footprint (FP16, both K and V, across all layers) = 2 * L * H_kv * d * 2 B = 2 * 32 * 8 * 128 * 2 = 131,072 B (128 KB). With 46 GB available for KV, that supports 46 * 2^30 / 131072 ≈ 376,832 tokens in aggregate. If average sequence uses 2000 tokens of KV, the server can hold ~188 concurrent sequences. At 32K/sequence, only ~11 sequences fit — the direct reason long-context LLM serving has tiny effective batch sizes.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: 256 KB is double the correct value; likely double-counts the (K and V) factor or misuses H.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: forgets to multiply by number of layers and (K and V).
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard KV cache arithmetic and its implication for batch size.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: KV cache scales linearly with tokens; the whole 'capacity' is per token per sequence position.

assumptions: FP16 KV storage (2 bytes per element).
L=32 layers, all with the same KV shape.
nonImplications: Does not imply the exact concurrent-sequence count matches production; batching efficiency and paging fragmentation eat some capacity.
Does not imply KV cache quantization is the only lever; MQA/GQA and shorter contexts also help.

sourceRefs.locator: Sec 2 — KV cache memory budget analysis

performanceClaim.scope: KV cache capacity calculation for a specific 32-layer GQA model on A100 80GB

questions.subtopic: Long context serving / KV bandwidth and capacity
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the primary bottlenecks that appear when scaling LLM inference to very long contexts.
questions.stem: Select all statements that correctly characterize challenges specific to long-context (say 32K+ token) LLM serving. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Decode-step attention time grows linearly with context length because the attention kernel reads the full growing KV cache each step; at long context, attention read bandwidth can rival weight read bandwidth per step, changing the per-step latency composition.
Long context has no impact on prefill latency: prefill is a single forward pass that always takes the same wall-clock time regardless of prompt length, so TTFT stays constant with longer prompts.
Per-token KV cache grows linearly with context length; at fixed HBM budget, doubling context length approximately halves the maximum concurrent batch size, directly cutting throughput.
TPOT is independent of context length because decode still processes only one new token per step; the KV cache size is a memory-only concern with no effect on per-step latency.

questions.explanation: A is correct: KV grows linearly with context, capping batch size. C is correct: attention read cost per decode step grows linearly with context (whole KV read), and at long context attention bytes can rival weight bytes, increasing TPOT. B is wrong: TPOT does grow with context because attention reads scale linearly. D is wrong: prefill time is roughly proportional to P (or P^2/M in the FlashAttention regime for attention); longer prompts increase TTFT.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: per-step attention bandwidth growth.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: prefill scales with prompt length.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: batch capacity cost.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: TPOT grows with context.

assumptions: 'Long context' means the KV cache is a significant fraction of HBM.
Attention kernel reads the full KV each decode step (no sliding window or sparse attention).
