nonImplications: Does not imply sliding-window or approximate attention cannot help; they are exactly the mitigations.
Does not imply KV quantization is quality-neutral.

sourceRefs.locator: Sec 4 — attention I/O at long context

performanceClaim.scope: Long-context LLM serving bottlenecks

questions.subtopic: KV cache OOM / Diagnosis and mitigations
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose KV cache OOM under long-context multi-tenant serving and identify effective mitigations.
questions.stem: A vLLM deployment on an 80GB GPU running Llama-3-70B (with GQA, 8 KV heads) is throwing frequent 'KV cache full' preemptions. Prompt/output stats and observed metrics: (Select all mitigations that would concretely reduce OOM/preemption rates.)
questions.profileData:
Model: Llama-3-70B, GQA (H_kv=8, d=128, L=80), FP16 KV.
  Per-token KV: 2 * 80 * 8 * 128 * 2 B = 320 KB.
  Deployment: TP=8 across 8 x H100 80GB (so per-GPU KV budget ≈ (80GB - weights_per_GPU - workspace) / 8 shard).
  Actually TP-8 means KV cache is also sharded (H_kv=8 goes to 1 KV head per GPU) → per-GPU per-token KV ≈ 40 KB.
  Workload: 4K-token prompts, 500-token outputs on average; target concurrent batch = 128.
  Observed: KV usage per GPU peaks at 99%, preemption rate 30%, tail TTFT p99 = 5x p50.

options.text: Switch from TP=8 to PP=8: pipeline parallelism replicates KV cache across all pipeline stages (each stage stores the whole per-request KV), providing 8x more KV capacity per pipeline stage.
Enable INT8 or FP8 KV cache: cuts per-token KV bytes ~2x, roughly doubling concurrent batch capacity at the cost of small accuracy loss.
Reduce max_concurrent_batch (batch admission cap) so that KV pressure doesn't reach 99%: this trades peak throughput for lower preemption / better tail TTFT.
Enable prefix caching if requests share long system prompts: shared prefill KV is reused across requests, cutting effective per-request KV cost for repeated prefixes.

questions.explanation: Options B, C, D are correct; option A is incorrect. A (Wrong): PP shards layers (each stage stores its layers' KV), it does not replicate. B (Correct): KV quant is the direct capacity lever. C (Correct): admission control trades throughput for stability. D (Correct): prefix caching reduces effective per-request KV. General context: In fact PP typically stores L/P layers' worth of KV per stage instead of L/T rows in TP.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: PP shards layers (each stage stores its layers' KV), it does not replicate.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: KV quant is the direct capacity lever.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: admission control trades throughput for stability.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: prefix caching reduces effective per-request KV.

assumptions: Standard vLLM configuration with PagedAttention.
Prefix caching is enabled and workload has shared prefixes.
nonImplications: Does not imply INT8 KV is quality-neutral.
Does not imply admission control is preferable to horizontal scaling; both are valid.

sourceRefs.locator: KV cache tuning: quant, prefix caching, admission

performanceClaim.scope: KV cache OOM diagnosis and mitigations

questions.learningObjective: Explain the paged KV cache abstraction used by vLLM's PagedAttention and its motivation.
questions.stem: vLLM's PagedAttention introduces a paged KV cache. Which description of the abstraction and its primary motivation is correct?

options.text: Paged KV cache stores KV entries in a hash table indexed by (request_id, position); the primary motivation is O(1) random access to individual entries, which enables sparse attention patterns not possible with contiguous storage.

Paged KV cache allocates one contiguous [max_seq_len, H_kv, d] slab per request and reserves virtual memory to grow it lazily; the primary motivation is compatibility with existing FlashAttention kernels that require contiguous memory.
Paged KV cache compresses KV entries by quantizing them to INT8 blockwise; the 'paging' refers to the quantization block boundaries, not to memory layout.

Paged KV cache divides KV memory into fixed-size blocks (e.g., 16 tokens per block) and gives each sequence a block table mapping logical positions to physical blocks. This eliminates external fragmentation and internal reservation of unused space that would otherwise result from pre-allocating each sequence's full max-length KV.

questions.explanation: Paged KV cache (PagedAttention, borrowing terminology from OS virtual memory) partitions KV memory into fixed-size physical blocks and gives each sequence a block table that maps logical positions to physical block indices. The motivation is memory efficiency: static per-sequence allocation of max-length KV wastes memory when actual outputs are shorter, and contiguous re-allocation causes fragmentation. Paging solves both problems and enables the sharing patterns (prefix caching, beam search) that vLLM uses.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: not a hash table; not for sparse attention.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: not per-request contiguous slabs; the whole point is to avoid that.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: paging is a memory layout, not quantization.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: fixed blocks + block table, motivated by memory efficiency.

assumptions: 'Paged' is used in the OS-VM sense: fixed-size blocks addressed via a page table.
Attention kernel must be aware of the block table (custom paged attention kernel).
nonImplications: Does not imply zero overhead; the block table adds indirection.
Does not imply the block size is universal; typical values are 8-32 tokens.

performanceClaim.scope: PagedAttention memory abstraction and motivation

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a PagedAttention kernel differs from a FlashAttention kernel and what block-table indirection costs at execution time.
questions.stem: The PagedAttention kernel differs from a standard FlashAttention kernel primarily in how it accesses KV cache. Which characterization is correct?

options.text: PagedAttention resolves each logical KV position to a physical block address via the per-sequence block table, then loads the block into SMEM and runs the same online-softmax + tiled attention math as FlashAttention. The extra cost is a table lookup per block (small), not per element; SMEM staging and math dataflow are essentially unchanged.

PagedAttention performs a scatter operation over the full KV cache to gather scattered blocks into a temporary contiguous buffer before running the attention math; the gather step is bandwidth-heavy and the primary source of PagedAttention overhead.

PagedAttention runs a completely different attention algorithm (approximate sparse attention) because contiguous access is required for exact softmax; the 'paged' name refers to a windowed truncation of the attention that skips distant tokens.

PagedAttention keeps the entire KV cache in host memory (paged in via zero-copy CUDA UVA) and only pulls in the currently needed positions per attention step; the block table is an operating-system-style page table mapping virtual to host addresses.

questions.explanation: PagedAttention (vLLM) is a kernel variant of FlashAttention/exact attention that adds one level of indirection: for each KV block position needed in the current tile, the kernel reads the block table to find the physical block address in HBM. The block is then loaded into SMEM and the attention math (online softmax + tiled QK^T + PV) proceeds as in FlashAttention. The lookup overhead is per block (typically 16 tokens per block), not per element, so it is amortized well.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: block-table lookup + otherwise-standard FlashAttention math.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no gather-to-contiguous step; blocks are loaded directly.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: PagedAttention is exact, not approximate.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: KV lives in HBM, not host memory; page table maps virtual position to HBM address.

assumptions: PagedAttention v1/v2 as in vLLM.
Block table is a small per-sequence array in HBM.
nonImplications: Does not imply zero indirection cost; there is a small overhead measurable in microbenchmarks.
Does not imply PagedAttention is universally slower or faster than contiguous FlashAttention per step; measured latency is very close.

performanceClaim.scope: PagedAttention kernel structure vs FlashAttention

questions.subtopic: PagedAttention design / Fixed-size blocks and sharing
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish correct claims about PagedAttention's design and its capabilities from common misconceptions.
questions.stem: Select all correct statements about PagedAttention's design. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: The block-table indirection allows different sequences to share physical blocks — used to implement prefix caching (across requests) and beam-search fork points (within a request).
PagedAttention decompresses KV blocks on-the-fly from a lossy quantized format; the 'paged' name refers to lossy compression pages, not memory blocks.

PagedAttention is compatible with FlashAttention-style tiled softmax: the paged attention kernel loads blocks into SMEM via the block table and runs the same online-softmax math. The paging overhead is a small per-block table lookup, not a per-element cost.

PagedAttention uses fixed-size KV blocks (e.g., 16 tokens per block) and a per-sequence block table mapping logical positions to physical block indices; internal waste per sequence is bounded by block_size - 1 tokens.

questions.explanation: Options A, C, D are correct; option B is incorrect. A (Correct): sharing enables prefix caching + beam search. B (Wrong): paging is not quantization/compression. C (Correct): block-table lookup as the only overhead vs FlashAttention. D (Correct): fixed blocks + block table + bounded internal waste.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: sharing enables prefix caching + beam search.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: paging is not quantization/compression.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: block-table lookup as the only overhead vs FlashAttention.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: fixed blocks + block table + bounded internal waste.

assumptions: PagedAttention as in vLLM (not a hypothetical variant).
Block size is a small fixed number (8-32 tokens).
nonImplications: Does not imply zero overhead vs FlashAttention with contiguous KV.
Does not imply block sharing is free of correctness constraints; copy-on-write is needed when shared blocks diverge.

performanceClaim.scope: PagedAttention design and sharing capabilities

questions.subtopic: Prefill vs decode / Compute vs memory characterization
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the compute and memory characteristics of prefill and decode phases in autoregressive LLM inference.
questions.stem: Which characterization of prefill vs decode in a batch-1 LLM inference is correct?

options.text: Both prefill and decode are memory-bandwidth bound because both phases read the same model weights from HBM per forward pass; the difference in wall time between them reflects only the number of tokens processed.
Prefill is memory-bound (streaming weights once) and decode is compute-bound (each token performs a full transformer forward with high arithmetic intensity on cached KV).

Prefill (processing a prompt of P tokens together) is typically compute-bound on the QKV / MLP GEMMs because arithmetic intensity per weight scales with P; decode (batch-1, one token at a time) is memory-bandwidth bound because each linear layer becomes a batch-1 GEMV with intensity ~1 flop/byte.

Prefill and decode both incur the same arithmetic intensity because they use the same weights and the same operators; the choice of prefill vs decode is entirely a scheduling artifact with no impact on where the bottleneck lies.

questions.explanation: Prefill: a prompt of P tokens is processed simultaneously. Each weight matrix W is used with a [P, D] input, so intensity per weight fetch scales with P; for even modest P this pushes prefill into the compute-bound region (GEMM). Decode: one new token per step at batch-1 means each weight matrix is used against a single [1, D] activation — a GEMV with ~1 flop/byte, well below the ridge point. This is the classic asymmetry that drives all decode-oriented optimizations (batching, quantization, speculative decoding).

optionExplanations.C: Correct: prefill compute-bound, decode memory-bandwidth bound.
optionExplanations.A: Wrong: intensity differs by a factor of P between the two phases.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: reverses the direction — decode is memory-bound, not compute-bound.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: arithmetic intensity depends on the activation shape at that step.

assumptions: Batch size 1 for a single request; batching changes decode intensity.
Standard dense (non-MoE) transformer forward.
nonImplications: Does not imply prefill is always faster than decode per token; prefill still processes many tokens.
Does not imply decode is always memory-bound at large batch; with big batch it can become compute-bound.

sourceRefs.locator: Sec 3 — batching in prefill and decode

performanceClaim.scope: Prefill vs decode compute vs memory characterization

questions.subtopic: Pipeline parallelism / Layer partition and bubble
questions.learningObjective: Explain how pipeline parallelism shards a model across devices and what causes pipeline bubbles.
questions.stem: Pipeline parallelism (PP) with P stages splits a model's layers across P devices. Which characterization of PP for LLM inference is correct?

options.text: PP partitions layers into P contiguous groups, one per device. In decode inference, a single-request forward passes sequentially through P stages, so per-request latency is not reduced (only memory is shared); throughput improves only with multiple in-flight requests, and imbalanced stages create bubbles.

PP partitions attention heads across devices (like TP) but with additional latency-hiding across P forward passes; per-token latency in decode is P times faster than a single-device baseline because P stages run concurrently.

In inference, PP has no bubble because there is no backward pass; a single request can flow through all P stages with perfectly overlapped stage execution, and per-token latency drops by P× under any load.

Each PP stage holds a copy of the full model and processes different tokens of the same request in parallel; the pipeline works because each token can be processed independently along the layer dimension after residual connections.

questions.explanation: PP partitions the model layer-wise: each device holds a contiguous group of layers. For a single request in decode, the forward is sequential across stages, so per-token latency is not reduced (in fact slightly increased by inter-stage transfer). PP improves throughput only by running multiple requests through the pipeline in parallel (each stage is busy with a different request at each moment). Imbalanced stage compute or memory creates 'bubbles' where some devices idle. In inference the backward-pass bubble of training does not exist, but pipeline scheduling still matters.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: layer-partition, sequential forward for one request, throughput-oriented benefit.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: describes something like TP, not PP; PP does not speed up single-request decode.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: single-request latency is not reduced by PP.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: PP does not replicate the model; each stage holds only its layer group.

assumptions: Standard layer-wise PP as in GPipe / PipeDream / Megatron-LM.
Stage transfer overhead is small relative to stage compute.
nonImplications: Does not imply PP is useless; it is essential when the model does not fit on one device.
Does not imply zero bubble; imbalance and inter-stage latency still create idle time.

performanceClaim.scope: Pipeline parallelism for LLM inference: layer partition, throughput vs latency

questions.subtopic: Prefix caching / KV cache reuse across requests
questions.learningObjective: Explain prefix caching, its correctness conditions, and its effect on TTFT.
questions.stem: Prefix caching (also called 'prompt caching' or 'radix cache' in SGLang) is a KV-cache reuse mechanism. Which description of its behavior and correctness conditions is correct?

options.text: Prefix caching stores the softmax outputs of past attention layers keyed by the prompt hash; when a new request's prompt matches, the softmax output is directly reused for the shared prefix, skipping both the QKV projections and the attention math.

Prefix caching stores the KV cache blocks of previously computed token positions and reuses them for new requests whose prompts share a token-identical prefix. Reuse is exact only if the shared prefix has identical token ids (any diff invalidates from that position onward). It reduces or eliminates the prefill of the shared prefix, cutting TTFT.

Prefix caching is a text-level LRU cache of the model's output strings keyed by prompt; it is only correct when the model temperature is 0 (deterministic decoding), and it cannot be applied when sampling is stochastic.

Prefix caching approximates the KV of a matching prompt with the closest cached embedding vector via cosine similarity; because the approximation is very close (typically >0.98 cosine similarity), the resulting output is nearly identical for most prompts.

questions.explanation: Prefix caching stores per-position KV blocks (from PagedAttention or equivalent) keyed by the sequence of prompt token ids. When a new request comes in whose prompt starts with an already-cached token sequence, the KV blocks for that shared prefix are reused directly — the prefill for those tokens is skipped, cutting TTFT. Reuse is exact and only when the token ids match; any divergence invalidates the reused cache from that position onward. SGLang's radix cache is a common efficient index structure for this.

optionExplanations.B: Correct: token-id-keyed KV reuse with exact-prefix condition.
optionExplanations.A: Wrong: softmax outputs are not cached; only KV.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: prefix caching is at KV level, not output-string level, and does not require T=0.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: no cosine-similarity approximation; that would break correctness.

assumptions: Prompts are tokenized identically across requests (same tokenizer, same normalization).
System stores KV in a form (paged blocks) that supports reuse.
nonImplications: Does not imply that prefix caching helps every workload; it only helps when prompt prefixes are shared.
Does not imply zero overhead; cache lookup and eviction have costs.

performanceClaim.scope: Prefix caching mechanism and TTFT benefit

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a serving scheduler handles KV cache pressure via preemption / swap-out and its trade-offs.
questions.stem: In a serving system running near KV-cache capacity, a burst of new prefill requests arrives. Which description of the scheduler's response is correct for vLLM-style continuous batching + paged KV?

options.text: The scheduler admits all new requests immediately and rewrites older sequences' KV cache in-place with the new prefill data; this is safe because older KV entries can always be recomputed later at negligible cost by re-prefilling those sequences.

The scheduler preempts one or more ongoing sequences (typically the ones with least urgency by policy) — either dropping their KV cache to be recomputed later, or swapping their KV blocks to host memory — and admits the new prefills into the freed KV blocks. Preempted sequences are resumed when capacity is available; this trades their added latency for aggregate throughput.

The scheduler compacts the KV cache by moving all blocks to contiguous memory, which frees up fragmented space for the new prefills; this defragmentation is fast because it uses async DMA copies within HBM.
The scheduler rejects all new requests until the cache pressure drops; ongoing decode continues unaffected. New requests receive an HTTP 503 response after a short timeout.

questions.explanation: Modern schedulers (Orca-inspired, implemented in vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM) manage KV cache pressure via preemption: when a new prefill's KV requirement plus existing KV exceeds capacity, the scheduler preempts (evicts or swaps to host memory) some ongoing sequences to admit new work. Recomputation-on-resume vs swap-to-host is a policy choice: recompute is simple but pays prefill cost twice for the preempted sequences; swap-to-host avoids recompute at the cost of PCIe traffic. Both policies are needed depending on prompt length and PCIe bandwidth.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: in-place overwrite would corrupt other sequences.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: preempt-and-resume with recompute or swap.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: paged KV avoids external fragmentation by design; compaction is not necessary.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: outright rejection is a coarse and suboptimal response.

assumptions: Paged KV cache with a block-level allocator.
Scheduler is aware of per-request KV footprint and priorities.
nonImplications: Does not imply preemption is free; it adds tail latency to preempted requests.
Does not imply every serving stack chooses the same preemption policy.

distractorRationales.C: Paged KV eliminates external fragmentation, making compaction unnecessary.

performanceClaim.scope: Serving scheduler preemption behavior under KV cache pressure

questions.subtopic: Speculative decoding / Acceptance rate and speedup
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how acceptance rate determines speedup in speculative decoding and where speedup is bounded.
questions.stem: In a spec-decoded run with k = 5 proposals per step, the observed acceptance rate per proposed token is p = 0.7. The target forward costs ~10 ms; the draft forward costs ~2 ms per token. Which statement about expected speedup is correct?
questions.profileData:
Setup:
  Target forward on k+1 positions:   10 ms
  Draft forward per token:            2 ms
  Proposals per verification:         k = 5
  Per-token acceptance probability:   p = 0.7 (independent Bernoulli approximation)

Expected accepted prefix length ≈ (1 - p^{k+1}) / (1 - p) for Bernoulli-independent acceptance.
  = (1 - 0.7^6) / 0.3 ≈ (1 - 0.117) / 0.3 ≈ 2.94 tokens
  Per-verification: 1 target step (10 ms) + 5 draft steps (5 * 2 = 10 ms) = 20 ms
  Expected accepted tokens per verification: ~2.94 + 1 (target's sample) = ~3.94
  Baseline: target alone = 10 ms per token

options.text: Speedup equals 1 / (1 - p) = 3.33x independent of k, because acceptance rate solely determines throughput; increasing k beyond 1 has no effect on wall time.
Speedup is exactly k = 5x because k tokens are proposed per target forward; the acceptance rate p only affects quality, not throughput.

Expected tokens per verification is ~3.94, at 20 ms per verification: ~0.20 tokens/ms. Baseline is 0.10 tokens/ms. Speedup ≈ 2x. Acceptance rate p is the dominant lever; as p → 1 speedup approaches (k+1) / (1 + draft-cost-fraction * (k+1)), bounded by the draft/target cost ratio.
Because the draft forward runs in parallel with the target forward on the same GPU, there is no draft overhead in wall time and speedup is (k+1) * p ≈ 4.2x.

questions.explanation: With Bernoulli-independent acceptance, expected accepted prefix length is (1 - p^{k+1})/(1 - p) ≈ 2.94 tokens; the target also samples one output on rejection, giving ~3.94 tokens per verification. At 20 ms per verification (target + draft), that's 0.20 tokens/ms vs baseline 0.10 → ~2x speedup. As p → 1, speedup approaches the limit (k+1)/(1 + draft-cost-share), so both draft cost and k matter. A cheap draft (low cost) and high p push toward the asymptote.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: k does affect throughput; the formula ignores k.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: p < 1 shortens expected accepted prefix; k tokens are never guaranteed.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: right arithmetic and correct sensitivity analysis.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: draft cannot run in parallel with target on the same critical path; draft is sequential per step.

assumptions: Bernoulli-independent per-token acceptance is a first-order approximation; real acceptance is position-dependent.
Draft and target run on the same GPU without overlap; some implementations overlap by pipelining, complicating the calculus.
nonImplications: Does not imply Bernoulli independence holds exactly.
Does not imply k should always be increased; larger k raises variance and can hurt tail latency.

performanceClaim.scope: Expected speedup of speculative decoding as a function of k, p, and draft cost

questions.learningObjective: Explain the mechanism of speculative decoding and its correctness property.
questions.stem: Which description of speculative decoding for LLM inference is correct?

options.text: A small 'draft' model is used to generate k candidate tokens at once by predicting all k positions in parallel; the target model is then used only to compute a probability for the whole k-token sequence, and the whole sequence is accepted if the joint probability exceeds a threshold.

Speculative decoding uses a distilled quantized version of the target model as the sole decoder; the 'speculative' name refers to running INT4 arithmetic that may be numerically wrong but recovers quality through calibration.

A smaller/faster draft model proposes k tokens autoregressively. The target model runs one forward pass on all k proposed positions (like a k-token prefill) and, using its own logits, accepts a prefix of the proposal by comparing probabilities per position via rejection sampling; the accepted prefix has the exact same distribution as target-only sampling.

The target model itself decodes in parallel over k positions by conditioning each of the k output positions on the same input hidden state; the 'draft' terminology refers to these draft positions being generated in one shot before being ranked.

questions.explanation: Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023) uses a small/fast draft model to propose k tokens autoregressively, then does a single target-model forward on all k positions (equivalent to k-token prefill for the target). Using rejection sampling comparing draft and target probabilities per position, a prefix of the proposal is accepted; the retained distribution is exactly the target model's sampling distribution. On acceptance of j <= k tokens, one target forward yields j+1 output tokens (j accepted plus one new sampled by target when rejection happens), improving throughput without changing sampling semantics.

optionExplanations.C: Correct: canonical speculative decoding mechanism.
optionExplanations.A: Wrong: draft model is used autoregressively for k steps; acceptance is per-token via rejection sampling.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: describes model quantization, not speculative decoding.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: describes non-autoregressive generation, not spec decoding.

assumptions: Both draft and target use the same vocabulary and tokenization.
Rejection sampling scheme correctly implemented.
nonImplications: Does not imply arbitrary speedup; benefit depends on the acceptance rate.
Does not imply the draft model's outputs are ever visible; only accepted tokens flow to the user.

performanceClaim.scope: Speculative decoding mechanism and correctness

questions.subtopic: Speculative decoding properties / Correctness and scope
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish correct claims about speculative decoding from common overclaims.
questions.stem: Select all correct statements about speculative decoding. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Speculative decoding always speeds up inference by a factor of (k+1) — the number of proposed tokens plus one — regardless of the draft model's quality or the workload characteristics.

Speculative decoding is most beneficial when the target model is memory-bandwidth bound (batch-1 decode), because the extra k-token verification is essentially free compared to a single-token forward. It is less beneficial at large batch when the target is already compute-bound.

Speculative decoding requires the draft and target models to share weights (be identically initialized) so that rejection sampling has an easy path to bit-exact agreement; using unrelated models breaks the algorithm's correctness guarantees.

When implemented with proper rejection sampling against the target model's logits, the sequences produced by speculative decoding have exactly the same distribution as target-only sampling — no quality loss.

questions.explanation: Options B, D are correct; options A, C are incorrect. A (Wrong): ignores acceptance rate and draft cost. B (Correct): memory-bound target maximizes the win. C (Wrong): draft can be arbitrary; only vocab needs to match. D (Correct): sampling distribution preserved.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: ignores acceptance rate and draft cost.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: memory-bound target maximizes the win.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: draft can be arbitrary; only vocab needs to match.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: sampling distribution preserved.

assumptions: 'Speculative decoding' refers to Leviathan et al. 2023 style rejection sampling.
Draft and target share vocab and tokenization.
nonImplications: Does not imply speedup is guaranteed; low acceptance rate can wipe out the win.
Does not imply that alternative variants (Medusa, EAGLE) share every property; they use different draft mechanisms but similar acceptance logic.

distractorRationales.A: Ignores acceptance rate and draft cost.

performanceClaim.scope: Speculative decoding correctness and scope of benefit

questions.subtopic: Tensor parallelism / Row-column sharding for MLP and Attention
questions.learningObjective: Explain how tensor parallelism shards MLP and attention weights across devices and what collective is required per layer.
questions.stem: In Megatron-LM-style tensor parallelism with TP degree T, the MLP block up projection W_up is column-parallel (sharded along output dim) and the MLP down projection W_down is row-parallel (sharded along input dim). Which characterization of the resulting dataflow is correct?

options.text: Each of the T devices holds the full [D, F] W_up and computes the full output; only W_down is sharded, requiring one AllGather per MLP block after the activation.

Column-parallel W_up requires an AllGather of x to every device (since each device needs the full input to multiply against its columns); row-parallel W_down then requires an AllGather of the intermediate; two AllGathers per MLP block are needed and TP scaling is bounded by interconnect bandwidth.

The column-then-row parallel arrangement is chosen because it requires no communication at all; the intermediate slices align exactly so that each device's partial down-output equals the correct global output for its shard, so all-to-all is unnecessary.

Column-parallel W_up: each device computes x @ W_up_shard producing 1/T of the intermediate columns; row-parallel W_down: each device multiplies its intermediate slice by its 1/T rows of W_down. A single AllReduce sums partial outputs across devices at the end of each MLP (and separately at the end of each attention block).

questions.explanation: The column-then-row parallel arrangement (Megatron-LM's design) works as follows: (1) The input x is fully replicated on all devices. (2) W_up column-parallel: each device holds F/T columns of W_up and produces 1/T slice of the intermediate. (3) Activation is elementwise, applied per-device. (4) W_down row-parallel: each device holds F/T rows of W_down and multiplies its intermediate slice, yielding a partial output. (5) One AllReduce sums partial outputs across devices. The same pattern applies to attention (QKV column-parallel, output-proj row-parallel with one AllReduce). This is one AllReduce per MLP and one per attention (2 per transformer block).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: W_up is sharded; the whole point is to shard both to save memory.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no AllGather is required; the sharded pattern is deliberately designed for a single AllReduce.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: an AllReduce is necessary to sum partial outputs.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: standard Megatron TP pattern with a single AllReduce per MLP.

assumptions: Standard Megatron-LM-style TP.
Input x is replicated across TP ranks at the start of each transformer block.
nonImplications: Does not imply TP is always the best parallel strategy; PP and DP have different trade-offs.
Does not imply zero communication overhead; AllReduce cost can be significant.

performanceClaim.scope: Megatron-style TP MLP dataflow and required collective

questions.learningObjective: Define TPOT (Time Per Output Token) and distinguish it from TTFT and throughput.
questions.stem: Which definition of TPOT (Time Per Output Token, also called inter-token latency) is correct?

options.text: TPOT is the total generation time (TTFT plus all decode steps) divided by the total number of output tokens; it is therefore equal to end-to-end latency per output token including the prefill amortization.
TPOT is the server's overall tokens-per-second throughput divided by the number of concurrent requests; it is a purely server-level metric that has no per-request interpretation.

TPOT is the average wall-clock time between consecutive output tokens after the first token, per request. It excludes TTFT and captures how fast the decode phase runs; for a request generating M tokens, total latency ≈ TTFT + (M-1) * TPOT.
TPOT is the elapsed time of the prefill phase divided by the number of prompt tokens; it measures per-prompt-token processing efficiency.

questions.explanation: TPOT (Time Per Output Token), also called inter-token latency, is the average wall-clock gap between successive output tokens after the first, per request. Total per-request latency = TTFT + (M-1) * TPOT for an M-token response. TPOT reflects decode-phase speed and is user-perceived as generation smoothness; it is directly bounded by KV-cache read bandwidth on batch-1 decode.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: conflates TTFT and TPOT; TPOT excludes TTFT by convention.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: describes throughput per concurrent user, not TPOT.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard TPOT definition.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: describes a prefill-phase efficiency metric, not TPOT.

assumptions: 'After the first token' is the standard convention; some tools compute TPOT including the first token.
Metric is per request; server-side aggregations report averages / percentiles.
nonImplications: Does not imply TPOT alone determines user experience; TTFT and total latency also matter.
Does not imply TPOT is constant across steps; long-context decode can slow down as KV grows.

distractorRationales.D: Confuses with a prefill efficiency metric.

performanceClaim.scope: TPOT metric definition

questions.learningObjective: Define TTFT precisely and use timeline data to diagnose which phase drives it.
questions.stem: The latency budget for one request is broken down in the timeline below. Which choice correctly identifies TTFT and its dominant contributor for this request?
questions.profileData:
Per-request timeline (single request, batch size 1):
  T0: request arrives at server
  T0 → T0 + 5 ms  : queueing (server busy with other requests)
  T0 + 5 ms  → T0 + 8 ms  : tokenization + input transfer
  T0 + 8 ms  → T0 + 190 ms: prefill of a 1024-token prompt on a single GPU
  T0 + 190 ms → T0 + 210 ms: first token generation (decode step 1) + detokenize + response send
  T0 + 210 ms → T0 + 500 ms: subsequent 30 decode steps (average 9.7 ms/token)

options.text: TTFT is the total decode time (about 310 ms in this trace); the dominant factor is the per-step decode latency, so mitigation should focus on speeding up decode via KV cache quantization or speculative decoding.

TTFT is only the queueing time (5 ms here); the prefill and decode contribute to throughput but not TTFT because those computations happen 'inside' the model and are amortized across all output tokens.

TTFT = time from request arrival to when the first output token is available (~210 ms here). It is dominated by the 182 ms prefill of the 1024-token prompt; mitigation focuses on prefill (chunked prefill, prefix caching, tensor parallelism).
TTFT is the average inter-token latency of subsequent decode steps (~9.7 ms/token in this trace); it excludes the prefill, which is a separate metric usually called 'time-to-prefill-complete'.

questions.explanation: TTFT (Time To First Token) is the wall-clock time from when the request arrives at the server to when the first output token is delivered. In this trace: 5 ms queue + 3 ms tokenize/transfer + 182 ms prefill + ~20 ms first-token generation/response = ~210 ms. The dominant component is the 182 ms prefill of the 1024-token prompt. Mitigations targeting TTFT focus on prefill: chunked prefill (overlap with decode of other requests), prefix caching (skip prefill for cache-hit prefixes), and tensor parallelism (parallelize prefill compute).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: this describes total generation latency, not TTFT.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: TTFT includes all wall-clock time until the first token, not just queueing.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: TTFT definition and its prefill-dominated composition here.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: that is TPOT (Time Per Output Token) / inter-token latency, not TTFT.

assumptions: 'First token' is delivered as soon as it is available (streaming).
Tokenization and detokenize are minor components and included in TTFT bookkeeping.
nonImplications: Does not imply that reducing prefill always reduces TTFT proportionally; other components (queueing under load) may become dominant.
Does not imply that TTFT is the only or most important metric; TPOT and throughput matter too.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses TTFT with total generation time.
distractorRationales.B: Reduces TTFT to queue time only.

performanceClaim.scope: TTFT definition and its contributor breakdown in a batch-1 request

questions.subtopic: Throughput vs latency trade-off / Batch-size lever
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the throughput vs latency trade-off in LLM serving and identify how batch size affects each metric.
questions.stem: Select all correct statements about the throughput vs latency trade-off in LLM decode serving. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: Beyond some batch size, the workload transitions from memory-bandwidth bound to compute-bound; further batch-size increases raise per-step compute time proportionally with fewer amortization gains, giving diminishing returns on aggregate throughput and larger per-request TPOT penalties.
Increasing batch size always reduces both TPOT and total request latency because more compute is used in parallel per step; there is no downside to arbitrarily large batches other than memory limits.

Increasing batch size amortizes weight-HBM reads across more requests, raising aggregate tokens/second (throughput), but each batched step takes slightly longer (because of extra compute and possibly attention I/O), so per-request TPOT increases mildly.
Latency and throughput are the same metric expressed in different units (1/latency = throughput); optimizing one always optimizes the other.

questions.explanation: Options A, C are correct; options B, D are incorrect. A (Correct): bandwidth→compute transition and diminishing returns. B (Wrong): larger batches raise TPOT. C (Correct): throughput up, per-request TPOT up. D (Wrong): throughput and latency are different metrics. General context: They are not reciprocals and can move independently.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: bandwidth→compute transition and diminishing returns.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: larger batches raise TPOT.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: throughput up, per-request TPOT up.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: throughput and latency are different metrics.

assumptions: 'Latency' = per-request TPOT or total request latency.
'Throughput' = aggregate output tokens/sec across all users.
nonImplications: Does not imply the optimal batch size is universal; it depends on SLA constraints.
Does not imply that continuous batching removes this trade-off; it only makes the batch composition dynamic.

performanceClaim.scope: Batch-size lever for throughput vs latency in LLM decode

questions.learningObjective: Explain why an ML compiler that ships a .so/.dll artifact must define a stable C ABI at the artifact boundary, not a C++ one, and what breaks when the boundary is not stable.
questions.stem: An AOT-compiled artifact (e.g., AOTInductor .so, TensorRT plan loader, IREE HAL module) exposes an entry point that must be loaded by processes built with unknown compiler toolchains. Which ABI-boundary discipline is standard, and why?

options.text: ABI stability is unnecessary because dynamic loaders (dlopen/LoadLibrary) automatically rewrite mangled symbols to match the host process's C++ compiler, meaning any C++ boundary works.

The artifact exposes a mangled C++ ABI with `std::vector<Tensor>` return types because C++ standard library types are guaranteed to be layout-compatible across all major compilers (GCC, Clang, MSVC) since C++17.

The artifact exposes a C ABI (plain `extern "C"` functions with POD structs and opaque handles). C++ name mangling, exception ABIs, and STL types differ across compilers/versions and would break linking or crash at library boundaries.
The artifact must be statically linked into the host process and cannot use a dynamic library at all; ABI concerns only arise when linking, not when loading precompiled kernels.

questions.explanation: C++ ABIs differ across compilers (GCC vs. MSVC), across libc++ vs libstdc++, and even across std versions. Name mangling, exception unwinding, and STL container layout are not portable. Serious dynamic-artifact stacks expose only a C ABI at the boundary: extern "C" entry points, POD structs, opaque handles created and destroyed on the artifact's side. Users can wrap that C ABI in a C++ facade inside the loading process, but the boundary itself is C.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: dynamic loaders do not rewrite mangled symbols; a mangled-symbol mismatch causes load-time or runtime linkage failure.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: `std::vector<T>` is not ABI-stable across compilers or STL implementations; passing it across .so boundaries is a known source of undefined behavior.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches the standard practice used by AOTInductor's C shim, TensorRT's C++ header + C API split, CUDA driver API, and IREE HAL C.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: dynamic libraries are widely used; ABI concerns are exactly why they exist and why they use C boundaries.

assumptions: The artifact will be loaded by a process compiled with a different toolchain or C++ standard than the compiler used to build the artifact.
nonImplications: Does not imply that internal implementations must be C; only the boundary must be C.
Does not imply ABI stability is only about C++; issues also arise with GPU driver ABIs, but those are shipped by vendors.

distractorRationales.B: False stability claim about STL types.

sourceRefs.locator: TensorRT C/C++ API split; ABI notes

questions.learningObjective: Explain why deep-learning runtimes use a caching memory allocator (a pool of previously freed device blocks) instead of calling cudaMalloc/cudaFree per tensor.
questions.stem: Deep-learning runtimes (PyTorch, TensorFlow, TVM) implement a caching memory allocator on the GPU rather than calling `cudaMalloc`/`cudaFree` for each tensor. Which reason is the strongest?

options.text: The CUDA driver limits the number of live allocations per process to 1024; a caching allocator sidesteps this by keeping a single large allocation for the lifetime of the process regardless of workload.

`cudaMalloc` returns memory that cannot be used as a kernel argument until a `cudaMemcpy` initializes it; a caching allocator writes zeros lazily so kernels can read uninitialized memory safely without additional API calls.

`cudaMalloc` and `cudaFree` are synchronous with respect to all CUDA streams and take microseconds to milliseconds; calling them on every tensor allocation would serialize the stream and dominate end-to-end latency. A caching allocator amortizes this by pooling freed blocks and reusing them without touching the driver.

A caching allocator eliminates memory fragmentation entirely because it always returns exactly the requested size and rounds up to a multiple of one byte, meaning no wasted padding ever occurs across tensor lifetimes.

questions.explanation: `cudaMalloc`/`cudaFree` synchronize with the device and cost microseconds to milliseconds — orders of magnitude more than a well-tuned pool lookup. A caching allocator holds freed device blocks in size-classed pools and reuses them on subsequent allocation requests, avoiding the driver call in the fast path. Fragmentation is a real concern; the allocator manages it via block splitting/coalescing but does not eliminate it (D is false). B and C fabricate driver behavior.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: there is no such 1024-allocation limit.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: cudaMalloc'd memory is usable as a kernel argument; nothing forces zero-init.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: this is the documented motivation for PyTorch's caching allocator and equivalent designs.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: caching allocators still have fragmentation; they mitigate it but do not eliminate it.

assumptions: The workload allocates and frees tensors frequently (training steps, iterative decoding), so per-step allocator cost matters.
nonImplications: Does not imply that caching allocators are always ideal; long-running services may need periodic empty-cache calls to release memory back to the OS.
Does not imply fragmentation is negligible; long training runs with variable shapes can suffer OOM from fragmentation.

performanceClaim.scope: Frequent-allocation ML workloads on NVIDIA GPUs

questions.learningObjective: Compare AOT artifact deployment (all lowering done ahead of first invocation) with JIT compilation (lowering triggered on the first suitable call), and identify the trade-offs.
questions.stem: Which statement most accurately contrasts an Ahead-of-Time (AOT) artifact (e.g., AOTInductor .so, TensorRT plan) with a JIT-compiled workflow (e.g., default torch.compile)?

options.text: JIT is always faster than AOT at steady state because JIT observes real inputs and re-optimizes on every call; AOT compiles once and cannot adapt, so its steady-state performance is capped below any JIT implementation.

AOT and JIT produce identical binaries; the only difference is the file extension, and either mode can be selected transparently at inference time without any change to compilation semantics or shape support.

AOT requires the source model be present at run time; the compiler is re-invoked from the artifact each time the runtime restarts, which is what enables cross-target dispatch on ARM and x86 from a single file.

The AOT artifact avoids first-call compilation latency and can be shipped independently of the compiler, but generally requires known shapes/dtypes at build time; JIT compiles lazily on first call, absorbing warmup cost in exchange for shape/dtype flexibility.

questions.explanation: AOT compilation lowers the model to a deployable artifact (shared library, plan file, VM executable) before deployment. The runtime then loads that artifact directly — no compiler needed, no first-call warmup — but the artifact is specialized to the shape/dtype/hardware assumptions used at build time. JIT trades first-call latency and a compiler dependency at run time for the ability to specialize to real observed inputs (dynamic shapes, guards). Neither strictly dominates the other at steady state.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: at steady state, an AOT-compiled artifact typically matches or beats JIT because it has already paid the compilation cost; JIT does not re-optimize per call.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: AOT and JIT differ in when compilation happens and what assumptions the artifact encodes.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: an AOT artifact does not require the source model or the compiler at run time — that's the point of AOT.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: describes the standard AOT vs JIT trade-off (compile-time vs run-time specialization).

assumptions: Both AOT and JIT stacks emit the same underlying kernels (Triton, cuBLAS, etc.) so we are comparing compilation phase, not code quality.
nonImplications: Does not imply that JIT is always slower to first-response; systems can cache JIT artifacts across process starts.
Does not imply AOT is impossible with dynamic shapes; some AOT stacks (AOTInductor with dynamic dims, TensorRT with optimization profiles) support ranges.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses JIT observation with per-call re-optimization.

sourceRefs.locator: AOTInductor deployment story (compile ahead of time, load .so at runtime)
TensorRT engine build vs. runtime deployment

questions.learningObjective: Explain what AOTInductor produces (a self-contained shared library that runs a compiled PyTorch model without a Python runtime) and how that differs from torch.compile in JIT mode.
questions.stem: Which statement best describes what AOTInductor produces and how it differs from the default JIT torch.compile flow?

options.text: AOTInductor ahead-of-time compiles an exported PyTorch model into a self-contained shared library (plus the generated kernels) that can be loaded and invoked from C++ without a Python interpreter or the Inductor compiler present at runtime; JIT torch.compile compiles on first call and requires Python + Inductor at run time.
AOTInductor is a re-implementation of the CUDA driver API; it lets torch.compile bypass cuBLAS and cuDNN by JIT-compiling all matmuls on the fly at each inference call.

AOTInductor is a smaller runtime that replaces Python entirely; it JIT-compiles PyTorch models at process start using an embedded MicroPython interpreter, producing the same kernels as torch.compile but launching them from within a compiled binary.

AOTInductor produces a Python-only artifact (a `.pyc` file) that still requires Python at runtime; the only difference from JIT torch.compile is that graph capture happens ahead of time while codegen happens on the first call.

questions.explanation: AOTInductor is the AOT compilation path for torch.compile: given an `torch.export`-produced graph, AOTInductor emits a shared library (.so) containing the generated kernels and a C-ABI entry point. The library is deployable without Python and without the Inductor compiler at run time. JIT torch.compile, by contrast, compiles lazily and depends on Python + Inductor at the deployment site.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: matches the AOTInductor design as described in the PyTorch docs.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: AOTInductor does not replace CUDA driver APIs.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: no embedded Python interpreter; it is a native artifact.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: it is not a .pyc; it is a native shared library.

assumptions: PyTorch 2.3 ~ 2.5 with the AOTInductor path (`torch._inductor.aot_compile` / `torch._export.aot_compile`).
nonImplications: Does not imply AOTInductor supports every torch.compile feature; some dynamic behaviors are restricted.
Does not imply zero build cost; users trade first-call latency for offline build time.

questions.learningObjective: Identify correct statements about executing an AOTInductor-compiled artifact at runtime.
questions.stem: Which statements about running an AOTInductor-compiled artifact are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The artifact automatically links against `libtorch.so` at runtime and requires the full PyTorch binary distribution to be present on the deployment machine; without libtorch the .so cannot be loaded.

The artifact exposes a C-ABI entry function; callers pass input tensors as device-memory pointers with shape/stride metadata and receive output tensors similarly, without requiring the Python runtime.
The artifact still requires the Inductor compiler at runtime; on first invocation Inductor is re-invoked to lower the graph, which is what allows the artifact to accept new shapes at inference time.

The artifact bundles the generated Triton/CUDA kernels needed to execute the model, and the runtime loads them via the shared library's loader; no separate kernel binaries need to be shipped alongside the .so.

questions.explanation: B: AOTInductor exposes a stable C interface for driving the compiled model, without requiring Python. D: The generated kernels are bundled with the .so and dispatched by the artifact itself. C is wrong: the whole point of AOT is that Inductor is not needed at runtime; new shapes work only if the artifact was built with dynamic dims. A is wrong: AOTInductor is designed to avoid a full libtorch dependency; it links against a minimal C shim.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: the artifact links against a minimal C shim, not full libtorch.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: stable C interface for calling into the artifact.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: Inductor is not present at runtime; artifacts run without the compiler.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: kernels are bundled into the artifact.

assumptions: PyTorch 2.3 ~ 2.5 AOTInductor path.
The artifact was built for the target GPU architecture.
nonImplications: Does not imply arbitrary shapes are supported; only those declared as dynamic at build time.
Does not imply the C ABI has been permanently frozen; the interface is stable within a major version but may evolve.

sourceRefs.locator: AOTInductor runtime and C ABI details

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish which decisions belong to compile-time (ahead-of-time lowering, kernel selection, memory planning) and which belong to run-time (dispatch, allocator calls, dynamic shape adaptation).
questions.stem: Which statement best characterizes the boundary between the compiler and the runtime in a typical ML compilation stack (e.g., IREE, TVM, XLA)?

options.text: The compiler emits target-specific kernels and a lowered artifact whose scheduling, buffer plan and kernel selection are fixed; the runtime dispatches kernels, manages memory and streams, and services shape-dependent branches within the pre-planned strategy.
The compiler and runtime are the same component; both perform kernel selection, memory allocation and dispatch in a single execution phase where lowering happens each time an input tensor arrives.

The compiler owns memory allocation and stream scheduling at run time, while the runtime is a thin wrapper that only records timing events and forwards inputs to precompiled kernels without touching allocation or streams.

The compiler performs only front-end parsing (op resolution, type inference); every optimization pass — including fusion, tiling and kernel selection — is deferred to the runtime and re-executed on every invocation.

questions.explanation: The canonical division of labor is: the compiler performs lowering, optimization, kernel selection and static memory planning ahead of time (or JIT-once), producing an artifact (bytecode, VM program, .so, plan file). The runtime consumes that artifact and handles device state at execution time — allocator calls, stream/event management, dispatch, and shape-dependent branches within the plan. Boundaries can shift (JIT vs AOT), but memory allocation and dispatch are runtime responsibilities in essentially every mainstream stack.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: describes the standard compiler-emits-artifact / runtime-executes-artifact split used by IREE, TVM, XLA, TensorRT, AOTInductor.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: conflates compiler and runtime; even JIT stacks separate the lowering phase from the execution phase.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: reverses the responsibilities. Compilers do not manage allocators or streams at run time.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: fusion, tiling and kernel selection are compile-time (or JIT-once) transformations, not per-invocation runtime work.

assumptions: A conventional two-phase (compile-then-run) ML system, not a purely interpreter-based one.
nonImplications: Does not imply that the boundary is rigid; some systems perform partial JIT specialization at first invocation, but the split of responsibilities still holds.
Does not imply that the runtime is stateless; runtimes typically own allocator pools, streams, and cached artifacts.

distractorRationales.D: Confuses AOT compile-time work with per-invocation dispatch.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about the sources of cold-start cost (compile, load, warmup) and how compilation caches reduce them across process restarts.
questions.stem: Which statements about cold-start cost and compilation caches for compiled ML workloads are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: AOT-compiled artifacts (TensorRT plan, AOTInductor .so) eliminate the JIT compile phase entirely at cold start because compilation happened offline; process init and weight load costs still remain.

Compilation caches guarantee that a cached hit produces exactly the same output tensors as a fresh compile; any bitwise difference between cached and fresh outputs is a compiler bug that must be fixed before shipping.

Cold-start cost consists of several distinct phases: process init (import framework, load driver), model artifact load (weights, graph), possibly compilation (JIT lowering), and warmup (autotune, cuBLAS handle init, kernel loading). Each has a different mitigation strategy.

A compilation cache stores previously compiled kernels or lowered graphs keyed by (source, shape/dtype/device, compiler-version) and hits skip the compile phase on subsequent process starts; a properly warm cache can turn a multi-minute torch.compile cold start into a fraction of that.

questions.explanation: Correct: A, C, D.  A: Correct: AOT removes JIT from the cold path. B: Wrong: bitwise equivalence between cached and fresh compilations is not guaranteed. C: Correct: standard decomposition of cold-start. D: Correct: compilation caches deliver large cold-start savings.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: AOT removes JIT from the cold path.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: bitwise equivalence between cached and fresh compilations is not guaranteed.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard decomposition of cold-start.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: compilation caches deliver large cold-start savings.

assumptions: A production system where cold-start latency (SLI/SLO) matters.
The runtime supports some form of compilation caching.
nonImplications: Does not imply caches are always safe across framework upgrades; version keys are essential to avoid stale hits.
Does not imply cache misses can be ignored; the first request after cache invalidation still pays the full cold-start cost.

sourceRefs.locator: AOTInductor deployment: zero JIT cost at start

performanceClaim.scope: Cold-start phases and cache impact for compiled ML workloads

questions.learningObjective: Reason about cross compilation in the ML compilation stack: compiling on a host machine for a target device that differs in ISA, GPU architecture, or OS.
questions.stem: Which statements about cross compilation for ML deployment are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Emitting portable IR (e.g., PTX, SPIR-V) and deferring final lowering to the target driver at load time is one strategy for handling cross compilation when the exact target architecture is unknown at build time.

Cross compilation means building an artifact on one host (e.g., x86 Linux with sm_80 dev box) that runs on a different target (e.g., aarch64 Linux with sm_75) — the compiler must be able to emit code for the target's ISA, GPU architecture, and OS ABI without executing on the target.

Autotuning that measures kernel latency on the target device cannot be replaced by pure static cost models; if the target is unavailable, cross compilation typically uses conservative heuristics or previously measured latency tables rather than online measurement.
Cross compilation is impossible for GPU code because NVCC (or ROCm) can only emit machine code that has already been JIT-compiled by the target driver at compile time on the target machine itself.

questions.explanation: Correct: A, B, C.  A: Correct: JIT-from-PTX / SPIR-V is a widespread strategy. B: Correct: canonical cross-compilation setup. C: Correct: autotuning-vs-static-cost is a live trade-off. D: Wrong: NVCC supports cross emission of PTX/SASS for multiple targets.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: JIT-from-PTX / SPIR-V is a widespread strategy.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: canonical cross-compilation setup.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: autotuning-vs-static-cost is a live trade-off.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: NVCC supports cross emission of PTX/SASS for multiple targets.

assumptions: The developer knows the target ISA, GPU architecture and OS ABI, or at least a range.
nonImplications: Does not imply cross compilation is always exact; specialization to actual target features may be reduced.
Does not imply autotuning is dead in cross-compile scenarios; some stacks record measurements offline on a fleet of target devices.

sourceRefs.locator: PTX, JIT, cross emission of sm_XX code
Cross-compilation flows for edge / mobile targets

questions.learningObjective: Describe how a custom operator is registered into a runtime so that both the compiler and the executor recognize it, and what obligations the author takes on.

softwareContext.framework: generic (ONNX Runtime custom op, TensorRT plugin, torch custom op)

questions.stem: When you add a custom operator to a runtime such as ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, or PyTorch, which combination best describes the author's responsibilities?

options.text: Only register a Python function of the same name; the runtime automatically infers the op schema from its Python signature and generates GPU kernels for all supported dtypes by tracing example inputs at first call.
Only implement the CUDA kernel; runtime frameworks introspect the .cu source to derive the op schema, differentiate the kernel symbolically, and register it into every backend transparently.
Ship the model with the op's PyTorch source; the compiler recompiles the source on every process start to derive schema, kernels, and backward pass, so no explicit registration is needed.

Provide (i) an op schema/signature so the compiler can type- and shape-check calls, (ii) a kernel implementation for each supported device/dtype registered into the runtime, and (iii) — if the op appears inside an autograd graph — a backward or functional counterpart. The runtime performs no automatic differentiation or shape inference for unknown ops.

questions.explanation: Custom operators require: (1) a schema describing inputs/outputs/types/attributes so the compiler and shape inference can reason about them; (2) at least one kernel per (device, dtype) combination to be supported, registered into the runtime; and (3) if used in autograd, either a differentiable formulation via primitive ops or a manual backward. None of the automated behaviors in A/B/D are how mainstream runtimes work.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: schemas are declared, not inferred; kernels are not auto-generated from a Python function.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no framework introspects .cu source to derive schema and backward.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: shipping source and recompiling on every start is neither typical nor what enables custom ops.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: reflects ONNX custom op API, TensorRT plugin API, and torch's custom op registration.

assumptions: The runtime supports pluggable custom ops (ONNX RT, TRT, PyTorch).
nonImplications: Does not imply the author must implement all dtypes; only those declared as supported by the registration.
Does not imply autograd is always required; inference-only custom ops need no backward.

questions.learningObjective: State the role of an operator dispatcher in an ML runtime (selecting an implementation based on device, dtype, layout) versus the role of an executor (issuing work on the device).
questions.stem: In a modern ML runtime such as PyTorch's ATen or an equivalent stack, what is the primary role of an operator dispatcher?

options.text: To synchronize CPU and GPU streams before every kernel launch so that the executor can guarantee sequential consistency across otherwise-asynchronous device queues.
To decide, based on the (op, device, dtype, layout, autograd key) tuple of a call, which concrete kernel implementation to invoke — i.e., to route from a logical op to a registered backend function.
To allocate output buffers on the target device and free intermediate tensors after each op returns, replacing the caching allocator with a per-op allocator.
To perform compile-time fusion of ops that share tensor shapes so that the executor only sees fused kernels instead of individual operator calls.

questions.explanation: A dispatcher is a routing layer: given an operator call at run time, it looks up the concrete implementation registered for the current (device, dtype, layout, autograd state, functorch transform, ...) — i.e., the 'dispatch key set'. The executor then issues that concrete kernel on the device. Allocation, synchronization and fusion are separate concerns (allocator, stream, compiler).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: cross-stream synchronization is not the dispatcher's job; it belongs to the runtime's stream/event API.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: this is the operator-dispatch pattern found in PyTorch ATen, TensorFlow, and most runtime kernel registries.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: the dispatcher does not manage the allocator; allocation is done by the runtime allocator (e.g., caching allocator).
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: fusion is a compile-time optimization; the dispatcher operates one op at a time in eager mode.

assumptions: A typical eager-mode ML framework with a dispatcher-driven op registry.
nonImplications: Does not imply that the dispatcher is cheap; PyTorch's dispatcher has measurable per-op overhead that motivates tracing/compilation.
Does not imply every framework has an explicit dispatcher; some fully-compiled runtimes have inlined direct calls.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about the trade-offs of calling external libraries (cuBLAS, cuDNN, cutlass, MKL) from a compiled runtime versus emitting compiler-generated kernels.
questions.stem: Which statements about calling into external libraries (cuBLAS, cuDNN, cutlass) from an ML compiler stack are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: External libraries expose stable numerical results across driver and library versions on the same hardware; the compiler can assume bitwise reproducibility of outputs across major versions of cuBLAS or cuDNN.

For standard GEMM/Conv patterns, a heavily-tuned vendor library often outperforms a compiler-generated kernel of comparable complexity because it ships hand-tuned tile shapes, algorithmic variants, and Tensor Core paths per architecture.

A compiler emitting its own fused kernel can beat an external GEMM library specifically when it fuses producer or epilogue ops into the matmul, because the external library sees only the isolated GEMM and cannot fuse across its boundaries.

Calling an external library from a compiled graph always eliminates the need for a caching allocator because the external library manages its own memory pool that the runtime can substitute in for its own allocator.

questions.explanation: Correct: B, C.  A: Wrong: numerical results can drift across cuBLAS/cuDNN versions. B: Correct: standard vendor-lib advantage. C: Correct: compiler advantage lies in fusion boundaries. D: Wrong: external libraries request workspace but do not replace the allocator.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: numerical results can drift across cuBLAS/cuDNN versions.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: standard vendor-lib advantage.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: compiler advantage lies in fusion boundaries.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: external libraries request workspace but do not replace the allocator.

assumptions: The reference stack is CUDA with NVIDIA vendor libraries; analogous points apply on other vendors.
nonImplications: Does not imply compilers can never beat vendor libs at GEMM in isolation; specialized shapes or dtypes sometimes favor Triton/Cutlass generation.
Does not imply fusion is always feasible; some epilogues are unsupported in specific library APIs.

distractorRationales.D: Confuses workspace with full allocator ownership.

sourceRefs.locator: TorchInductor + external kernels; fusion boundary discussion

performanceClaim.scope: GEMM/Conv comparison of vendor-lib vs compiler codegen with and without epilogue fusion

questions.learningObjective: Explain the design and cost of a CPU fallback path when the compiler encounters an op with no GPU implementation.
questions.stem: A compiled GPU inference graph contains a single op with no GPU kernel; the runtime supports a CPU fallback for that op. Which description most accurately captures what happens at execution time?

options.text: The runtime executes the op on both the GPU (using a zero-fill placeholder) and the CPU in parallel, then compares the outputs at run time to decide which to keep; this pattern doubles memory usage but eliminates transfer overhead entirely.

The GPU driver internally emulates the CPU op on the GPU by executing the CPU instruction stream on a special 'compatibility SM' with no host↔device transfer, incurring only a constant driver overhead of roughly 1 µs per op regardless of tensor size.

The runtime silently drops the op from the graph; the missing computation is lossy but tolerable in practice because most such ops (e.g., control-flow or shape ops) do not affect the model's output tensor values downstream.

The runtime copies the op's input tensors from device to host, runs the CPU implementation, then copies the result back to device before the next GPU op resumes. Every fallback op adds a round-trip H2D/D2H transfer that can dominate its execution cost.

questions.explanation: Standard CPU fallback issues D2H transfers for the op's inputs, runs the CPU kernel, and issues H2D transfers for the outputs before the next GPU op. Each fallback introduces synchronization and PCIe transfer cost that can dominate the actual op cost, which is why runtimes such as ONNX Runtime, TensorRT and torch.compile aim to minimize fallback ops or group them into a single CPU subgraph.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: parallel dual-execution is not a standard fallback strategy.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: GPUs cannot emulate arbitrary CPU code on 'compatibility SMs'; no such feature exists.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: runtimes do not silently drop ops.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: standard CPU-fallback semantics.

assumptions: The graph is otherwise GPU-resident; only the one op lacks a GPU kernel.
nonImplications: Does not imply fallback is always bad; for ops that are inherently CPU-appropriate (e.g., string preprocessing) it may be the only viable path.
Does not imply the copy cost is always dominant; large fallback ops can amortize the transfer.
