performanceClaim.scope: Fine-grained CPU fallback ops in an otherwise-GPU-resident graph

questions.learningObjective: Reason about executing a single model across heterogeneous devices (CPU + GPU + specialized accelerator) coordinated by a runtime.
questions.stem: Which statements about heterogeneous execution (a single model spanning CPU + GPU or CPU + NPU) are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Some accelerators (NPUs) have restricted op coverage; the runtime must decide, on a per-op basis, whether the op runs on the NPU (fast for supported ops) or falls back to CPU/GPU (slower but universal), and the partitioning cost model must model this asymmetry.

A partitioning pass typically groups ops into 'subgraphs' assigned to one device each, minimizing cross-device edges; the runtime executes each subgraph on its device and inserts transfer ops between them.

Cross-device edges are essentially free on modern PCIe 4.0 and NVLink; therefore the partitioning cost model can ignore transfer cost and choose the fastest device for each op independently, giving a partition that is optimal by construction.

Heterogeneous execution requires all devices to share a unified virtual memory space with cache coherence; without hardware support such as CXL, correct execution is impossible on machines with discrete GPUs.

questions.explanation: Correct: A, B.  A: Correct: NPU op-coverage asymmetry is a real constraint. B: Correct: standard subgraph partitioning approach. C: Wrong: cross-device transfer and synchronization cost is significant and cannot be ignored. D: Wrong: cache coherence is not required; explicit transfer suffices.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: NPU op-coverage asymmetry is a real constraint.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: standard subgraph partitioning approach.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: cross-device transfer and synchronization cost is significant and cannot be ignored.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: cache coherence is not required; explicit transfer suffices.

assumptions: The runtime supports partitioning into per-device subgraphs and inserting explicit transfers.
nonImplications: Does not imply hardware coherence (CXL, unified memory) is never useful; it does reduce programming complexity, but is not required.
Does not imply the coarsest partition is always best; extreme coarsening may under-utilize a fast device.

distractorRationales.D: Overstates the hardware requirement for heterogeneous execution.

sourceRefs.locator: ONNX Runtime execution providers and subgraph partitioning

performanceClaim.scope: Heterogeneous execution with partitioned subgraphs and explicit device transfers

questions.learningObjective: Describe IREE's design as an MLIR-based end-to-end compilation and runtime stack with an explicit compiler/runtime separation and a hardware abstraction layer (HAL).
questions.stem: Which statement best captures IREE's architecture?

options.text: IREE is a Python-based interpreter that JIT-compiles PyTorch models directly to CUDA at each inference call; it does not use MLIR and does not target hardware other than NVIDIA GPUs.

IREE is an MLIR-based compilation pipeline that lowers input (e.g., StableHLO, TOSA) to a target-specific VM module plus binary kernels; the IREE runtime consists of a bytecode VM and a Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) that abstracts over Vulkan, CUDA, ROCm, CPU and WebGPU backends.
IREE is a thin wrapper around cuDNN that exposes an ONNX-compatible API; it has no MLIR pipeline of its own and forwards all ops to cuDNN kernels.
IREE is a training framework based on JAX's tracing; it does not provide inference deployment and cannot produce a compiled artifact for embedded targets such as WebGPU or edge accelerators.

questions.explanation: IREE (Intermediate Representation Execution Environment) is an MLIR-based compiler + runtime. It ingests a high-level dialect (StableHLO / TOSA / Torch-MLIR), lowers through several MLIR dialects, and emits an IREE VM module plus compiled binary payloads (SPIR-V, PTX, LLVM-object, WebGPU, etc.). The runtime consists of a bytecode VM to dispatch work plus a HAL to abstract device backends. This gives it a strong compiler/runtime separation and multi-backend portability.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: IREE is MLIR-based, not a Python interpreter, and supports many backends.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: matches the IREE project overview.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: IREE has its own MLIR pipeline and does not merely wrap cuDNN.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: IREE is inference-focused with strong edge and WebGPU support.

assumptions: IREE 2024+ mainline design.
nonImplications: Does not imply IREE always outperforms other stacks; performance is workload- and target-dependent.
Does not imply IREE is the only MLIR-based ML compiler; XLA, Torch-MLIR and others exist in the same space.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish ONNX as an interchange format from any specific runtime (ONNX Runtime, TensorRT importer) that consumes ONNX.
questions.stem: Which statement most accurately describes ONNX's role in the deployment stack?

options.text: ONNX is a high-performance inference runtime that runs models directly on GPU or CPU; converting to another format such as TensorRT is unnecessary because ONNX already ships GPU kernels for every op.

ONNX is a serialization format for a graph of standardized operators (with a versioned opset) that different runtimes and compilers can import; performance depends on the runtime that consumes the model, not on ONNX itself.
ONNX is a JIT compiler that lowers PyTorch or TensorFlow models to Triton at load time on the deployment machine; the resulting kernels are cached in the ONNX file for subsequent loads.
ONNX is a proprietary format used only by Microsoft's ONNX Runtime; other runtimes cannot import it and must convert through TorchScript or SavedModel first.

questions.explanation: ONNX is an open interchange format — a protobuf-encoded graph of standardized operators with an opset version. Multiple runtimes (ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, TVM, IREE, OpenVINO, etc.) can import ONNX and execute it with their own kernels. Performance is a property of the consuming runtime, not of the ONNX file, and 'interchange format ≠ high-performance runtime' is one of the module's canonical boundaries.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: ONNX is a format, not a runtime; ONNX Runtime is a separate project that consumes it.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: standard definition of ONNX.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: ONNX does not lower to Triton; it is a format, not a JIT compiler.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: ONNX is open and consumed by many runtimes.

assumptions: The user is comparing 'the ONNX file' to 'the runtime that loads it'.
nonImplications: Does not imply every op is portable across all runtimes; consumers may not support the full opset.
Does not imply ONNX cannot be compiled AOT; runtimes like TensorRT can build an engine from ONNX at ahead-of-time.

sourceRefs.locator: Overview: interchange format, opset, model IR

questions.learningObjective: Identify correct statements about ONNX shape inference and its role in deployment.
questions.stem: Which statements about ONNX shape inference are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Static shape inference results are useful for downstream compilers such as TensorRT or ONNX Runtime's optimizer because they enable buffer planning, fusion decisions and kernel selection without waiting for runtime inputs.
Shape inference in ONNX is a runtime-only operation performed by every consumer at load time; the exported ONNX file itself contains no shape metadata whatsoever for intermediate tensors.

ONNX shape inference is a static, per-op procedure defined by each operator's schema; it propagates known input shapes and dtypes to output shapes and dtypes but can leave some dimensions symbolic when they depend on runtime tensors.

ONNX shape inference always produces fully concrete integer shapes for every intermediate tensor at export time; symbolic dimensions such as `batch` are resolved by the exporter before the model is written.

questions.explanation: A is correct: shape inference is per-op and driven by operator schemas; symbolic (named) dimensions remain when they depend on unknown quantities. C is correct: knowing shapes statically lets downstream compilers plan buffers and select kernels ahead of time. B is wrong: dynamic axes (batch, seq_len) commonly remain symbolic. D is wrong: exported ONNX models carry `value_info` shape metadata for intermediates when known.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: standard downstream use case.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: ONNX files store shape metadata; runtime consumers may extend it but do not start empty.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches the ONNX shape-inference specification.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: symbolic dims are a first-class feature and often remain post-export.

assumptions: The model uses standard ai.onnx opset ops with published schemas.
nonImplications: Does not imply every op has full shape inference implemented; custom ops may lack it.
Does not imply inferred shapes are always tight; unions and unknowns are permitted.

distractorRationales.B: Wrong claim about absence of metadata.

questions.subtopic: ONNX IR version vs opset version
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the ONNX IR (file format) version from the operator opset version, and identify a common source of load-time incompatibility.
questions.stem: A user tries to load an ONNX file and gets an error about unsupported version. Which distinction between the ONNX **IR version** and the **opset version** best explains the diagnostic they should perform?

options.text: IR version and opset version are synonyms in ONNX; the diagnostic is to check `model.ir_version` and upgrade the consumer if it differs by more than 1.

The IR version governs the model file/graph format (how ModelProto, GraphProto, NodeProto are laid out); the opset version governs operator semantics. A load-time incompatibility can come from either — the consumer's ONNX library too old to parse the IR, or too old to know the declared opset — so the diagnostic must inspect both fields in `model.ir_version` and `model.opset_import`.

The opset version is a lower bound on IR version and always exactly one greater; the diagnostic is therefore to update the opset by +1 and re-export the model, which is guaranteed to resolve any version error.
IR version is only used for training checkpoints; inference models omit IR version entirely, so the diagnostic is to check whether the file was accidentally saved as a training checkpoint.

questions.explanation: ONNX distinguishes the IR version (`ir_version`, versioning of the model protobuf format itself) from the opset version (`opset_import[i].version`, versioning of the operator schema library). Both evolve independently; a mismatch on either can make a model unloadable. The correct diagnostic looks at both. Options A/B/C fabricate relationships that do not exist in the ONNX spec.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: IR version and opset version are separate axes.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: two-axis versioning per the ONNX specification.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: no such exact relationship exists.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: IR version is present on all ONNX models.

assumptions: The file is a well-formed ONNX protobuf.
nonImplications: Does not imply every version mismatch is fatal; some ORT versions can be forward-compatible within an opset range.
Does not imply upgrading ONNX always fixes the issue; some old runtimes are the constraint.

sourceRefs.locator: Versioning: IR version and opset version

questions.learningObjective: Explain the meaning of the ONNX opset version in a model file and the compatibility contract between opset producers and consumers.
questions.stem: An ONNX model advertises `opset_import: [{domain: "", version: 17}]` in its metadata. What does the opset version encode, and what compatibility guarantee follows?

options.text: It specifies the ONNX Runtime binary version that must be installed to load the model; opset 17 corresponds to ONNX Runtime version 17.x and models built with a mismatched runtime version fail to load.

It specifies the version of the model's weight file format; opset changes only affect serialization layout, not operator semantics, so any runtime version can consume the file if it understands protobuf.

It specifies the version of each operator's schema used by the model — signatures, attribute defaults, and semantics of ops in the default (ai.onnx) domain at opset 17. A runtime that claims to support opset ≥ 17 must be able to execute those ops with those semantics; older runtimes may lack ops introduced after their supported opset.
It specifies the version of the underlying framework that exported the model; a model exported by PyTorch 1.13 must be loaded by an ONNX Runtime linked against PyTorch 1.13 for correctness.

questions.explanation: The `opset_import` list declares, per domain, which version of each op's schema the model relies on. Op schemas evolve — new ops are added, attributes change, defaults shift, behaviors can be tightened. A runtime advertises which opset ranges it supports and must respect the exact schema of the declared opset for correct execution. Opset is not tied to runtime binary version, weight format, or framework version.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: opset version is orthogonal to runtime binary version.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: opset changes affect operator semantics, not just serialization.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard definition per ONNX operator specification.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: opset is about ONNX operator schemas, not the exporter framework.

assumptions: The empty domain "" refers to the standard ai.onnx op set.
nonImplications: Does not imply higher opsets are always better; some ops become deprecated in later opsets.
Does not imply consumers must support every opset ≤ 17; they typically support a range.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses opset with runtime binary version.

questions.learningObjective: Describe what typically goes into a model deployment package (weights + graph + metadata) and why the packaging boundary matters for reproducibility.
questions.stem: Which is the most complete description of what a well-packaged inference model artifact typically contains?

options.text: Only the weight tensors serialized as a single binary blob; graph structure and signatures are inferred by the runtime at load time by tracing the model on a synthetic input tensor of zeros.
Only the Python source code of the model; runtime re-instantiates and initializes weights from a random seed at deployment because random weights are close enough to the trained ones for inference.

(i) The graph structure or compiled program; (ii) the weight tensors with dtype/shape/layout metadata; (iii) input/output signatures (names, dtypes, shape specs); (iv) preprocessing/postprocessing metadata (tokenizer config, normalization stats, calibration scales for quantized models) — plus a version tag identifying the schema of the archive itself.
Only a URL pointing to the model in the training framework's registry; the runtime downloads weights and code fresh on every process start to guarantee freshness of the artifact.

questions.explanation: A robust deployment artifact contains structure (graph or compiled program), weights (with metadata), signatures, and preprocessing/postprocessing metadata, plus an archive version. Options A/B/D describe non-viable packaging schemes: shipping only weights would leave graph and pre/postprocessing undefined; shipping only source and random-initializing weights is nonsensical; downloading on every start couples deployment to network availability and defeats reproducibility.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: weights alone are insufficient.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: random init is not equivalent to trained weights.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches standard packaging (SavedModel, TorchScript, ONNX, safetensors + config).
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: network-dependent deployment breaks reproducibility.

assumptions: Production deployment where reproducibility, portability and offline operation matter.
nonImplications: Does not imply a single format fits every use case; the LLM community often uses safetensors + tokenizer config + generation config as multiple files rather than one bundle.
Does not imply preprocessing metadata is always separable from the model; some vendors embed it in the compiled artifact.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a runtime decides where to place each op and tensor when the graph mixes CPU-only ops, GPU-native ops, and host↔device transfers.
questions.stem: A model graph has some ops with only a CPU implementation and others with only a GPU implementation. Which of the following statements about device placement are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Placement decisions should ideally minimize the total number of host↔device transitions along the critical path, sometimes at the cost of running an op on a slower device — the transfer cost can exceed the op-level savings.

A device-placement pass typically inserts explicit host↔device transfer ops (e.g., MemcpyToHost / MemcpyToDevice) at boundaries between differently placed ops, and the emitted plan records those transfers so the runtime does not have to guess them.

Placing CPU-only ops on the GPU can be forced by the runtime by 'promoting' the CPU kernel implementation to a GPU kernel automatically; no additional lowering is needed because the runtime treats device tags as advisory hints only.
Alternating between CPU and GPU ops in the middle of a hot loop causes host↔device transfer traffic across PCIe/NVLink and can dominate the end-to-end latency, even if each individual kernel is fast.

questions.explanation: Standard device-placement passes insert transfer ops at device boundaries (A). Alternating device execution introduces PCIe/NVLink transfer overhead that often dominates fine-grained ops (C). Consequently, placement heuristics minimize the number of device transitions on the hot path (D). Option (B) is false: 'device tags' are not advisory — an op with only a CPU implementation cannot be run on the GPU without providing a GPU kernel; the runtime cannot magically synthesize one.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: this is the standard placement heuristic (minimize crossings on the hot path).
optionExplanations.B: Correct: transfer-op insertion is standard in ONNX Runtime, XLA HloRunner, TensorRT (with explicit host tensors), and IREE.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: a CPU-only op needs a genuine GPU implementation to run on the GPU; there is no automatic 'promotion'.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: PCIe transfer cost is a well-known bottleneck for graphs with fine-grained device transitions.

assumptions: The runtime supports mixed CPU/GPU execution (typical of ONNX Runtime, XLA, IREE).
The graph is executed on a single machine with a distinct host and device memory space.
nonImplications: Does not imply that every CPU op must be moved to GPU; small ops on the CPU can be preferable to a round-trip.
Does not imply the runtime always uses PCIe; NVLink or unified memory may reduce but not eliminate transfer cost.

sourceRefs.locator: Device placement and Memcpy nodes in ONNX Runtime
PCIe transfer cost and pinned memory guidance
Placement pass and HAL buffer transfers

performanceClaim.scope: Mixed CPU/GPU graphs with fine-grained device alternation on PCIe-attached GPUs

questions.learningObjective: Describe the role of a kernel registry (a mapping from op signature to concrete implementation) in a runtime that supports multiple backends and dtypes.
questions.stem: In an ML runtime, the 'kernel registry' is best described as which of the following?

options.text: A mapping from (op name, device, dtype, layout, …) to a concrete function pointer or callable that implements the op; the dispatcher consults it at run time to pick the correct backend implementation.
A cache of compiled kernels keyed by input pointer addresses; hits skip recompilation while misses trigger a JIT compile on the current CUDA stream.
A profiling database of measured kernel latencies used by the compiler's cost model; it does not affect run-time dispatch decisions and is only consulted during autotuning.
A structured hardware descriptor of the physical device (SM count, warp size) that the runtime uses to select launch configurations for kernels declared as `device-agnostic`.

questions.explanation: A kernel registry is a table (usually populated at library load time via registration macros or plugin discovery) that maps op signatures to implementations. When a runtime dispatches an op, it queries this registry with the current tensor descriptors to select the correct kernel — for example ONNX Runtime's `KernelRegistry`, TVM's `PackedFunc` op registry, or PyTorch's ATen dispatch table. It is a runtime data structure, not a cost model, cache, or hardware descriptor.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: standard kernel-registry semantics.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: this describes a JIT compilation cache, not a registry.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: describes an autotuning database.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: describes a device capability record.

assumptions: The runtime supports multiple backends or dtypes and needs to route calls dynamically.
nonImplications: Does not imply that the registry is a single flat table; PyTorch's dispatcher has layered dispatch keys.
Does not imply registrations happen at compile time; many runtimes register kernels at library load via static initializers or plugin discovery.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a runtime handles dynamic (unknown-at-compile-time) shapes: symbolic dim tracking, allocator reservation, and specialization vs generalization trade-offs.
questions.stem: Which statements about how modern ML runtimes handle dynamic shapes are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Fully-dynamic shapes and fully-static shapes are equivalent in cost: any modern compiler can generate a single kernel that is as fast on unknown shapes as on known ones, because dynamic-shape codegen has no runtime overhead versus fully specialized codegen.

Bucketing (grouping inputs into a small set of pre-compiled shape classes) is a standard practical trade-off: it retains most of the specialization benefit while covering a large range of real workloads, at the cost of build time proportional to the number of buckets.

A shape runtime maintains symbolic descriptors for tensor dimensions (batch = N, seq_len = S) and evaluates them at run time based on actual input shapes; downstream kernels can be parameterized on those symbols or specialized.

Compilers typically declare a set of shape ranges (min / opt / max, or bucketed shapes) at build time; runtime inputs falling within a supported range use the generalized kernel, while inputs outside the range typically trigger a fallback, recompilation, or error.

questions.explanation: Correct: B, C, D.  A: Wrong: dynamic and static shapes are not zero-cost equivalent. B: Correct: bucketing is a mainstream practical technique. C: Correct: symbolic dim descriptors are the standard tool. D: Correct: shape ranges must be declared at build.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: dynamic and static shapes are not zero-cost equivalent.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: bucketing is a mainstream practical technique.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: symbolic dim descriptors are the standard tool.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: shape ranges must be declared at build.

assumptions: The runtime supports dynamic shapes (most modern stacks do to some degree).
nonImplications: Does not imply dynamic-shape kernels are always slow; the gap is often small for large ops.
Does not imply bucketing works for all workloads; extreme shape variability may exhaust the bucket budget.

performanceClaim.scope: Dynamic-vs-static kernel cost, bucketing trade-off in deployment

questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of StableHLO as a compiler-portability boundary between ML frameworks (JAX, PyTorch export, TF) and compilers (XLA, IREE, others).
questions.stem: How is StableHLO positioned in the OpenXLA / IREE ecosystem?

options.text: StableHLO is a runtime engine that executes MLIR modules directly on GPU without any additional lowering; it replaces XLA's Runtime and cannot be used with any other backend such as IREE.
StableHLO is the low-level LLVM IR that XLA compiles its HLO into during backend code generation; it exposes hardware-specific instructions and is not intended to be portable across accelerators.

StableHLO is a versioned, stable operator set (specified as an MLIR dialect) intended to serve as a portable IR between ML frameworks and compilers, providing forward/backward compatibility guarantees so that a producer and a consumer built at different times can still interoperate.
StableHLO is a version-agnostic Python DSL layered on top of PyTorch; it converts arbitrary Python control flow into JAX-style pure functions at import time and requires no compiler.

questions.explanation: StableHLO is an MLIR dialect specifying a stable set of ML operators with explicit versioning and compatibility guarantees. Its purpose is to be the interchange layer between framework front-ends and downstream compilers (XLA, IREE, or others), so a model serialized in StableHLO by one version of a framework can be consumed by a compiler shipped at a different time.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: it is not a runtime; downstream compilers still lower to their own backends.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: StableHLO is a high-level ML operator dialect, not LLVM IR.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches the StableHLO project mission.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: it is an IR dialect, not a Python DSL.

assumptions: The ecosystem in question is OpenXLA / IREE / MLIR-based compilers.
nonImplications: Does not imply StableHLO covers every op needed by every model; some ops still require framework-specific extensions.
Does not imply StableHLO replaces HLO entirely; XLA still consumes it and may lower via HLO internally.

questions.learningObjective: State the semantics of a CUDA stream (an in-order queue of device work) and a CUDA event (a synchronization point recordable on a stream), and their role in a runtime.
questions.stem: Which statement most accurately describes CUDA streams and events in the context of an ML runtime that overlaps kernel execution with data transfers?

options.text: A stream represents a physical hardware queue with a fixed one-to-one binding to a specific SM group; events are per-SM performance counters that record occupancy and warp-stall statistics for later Nsight analysis.

A stream is a mutable shared buffer that host and device both read/write; events are memory fences that flush the L2 cache to global memory before subsequent kernels begin executing on the same device.

A stream is an in-order queue of operations on the device — work enqueued on the same stream executes in order, work on different streams may execute concurrently; events are recorded on streams as synchronization markers that other streams (or the host) can wait on.

Streams and events are optional debugging APIs whose only function is to expose timing information to profilers; kernel execution order is instead determined by the CUDA driver's global scheduler regardless of stream assignment.

questions.explanation: A CUDA stream is an in-order queue of device operations. Operations within the same stream execute in issue order; operations across different streams may overlap (subject to hardware and driver policies). CUDA events are recorded on streams (`cudaEventRecord(event, stream)`) and act as synchronization markers — another stream can wait on the event, or the host can block until it completes. Overlapping copy-and-compute uses one stream for H2D and another for the kernel, synchronized by events.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: streams are logical queues, not physical SM bindings; events are not performance counters.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: streams are not shared host/device buffers, and events are not L2 fences.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches the CUDA C++ Programming Guide description of streams and events.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: streams determine execution order (within-stream in-order); they are not debug-only.

assumptions: A single-device, single-process CUDA context.
nonImplications: Does not imply cross-stream ops always run concurrently; concurrency depends on GPU resources and dependencies.
Does not imply events replace `cudaStreamSynchronize`; both are valid tools for different granularities.

sourceRefs.locator: Concurrent kernel execution and overlap using streams

questions.learningObjective: Identify correct and incorrect statements about host/device synchronization in a CUDA-based ML runtime.
questions.stem: Which statements about host/device synchronization in a CUDA runtime are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Under legacy default-stream semantics, `cudaMemcpy` (blocking) can be issued while a kernel is executing on a user-created stream and always returns immediately without waiting for that kernel — the two operations proceed independently.
`cudaStreamSynchronize(stream)` blocks the calling host thread until all previously enqueued work on `stream` has completed, but does not affect work on other streams.
`cudaDeviceSynchronize()` waits for all streams on the current device to drain; overusing it in a hot loop serializes host and device and defeats stream-level overlap.

A `cudaMemcpyAsync` on the default stream is guaranteed to be fully overlapped with any kernel executing on another user-created stream, even without explicit event synchronization or the use of pinned host memory.

questions.explanation: Correct: B, C.  A: Wrong: legacy default stream synchronizes with other streams; the blocking `cudaMemcpy` will wait for the kernel. B: Correct: matches `cudaStreamSynchronize` semantics. C: Correct: overusing device-wide sync serializes execution. D: Wrong: async is necessary but not sufficient for overlap — pinned memory and correct stream placement are also required.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: legacy default stream synchronizes with other streams; the blocking `cudaMemcpy` will wait for the kernel.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: matches `cudaStreamSynchronize` semantics.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: overusing device-wide sync serializes execution.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: async is necessary but not sufficient for overlap — pinned memory and correct stream placement are also required.

assumptions: CUDA runtime API in its documented behavior; legacy default-stream mode unless otherwise specified.
Single-process, single-device unless noted.
nonImplications: Does not imply per-thread default stream (`--default-stream per-thread`) has the same semantics; that mode changes the default-stream synchronization behavior.
Does not imply pinned memory is always desirable; it consumes physical RAM.

distractorRationales.D: Confuses async API with overlap guarantee.

sourceRefs.locator: Stream synchronization semantics; default stream behavior
Asynchronous memcpy and pinned memory requirement

questions.learningObjective: Describe the TensorRT deployment pipeline: the builder produces an engine (plan file) from a network description; the runtime loads and executes the engine.
questions.stem: In the TensorRT workflow, which sequence best describes the roles of the builder, engine and runtime?

options.text: The builder and the runtime are the same object in TensorRT; every inference call re-optimizes the graph on the currently observed inputs, which is what allows TensorRT to adapt to shape variations at run time without recompilation.
TensorRT builds and runs entirely on the CPU; the GPU is only used for peripheral memory transfer, and the actual compute is executed by CUDA-backed CPU kernels that emulate GPU instructions.

The engine is a text-format description of the model that the runtime interprets line by line; kernel selection happens on every execution, so plan files are portable across GPUs but slower than a JIT compiler.

The builder consumes a network description (e.g., parsed ONNX or the TensorRT network API), runs optimizations (layer fusion, kernel selection, precision calibration) and produces a serialized engine (plan file); the runtime deserializes the engine on the target device and creates an execution context that runs inference.

questions.explanation: TensorRT's builder is a compile-time component that takes a network description and produces a serialized engine (plan). Optimizations — layer fusion, kernel selection from a tactic set, precision calibration, memory planning — are performed during build. At deployment the runtime deserializes the plan and creates one or more execution contexts that run inference. The plan file is a compiled binary artifact, and it is generally not portable across different GPU architectures without rebuild.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: TensorRT does not re-optimize per inference call.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: TensorRT executes kernels on the GPU.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: the plan is binary and pre-optimized; the runtime does not select kernels per call.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: standard TensorRT builder → engine → runtime pipeline.

assumptions: The user is running the standard TensorRT flow (not TensorRT-LLM's specialized flow, though it is similar).
nonImplications: Does not imply plan files are portable across GPU generations; they are typically architecture- and TRT-version-specific.
Does not imply build time is negligible; large models can take minutes to hours to build.

sourceRefs.locator: TensorRT builder, engine, and execution context

questions.subtopic: TensorRT build cost vs runtime cost
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the split between one-time build cost and per-inference runtime cost in TensorRT, and identify a common misdiagnosis when comparing to eager PyTorch.
questions.stem: A team benchmarks their model as follows: 'TensorRT 8 min, PyTorch eager 0.2 s'. What is the most likely source of confusion in this comparison?

options.text: The 8 minutes is the TensorRT engine build cost, which is a one-time offline compilation of the model; the correct comparison against PyTorch eager is per-inference latency of the deserialized engine, not build time. Build cost and inference latency should never be added together for the deployment comparison.
TensorRT's build step must be repeated on every inference call, whereas PyTorch eager amortizes it via warmup, which is why the 8-minute number is a per-call cost that dominates end-to-end latency.

PyTorch eager is missing calls to `torch.cuda.synchronize()`, so the 0.2 s is entirely CPU-side dispatch cost; TensorRT does not require synchronization, so its 8 minutes is a true GPU-side execution time.

TensorRT is always slower than PyTorch eager for BERT-sized models on modern GPUs; the 0.2 s PyTorch number reflects steady-state kernel launches, whereas TensorRT's kernel selection heuristics never converge to a competitive plan for transformer workloads.

questions.explanation: TensorRT's builder can spend minutes or more selecting tactics, calibrating precision and running optimization passes; this is a one-time offline cost. The relevant comparison for deployment is per-inference latency of the deserialized engine (typically milliseconds or less). Conflating build cost with inference cost is a common miscommunication in benchmarks.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: the standard build-vs-runtime split.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: build is one-time offline, not per-call.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: fabricates PyTorch measurement error.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: TensorRT commonly outperforms PyTorch eager on transformers.

assumptions: The 8-minute number is the reported TensorRT build time, not an inference latency.
nonImplications: Does not imply build time is irrelevant; long build times matter for iterative development and canary deploys.
Does not imply eager PyTorch is always slower at inference; small models with tiny kernels may favor eager.

distractorRationales.B: Wrong split of one-time vs per-call.

sourceRefs.locator: Builder cost vs. runtime cost; engine deserialization

questions.learningObjective: Reason about the portability constraints of a serialized TensorRT engine across GPU architectures, driver versions and TensorRT major versions.
questions.stem: Which statements about the portability of a serialized TensorRT engine (plan file) are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Dynamic input shape ranges (optimization profiles) supported by the runtime are baked into the plan at build time; if the runtime feeds a shape outside the built ranges the engine cannot execute it and must be rebuilt.
The plan file is a wrapper around the ONNX file it was built from; deleting the ONNX file makes the plan invalid because the runtime re-parses ONNX on deserialization.

A plan file built for one GPU compute capability (e.g., sm_80, A100) is not guaranteed to run on a different one (e.g., sm_90, H100); the builder emits kernels for the target architecture used at build time.

A plan file built with TensorRT major version X is not generally deserializable by a TensorRT runtime of major version Y ≠ X, because plan serialization is not backward/forward compatible across major versions.

questions.explanation: Plan files are architecture-specific (A), TensorRT-major-version-specific (B), and shape-range-specific (C). D is false: the plan is self-contained — it does not require the source ONNX at runtime.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: optimization profiles are baked in at build.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: the plan is self-contained and does not need the source ONNX.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: TensorRT documentation states plans are compute-capability-specific.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: cross-major-version compatibility is not guaranteed.

assumptions: Standard TensorRT deployment without explicit version-compatibility mode enabled.
nonImplications: Does not imply cross-arch is never possible; TensorRT has optional 'hardware compatibility' modes that trade performance for wider portability.
Does not imply cross-minor-version is broken; minor-version compatibility is typically maintained.

distractorRationales.B: Fabricates dependency on the source file.

questions.learningObjective: Describe TVM's Relax VM: a bytecode VM that dispatches PackedFunc kernels and manages allocators and streams for a compiled model.
questions.stem: In TVM's Unity stack, what is the Relax VM (`tvm.relax.VirtualMachine`) primarily responsible for?

options.text: Executing a compiled Relax program by interpreting a VM bytecode that invokes precompiled PackedFunc kernels, allocating tensors via a runtime allocator, dispatching to different devices via device contexts, and handling dynamic shape branches.
Providing an interactive Python REPL for authoring Relax IR; it does not participate in inference execution, which is instead handled by the CUDA driver directly via nvptx-loaded kernels.
Replacing PyTorch's autograd engine so TVM can compute gradients through Relax; it does not run inference and is deprecated in favor of the tvm.te module for actual execution.

Performing operator-fusion optimization on the input Relax IR during graph construction; the VM lowers the fused graph to a monolithic C++ function that is JIT-compiled into a shared library at each call site.

questions.explanation: The Relax VM is the runtime execution engine. It consumes a VMExecutable (compiled Relax bytecode + a set of PackedFunc kernels), interprets the bytecode instructions (call_packed, alloc_tensor, alloc_storage, if_true, ret), dispatches to devices via device contexts, and manages storage/memory. Optimization (fusion, layout, etc.) happens in the compilation pipeline before the VMExecutable is produced.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: VMExecutable + bytecode + PackedFunc dispatch model.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: the VM is an execution engine, not a REPL.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: Relax VM is not an autograd engine.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: fusion is a compile-time pass, not a VM responsibility.

assumptions: TVM Unity's Relax + VM design as of 2024.
nonImplications: Does not imply the VM must always be used; TVM also supports GraphExecutor for simpler workloads.
Does not imply VM overhead dominates for large kernels.

sourceRefs.locator: Relax VM design and instruction set

questions.subtopic: Virtual Machine runtime (TVM Relax VM / IREE VM)
questions.learningObjective: Explain why deep-learning runtimes such as TVM Relax VM or IREE use a bytecode virtual machine to interpret a compiled program, rather than directly linking a monolithic function.
questions.stem: TVM Relax and IREE both ship 'virtual machine' style runtimes that interpret compiled bytecode rather than emitting a single monolithic native function. Which motivation best explains this design?

options.text: Interpreting bytecode is faster than native execution because the VM bypasses the operating-system's process scheduling, letting each op run at higher priority than in a native binary.
A VM eliminates the need for a memory allocator by executing every op in a single pre-allocated buffer, which is the reason VM-based runtimes have lower memory footprints than native ones.
A VM is mandatory whenever the target is a GPU because GPU code cannot be dispatched from natively compiled host code and must be issued through a bytecode interpreter.

A VM lets the runtime express host-side control flow (if/while, dynamic shape branches, allocator calls, external function invocation) around a set of precompiled kernels, decoupling model control flow from any single native ABI.

questions.explanation: A bytecode VM is used to represent the host-side program: control flow, dynamic shape dispatch, allocator/free ops, external calls, and invocation of precompiled device kernels. This keeps the model portable across host targets (x86, aarch64, wasm), simplifies serialization (the VM program is a data artifact), and separates the fixed set of kernels from the flexible host program. Compute kernels themselves are still native code.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: interpreted bytecode is not faster than native code per se; the VM is chosen for portability and expressiveness, not raw throughput.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: VMs still call into allocators; they do not remove the need for allocation.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: native binaries can and do dispatch GPU kernels (e.g., CUDA runtime API from C++).
optionExplanations.D: Correct: describes the standard motivation used in the TVM Relax and IREE design docs.

assumptions: The VM in question is a coarse-grained bytecode VM that dispatches kernels, not a fine-grained instruction VM like the JVM.
nonImplications: Does not imply that AOT-native artifacts (e.g., AOTInductor .so) are inferior; they trade portability for lower host overhead.
Does not imply the VM is always the bottleneck; for large models kernel time dwarfs VM overhead.

questions.learningObjective: Triage an accuracy regression across a model update by systematically bisecting the change (weights, kernel, precision, framework version).
questions.stem: A model that previously achieved 78.5% accuracy on the validation set now reports 76.2% after a joint change (new PyTorch version, new torch.compile mode, new BF16 mixed-precision recipe, retrained weights). What is the most defensible triage plan?

options.text: Immediately blame the new torch.compile mode and revert it; if accuracy comes back that confirms the compile mode is the cause. Bisecting other axes is unnecessary because compile changes are the most common source of accuracy drift in practice.

Rerun the evaluation five times and average the accuracy. Accuracy drift of 2.3 percentage points is within the noise of any modern evaluation harness, so the reported regression is almost certainly a random fluctuation and no code investigation is needed.

Bisect the axes one at a time: (1) hold everything else at old and switch back to old weights → see if accuracy recovers; (2) restore old PyTorch version; (3) disable mixed precision. This isolates which axis is responsible before any deep debugging. Only after the axis is known should we look at kernel-level differences.

Skip axis bisection and instead directly compare the softmax outputs on 10 validation samples with `torch.testing.assert_close`; any bitwise difference would identify the exact op responsible for the accuracy drop, bypassing the need for controlled experiments.

questions.explanation: The correct discipline is to bisect the confounded change into single-variable experiments. Blaming any one axis without evidence (A) risks reverting the wrong change. Attributing a 2.3-point drop to noise (B) is inappropriate without measuring variance. Bitwise comparison of softmax outputs (C) is neither guaranteed to isolate the cause nor to be zero across correct compiler transformations. Systematic bisection is the standard practice.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: presumptive blame without evidence.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: 2.3-point drops rarely fall within evaluation noise on standard benchmarks; even if so, variance must be measured.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: bisect confounded axes.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: bitwise comparison does not isolate the cause.

assumptions: The evaluation harness is deterministic given fixed inputs and seeds.
nonImplications: Does not imply bisection order is unique; sometimes reversing weights is the cheapest first step, sometimes disabling compile is.
Does not imply per-op comparison is useless; it becomes valuable after the axis is isolated.

distractorRationales.D: Skips isolation and misuses bitwise comparison.

questions.subtopic: Async timing pitfall in benchmark code
questions.learningObjective: Identify a subtle timing bug in a benchmark loop where the CPU timer records the wrong quantity because of async launch and CUDA stream ordering.
questions.stem: The benchmark below prints `per-iter mean: 0.041 ms`, but the model is a 4096×4096 FP16 matmul that could not possibly run in 41 µs on the target GPU. Which change is required to make the measurement meaningful?
questions.codeSnippet:
import torch, time
x = torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
w = torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)

# Warmup
for _ in range(3):
    y = x @ w

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(100):
    y = x @ w
t1 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"per-iter mean: {(t1 - t0) / 100 * 1000:.3f} ms")

# Prints: per-iter mean: 0.041 ms
questions.profileData: Reported per-iter mean: 0.041 ms; expected ~2-3 ms based on 4096-square FP16 matmul on the target GPU.

options.text: Move the `time.perf_counter()` reads into a `with torch.no_grad():` block. The measurement is wrong because autograd tracking is running in the background, and disabling it eliminates the async accounting problem entirely.

Add `torch.cuda.synchronize()` immediately before `t0` and immediately before `t1`. The CPU timer currently ends before the GPU has finished the queued kernels; the pre-timer sync flushes prior work, and the pre-t1 sync waits for all 100 kernels to finish, so the interval reflects real GPU wall-time.
Replace `time.perf_counter()` with `time.time()`, which has higher resolution on Linux and can measure microsecond-level events. `perf_counter` under-reports for durations shorter than 100 µs.

Run the loop 10 000 times instead of 100. The current 100-iter loop is too short to amortize warmup; with more iterations, the per-iter mean will asymptotically approach the correct value without any change to the timing methodology.

questions.explanation: CUDA launches are asynchronous. The `t1` capture happens right after the CPU has enqueued 100 kernels, not after the GPU has executed them. The visible cost is only the ~0.04 ms of dispatch overhead per launch. Correct methodology synchronizes before the start marker (to flush prior work), enqueues the loop, and synchronizes before the end marker. Option A conflates autograd with async accounting; C is false (perf_counter resolution is fine); D does not fix the fundamental issue.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: no_grad has no effect on CUDA async semantics.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: async launch + missing synchronize is the exact bug pattern.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: perf_counter is high-resolution and appropriate for microsecond timing.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: more iterations still measure dispatch cost if sync is missing.

assumptions: The kernel is a real cuBLAS matmul and is compute-heavy at this shape.
The target GPU has no anomalously fast FP16 GEMM implementation.
nonImplications: Does not imply CUDA events are unnecessary; they can replace or complement the sync pattern.
Does not imply autograd is free; it does add dispatcher overhead but not the 40× discrepancy here.

distractorRationales.D: Iteration count does not fix missing sync.

sourceRefs.locator: Synchronization when timing PyTorch CUDA workloads

performanceClaim.scope: Timing a 4096²  FP16 matmul loop without proper CUDA synchronization

questions.subtopic: Graph break and recompile log diagnosis
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose torch.compile graph breaks and recompiles from the TORCH_LOGS='+dynamo,recompiles' output and identify remediation strategies.
questions.stem: The following TORCH_LOGS output was captured for a torch.compile'd function processing a variable-length batch. Which conclusions are correct? (Select all that apply.)
questions.profileData:
TORCH_LOGS='+dynamo,recompiles' output for f(x, mask):

[0] torch._dynamo.convert_frame: Recompiling function f (call 1) — new signature
[0] torch._dynamo.symbolic_convert: graph break on `if mask.any():` — data-dependent branch
[0] torch._inductor: compiled subgraph #0 (before break), #1 (after break)

[1] torch._dynamo.convert_frame: Recompiling function f (call 2) — guard failure: tensor 'x' size changed 128 → 256
[1] torch._inductor: recompile of #0 and #1

[2] torch._dynamo.convert_frame: Recompiling function f (call 3) — guard failure: tensor 'x' size changed 256 → 128
[2] torch._inductor: cache hit on #0 (size 128 already compiled), cache hit on #1

options.text: The 'cache hit' at call 3 shows that torch.compile keeps compiled subgraphs indexed by (shape, dtype) guard set — bouncing between two sizes stops paying compile cost after both have been seen once, but each still uses shape-specific code.

Replacing `if mask.any():` with `torch.where(mask, x, 0)` — an eager pattern that avoids the graph break — would still cause the same recompiles because guard failures on tensor shapes are unrelated to control flow.

The `if mask.any():` triggers a graph break because it is a data-dependent Python control flow; the compiled region is split into two subgraphs (#0 before and #1 after) with eager execution of the branch decision itself in between.

The recompile at call 2 is due to a shape guard failure (128 → 256); enabling dynamic shapes for `x` (`torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic(x, 0)`) would avoid the recompile by generating a shape-generic compiled graph that handles both sizes.

questions.explanation: C: data-dependent Python control flow forces a graph break, splitting compilation into subgraphs #0 and #1. D: enabling dynamic shape via `mark_dynamic` avoids per-shape recompiles by generating one shape-generic compiled graph. A: torch.compile keeps compiled subgraphs indexed by shape/dtype guards, so bouncing between two known sizes stops paying compile cost after both have been seen (the log shows 'cache hit on #0' at call 3). B is wrong because rewriting `if mask.any():` to `torch.where` removes the graph break (unlocking fusion across the branch); that is a real, separate benefit from what shape guards do, so the claim that 'rewriting has no effect on compile behavior' conflates the two orthogonal mechanisms.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: cache-indexed compiles stabilize after all shapes seen.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: the rewrite eliminates the graph break (unlocking fusion across the branch); the claim that 'rewriting has no effect' conflates two orthogonal mechanisms.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: data-dependent branch = graph break.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: mark_dynamic avoids shape-guard recompiles.

assumptions: PyTorch 2.3 ~ 2.5 torch.compile behavior.
cache_size_limit is not being exceeded by the two shapes in the log.
nonImplications: Does not imply mark_dynamic has zero cost; the compiled shape-generic kernel can be slower per iteration.
Does not imply graph breaks are always bad; some are unavoidable and negligible.

distractorRationales.B: Conflates shape guard with graph break impact.

sourceRefs.locator: torch._dynamo recompile / guard failure / graph break docs

performanceClaim.scope: torch.compile dynamo/recompile log interpretation

questions.learningObjective: Interpret L1/L2 cache hit-rate metrics in Nsight Compute and decide whether the metric points to a real optimization opportunity or is expected for the workload.
questions.stem: Two elementwise FP32 kernels have identical implementations except for input size. Nsight Compute reports the following. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.profileData:
Kernel A: single-pass streaming over 1 GB (much larger than L2)
  L1 Hit Rate: 40 %
  L2 Hit Rate: 5 %
  DRAM Throughput: 92 %

Kernel B: single-pass streaming over 8 MB (fits in L2)
  L1 Hit Rate: 42 %
  L2 Hit Rate: 78 %
  DRAM Throughput: 22 %

options.text: Kernel A's low L2 hit rate is a bug; adding a shared-memory blocking scheme (loading tiles into shared memory) will let the L2 hit rate climb to Kernel B's level, unlocking a proportional speedup.
Kernel B is compute-bound because its DRAM throughput is only 22%; the correct optimization is to add more math per element to raise arithmetic intensity toward the ridge point of the roofline.

The L2 hit rates prove the L2 is unreliable on Ampere; disabling the L2 (via `cudaFuncSetAttribute` with CU_CTX_CACHE_L2_NONE) will make DRAM utilization consistent between the two kernels and improve total throughput.

Kernel A's low L2 hit rate is expected for a single-pass stream over data larger than L2 — each cache line is touched once and evicted before reuse. The kernel is memory-bound at 92% DRAM and shared-memory blocking cannot reduce the total number of unique bytes that must be read.

questions.explanation: For a single-pass streaming kernel over data much larger than L2, cache is not reusable — the working set exceeds L2 capacity so lines are evicted before reuse. Low L2 hit rate is expected and not fixable by better locality. Kernel A's 92% DRAM utilization confirms it is near HBM peak. Blocking helps when there is reuse to expose, which is not the case here. Options A/B/C fabricate mechanisms: A misapplies blocking, B confuses low DRAM with compute-bound (it's simply that Kernel B mostly hits L2), C fabricates an L2-disable API.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: no data reuse to expose in a single-pass stream over data >> L2.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: Kernel B's low DRAM is because L2 is serving reads, not because it's compute-bound.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: disabling L2 is not a real optimization path.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: matches roofline / working-set analysis for streaming.

assumptions: A100 has ~40 MB L2 cache; 1 GB is well beyond it, 8 MB fits comfortably.
The elementwise kernel has no cross-element reuse in either case.
nonImplications: Does not imply cache-blocking is useless in general; it is critical for GEMM/attention where reuse exists.
Does not imply L2 hit rate is uninformative; combined with working-set size it is a meaningful diagnostic.

distractorRationales.A: Applies blocking where no reuse exists.

Working set vs cache size and locality optimization limits

questions.subtopic: Compile time as a benchmark axis
questions.learningObjective: Reason about when compile time should be reported alongside inference latency in benchmarks and how the choice affects fair comparison.
questions.stem: Which statements about compile time in ML performance benchmarks are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Reporting only steady-state inference latency without disclosing compile time can hide significant real-world cost, particularly for auto-tuners (TVM Ansor, TensorRT builder tactic search) that can take minutes to hours per shape/model.

Compile time is fully amortizable in every deployment scenario: since the model is compiled once and served millions of times, per-request amortized compile time is always negligible and does not need to be reported.

For iterative research workflows (e.g., quickly iterating on model architecture), long compile times can dominate wall-clock development cost; a fair benchmark for these workflows must include compile time.
Benchmarks that compare compilers with different compile-time budgets (10 s vs 30 min) but the same inference latency should be treated as equivalent for deployment because compile is offline.

questions.explanation: A: hiding compile time misleads readers. C: for iterative workflows compile dominates. B is too strong (there are common cases — canary deploys, autoscaling, per-tenant compile — where amortization fails). D is also wrong: even for deployment, a 30-minute compile impacts release cadence, canary strategy and rollback speed; the tradeoff is real, even if not per-request.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: standard reporting caveat.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: canary deploys, autoscaling, per-tenant models all amortize poorly.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: developer workflows are compile-cost-sensitive.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: compile time affects release cadence and operational agility.

assumptions: The benchmark is representative of a real workflow (development, canary, per-tenant, or steady-state).
nonImplications: Does not imply compile time must always be equal to inference; different scenarios weight them differently.
Does not imply short compile is always preferable; some workloads benefit from investing time in tuning.

distractorRationales.D: Ignores operational impact of long compiles.

questions.subtopic: CUDA Event vs CPU Timer: single-kernel timing
questions.learningObjective: Choose between CUDA events and CPU timers when timing a single small CUDA kernel; understand the precision and semantic implications.
questions.stem: You want to time a single small CUDA kernel (expected duration ~30 µs) that runs on a non-default stream in the middle of a larger workload. Which measurement approach is most accurate, and why?
questions.profileData:
Setup:
  - Kernel duration expected ~30 µs
  - Runs on user stream `s1`, while stream `s2` runs concurrent work
  - Wall-clock question: time _only_ this one kernel, not the concurrent work

Candidate approaches:
  (i)   time.perf_counter() around a single non-synced launch
  (ii)  time.perf_counter() around launch + torch.cuda.synchronize() (device-wide)
  (iii) cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), event.record(s1) before and after kernel, elapsed_time after event.synchronize()
  (iv)  time.perf_counter() around launch + s1.synchronize()

options.text: Approach (i) is best because it eliminates any synchronization overhead; the reported time is exactly the wall-clock cost of the launch and it also captures the GPU-side execution because CUDA launches block the host until completion when the kernel is small enough (<100 µs).

Approach (iii) is best: CUDA events recorded on `s1` around the kernel isolate its execution on that stream, are timed by the GPU with ~0.5 µs resolution, and are unaffected by concurrent work on `s2`. Approaches using device-wide synchronize would also charge concurrent work on other streams.

Approach (ii) is best because a device-wide synchronize also flushes work on `s2` before recording the end time, which gives the most accurate measurement of _only_ the kernel of interest by ensuring the entire GPU is idle at the endpoints.

Approach (iv) is best because a stream-scoped synchronize combined with a CPU timer captures the full CPU dispatch cost plus GPU execution; CUDA events cannot record a stream because `cudaEventRecord` only accepts the default stream in single-context CUDA programs.

questions.explanation: CUDA events with `enable_timing=True` are recorded onto the target stream and time GPU-side execution with sub-microsecond resolution. They isolate `s1`'s work and are not perturbed by concurrent work on `s2`. A device-wide synchronize (ii) forces all streams to drain and, combined with a CPU timer, over-charges the measurement with `s2`'s work. Approach (i) is completely wrong (CUDA launches are async). Approach (iv) is misleading: `s1.synchronize()` waits for `s1` only, but the CPU timer also captures dispatch and driver-visible latency, and CUDA events can be recorded on any stream (D's premise is false).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: kernel launches are always asynchronous; a CPU timer around a launch measures dispatch, not execution.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: stream-scoped CUDA events give per-stream isolation and high timing resolution.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: device-wide synchronize charges `s2`'s concurrent work into the measurement, over-reporting the target kernel's cost.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: CUDA events can be recorded on any stream, not only the default stream.

assumptions: Modern CUDA runtime; `cudaEventRecord` supports non-default streams.
Concurrent work on `s2` may overlap in wall clock but is not the measurement target.
nonImplications: Does not imply CUDA events are always the right tool; for coarse workflow-level timing, CPU timers with synchronize are fine.
Does not imply event timing has zero overhead; event record itself adds a few hundred nanoseconds of driver work.

distractorRationales.D: False claim about event stream restrictions.

performanceClaim.scope: Single small CUDA kernel timing with concurrent streams

questions.learningObjective: Identify sources of non-determinism in GPU-based ML training/inference and which knobs (deterministic algorithms flag, atomic-free kernels, seed control) address them.
questions.stem: Which statements about non-determinism on GPU ML workloads are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Setting `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` to hide GPUs from a single-GPU training job re-partitions the kernel launch grid and changes the per-warp thread count, which is what causes non-determinism in FP reductions on a single device.

Reductions implemented with cross-block `atomicAdd` on floats are non-associative and can produce different low-order bits across runs even with the same input, because the order of concurrent atomic operations is not fixed.

Setting `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` and seeding RNGs is sufficient to guarantee bit-identical outputs across GPU model changes (A100 → H100); once the flag is set, PyTorch reroutes any non-deterministic op through a deterministic kernel that is cross-architecture identical.

cuDNN convolution algorithm selection (via benchmark mode) can pick different algorithms across runs with the same input; disabling benchmark mode (or using `torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True`) locks the algorithm choice and reduces one source of non-determinism.

questions.explanation: Options B, D are correct; options A, C are incorrect. A (Wrong): `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` only masks which physical devices the CUDA runtime exposes to the process — it does NOT modify the launch grid, per-kernel thread count, or per-warp reduction shape on a single visible GPU. The canonical caveat "determinism only guaranteed under identical execution configurations (device count, kernel launch bounds, cuBLAS/cuDNN algorithm choice)" is real, but this option pins the caveat to a mechanism that CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES does not have. B (Correct): cross-block atomicAdd is a known non-determinism source. C (Wrong): cross-architecture bit-identity is not a guarantee. D (Correct): cuDNN benchmark mode is a known non-determinism source; deterministic mode addresses it.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong mechanism: `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` only masks which physical devices the CUDA runtime exposes to the process — it does NOT modify the launch grid, per-kernel thread count, or per-warp reduction shape on a single visible GPU. The canonical caveat "determinism only guaranteed under identical execution configurations (device count, kernel launch bounds, cuBLAS/cuDNN algorithm choice)" is real, but this option pins the caveat to a mechanism that CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES does not have.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: cross-block atomicAdd is a known non-determinism source.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: cross-architecture bit-identity is not a guarantee.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: cuDNN benchmark mode is a known non-determinism source; deterministic mode addresses it.

assumptions: Standard PyTorch 2.0+ with cuDNN backend for convolutions.
nonImplications: Does not imply determinism is free; deterministic kernels are often slower.
Does not imply seed control is unnecessary; RNG seed is orthogonal to op determinism.

questions.learningObjective: Identify correct properties of differential testing (running two implementations of the same spec on many random inputs and comparing outputs) versus golden testing.
questions.stem: Which statements about differential testing (as applied to kernel/compiler correctness) are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Differential testing between an implementation and itself (e.g., torch.compile vs eager) always yields identical outputs by construction; any discrepancy indicates a compiler bug that must be fixed before shipping, with no room for numerical tolerance.
Differential testing eliminates the need for golden tests entirely because random inputs provide statistically stronger coverage than any fixed input set.

Differential testing compares outputs of two independent implementations of the same specification on many (often randomly generated) inputs; it is especially effective at surfacing corner-case bugs (empty shapes, extreme values, unusual strides) that a single golden test might miss.

A differential-testing framework must record inputs that trigger a discrepancy so that the failure can be reproduced deterministically; without seed recording, non-deterministic failures degrade to noise and cannot be triaged.

questions.explanation: Correct: C, D.  A: Wrong: eager vs compiled comparisons expect tolerance, not bit equality. B: Wrong: golden and differential tests are complementary. C: Correct: standard scope and value proposition. D: Correct: reproducibility discipline is essential.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: eager vs compiled comparisons expect tolerance, not bit equality.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: golden and differential tests are complementary.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard scope and value proposition.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: reproducibility discipline is essential.

assumptions: The two implementations are actually independent, not two builds of the same code path.
nonImplications: Does not imply differential testing catches all bugs; some bugs are input-distribution-dependent.
Does not imply golden tests are obsolete; they cover named regressions and reproducibility.

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose dynamic-shape performance regressions in compiled workloads from a mix of graph-break/recompile logs and per-shape latency data.
questions.stem: A torch.compile-wrapped inference service handles requests of varying seq_len. In production, latency has become erratic. The following profiler output is captured. Which conclusions are supported? (Select all that apply.)
questions.profileData:
Per-request torch.compile trace (500 requests, various seq_len):
  Seq_len distribution: 128, 256, 384, 512, 640, 768, 896, 1024 (roughly uniform)
  torch._dynamo.utils.count_calls_to_compile: 8 recompiles (one per unique seq_len)
  torch._dynamo.config.cache_size_limit: default (8)
  Median latency:  4.2 ms  (steady state after warmup)
  p95 latency:     42.6 ms
  p99 latency:     58.1 ms
  First-time-seen seq_len latencies:  350 - 900 ms
  Recompile reason in logs: "tensor size mismatch, previous s0 = 128, new s0 = 256" (× 7)

options.text: Enabling dynamic shapes (e.g., `torch.compile(dynamic=True)` or `torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic`) would allow one compiled graph to cover multiple seq_lens, converting the recompile spikes into a single warmup cost and stabilizing p95/p99.

The `cache_size_limit` of 8 is currently being fully consumed and the FX cache is thrashing on the present 8-shape workload; each of the 8 shapes is being evicted and recompiled every invocation, which is why recompilation is being observed.

The recompile latencies (~350–900 ms) are counted inside the per-request latency measurement, so the p95/p99 are dominated by compile-time cost, not actual GPU execution. Removing the compile cost by pre-warming all seq_lens or enabling dynamic shapes would fix the tail.

The 8 recompiles correspond to shape-specialized graphs — one per unique seq_len — because dynamic shape was not enabled (or a guard forced specialization); the p99 spikes correspond to first-time-seen shapes paying the JIT cost.

questions.explanation: Options A, C, D are correct; option B is incorrect. A (Correct): dynamic-shape compile addresses the root cause. B (Wrong): with exactly 8 distinct shapes and cache_size_limit=8, the cache is at capacity but NOT evicting — each shape's compiled artifact is still resident, so no thrashing/eviction is occurring. Recompilation being observed must therefore come from a different cause (guard failures on non-shape state, dynamic=True disabled, or a Python-level cache miss unrelated to size_limit). The "currently thrashing" claim is factually wrong given the present state. C (Correct): JIT cost is inside the request latency for first-time-seen shapes. D (Correct): matches the guard-based recompile behavior. General context: If shape diversity were higher, C's concern would be legitimate, but the specific data given here does not evidence eviction — the observed pattern is one-time recompile cost, not thrashing.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: dynamic-shape compile addresses the root cause.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: with exactly 8 distinct shapes and cache_size_limit=8, the cache is at capacity but NOT evicting — each shape's compiled artifact is still resident, so no thrashing/eviction is occurring. Recompilation being observed must therefore come from a different cause (guard failures on non-shape state, dynamic=True disabled, or a Python-level cache miss unrelated to size_limit). The "currently thrashing" claim is factually wrong given the present state.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: JIT cost is inside the request latency for first-time-seen shapes.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: matches the guard-based recompile behavior.

assumptions: Static-shape torch.compile mode (no explicit dynamic=True or mark_dynamic).
cache_size_limit default in 2.3~2.5 is around 8.
nonImplications: Does not imply dynamic=True has no drawbacks; guards and shape-generic kernels can be slower per iteration.
Does not imply larger cache_size_limit is always the right fix; it hides but does not eliminate compile cost.

distractorRationales.B: Concern would apply to a different data regime; not supported by these numbers.

performanceClaim.scope: torch.compile inference with static-shape guards under varying seq_len

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish end-to-end latency from microbenchmark latency and identify when a microbenchmark speedup does not translate to end-to-end speedup.
questions.stem: A team reports a 4.7× speedup on a fused LayerNorm+bias microbenchmark and concludes the end-to-end model inference will speed up by 4.7×. Which critique is most accurate?

options.text: Kernel and end-to-end speedups can differ substantially: only the fraction of end-to-end time actually spent in that kernel is affected by the microbenchmark improvement (Amdahl's law). If LayerNorm is 5% of end-to-end time, a 4.7× kernel speedup translates into at most ≈ 4% end-to-end improvement, not 4.7×.

The microbenchmark speedup is an underestimate: fusing LayerNorm with adjacent bias unlocks cache reuse in following ops as well, so the end-to-end speedup is typically 2-3× larger than the microbenchmark number.

Since the microbenchmark speedup is 4.7×, the end-to-end speedup will be exactly 4.7× minus the launch-overhead constant of 5 µs times the number of layers; for typical 32-layer models this gives ≈ 4.6× end-to-end.

The 4.7× is correct because kernel-level speedups compose multiplicatively into end-to-end speedup as long as at least one op is sped up; the only limit is the Amdahl fraction of the sped-up op, and LayerNorm is a mainstream op so its fraction is always high.

questions.explanation: End-to-end speedup follows Amdahl's law: if the optimized op consumes fraction f of end-to-end time and is sped up by k, the end-to-end speedup is at most 1 / ((1-f) + f/k). For a small f the achievable end-to-end speedup is bounded well below k. Options A, B, C fabricate compositional or additive relationships that don't hold.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: Amdahl's law bounds the end-to-end improvement.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: cross-op cache effects exist but typically shrink, not amplify, the reported gain in end-to-end.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: no such fixed launch-overhead subtraction rule.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: kernel and end-to-end speedups do not compose multiplicatively without weighting by time fraction.

assumptions: The microbenchmark measures the kernel in isolation, not with surrounding realistic context.
The end-to-end pipeline includes many other kernels.
nonImplications: Does not imply LayerNorm optimization is useless; even a small end-to-end gain matters at scale.
Does not imply Amdahl is the only concern; batch effects and cross-op memory traffic can also cause divergence.

performanceClaim.scope: Kernel-level microbenchmark speedup vs end-to-end speedup under Amdahl's law

questions.learningObjective: Interpret generated Triton code emitted by TorchInductor and identify what the code does and does not tell you about performance.
questions.stem: Which statements about inspecting the generated Triton code from TorchInductor are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Autotuning parameters (BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N, num_warps, num_stages) affect performance substantially; the generated code often includes an `@triton.autotune` decorator listing candidate configurations, and the actual runtime chooses among them on the first call.

The generated Triton code is the same across all PyTorch 2.x versions: TorchInductor's codegen strategy has been frozen since 2.0, so any performance change between minor versions must come from other components (allocator, dispatcher) rather than from codegen changes.

The generated Triton kernel exposes the fused iteration space (block sizes, program dimensions) and the sequence of `tl.load`, arithmetic, and `tl.store` calls; seeing multiple fused elementwise ops inside one kernel confirms that Inductor's scheduler recognized producer-consumer reuse.

The generated Triton code alone determines steady-state performance: any two kernels with the same Triton source will run at the same latency on the same GPU regardless of tuning parameters or launch configuration.

questions.explanation: A: the Triton source directly exposes fusion structure. C: autotune decorators and their configurations govern runtime performance. B is wrong: the same source can produce very different performance depending on autotune choices, and launch parameters (grid shape) also matter. D is wrong: Inductor's codegen has evolved substantially across PyTorch 2.x versions.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: autotune governs runtime performance.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: Inductor codegen evolves across versions.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: fusion structure is visible in source.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: autotune selection matters.

assumptions: PyTorch 2.3 ~ 2.5 Inductor with Triton backend on CUDA.
nonImplications: Does not imply Triton source review replaces profiling; source shows intent, profiling measures behavior.
Does not imply autotune always finds the optimal config; heuristic search has limits.

performanceClaim.scope: TorchInductor generated Triton code and autotune impact

questions.learningObjective: Design a golden test for a custom kernel by choosing an appropriate reference implementation, deterministic inputs, and tolerance schema.
questions.stem: You are writing a golden test for a new fused Triton `LayerNorm(x) * gamma + beta` kernel. Which combination of design choices best matches golden-test discipline?
questions.codeSnippet:
# Custom Triton kernel under test:
def fused_ln_gamma_beta(x, gamma, beta, eps=1e-5):
    ...

# Reference options:
#   (i)  torch.nn.functional.layer_norm on CUDA in FP32
#   (ii) A hand-written numpy CPU LayerNorm in FP64
#   (iii) An older version of the same Triton kernel

# Input options:
#   (a) torch.randn seeded with a fixed torch.manual_seed(0)
#   (b) Different random inputs every test invocation

# Tolerance options:
#   (α) rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-2 (BF16-appropriate)
#   (β) rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-6 (FP32/FP64-appropriate)
#   (γ) tolerance derived from the input dtype (FP32 rtol~1e-5, BF16 rtol~1e-2)

options.text: Reference (i) — torch.nn.functional.layer_norm; input (a) — fixed seed; tolerance (β) — strict FP32/FP64 tolerance regardless of the actual input dtype. Golden tests should always assert bitwise-close equality; letting BF16 tests pass at 1e-2 masks real bugs.

Reference (iii) — an older version of the same kernel; input (b) — random each run; tolerance (β) — FP32 strict. Using the same-family reference guarantees the closest numerical match, and random inputs each run maximize coverage across the input distribution over CI history.

Reference (ii) — numpy CPU FP64; input (a) — fixed seed; tolerance (γ) — dtype-driven. A high-precision independent reference plus deterministic inputs plus dtype-appropriate tolerance is the strongest correctness signal, with the extra property that a floating-point-order difference between the CUDA implementation and the reference does not falsely fail the test.

Reference — none; input (b) — random; tolerance (α) — loose BF16 tolerance. Golden tests are only useful for detecting NaN/Inf; numerical correctness is validated by end-to-end model accuracy on validation datasets, not by per-kernel numerical checks.

questions.explanation: A robust golden test uses (i) an independent high-precision reference so the test does not merely re-check the buggy implementation against itself, (ii) deterministic inputs so failures are reproducible, and (iii) tolerances matched to the numeric dtype under test. Applying an FP64 tolerance to a BF16 kernel would guarantee failure; applying a BF16 tolerance to an FP32 test would hide bugs. Option B is anti-pattern (same-family reference); C sets a wrong tolerance floor; D abandons numerical validation entirely.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: applying FP64 tolerance to BF16 kernels guarantees false failures.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: same-family reference invites shared bugs; random inputs make failure debugging painful.
