optionExplanations.C: Correct: independent + high-precision + deterministic + dtype-appropriate.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: eliminates per-kernel correctness signal.

assumptions: The CUDA implementation is being validated against a reference for correctness.
The test runs in CI where reproducibility matters.
nonImplications: Does not imply CPU/FP64 references are always feasible; some ops have no straightforward CPU reference.
Does not imply differential testing on random inputs is bad; it is complementary, not a replacement for a golden test.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about what information a TorchInductor IR dump reveals and what it does not, and how to use it for debugging compilation issues.
questions.stem: You dump the TorchInductor IR (via `TORCH_COMPILE_DEBUG=1` or `torch._inductor.config.debug = True`) for a compiled function. Which statement most accurately describes what the dumps reveal for debugging?

options.text: The dumps only contain the model's weights in a compressed format; they do not expose graph structure or generated code and are intended only as a runtime cache for the compiler.

The dumps include a full PTX assembly listing with per-instruction SASS mapping and dynamic register allocation; they are the primary tool for register-pressure debugging and replace nvcc `--ptxas-options=-v` output entirely.
The dumps are text protobuf files identical to ONNX and can be re-imported into any ONNX-compatible runtime; this is the standard way to convert a torch.compile'd model to TensorRT for deployment.

The dumps show the FX graph (post-AOTAutograd), the scheduler decisions, and the generated Triton/C++ code. They let you verify which ops fused together, which were emitted as separate kernels, and where the compiler fell back to eager or an external kernel — invaluable for diagnosing missing-fusion or unexpected-kernel-launch bugs.

questions.explanation: TorchInductor's debug dumps show the FX graph after AOTAutograd, the scheduler's fusion decisions, and the actual generated Triton (for CUDA) or C++ (for CPU) code. This lets you verify fusion, kernel count, and codegen behavior — the primary use case is diagnosing performance regressions or missing fusions. Options B/C/D fabricate contents that these dumps do not have (PTX/SASS, ONNX serialization, or weight caches).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: the dumps contain graph and generated code, not just weights.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: PTX/SASS analysis uses ptxas -v and Nsight Compute; Inductor dumps stop at the Triton source level.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: the dumps are not ONNX-compatible.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: describes the actual dump contents and their diagnostic use.

assumptions: PyTorch 2.3 ~ 2.5 default Inductor debug dump layout.
nonImplications: Does not imply IR dumps replace runtime profiling; they show static compiler decisions, not measured behavior.
Does not imply the dumps expose everything; some internal state (e.g., autotuning history) may require additional flags.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses IR dump with ONNX export.

sourceRefs.locator: Inductor scheduler and generated code debugging story

questions.subtopic: Launch overhead / Nsight Systems timeline diagnosis
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a launch-overhead-limited workload from an Nsight Systems timeline showing many small kernels with large CPU-side gaps.
questions.stem: A user profiles a training step with Nsight Systems and observes the timeline data shown. Which diagnosis and mitigation set is most appropriate?
questions.profileData:
Nsight Systems timeline (aggregated, one training step):
  Total wall time: 50 ms
  Number of CUDA kernel launches: 1000
  Mean kernel duration: 30 µs
  Mean CPU-side gap between consecutive launches: 20 µs
  Sum of kernel durations: ≈ 30 ms
  Sum of CPU-side launch gaps: ≈ 20 ms
  GPU utilization (Nsight measure): ≈ 60%
  No PCIe/host-device transfers visible in the trace
  No CPU dataloader stall visible in the trace

options.text: Launch-overhead limited: ~20 ms (40%) is CPU-side dispatch between many small kernels. Mitigate with fusion, CUDA Graphs, or larger per-kernel work.

The workload is compute-bound; the fix is to add more math per kernel to shift the compute-to-memory ratio, since compute-bound kernels benefit directly from higher arithmetic intensity per iteration.

The workload is I/O bound (SSD/PCIe); reducing dataloader thread count will help, because the trace's 40% idle time reflects host-side dataloader blocking behind slower storage or PCIe transfer bandwidth.

The workload is memory-bandwidth limited; the 40% idle time on the GPU indicates HBM is saturated in a way that stalls SM issue slots, and the correct mitigation is to shrink model weights via quantization to lower HBM pressure.

questions.explanation: Kernel duration (30 µs) is short compared to the CPU-side gap (20 µs), and there are many launches. The 20 ms cumulative gap time matches CPU-side dispatch overhead. Neither PCIe transfers nor dataloader stalls appear. The right levers reduce launch count (fusion, torch.compile), amortize per-launch cost (CUDA Graphs), or make each kernel do more work.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: this matches the timeline signature of a launch-overhead-limited workload and lists the standard mitigations.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: compute-bound kernels would show high SM utilization inside each kernel; the idle-between-kernels pattern points to launch overhead.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: the trace shows no I/O or dataloader stalls; the gap is CPU-dispatch time.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: HBM saturation would show up as high kernel duration with high memory-throughput metrics, not as CPU-side idle gaps between launches.

assumptions: Nsight's 'GPU utilization' metric here reflects the fraction of wall time during which any SM is running a kernel; 60% ≈ 30/50 ms.
The 'CPU-side gap' truly measures time between one kernel's end and the next kernel's start on the same stream, not synchronization waits.
nonImplications: Does not imply that CUDA Graphs is always the best fix; some workloads (variable shapes, control flow) cannot easily use them.
Does not imply that fusion is always feasible; some ops have unfusable boundaries (custom ops, reductions across streams).

distractorRationales.C: Fabricates I/O root cause absent from the trace.
distractorRationales.D: Confuses HBM saturation with CPU dispatch idle.

sourceRefs.locator: Nsight Systems timeline analysis and launch overhead patterns
Kernel launch overhead and CUDA Graphs

performanceClaim.scope: Launch-overhead-limited training step, 1000 kernels/step, 30 µs mean kernel, 20 µs mean gap

questions.subtopic: NaN / Inf detection and root-cause analysis
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the appearance of NaN in a Transformer forward pass using loss / activation statistics and localize the source op.
questions.stem: In mid-training a 7B Transformer, loss becomes NaN at step 4213 after being stable for hundreds of prior steps. Activation-hook profiling records per-layer max-abs statistics as shown. Which diagnosis is best supported?
questions.profileData:
Per-layer max(|activation|) at step 4212 (last healthy) vs step 4213 (NaN):
  layer 22 attn_scores:  before-softmax   step 4212 = 12.4       step 4213 = 27.8
  layer 22 attn_scores:  after-softmax    step 4212 = 0.94       step 4213 = NaN
  layer 22 attn_probs @ V                   step 4212 = 5.1        step 4213 = NaN (propagated)
  All prior layers (0-21):                                              finite in both steps
  Precision: fp16 activations, fp32 master weights, GradScaler enabled

options.text: The GradScaler failed to scale the loss and gradients underflowed to zero at step 4213; disabling GradScaler will fix the NaN because zero-gradient training is stable at any precision.

The attention scores at layer 22 exceeded FP16 range (max ≈ 65504) between steps 4212 and 4213, causing softmax input to overflow to Inf on one entry and produce NaN after normalization; typical fixes include upcasting attn_scores to FP32 before softmax (or using an implementation that fuses safe softmax with FP32 accumulator, e.g., FlashAttention).
Softmax over a vector with max ≈ 27.8 always overflows to Inf regardless of precision because exp(27.8) exceeds FP32 range; the fix is to switch entirely to FP64 for all training compute.
The NaN is a numerical fluke unrelated to the profile data; retraining from an earlier checkpoint with a different seed will always resolve NaN issues without changing precision or fusing softmax.

questions.explanation: FP16 max is ~65504, and exp(27.8) ≈ 1.19e12 — well beyond FP16 range. In naive softmax implementations, an FP16 attention-score around 27+ causes exp(x) to overflow to +Inf, and the subsequent normalization produces NaN. The standard mitigation is to upcast the softmax to FP32 or use a FlashAttention-style safe softmax that subtracts the running max in higher precision. Option A misattributes to GradScaler. B is fatalistic. C falsely claims FP32 also overflows (exp(27.8) is only ~1e12, far under FP32 max ~3.4e38).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: GradScaler manages loss scaling; it does not gate attention-score overflow.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: FP16 range + exp of large logit is a classic overflow-to-NaN pattern.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: FP32 easily represents exp(27.8) ≈ 1e12.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: root-cause is diagnosable and fixable.

assumptions: Naive softmax (no safe-softmax max-subtract) at FP16.
The profile data reflects genuine max-abs activation statistics.
nonImplications: Does not imply FlashAttention is required; any safe-softmax variant with FP32 accum works.
Does not imply FP16 training is doomed; safe softmax + gradient clipping is sufficient in most cases.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses gradient scaling with forward overflow.

sourceRefs.locator: Safe softmax with max-subtract for numerical stability
FP16 dynamic range and softmax stability

questions.learningObjective: Interpret Nsight Compute metrics (SM utilization, achieved occupancy, DRAM throughput, L1 hit rate) to conclude that an elementwise kernel is DRAM-bandwidth bound and choose the right mitigation.
questions.stem: Nsight Compute reports the following metrics for an FP32 elementwise kernel `out[i] = sqrt(in[i])` on A100. Which is the best-supported diagnosis and mitigation?
questions.profileData:
Kernel: fp32_elementwise_sqrt
  SM Utilization           : 12 %
  Achieved Occupancy       : 0.85
  DRAM Throughput          : 92 % of peak
  L1 Cache Hit Rate        : 40 %
  L2 Cache Hit Rate        : 8 %
  Warp Stall Reason (top-1): Long Scoreboard (memory latency)

options.text: SM utilization is 12%; increasing block size until SMs reach 100% utilization will improve performance proportionally, since more warps per SM directly translates to higher throughput on any streaming kernel.
L1 hit rate (40%) is the primary bottleneck; increasing per-block shared-memory usage will lift the L1 hit rate and speed up the kernel by satisfying more accesses from on-chip cache instead of HBM.
DRAM-bandwidth bound: 92% DRAM throughput near peak, low SM utilization from memory stalls; occupancy and math cannot help — reduce bytes moved (fusion, lower dtype).

Achieved occupancy 0.85 is too low; further reducing register usage per thread will raise it to 1.0 and unlock roughly 20% speedup by allowing more warps to reside per SM and hide latency more thoroughly.

questions.explanation: The signature of a memory-bound kernel is: high DRAM throughput (near peak), low SM utilization (SMs stall waiting for memory), decent occupancy (not the bottleneck), and long scoreboard stalls (memory latency). Elementwise sqrt streams data through HBM with no reuse; increasing occupancy or adding math to each element cannot exceed AI × BW. The lever is to reduce HBM traffic — usually via fusion into a producing op, kernel elision, or a lower-precision dtype if hardware supports it.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: low SM utilization is a symptom of memory-bound streaming, not an occupancy problem; raising occupancy does not increase HBM bandwidth.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: an elementwise streaming kernel with each element read once has no meaningful reuse; L1 hit rate is naturally low and not the bottleneck.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches the memory-bound Nsight signature and lists the correct mitigations.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: 0.85 achieved occupancy is high; raising it further will not add throughput because the kernel is already HBM-limited.

assumptions: A100 with HBM2e ≈ 2.0 TB/s peak; 92% of peak ≈ 1.84 TB/s.
The kernel touches each element exactly once for read and once for write (no reuse).
nonImplications: Does not imply that FP16 sqrt is always faster; the fused pipeline or downstream op determines whether reducing bytes moved helps.
Does not imply that fusion is always feasible; boundary conditions (custom ops, unsupported dtypes) can block it.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses SM utilization signal with occupancy fix.

sourceRefs.locator: Nsight Compute memory workload analysis / speed-of-light metrics

performanceClaim.scope: FP32 elementwise sqrt streaming kernel on A100 with DRAM near saturation

questions.learningObjective: Choose a robust statistic (median or a percentile) rather than mean when reporting kernel latency in the presence of outliers.
questions.stem: Given the following 20 warmed-up per-iter latencies of the same kernel, which single number is the most defensible headline for a report and why?

options.text: The mean (2.98 ms) is a good headline because it summarizes all 20 samples in a single number, and mean is the standard statistic in scientific reporting.
The p99 (12.4 ms) is a good headline because it represents worst-case behavior and captures the tail; when in doubt, always report the worst observed sample as the summary number.
The std (2.5 ms) is the most useful headline because it captures the spread; readers can infer any percentile from mean ± std under the assumption of a normal distribution of kernel latencies.

The median (2.18 ms) is the most defensible headline: it is robust to the two obvious outliers (5.80 ms and 12.4 ms), agrees with the bulk of the distribution, and does not overstate steady-state cost. Ideally the report should include median plus one or more tail percentiles (p95, p99) rather than a single number.

questions.explanation: With 20 samples containing 2 clear outliers, the mean is pulled far above the bulk of the distribution (2.98 vs 2.18 ms). Median (or a robust central estimator like trimmed mean) reflects the typical steady-state behavior; tail percentiles capture the rare bad case. Reporting only mean or only p99 misleads. Standard deviation assumes normality which does not hold for latency (usually right-skewed with a heavy tail).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: mean is not robust to outliers common in latency distributions.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: p99 on 20 samples is essentially one worst-case sample; unstable and not representative.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: latency distributions are right-skewed; std does not encode percentiles under a normal assumption that fails.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: median (with additional tail percentiles) is the standard robust choice.

assumptions: The two outliers (5.80 ms, 12.4 ms) reflect infrequent noise events (GC, driver events), not the target measurement.
nonImplications: Does not imply mean is never useful; for total-throughput calculations it can be appropriate.
Does not imply p99 should be ignored; it is essential for latency SLOs, just not as a stand-alone headline.

distractorRationales.B: Single-sample p99 with n=20 is unstable.

performanceClaim.scope: Kernel latency reporting statistics under a right-skewed distribution

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose whether a kernel with low achieved occupancy is actually occupancy-limited or is memory-bound at high occupancy.
questions.stem: Nsight Compute reports the following metrics for a compute-heavy FP16 GEMM kernel on A100. Which diagnosis best matches the data?
questions.profileData:
Kernel: hgemm_128x128
  SM Utilization      : 96 %
  Achieved Occupancy  : 0.30
  DRAM Throughput     : 25 % of peak
  L2 Hit Rate         : 65 %
  Warp Stall Reason (top-1): Not Selected (waiting for issue slot)
  Registers per thread: 168
  Shared memory per block: 96 KB

options.text: Low occupancy (0.30) is the bottleneck; force lower register usage to raise occupancy to 1.0, which will unlock roughly 3× speedup as more warps become resident on each SM.

SM utilization is 96% and stall reason is 'not selected' (issue slot pressure), indicating the SMs are saturated with the current small number of resident warps — occupancy 0.30 is intentional (large tiles need many registers/shared memory) and reflects the standard trade-off in high-performance GEMM. The kernel is close to optimal and lowering register usage would not help.

The kernel is memory-bound; the 25% DRAM throughput plus 65% L2 hit rate indicate the kernel is saturating HBM through L2; reducing register usage would only worsen the situation by evicting more L2 data through spills.
The kernel is achieving 0.30 × 96% = 28.8% of peak; scaling occupancy to 1.0 would give 96% peak, which is the standard optimization target for any GEMM on any GPU generation.

questions.explanation: High-performance GEMM kernels use large tiles that consume many registers and shared memory per block. This deliberately caps occupancy at a low fraction, but SMs remain fully busy (96% utilization) because each warp does much more work per iteration. Stall reason 'not selected' means warps are waiting only for an issue slot, not for memory. Raising occupancy by reducing register usage would force smaller tiles, more memory traffic, and typically worse GEMM throughput. Options A/B/D misread the metrics.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: raising occupancy doesn't help when SM is already 96% utilized.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: occupancy-vs-tile-size trade-off is standard in GEMM design.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: 25% DRAM throughput is not saturation; the top stall is not a memory reason.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: linearly combining occupancy and SM utilization is not how peak performance is computed.

assumptions: Kernel is a well-tuned tile-based GEMM.
The metrics reported by Nsight Compute are on a warmed-up steady-state kernel launch.
nonImplications: Does not imply low occupancy is always fine; for latency-bound (memory-latency) kernels, higher occupancy usually helps hide latency.
Does not imply the kernel is at peak throughput; other Nsight sections (SoL, math pipe utilization) would need to confirm.

performanceClaim.scope: Tile-based FP16 GEMM on A100; occupancy vs tile size trade-off

questions.learningObjective: Reason about how many samples are needed to estimate a p99 latency with reasonable confidence, and identify a common under-sampling mistake.
questions.stem: A team claims a service's p99 latency is 3.4 ms based on a benchmark of 100 samples. What is the correct critique of this claim, purely from a statistical standpoint?

options.text: There is no critique — 100 samples is more than enough to estimate p99 within one significant figure, since p99 is defined as the 99th-largest value in any sample regardless of N and the estimator is unbiased for N ≥ 30.

The critique is that the p99 must be reported alongside a p50 that is exactly 100× smaller, otherwise the p99 is meaningless. Since 3.4 ms is given, one can only accept the number if the p50 is 34 µs; otherwise the sample is biased.
100 samples are too many; percentile estimators become less accurate as N grows due to increased opportunity for outliers in the tail. A benchmark should use exactly 10 samples to minimize variance.

With N = 100, the p99 estimator is highly unstable: the empirical p99 corresponds to (roughly) the 1-2 slowest samples, and its variance is on the order of the tail spread. A defensible p99 estimate needs on the order of 10³-10⁴ samples, and reporting should include a confidence interval.

questions.explanation: The empirical p99 with N = 100 samples is essentially one specific sample (the 99th-order statistic), so its variance is large — comparable to the tail spread of the underlying distribution. To estimate p99 with reasonable confidence you typically want at least 10³-10⁴ samples, and to communicate uncertainty you report a confidence interval. Options A, C, D fabricate rules that do not exist in statistics.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: 100 samples give an unstable p99.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no such p50/p99 ratio constraint exists.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: fewer samples yield more, not less, variance.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: matches basic sampling theory for order statistics.

assumptions: The samples are i.i.d. from the underlying latency distribution.
nonImplications: Does not imply 100 samples are useless for any purpose; median and IQR are decently estimable with N = 100.
Does not imply that larger N is always feasible; some scenarios have limited samples and require accepting wider CIs.

sourceRefs.locator: Percentile reporting practices in profiler documentation

performanceClaim.scope: Estimating p99 latency from a finite sample

questions.subtopic: PyTorch Profiler vs Nsight Systems: choosing the right tool
questions.learningObjective: Compare PyTorch Profiler with Nsight Systems/Compute and choose the appropriate tool for a given debugging task.

softwareContext.framework: PyTorch Profiler / Nsight Systems / Nsight Compute

questions.stem: Which statements about the split between PyTorch Profiler, Nsight Systems, and Nsight Compute are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Nsight Compute samples inside a single kernel (SM utilization, warp stall reasons, memory throughput, cache hit rate); it is the right tool for optimizing a specific kernel that you have already identified as the bottleneck via Nsight Systems or PyTorch Profiler.
All three tools show the same information — kernel timeline, SM utilization, and warp stall reasons — with different UIs; picking one is a matter of preference and not of debugging need.

PyTorch Profiler is the appropriate tool when you need op-level attribution (which aten op or Python line launched which kernel) and a timeline view that unifies CPU-side dispatcher work, autograd events, and CUDA kernel launches.

Nsight Systems is oriented at system-level tracing (CPU, GPU, CUDA API, NVTX, cuDNN library calls, stream utilization); it is the right tool for diagnosing CPU launch gaps, PCIe bottlenecks, and cross-stream concurrency issues.

questions.explanation: Correct: A, C, D.  A: Correct: per-kernel deep dive is Nsight Compute's scope. B: Wrong: tools do not fully overlap. C: Correct: op-level attribution is PyTorch Profiler's strength. D: Correct: system tracing is Nsight Systems's scope.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: per-kernel deep dive is Nsight Compute's scope.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: tools do not fully overlap.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: op-level attribution is PyTorch Profiler's strength.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: system tracing is Nsight Systems's scope.

assumptions: Modern versions of all three tools as of 2024-2025.
nonImplications: Does not imply one tool is 'best'; the workflow typically composes them (system → op → kernel).
Does not imply the tools always agree numerically; slightly different measurement scopes can produce different numbers.

questions.subtopic: Race condition in a CUDA kernel
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a race condition in a CUDA kernel from symptoms (non-deterministic output, small numerical drift across runs) and identify the missing synchronization primitive.
questions.stem: A CUDA reduction kernel produces slightly different outputs across runs with the same input (differences beyond floating-point tolerance and inconsistent across GPU model). The relevant kernel snippet is shown. What is the root cause?

options.text: The bug is that `smem` is not initialized to zero before the load; on some GPUs uninitialized shared memory contains garbage, and threads with `i >= N` read stale bank contents instead of writing zero.

The `atomicAdd` on `out` is non-associative for floats, and different launch orderings produce different accumulation orders; adding a `__threadfence()` before the atomicAdd would enforce a canonical order and eliminate the non-determinism.

Missing `__syncthreads()` between the load and the reduction loop (and inside the loop). Without the barrier, threads with different warp scheduling can read `smem[tid + s]` before other threads have finished writing it, producing non-deterministic partial sums. Adding `__syncthreads()` after the load and at the end of each loop iteration fixes the race.

The kernel uses `blockDim.x = 256` implicitly but should use `blockDim.x = 32` to match the warp size; different warp counts produce different rounding orders and this is the source of the observed non-determinism.

questions.explanation: The clear bug is missing `__syncthreads()` after the load-into-smem step and at the end of each reduction iteration. Threads within a block are not guaranteed to be synchronized in lockstep beyond a warp; without the barrier, some threads may read `smem[tid + s]` while others are still writing it. This produces non-deterministic results that vary by launch scheduling. The other options describe unrelated concerns: atomicAdd on floats is non-associative but the observed non-determinism inside the block is the real bug (B); shared memory is defined to hold whatever the thread writes (C); warp size ≠ block size (D).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: shared memory reads only what is written by threads within the block.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: atomicAdd non-associativity produces small drift but not the racy behavior seen here.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: identifies the missing barriers and their necessity.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: block size is a separate concern from synchronization.

assumptions: Compute capability ≥ sm_70 (Volta+), where independent warp scheduling makes intra-block races more visible.
The kernel is launched with a block size ≥ 32 (larger than a single warp).
nonImplications: Does not imply that atomicAdd should be avoided; it is fine in this pattern given proper intra-block sync.
Does not imply that adding syncthreads has zero cost; barriers introduce a small stall but are required for correctness.

distractorRationales.D: Confuses block size with warp size.

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose register-spill-induced slowdown from Nsight Compute metrics and compiler diagnostics.
questions.stem: A custom CUDA kernel's Nsight Compute report and compiler output are shown. Which mitigation is most directly indicated?
questions.profileData:
Compiler output (nvcc --ptxas-options=-v):
  ptxas info: Used 168 registers, 96 KB shared, 40 stack frame, 320 bytes spill stores, 480 bytes spill loads

Nsight Compute metrics:
  Achieved Occupancy: 0.12
  Warp Stall Reason (top): Long Scoreboard (memory latency)
  L1 Local Load Traffic: 22% of L1 traffic (unusually high; local memory is where spills go)
  DRAM Throughput: 30%
  SM Utilization: 40%

options.text: 40% SM utilization indicates the kernel is under-scheduled by the GPU driver; setting CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=0 and using per-thread default streams will bring SM utilization to 100% and fix the underlying issue.

The 0.12 occupancy directly bounds SM throughput; raising `blockDim` (larger blocks) will proportionally increase performance because more threads per block always means more concurrent warps hiding latency.

Register spilling to local memory (evident from the 40-byte stack frame + 320/480 spill stores/loads and the abnormally high L1 local-load traffic) is causing costly memory traffic disguised as 'Long Scoreboard' stalls. Mitigations: reduce register usage via `__launch_bounds__` or `-maxrregcount`, refactor to fewer live variables, or restructure the algorithm to shrink working set.

The kernel is memory-bound at 30% DRAM throughput; the fix is to remove the shared-memory usage entirely because shared memory competes with registers for chip area, so shrinking shared memory automatically frees more registers per thread.

questions.explanation: The compiler diagnostic shows explicit register spills (stack frame + spill stores/loads). Nsight Compute confirms unusual L1 local-load traffic — local memory (in CUDA terminology) is where spilled registers live. The 'Long Scoreboard' stall is caused by these spills going through L1/L2/DRAM. Reducing register usage (via `__launch_bounds__`, refactoring, or algorithmic changes) directly addresses the root cause. B, C, D fabricate mechanisms or misdiagnose.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING and default streams do not affect SM occupancy.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: raising blockDim doesn't fix per-thread register pressure.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard register-spill diagnosis and mitigation.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: shared memory and register file are separate hardware resources; removing shared memory does not free registers.

assumptions: The kernel was compiled with default optimization and the ptxas verbose output is accurate.
nonImplications: Does not imply `__launch_bounds__` always helps; it can force higher spills if the underlying algorithm needs many live values.
Does not imply spills are always fatal; small spills can be masked by warp scheduling.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses block size with register pressure.
distractorRationales.D: Confuses shared memory with register file.

sourceRefs.locator: Register pressure and local-memory traffic analysis

performanceClaim.scope: Register-spill-induced slowdown on Ampere kernel

questions.subtopic: Roofline analysis of a memory-bound kernel
questions.learningObjective: Compute arithmetic intensity, place a kernel on a roofline chart, and identify whether measured throughput is close to the roofline.
questions.stem: An FP32 elementwise kernel `out[i] = 3.0f * in[i] + 2.0f` runs on A100 (peak FP32 = 19.5 TFLOP/s, peak HBM = 2.0 TB/s). It reads 64 MB, writes 64 MB, and measures 40 ms. What is the arithmetic intensity and what does the roofline analysis say?
questions.profileData:
Kernel: fma_bias
  Input:  16,777,216 FP32 elements (64 MB read)
  Output: 16,777,216 FP32 elements (64 MB written)
  Ops per element: 1 fused multiply-add = 2 FLOPs
  Measured wall time: 40 ms
  A100 peak FP32: 19.5 TFLOP/s
  A100 peak HBM:  2.0 TB/s
  Roofline ridge point: 19.5e12 / 2.0e12 = ~9.75 FLOP/byte

options.text: Arithmetic intensity ≈ 0.125 FLOP/byte (2 FLOPs / 16 bytes per element pair). The roofline predicts a compute-bound region since 0.125 > 9.75; the kernel should achieve near 19.5 TFLOP/s and the measured 40 ms indicates a bug.

Arithmetic intensity depends on the number of thread blocks and cannot be computed from bytes and FLOPs alone; roofline analysis is not applicable to elementwise kernels because they never hit the roof.
Arithmetic intensity ≈ 0.5 FLOP/byte (2 FLOPs / 4 bytes per element). The kernel is compute-bound and should achieve near 19.5 TFLOP/s; 40 ms is expected for this problem size.

Arithmetic intensity ≈ 0.25 FLOP/byte. The kernel is well below the ridge point (0.25 << 9.75), so it is memory-bound: expected time = 128 MB / 2.0 TB/s ≈ 62 µs (peak). Measured 40 ms is roughly 640× slower than peak — the kernel is highly inefficient or the measurement is wrong (launch overhead, missing sync, tiny grid).

questions.explanation: Elementwise `y = a*x + b` performs 2 FLOPs per output element, reading 4 bytes and writing 4 bytes (8 bytes total per element). Arithmetic intensity = 2 / 8 = 0.25 FLOP/byte, far below the A100 ridge point of ~9.75 FLOP/byte — the kernel is deeply memory-bound. Peak-bound time for 128 MB of traffic at 2.0 TB/s is ~62 µs. The measured 40 ms is ~640× slower than roofline peak, indicating a serious inefficiency (launch overhead dominates, or the measurement contains async-timing errors, or the grid is undersized). Options A and C mis-count the byte traffic (A: 16 bytes per pair double-counts; C: 4 bytes per element counts only one side) and mis-diagnose the kernel as compute-bound; option B wrongly claims roofline is inapplicable to elementwise kernels; option D states the correct arithmetic intensity and the memory-bound diagnosis.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: 0.125 is well below 9.75, so the kernel is memory-bound, not compute-bound.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: roofline applies to all kernels; elementwise kernels typically sit at the memory-bound side.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: 4 bytes per element counts only one side; must include read and write.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: intensity + roofline + comparison to peak-bound time.

assumptions: A100 peak FP32 and HBM numbers used above are from NVIDIA specs.
The 'measured' time is a valid wall-clock number (not itself buggy).
nonImplications: Does not imply the kernel can achieve peak HBM in practice; L2 hit rate and coalescing may cap effective bandwidth.
Does not imply the measurement is definitely wrong; it might reflect a badly-configured launch.

performanceClaim.scope: FP32 elementwise FMA on A100; roofline vs measured 40 ms

questions.learningObjective: Design a shape-coverage matrix for testing a GPU kernel so that the test suite covers boundary shapes, tile-boundary shapes, and typical production shapes.
questions.stem: You are writing shape-coverage tests for a fused pointwise kernel with a compile-time tile size of 128. Which shape set is most likely to catch bugs before production?

options.text: Only power-of-two shapes: 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048. These are the most common in ML workloads; if the kernel works on power-of-two sizes it will work on all others by symmetry, so covering non-power-of-two is redundant.
Only very large shapes (≥ 10⁶ elements) to make sure the kernel utilizes the GPU; small shapes never expose bugs because they finish quickly, and testing them wastes CI time.

A matrix that includes: 0 (empty), 1 (singleton), tile-boundary sizes (127, 128, 129, 255, 256, 257), a couple of large production sizes, and a random-shape fuzz set. This covers boundary handling (mask logic), off-tile-multiple handling, and typical inputs.

The exact production shape set (e.g., `M=32, N=4096`), because tests should validate the actual deployment path. Covering other shapes wastes CI cycles and is not required if the kernel is only used with fixed shapes at inference time.

questions.explanation: Kernel bugs commonly appear at boundaries: empty tensors, singletons, tile-boundary values (n = tile, n = tile+1, n = tile-1), and interactions between mask logic and the last tile. A well-designed shape matrix covers those edge cases plus a fuzz set. Options A/B/D miss important classes of bugs: A ignores mask logic for non-tile-multiples; B fails to exercise the edge cases; D is fragile against future changes to production shapes.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: mask logic bugs surface at non-power-of-two shapes.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: small shapes exercise edge cases that large shapes may bypass.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: boundary + production + fuzz coverage is the standard discipline.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: production shapes only make the test fragile to workload changes.

assumptions: Kernel has a compile-time tile size and uses masked loads/stores at tile boundaries.
nonImplications: Does not imply exhaustive shape coverage is needed; a well-chosen boundary set + fuzz is sufficient.
Does not imply CI time is unlimited; parameterized tests can prune redundant shapes.

sourceRefs.locator: Kernel boundary handling and mask logic

questions.subtopic: Multi-stream timing pitfall with CUDA events
questions.learningObjective: Reason about a subtle event-timing bug where an event recorded on one stream is elapsed against an event recorded on another stream, giving a wall-time reading that is not the intended per-stream cost.
questions.stem: A user times a kernel on stream `s1` using events but sees inconsistent numbers depending on what runs concurrently on `s2`. Which explanation best matches the reported profile data below?
questions.profileData:
Scenario:
  start_evt.record()   # recorded on the current (default/legacy) stream
  kernel_A_on_s1()     # launched on stream s1
  end_evt.record()     # recorded on the current stream, NOT on s1
  end_evt.synchronize()
  elapsed = start_evt.elapsed_time(end_evt)

Observed:
  When s2 is idle:  elapsed ≈ 2.5 ms (matches expected kernel A wall time)
  When s2 runs a 100 ms independent kernel concurrently:  elapsed ≈ 100 ms

options.text: The events are recorded on the default (legacy) stream, not on `s1`. Under legacy default-stream semantics the default stream synchronizes with all other streams, so `end_evt.record()` waits for `s2`'s 100 ms kernel to complete before recording. Fix: record the events on `s1` (`start_evt.record(s1)` / `end_evt.record(s1)`).

CUDA events do not have per-stream isolation; any concurrent GPU work always contributes to the elapsed time even when events are recorded correctly on the target stream, so the discrepancy is expected and cannot be fixed with better placement.
`elapsed_time` reports the union of GPU activity between the two events; the fix is to divide the reported value by the number of streams that had work in the interval (2 streams → divide by 2).

The `synchronize()` on the end event drains the entire device; the reported 100 ms is the sum of s1 and s2 execution because synchronize serializes them. Fix: replace `end_evt.synchronize()` with `end_evt.query()` in a busy loop.

questions.explanation: The bug is that the events are recorded on the current stream (the default/legacy stream), not on `s1`. Under legacy default-stream semantics, the default stream synchronizes with all user streams; `end_evt.record()` therefore waits for `s2`'s outstanding work as well. Recording the events on `s1` explicitly (`start_evt.record(s1)`, `end_evt.record(s1)`) isolates the measurement to `s1`'s progress. Option A is false (events are per-stream when recorded on that stream). Option C fabricates dividing semantics. Option D misattributes the cause to synchronize.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: default-stream event record + legacy semantics = accidental cross-stream sync.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: correctly-placed events do isolate the target stream.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: no such union-and-divide semantics exists.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: synchronize on an event only waits until that event completes, not the whole device.

assumptions: Legacy default-stream semantics (not per-thread default stream mode).
`s1` and `s2` are user-created streams distinct from the default stream.
nonImplications: Does not imply per-thread default stream mode has the same issue; that mode changes default-stream semantics.
Does not imply s2 concurrent work has zero impact; on shared resources some indirect slowdown remains, but not a 100 ms serialization.

distractorRationales.D: Confuses event.sync scope with device sync.

performanceClaim.scope: Event-based timing on multi-stream workloads under legacy default-stream semantics

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a CPU-based timer around a CUDA kernel launch loop under-reports GPU execution time and how to obtain a correct measurement.
questions.stem: A user times a matmul on CUDA two different ways. Attempt 1 reports 0.008 ms per iteration; Attempt 2 reports 3.412 ms per iteration. Which measurement reflects actual GPU execution time and what explains the discrepancy?
questions.codeSnippet:
import torch, time

x = torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda")
w = torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda")

# Attempt 1: CPU timer only, no synchronization
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(10):
    y = x @ w
t1 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"Attempt 1 mean per iter: {(t1 - t0) / 10 * 1000:.3f} ms")

# Attempt 2: synchronize on both sides
torch.cuda.synchronize()
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(10):
    y = x @ w
torch.cuda.synchronize()
t1 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"Attempt 2 mean per iter: {(t1 - t0) / 10 * 1000:.3f} ms")

# Output:
#   Attempt 1 mean per iter: 0.008 ms
#   Attempt 2 mean per iter: 3.412 ms
questions.profileData: Reported per-iter times: Attempt 1 = 0.008 ms; Attempt 2 = 3.412 ms

options.text: Attempt 2 is correct. CUDA launches are asynchronous; without `torch.cuda.synchronize()`, the CPU timer captures dispatch cost, not GPU execution time.

Attempt 1 is correct. Modern GPUs execute matmul in single-digit microseconds thanks to Tensor Cores and cuBLAS's autotuning; Attempt 2 is measuring the added synchronize overhead rather than the actual per-iter kernel duration.

Both are incorrect. `torch.cuda.synchronize()` returns before kernels finish because it only waits for launches on the default stream; only `torch.cuda.Event.elapsed_time` is a valid method for CUDA-side timing measurements.

Attempt 1 is correct because JIT warmup happens after the 10th iteration and pre-warmup runs are much slower; Attempt 2 unfortunately measures pre-warmup kernels because `synchronize()` resets the JIT cache between the two measurements.

questions.explanation: CUDA kernel launches are asynchronous: the CPU function `x @ w` returns after enqueuing the kernel on the stream, not after the GPU completes it. A CPU timer around such launches captures dispatch cost (microseconds), not GPU execution time. Synchronizing before starting the timer flushes prior work; synchronizing before stopping the timer ensures all in-flight kernels finish; the delta then reflects the actual wall time for GPU execution.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: describes the async-launch model and the synchronization discipline needed for CPU-timer accuracy.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: 8 µs per 4096-square FP32 matmul is physically implausible on any current GPU (~ 137 GFLOPs at that time would exceed HBM constraints).
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: `torch.cuda.synchronize()` blocks until the stream is fully drained; it is a valid synchronization primitive.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: PyTorch's cuBLAS matmul dispatch has essentially no per-iteration JIT compilation; warmup effects exist but do not explain a 400× difference.

assumptions: The matmul kernel is compute-heavy enough that GPU work dominates once measured correctly.
No CUDA Graphs capture is active (which would alter the timing model).
nonImplications: Does not imply that CPU timers are useless; wrapped with synchronize they are fine for aggregate measurements.
Does not imply that `torch.cuda.Event` is unnecessary; events remain preferable for high-resolution single-kernel timing.

sourceRefs.locator: Asynchronous kernel launches; timing methodology chapter
Guidance on CUDA synchronization for timing

performanceClaim.scope: CPU timer around CUDA async launches on any current NVIDIA GPU

questions.subtopic: Numerical tolerance / Golden test for FP16 GEMM
questions.learningObjective: Choose realistic tolerance thresholds when validating a custom FP16 GEMM implementation against a reference (e.g., cuBLAS) with a large K reduction.
questions.stem:
A custom FP16 matmul kernel using FP32 accumulators is compared against `x @ w` on FP16 tensors with `K = 1024`. The following tolerance check fails:

`torch.testing.assert_close(out_ref, out_test, atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-6)`

What is the most likely reason and what is a correct fix?
questions.codeSnippet:
import torch

x = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
w = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)

out_ref  = x @ w                       # cuBLAS FP16 (Tensor Core), FP32 accum
out_test = my_flash_matmul(x, w)       # custom kernel, also FP32 accum

# Fails:
torch.testing.assert_close(out_ref, out_test, atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-6)

options.text: The FP32 accumulator in `my_flash_matmul` is the problem — reducing at higher precision produces different results from cuBLAS; the correct fix is to accumulate in FP16 so both implementations round identically after every multiply-add.

The kernel has a bug; two correct FP16 matmul implementations should produce bit-identical results across all accumulation orders because IEEE 754 guarantees deterministic rounding for FP16 sums up to at least K=2048.
FP16 GEMM reductions over K=1024 differ across implementations due to accumulation order and rounding; realistic tolerances are ~1e-2 (atol/rtol), not FP64-scale 1e-5/1e-6.

`torch.testing.assert_close` requires `check_dtype=False` to correctly compare tensors that were computed via a Tensor-Core path; adding this flag eliminates the failure regardless of numerical difference between the two outputs.

questions.explanation: FP16 matmul with K=1024 involves 1024 partial products summed in some order. Different implementations (cuBLAS kernels, custom Triton, cutlass) traverse the K dimension with different tile shapes and reduction trees; combined with FP16 rounding, the results differ in the low bits. Tolerances of 1e-5 atol / 1e-6 rtol correspond to FP64 accuracy. For FP16 GEMM, tolerances in the 1e-2 to 1e-3 range are typical for random Gaussian inputs of moderate K.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: FP32 accumulation is actually the higher-accuracy choice and matches what cuBLAS does for FP16 Tensor-Core matmul. Downgrading to FP16 accum increases, not decreases, the error.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: FP16 (and FP32 accumulated FP16) matmul is not bitwise-reproducible across implementations because floating-point addition is not associative.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches the standard numerical-analysis view of FP16 GEMM tolerance.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: `check_dtype=False` skips dtype comparison; the numerical mismatch remains. The failure is about the values themselves.

assumptions: `x` and `w` are Gaussian-distributed FP16 tensors of moderate magnitude.
Both implementations use FP16 storage and (approximately) FP32 accumulation via Tensor Cores or their emulation.
nonImplications: Does not imply that any error is acceptable; if `atol > 1` for magnitudes ~ 1, the kernel is wrong.
Does not imply that FP16 accumulation is never appropriate; small-K reductions may fit within FP16 dynamic range.

distractorRationales.A: Reverses the correct causal direction: FP32 accum is more accurate, not less.

questions.learningObjective: Choose a realistic tolerance when validating a BF16 GEMM+bias implementation against an FP32 reference; distinguish rounding-mode and accumulation-order effects.
questions.stem: You compare a custom BF16 GEMM+bias kernel (with FP32 accumulator) against a reference `x @ w + b` cast to BF16 for `M=2048, K=4096, N=4096`. The naive check `torch.testing.assert_close(out_ref, out_test, atol=1e-3, rtol=1e-3)` fails on some rows. What is the most principled adjustment?
questions.codeSnippet:
x = torch.randn(2048, 4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
w = torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
b = torch.randn(4096,       device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)

out_ref = (x @ w + b).to(torch.bfloat16)          # reference
out_test = my_bf16_gemm_bias(x, w, b)             # kernel under test (FP32 accum)

torch.testing.assert_close(out_ref, out_test, atol=1e-3, rtol=1e-3)   # fails on some rows

options.text: Compare in FP32 by upcasting `out_test` to FP32 and using the FP32 tolerance `atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-6`. The dtype of the output tensor governs the achievable precision, so casting up to FP32 automatically tightens error bounds without changing the underlying kernel.

Raise tolerance to something like `atol=1e-2, rtol=1e-2` (BF16-scale). BF16 mantissa is only 7 bits; K=4096 accumulations amplify rounding, and different tile shapes/reduction orders in cuBLAS vs the custom kernel produce differences well above 1e-3 at large K.

Sort each row of both outputs before comparing to remove accumulation-order effects; sorted-tolerance comparisons ignore permutations that arise from different tile scheduling in the two GEMMs, making BF16 GEMMs bit-comparable.

The failure indicates a real bug: BF16 GEMMs with FP32 accumulators are bit-identical across all implementations because Tensor Cores use a standardized rounding mode; any mismatch indicates a saturation or overflow bug that must be found.

questions.explanation: Correct: B.  A: Wrong: upcasting after the reduction cannot recover lost precision. B: Correct: BF16-scale tolerance for K=4096 GEMMs. C: Wrong: sorting reorders values but does not model the actual arithmetic. D: Wrong: BF16 GEMM is not bit-reproducible across implementations.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: upcasting after the reduction cannot recover lost precision.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: BF16-scale tolerance for K=4096 GEMMs.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: sorting reorders values but does not model the actual arithmetic.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: BF16 GEMM is not bit-reproducible across implementations.

assumptions: Random Gaussian inputs of moderate magnitude.
Both implementations use FP32 accumulation (as is standard for BF16 Tensor Core paths).
nonImplications: Does not imply 1e-2 is the right tolerance for every dtype; FP32 GEMMs are typically 1e-4 to 1e-5 range.
Does not imply BF16 kernels are always numerically 'good enough'; downstream ops (softmax) may amplify these errors.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses post-hoc casting with in-place higher-precision.

sourceRefs.locator: Numerical accuracy and mixed-precision GEMM tolerance

questions.learningObjective: Explain the sources of the very different timings between a single-run measurement and the amortized mean of a many-run loop, and describe a correct benchmarking discipline.
questions.stem: A user benchmarks a matmul with CUDA events. The first single-run timing is 43.2 ms, but a subsequent 100-run mean is 3.4 ms per iteration. Which explanation is best supported and what is the correct benchmarking practice?
questions.codeSnippet:
import torch

x = torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda")
w = torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda")

start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
end   = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)

# Single run
start.record()
y = x @ w
end.record()
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(f"single-run: {start.elapsed_time(end):.3f} ms")

# 100 runs
start.record()
for _ in range(100):
    y = x @ w
end.record()
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(f"100-run mean: {start.elapsed_time(end) / 100:.3f} ms")

# Output:
#   single-run: 43.2 ms
#   100-run mean: 3.4 ms
questions.profileData: single-run: 43.2 ms; 100-run mean: 3.4 ms

options.text: `start.elapsed_time(end)` returns the cumulative time between events, not the last kernel; the 100-run mean is thus miscomputed by dividing by 100 and cannot be interpreted as per-iteration cost in any meaningful way.
First-run cost includes one-time setup (cuBLAS handle init, algo selection/autotune, kernel loading); benchmark should warm up and report a robust statistic (median) over remaining runs.

Modern GPUs cache kernel results across launches; the 2nd through 100th runs return the same output without recomputation, so the loop measurement effectively times cache lookup latency rather than actual matmul execution.

The 100-run version invokes `torch.compile` automatically after 10 iterations and benefits from a fused kernel that the single run does not use, since PyTorch's runtime silently promotes hot loops to compiled variants for throughput.

questions.explanation: The single-run cost is dominated by one-time initialization: on the first cuBLAS matmul, PyTorch may allocate a cuBLAS handle, run algorithm heuristics or autotune, and load the kernel binary. Subsequent runs skip these costs and reflect steady-state execution time. Correct benchmark practice: warm up several iterations, synchronize, then time a batch of runs and report a robust statistic (median, or e.g., p50 / p95 over multiple batches).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: `elapsed_time(end)` returns the interval between two recorded events; dividing by 100 is meaningful when the events bracket 100 iterations.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: describes the standard warmup pattern and recommended reporting statistic.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: GPUs do not cache tensor results; each launch recomputes the matmul.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: `torch.compile` is not invoked implicitly by a loop; the loop runs the same eager matmul each iteration.

assumptions: PyTorch's default cuBLAS backend is used, not TensorRT or a custom kernel.
There is no explicit `torch.compile` in the code.
nonImplications: Does not imply that a first-run cost is a bug; it is a normal cost that a warmup absorbs.
Does not imply that the mean is always the best statistic; percentile-based reporting is often preferable for tail-sensitive workloads.

performanceClaim.scope: First-run vs steady-state benchmark discrepancy for CUDA matmul

questions.learningObjective: Interpret Nsight Compute warp stall reasons and translate them to actionable optimization steps.
questions.stem: Nsight Compute reports the following warp stall breakdown for a custom kernel. Which conclusions and next steps are correct? (Select all that apply.)
questions.profileData:
Kernel: my_reduce_kernel
  Warp stall breakdown (% cycles per stall reason):
    Long Scoreboard (memory latency)  : 42 %
    Barrier                            : 18 %
    Wait                               : 12 %
    Not Selected                       :  8 %
    Short Scoreboard                   :  6 %
    Others (Selected, Drain, ...)      : 14 %
  DRAM Throughput: 45 %
  L2 Hit Rate: 30 %

options.text: 'Long Scoreboard' means the kernel is compute-bound on the FP32 unit; warps are waiting for math to complete. The right mitigation is to add more math per thread to fill in the pipeline.

The dominant stall reason 'Long Scoreboard' points to memory-load latency: warps are waiting for global-memory loads. Mitigations include improving L2 hit rate (better data reuse or blocking), using async cp.async / prefetching, and increasing warps-per-SM to hide latency.

'Barrier' stall at 18% suggests __syncthreads() is taking a large fraction of time; reducing block size or eliminating synchronization is always the right response to any Barrier stall regardless of the algorithm's synchronization needs.

A 45% DRAM throughput combined with 30% L2 hit rate indicates room to reduce memory traffic (e.g., staging in shared memory) — this would attack the top stall reason at the source rather than raising occupancy to hide it.

questions.explanation: Correct: B, D.  A: Wrong: 'Long Scoreboard' = memory, not compute. B: Correct: standard Long-Scoreboard interpretation. C: Wrong: barriers exist for correctness; removing them is not a general fix. D: Correct: reducing memory traffic attacks the root cause.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: 'Long Scoreboard' = memory, not compute.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: standard Long-Scoreboard interpretation.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: barriers exist for correctness; removing them is not a general fix.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: reducing memory traffic attacks the root cause.

assumptions: Ampere/Hopper stall taxonomy as documented in Nsight Compute reference.
The workload is real and not measurement noise.
nonImplications: Does not imply 'Long Scoreboard' can always be eliminated; some workloads have irreducible memory latency.
Does not imply higher occupancy is always desirable.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses memory latency stall with compute stall.

performanceClaim.scope: Warp stall interpretation on Ampere/Hopper Nsight Compute output

questions.learningObjective: Identify All-to-All as the collective that permutes per-rank shards and its canonical role in MoE dispatch.
questions.stem: An expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts layer places each expert on a distinct rank. During the forward pass, every rank must send each of its tokens to the rank that owns the routed expert, and later return the transformed token to the origin rank. Which collective correctly describes this dispatch/combine pattern and its semantics?

options.text: AllReduce (sum): every rank sums the routing probabilities across all ranks so that each expert receives the aggregate contribution of every token in the global batch.
AllGather: every rank broadcasts its full token buffer to every peer so that each expert can locally scan its assigned tokens.
Broadcast from rank 0: rank 0 collects tokens, distributes them to the experts on all other ranks, and gathers the results back.
All-to-All: every rank sends a distinct per-destination shard (the tokens routed to that destination's expert) and receives a distinct per-source shard from every peer; no reduction is performed.

questions.explanation: MoE dispatch requires a permutation of tokens across ranks (each destination rank gets only the tokens routed to its expert), which is exactly All-to-All's semantics. AllReduce would destroy per-token identity; AllGather would replicate every token on every rank (N× memory), which is wasteful and semantically wrong for routing; broadcast from rank 0 creates a bottleneck and is not what expert-parallel frameworks implement.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: MoE dispatch needs per-token routing, not a reduction across ranks.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: AllGather would replicate every token on every rank; experts would receive tokens not routed to them.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: rank-0-only broadcast serializes the pattern and does not match any modern MoE implementation.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: All-to-All permutes disjoint shards without reduction, which matches MoE dispatch and combine.

assumptions: One expert per rank (or a bijection between ranks and expert groups).
Tokens have already been sorted by destination rank before the collective.
nonImplications: Does not imply that All-to-All is always the fastest dispatch (top-k routing produces uneven shard sizes and can suffer load imbalance).
Does not imply that a subsequent All-to-All for the combine step doubles the bandwidth cost per token linearly with N.

distractorRationales.C: Ignores the parallel nature of expert-parallel dispatch.

sourceRefs.locator: § discussion of All-to-All patterns for expert-parallel workloads

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the semantics of AllReduce and AllGather as collective operations over a device group.
questions.stem: N ranks each hold a tensor T_i of identical shape S. After the collective, each rank must observe a specific result. Which statement correctly distinguishes AllReduce (sum) from AllGather along a new leading axis?

options.text: After AllReduce and after AllGather, every rank holds a tensor of shape [N, *S]; AllReduce differs only in that it also multiplies each slice by 1/N so that a subsequent local sum yields the reduction.
After AllReduce (sum), every rank holds a tensor of shape S equal to Σ_i T_i; after AllGather, every rank holds a tensor of shape [N, *S] containing all T_i stacked.
After AllReduce (sum), every rank holds a tensor of shape [N, *S] equal to the concatenation of the T_i; after AllGather, every rank holds only its own T_i annotated with the ranks of the peers.

AllReduce and AllGather are semantically identical; the difference is purely an implementation choice — AllGather is a synonym used by MPI while AllReduce is the corresponding NCCL name for the same operation.

questions.explanation: AllReduce combines per-rank inputs via an associative reduction, producing a tensor of the same shape S on every rank whose value is the reduction (here Σ_i T_i). AllGather is pure data movement: every rank ends with a tensor containing all N inputs (typically shape [N, *S] when stacking on a new axis, or [N·d, *rest] when concatenating along an existing one).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: AllReduce output has shape S, not [N, *S], and it does not silently scale by 1/N.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: matches the standard collective-communication semantics for AllReduce and AllGather.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: swaps the two definitions.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: MPI and NCCL both define AllReduce and AllGather as distinct primitives with different semantics.

assumptions: All ranks participate with tensors of the same shape and dtype.
The reduction operator for AllReduce is the standard element-wise sum.
nonImplications: Does not imply that ring-AllReduce internally materializes the gathered tensor on any rank.
Does not imply that AllReduce with mean is unavailable; it is standard in DL frameworks.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses shape and adds a spurious 1/N scaling.

sourceRefs.locator: Ch. 6 discussion of collective communication primitives
§2 background on collective operations for ML

questions.learningObjective: Delineate the responsibilities of an SPMD-style compiler versus a distributed runtime (e.g. NCCL / MPI stack).
questions.stem: Which THREE of the following statements about the division of responsibilities between an SPMD-style compiler (e.g. XLA + GSPMD emitting StableHLO) and a distributed runtime (e.g. NCCL) are correct?

options.text: The compiler decides which collectives (AllReduce, AllGather, All-to-All, ReduceScatter) to insert and at which mesh axes, based on sharding specs; the runtime chooses the internal algorithm (ring, tree, recursive halving) at execution time.
Algorithm selection, message-chunk sizes, and NIC/NVLink lane assignment inside a collective are runtime concerns and are not visible at the SPMD IR level.
Fault tolerance (dead-rank detection, retry, checkpoint restore) is a runtime/framework responsibility; the SPMD compiler does not manage process lifecycle.
Because the compiler needs to reason about performance, it must know each device's NVSwitch domain and PCIe topology at compile time; without this, the emitted IR is topology-incorrect.

questions.explanation: A, B, C reflect the standard division. The compiler operates at the mesh-axis / collective-op level; runtime handles algorithm choice, chunking, NIC selection, and fault tolerance. D is wrong: the IR references mesh axes, not physical devices; topology-aware mapping is a runtime concern (though cost models may consult topology when available).

optionExplanations.A: Correct: compile-time inserts collectives; runtime picks algorithm.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: internal algorithm parameters live at the runtime.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: fault tolerance is a runtime/framework concern.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: physical topology awareness lives at the runtime; compiler references mesh axes.

assumptions: Modern SPMD compiler stack (XLA + GSPMD, StableHLO) and NCCL/MPI-style runtime.
IR-level collectives are algorithm-agnostic.
nonImplications: Does not imply the compiler has no cost model; cost models can consult mesh shape.
Does not imply the runtime cannot be topology-aware; NCCL is notably topology-aware.

distractorRationales.D: Wrongly places topology-mapping at compile time.

sourceRefs.locator: Collective ops at IR level are algorithm-agnostic
Ch. 6 runtime algorithm selection for collectives

questions.learningObjective: Explain the motivation for gradient bucketing in data-parallel training and the trade-off it induces.
questions.stem: A model has ~2000 parameter tensors, most of them small (≤ 64 KB). A data-parallel runtime issues a separate AllReduce for each and observes that the collective phase is bottlenecked. Which best explains why grouping gradients into ~25 MB buckets improves performance, and what the primary trade-off is?

options.text: Bucketing eliminates the per-collective bandwidth term entirely because a fused AllReduce sends only one tensor's worth of bytes regardless of the payload; the trade-off is that the reduction becomes approximate at large bucket sizes.
Bucketing is required by NCCL: NCCL only supports one AllReduce per iteration, so all gradients must be packed into a single buffer; the trade-off is code complexity.
Bucketing improves gradient accuracy by summing more terms before the AllReduce averages them, reducing gradient variance; the trade-off is that it delays the optimizer step.

Bucketing amortizes the per-collective latency term (α) across many small tensors, better utilizing link bandwidth; the trade-off is that the collective must wait until every tensor in the bucket is produced by backward, which shrinks the overlap window with backward compute if the bucket spans too many layers.

questions.explanation: Small tensors are in the latency-dominated regime of the α + βS cost model. Packing them into a bucket amortizes α and lets the payload dominate the wall-clock time. The main trade-off is temporal: a bucket cannot be dispatched until all its tensors are produced during backward, so overly large buckets narrow the compute/communication overlap window.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: bucketing does not remove the bandwidth term; it moves the same bytes and remains numerically exact (up to FP ordering).
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: NCCL supports many AllReduces per iteration.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: AllReduce is deterministic given its inputs; bucketing does not reduce gradient variance.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: latency amortization is the mechanism; overlap-window shrinkage is the trade-off.

assumptions: Cost model α + βS applies with a non-negligible α.
Backward proceeds output → input in layer order.
nonImplications: Does not imply that maximally large buckets are always best.
Does not imply that bucketing is unnecessary when compute/comm overlap is enabled; they are complementary.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses latency amortization with bandwidth reduction.
distractorRationales.C: Confuses performance optimization with accuracy improvement.

sourceRefs.locator: Ch. 6 α + βS collective communication cost model

questions.learningObjective: Compute the per-rank bandwidth term of a ring-AllReduce for a tensor of S bytes across N ranks.

hardwareContext.architecture: Ring topology (e.g. NVLink ring, InfiniBand ring)
requiredFeatures: symmetric point-to-point bandwidth BW between neighbors

questions.stem: A tensor of S bytes is AllReduce-summed over N ranks via the ring algorithm (ReduceScatter + AllGather), on a ring where each neighbor link has effective bandwidth BW. Ignoring the fixed latency term, which expression best approximates the per-rank bandwidth-limited time?

options.text: S / BW, because the tensor is only transmitted once around the ring.
N · S / BW, because each rank has to forward the full tensor to every other rank.
2·(N-1)/N · S / BW, from ReduceScatter (N-1)/N · S and AllGather (N-1)/N · S.
log₂(N) · S / BW, because the ring implements a recursive halving reduction internally.

questions.explanation: The ring algorithm splits the payload into N chunks. During ReduceScatter, each chunk travels through N-1 hops but each rank only sends/receives (N-1)/N · S bytes total. AllGather then propagates the reduced chunks through another (N-1)/N · S bytes. Total bandwidth cost per rank ≈ 2·(N-1)/N · S, approaching 2S for large N; not S, not N·S, and not log₂(N)·S.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: the tensor is transmitted twice (once during reduce-scatter and once during all-gather).
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: describes a naive scheme where each rank sends the whole tensor to each of N-1 peers.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: the classical ring-AllReduce bandwidth cost.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: log₂(N) scaling belongs to recursive halving / doubling on a hypercube-like topology, not to a ring.

assumptions: Fixed latency term α per phase is negligible relative to the bandwidth term.
Even chunking by N; edge effects of remainder chunks are ignored.
nonImplications: Does not imply the wall-clock time is independent of N (the latency term α·2(N-1) still scales with N).
Does not imply that ring is optimal for all N and S; for very small S the latency-dominated regime favors trees.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses ring with an all-to-all broadcast.

performanceClaim.scope: Ring-AllReduce bandwidth term for a payload of S bytes on N ranks

questions.learningObjective: Compare the per-rank bandwidth costs of ring-AllGather, ring-ReduceScatter and ring-AllReduce and the relationships between them.
questions.stem: For a total payload of S bytes on N ranks arranged as a ring, ignoring the latency term α, which THREE of the following statements about per-rank bandwidth cost are correct?

options.text: Ring-AllReduce cost equals the sum of ring-ReduceScatter and ring-AllGather, i.e. 2·(N-1)/N · S per rank.
Ring-AllGather per rank must move N · S bytes because every rank has to see every other rank's full copy of the payload.
Ring-AllGather per rank sends and receives (N-1)/N · S bytes (each rank starts with its own S/N shard and must receive the remaining (N-1)·(S/N)).
Ring-ReduceScatter per rank moves (N-1)/N · S bytes, matching AllGather's per-rank cost.

questions.explanation: A, B, C are the standard ring-collective costs. AllGather receives S − S/N = (N-1)/N · S per rank. ReduceScatter on a ring pipelines partial reductions with the same per-rank byte movement, (N-1)/N · S. AllReduce = ReduceScatter + AllGather = 2·(N-1)/N · S per rank. D is wrong: no rank ends with N·S bytes; every rank ends with S bytes (the whole payload once).

optionExplanations.A: Correct: sum of the two phases.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: overcounts by a factor N (confuses per-hop volume with per-rank end state).
optionExplanations.C: Correct: canonical AllGather cost on a ring.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: canonical ReduceScatter cost.

assumptions: The ring implementation is used (no tree/hypercube).
Latency term α is negligible relative to the bandwidth term.
S is evenly divisible by N.
nonImplications: Does not imply the same equalities on hypercube/tree topologies.
Does not imply the wall-clock cost is exactly (N-1)/N · S / BW; contention and pipelining stalls can push it higher.

sourceRefs.locator: Ch. 6 cost analysis of ring collectives

performanceClaim.scope: Ring collectives on N ranks with payload S

questions.learningObjective: Apply the α + βS communication cost model to distinguish latency-dominated from bandwidth-dominated regimes for small vs large collectives.

hardwareContext.architecture: Point-to-point link, α = 10 μs, β = 10 GB/s (⇒ 1/β = 0.1 ns/byte)

questions.stem: A collective has an effective point-to-point cost model T(S) = α + β·S with α = 10 μs and effective bandwidth 10 GB/s (β = 100 ps/byte). Consider two payloads: S1 = 1 KB and S2 = 10 MB. Which statement is correct?

options.text: T(1 KB) ≈ 10 ms; T(10 MB) ≈ 10 μs. Larger payloads amortize α so effectively no time is spent on very large messages, and small ones are dominated by α scaled up by S.
T(1 KB) ≈ 100 ns (bandwidth-dominated at any size); T(10 MB) ≈ 1 ms. Since 10 GB/s bandwidth is high, α is negligible at all payload sizes and the cost ratio equals the byte ratio.
T(1 KB) ≈ 10 μs (latency-dominated); T(10 MB) ≈ 1 ms (bandwidth-dominated). Increasing S1 tenfold to 10 KB barely changes T because α ≫ β·S in this regime.
T(1 KB) ≈ 1 μs; T(10 MB) ≈ 100 s. The bandwidth term should be interpreted as S · β with β=10 GB, giving super-linear scaling with S.

questions.explanation: T(S) = α + β·S. Compute: β = 100 ps/byte ⇒ β·(1 KB) = 100 ps × 1024 ≈ 100 ns, so T(1 KB) ≈ 10 μs + 0.1 μs ≈ 10 μs (α dominates). β·(10 MB) = 100 ps × 10⁷ = 10⁶ ns = 1 ms, so T(10 MB) ≈ 10 μs + 1 ms ≈ 1 ms (β·S dominates). In the small-message regime, S can change by 10× and T barely moves — bucketing is designed to exit this regime.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: units and direction of the model are inverted.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: at 1 KB, α (10 μs) is orders of magnitude larger than β·S (100 ns), so latency dominates.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches the two regimes and the (in)variance of T with S when α dominates.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: misinterprets β as 10 GB (giving super-linear scaling).

assumptions: α and β are constants over the size range considered.
No pipelining or concurrent messages.
nonImplications: Does not imply the crossover S* = α/β is a hardware constant across collectives (algorithms change effective α, β).
Does not imply that a real GPU collective always achieves peak β; contention and topology can reduce effective β.

performanceClaim.scope: α + βS model with α=10 μs, β=100 ps/byte

questions.learningObjective: Explain GSPMD's sharding-propagation design: how user annotations become a fully sharded graph.
questions.stem: The GSPMD paper describes a sharding-propagation pass that turns a partially-annotated graph into a fully sharded one. What is the core design intent of propagation, as argued by the paper?

options.text: To search over all possible partitioning strategies at runtime and pick the one with the lowest measured latency, so annotations serve only as a starting point for a runtime autotuner.
To transform every collective into a point-to-point send/recv so that any topology can be supported, at the cost of removing NCCL AllReduce optimizations.
To bypass the XLA compiler entirely and generate CUDA code directly from the sharding annotations, avoiding HLO-level intermediate representation.

To eliminate the need for the user to annotate every tensor: given a small number of sharding hints, the compiler pushes constraints through operators (respecting each op's propagation rules) and inserts reshard collectives at boundaries where required and produced sharding disagree.

questions.explanation: The GSPMD paper's key design intent is that user annotations are sparse (a few key tensors), and the compiler propagates them algorithmically through operator-specific rules, inserting reshard collectives where downstream ops require a different sharding than what upstream produced. This is a compile-time transformation over HLO; the goal is expressive-but-lightweight user interface plus a systematic partitioner.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: GSPMD is a compile-time system, not a runtime autotuner.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: GSPMD emits standard collectives (AllReduce, AllGather, etc.), not raw point-to-point.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: GSPMD operates over HLO, does not bypass XLA.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: the paper's stated propagation-and-reshard design.

assumptions: The reader is familiar with GSPMD/XLA's operator-level sharding rules.
'Annotation' means an sharding attribute attached to a tensor in HLO.
nonImplications: Does not imply propagation always produces the globally optimal partitioning; it uses heuristics.
Does not imply that every graph is expressible in SPMD; some patterns benefit from user re-annotation.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses GSPMD with a runtime search system.
distractorRationales.C: Fabricates a compilation flow that skips HLO.

sourceRefs.locator: §3 sharding propagation algorithm and its role

questions.learningObjective: Understand that GSPMD treats user sharding annotations as hints that may be refined or overridden by propagation, rather than as strict per-tensor placement decisions.
questions.stem: The GSPMD paper describes user sharding annotations as 'hints'. What is the design rationale for this choice, according to the paper?

options.text: Users only annotate a small number of representative tensors; the compiler propagates sharding to the rest of the graph and inserts reshard collectives where a downstream consumer requires a different sharding than upstream produced, so annotations guide but do not exhaustively specify the partitioning.
Because sharding is dynamic (may change per step), the compiler treats annotations as advisory and re-selects sharding at each iteration based on measured runtime performance.
GSPMD deliberately ignores user annotations on more than one tensor per op; if a user annotates multiple inputs of a matmul, the compiler will randomly pick one and drop the others to avoid conflict.

The compiler treats annotations as strict placement constraints and errors out whenever the propagation cannot find a global sharding consistent with every annotation, forcing the user to re-annotate.

questions.explanation: GSPMD's design intent is to keep the user interface lightweight: annotations mark a few strategic tensors, and the compiler propagates. Where downstream ops need a different sharding, the partitioner inserts reshard collectives rather than requiring the user to annotate every tensor or matching them exactly across boundaries. A invents a runtime re-selection mechanism. C fabricates a drop-annotations policy. D treats annotations as strict constraints, which conflicts with the paper's reshard-insertion design.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: the paper's stated role of annotations as sparse hints, resolved by propagation and reshard insertion.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no runtime re-selection is described.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: no drop-multiple-annotations policy exists.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: reshards exist precisely so strict-matching is not required.

assumptions: Familiarity with GSPMD paper §3.2–§3.3.
The reader distinguishes producer-sharding, consumer-required-sharding, and inserted reshards.
nonImplications: Does not imply the partitioner ignores annotations; annotated tensors' shardings are respected at their declaration site.
Does not imply propagation is unique; heuristics choose among consistent assignments.

sourceRefs.locator: §3.2–§3.3 propagation and reshard-based resolution of annotations

questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of a Device Mesh as a logical named-axis grid decoupled from the physical topology.
questions.stem: In GSPMD / XLA-style SPMD, a job runs on 32 GPUs organized as a Device Mesh of shape [8, 4] with named axes ('data', 'model'). Which statement about the Mesh abstraction is correct?

options.text: The Device Mesh is a logical grid: sharding specs reference axis names, and the runtime is free to map mesh coordinates to physical devices in different ways (e.g. to align an axis with fast NVLink links).
Once axes are named 'data' and 'model', the compiler forbids sharding any tensor along the 'model' axis if it is also sharded along the 'data' axis; sharding must be exclusive to a single mesh axis.
The Device Mesh is a physical topology descriptor: axes must be named to match the underlying NVLink/PCIe layout, and changing axis assignments requires physically recabling the cluster.
The Mesh is a NCCL runtime object; the compiler IR does not represent it, so all mesh-related decisions happen at runtime and cannot influence which collectives are inserted.

questions.explanation: The Device Mesh is a logical named-axis abstraction. Sharding specs reference axis names (e.g. sharding a weight along 'model'); the runtime chooses how to map mesh coordinates to physical devices, typically to align high-bandwidth axes (like 'model' which sees frequent AllReduces) with fast intra-node links. A is a physical-topology confusion. B is wrong: a tensor can be sharded along multiple axes simultaneously (e.g. sharded on both 'data' and 'model'). D is wrong: the mesh is a compile-time IR concept that drives partitioning.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: mesh is logical; physical mapping is separate.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: multi-axis sharding is common and supported.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: mesh axes do not represent physical wiring.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: the mesh is represented at the IR / compile-time level.

assumptions: Sharding specs reference mesh axes by name.
