nonImplications: Does not imply that any mapping performs equally well; aligning collectives with fast links matters.
Does not imply that mesh shape can be changed mid-execution.

distractorRationales.D: Ignores the compiler-level role of the mesh.

sourceRefs.locator: Sharding specs referencing named mesh axes

questions.learningObjective: Identify the preconditions under which a compiler or DDP-style runtime can overlap gradient AllReduce with the backward compute of earlier layers.

hardwareContext.architecture: Multi-GPU node with NVLink and/or NIC

questions.stem: A data-parallel training runtime wants to overlap gradient AllReduce with the backward compute of earlier layers. Which two conditions are together sufficient for the accelerator scheduler to actually run them concurrently? (Select exactly TWO.)

options.text: The accelerator has a dedicated communication core separate from its compute cores; on GPUs without such a core, overlap is impossible.
The gradient AllReduce is launched on a stream distinct from the backward-compute stream, and the collective backend supports non-blocking asynchronous execution.

The reduced gradient is not consumed by any op earlier than the optimizer step (or a later synchronization point), so the runtime does not have to insert a wait between the AllReduce and the ongoing backward compute.
The compiler reorders the backward pass so that all AllReduce operations are executed after the entire backward compute has finished, then a single fused AllReduce is emitted.

questions.explanation: For actual concurrency, the collective must be on a stream independent of compute AND the reduced result must not be required by ongoing backward compute (only by the optimizer). Both conditions are necessary; together they are sufficient for the scheduler to execute the two streams in parallel. C describes serialization (the opposite of overlap). D is a hardware fallacy: overlap is achieved via distinct streams and DMA engines, not a separate 'communication core'.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: no dedicated communication core is required; NVLink/PCIe DMA runs concurrently with SM compute.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: distinct streams + async launch is the standard mechanism for GPU stream-level concurrency.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: without dependency on the reduced result, the compute stream can continue without waiting.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: this defeats the purpose of overlap by fully serializing the two phases.

assumptions: Backend supports non-blocking collectives (e.g. NCCL on a separate stream).
Link bandwidth is not saturated by compute stream memory traffic.
nonImplications: Does not imply that overlap always yields net speedup; if compute is short relative to communication, gains are small.
Does not imply bucketing is unnecessary; bucketing amortizes launch/latency overhead orthogonally to overlap.

distractorRationales.A: Hardware fallacy about dedicated communication cores.

sourceRefs.locator: §4 overlap of collectives with partitioned compute

questions.learningObjective: Explain the pipeline-parallel bubble and how microbatching reduces it.
questions.stem: A model is split across P=8 pipeline stages, one per GPU. A training step consists of M microbatches processed in a GPipe-style schedule. Which statement about the pipeline bubble is correct?

options.text: The bubble is exactly 1/P of total time regardless of M; it can only be removed by reducing P, which defeats the purpose of pipeline parallelism.
The bubble fraction is approximately (P-1)/(P + M - 1) of total time; increasing M shrinks this fraction, at the cost of holding activations for more in-flight microbatches (or paying recomputation).
Pipeline parallelism reduces the wall-clock time of a single microbatch's forward+backward pass by a factor of P relative to single-GPU execution, so the bubble is a negligible overhead in practice.
The bubble is a compiler artifact; an optimizing compiler can eliminate it completely for any P and M by fusing stages into a single kernel.

questions.explanation: In GPipe, the pipeline needs P-1 steps to fill and P-1 to drain, giving a total time of (P-1) + M + (P-1) = P + M - 1 stage-times for M microbatches, of which (P-1) is spent doing useful work per stage and (P-1) is fill/drain — hence bubble fraction (P-1)/(P + M - 1). Larger M dilutes the bubble but keeps more activations alive (memory cost). Pipelining does not shorten a single microbatch's latency — it raises throughput.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: bubble fraction depends on M, not just P.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: canonical GPipe bubble fraction, plus the memory trade-off.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: pipeline parallelism raises throughput, not single-microbatch latency.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: bubble is intrinsic to fill/drain, not a compiler artifact.

assumptions: Stages have equal cost.
Communication is overlapped or negligible relative to stage compute.
nonImplications: Does not imply that 1F1B or interleaved pipelines have the same bubble; they change the constant but not the fundamental fill/drain requirement.
Does not imply larger M is always better; memory pressure eventually forces recomputation or activation offloading.

sourceRefs.locator: § discussion of pipelining vs SPMD partitioning trade-offs

performanceClaim.scope: GPipe-style schedule bubble analysis

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish ReduceScatter from AllReduce and identify how the two compose.
questions.stem: Given N ranks each holding a tensor of shape S, which statement about ReduceScatter is correct?

options.text: ReduceScatter reduces the N tensors elementwise and delivers the full reduced tensor of shape S to rank 0 only; other ranks receive nothing.
ReduceScatter is a naming alias for All-to-All when the payload contains only one element per rank; the two are semantically identical for scalar payloads.
ReduceScatter is equivalent to AllGather followed by a local reduction on each rank, so it always ends with every rank holding the full reduced tensor of shape S.
ReduceScatter reduces the N tensors elementwise and gives each rank a disjoint 1/N-shard of the result, so AllReduce = ReduceScatter followed by AllGather.

questions.explanation: ReduceScatter is a hybrid primitive: it applies an associative reduction across ranks and then distributes disjoint shards of the reduced tensor to each rank. Because AllGather concatenates those shards on every rank, AllReduce is semantically ReduceScatter ∘ AllGather. Ring-AllReduce is often implemented exactly this way.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: that describes Reduce (single-recipient), not ReduceScatter.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: All-to-All permutes payloads without any reduction; the two have distinct semantics.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: no rank ends with the full reduced tensor after ReduceScatter alone.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: reduces then distributes 1/N-shards, and ReduceScatter ∘ AllGather = AllReduce.

assumptions: All ranks contribute tensors of identical shape and dtype.
The scatter axis divides the tensor evenly into N shards.
nonImplications: Does not imply that ReduceScatter and AllReduce cost the same; ReduceScatter's ring-cost is (N-1)/N · S per rank, half of AllReduce.
Does not imply that ReduceScatter is exclusive to FSDP; it is the first half of ring-AllReduce.

sourceRefs.locator: Ch. 6, ReduceScatter and its role in ring-AllReduce
§3 partitioning uses ReduceScatter in weight-sharded configurations

questions.learningObjective: Reason about the collectives that a partitioner must insert to reshard a tensor between two different sharding specifications on the same device mesh.

hardwareContext.architecture: Multi-GPU cluster with a 1-D device mesh of size N

questions.stem: A tensor T of shape [D0, D1] lives on an N-device 1-D mesh. Consider the following reshard requests. Which TWO of the following mappings between reshard requests and required collectives are correct?

options.text: From 'sharded along D0' to 'sharded along D1' (both along the same mesh axis): the partitioner inserts a local reshape only, since the total per-rank byte count is unchanged.
From 'fully replicated' to 'sharded along D0': the partitioner inserts an AllReduce (sum) followed by a local slice, in order to guarantee that no rank keeps a stale replica.
From 'sharded along D0 (each rank has [D0/N, D1])' to 'fully replicated on all ranks': the partitioner inserts an AllGather along the mesh axis.
From 'partial-sum on all ranks (each rank has a partially reduced [D0, D1] whose sum equals T)' to 'fully replicated': the partitioner inserts an AllReduce along the mesh axis.

questions.explanation: A and B are the canonical reshards emitted by GSPMD-style partitioners: sharded→replicated is AllGather (assembling shards); partial→replicated is AllReduce (summing partial contributions). C is wrong: changing the sharded dimension across the same mesh axis requires All-to-All (a permutation), not a local reshape. D is wrong: replicated→sharded is a local slice with no collective, since every rank already has the full tensor.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: this requires All-to-All, not a local reshape.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: replicated→sharded needs no collective, only a local slice.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard sharded→replicated reshard is AllGather.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: partial→replicated is AllReduce.

assumptions: The mesh is 1-D of size N.
Sharding is uniform (no residual).
nonImplications: Does not imply that the partitioner always chooses the cheapest reshard; consumer-driven decisions can propagate cost upstream.
Does not imply that a partial-sum tensor is invalid — it is a valid intermediate sharding.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses per-rank byte count with reshard cost.
distractorRationales.B: Overcompensates by inserting a spurious AllReduce.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish SPMD-style compiler-driven parallelization (as in GSPMD) from manual multi-controller / MPMD approaches.
questions.stem: Consider GSPMD-style SPMD partitioning versus manual/MPMD-style parallelization for a large model. Which THREE of the following statements are correct?

options.text: SPMD forbids per-rank differences of any kind; if any operator would have to execute differently on different ranks, the program cannot be expressed in SPMD and must fall back to MPMD.

Manual / MPMD-style parallelism generally requires the user to author per-rank code paths and to explicitly place ops and issue collectives, which is more expressive but more error-prone than SPMD annotations.

SPMD partitioning transforms a single-device-semantics program into a single per-rank program in which each op has been rewritten according to sharding annotations, and reshard boundaries are compiled into explicit collectives.
GSPMD relies on sharding annotations that the user places on some tensors/ops; the partitioner then propagates these annotations to the rest of the graph.

questions.explanation: A, B, D reflect the GSPMD design: (A) one SPMD program per rank, generated by a partitioner that inserts collectives at reshard boundaries; (B) user-provided annotations propagated by the compiler; (D) manual approaches trade expressive freedom for more per-rank code complexity. C is false: SPMD permits per-rank parameterization (rank id, shard offsets, even control-flow specialization) — 'single program' does not mean 'identical execution on every rank'.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: SPMD allows per-rank differences via rank-id-dependent computation.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: MPMD is more expressive but more manual.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard SPMD partitioning transforms operators and inserts collectives.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: annotations are user hints; propagation is compiler responsibility.

assumptions: The compiler is at least as expressive as XLA/HLO with sharding attributes.
Users understand that annotations are hints, not exhaustive specifications.
nonImplications: Does not imply that SPMD is universally faster than MPMD; certain asymmetric patterns can be more natural in MPMD.
Does not imply that annotations alone determine performance; the partitioner's cost model matters.

sourceRefs.locator: §1–§3 SPMD design and comparison with manual approaches

questions.learningObjective: Explain the design intent of Ansor's task scheduler for allocating autotuning budget across subgraphs.
questions.stem: The Ansor paper introduces a 'task scheduler' that allocates autotuning budget across the subgraphs of a full model. Which TWO of the following statements correctly describe the task scheduler's design intent, as argued in the paper?

options.text: The task scheduler distributes budget non-uniformly, favouring subgraphs whose expected marginal improvement × contribution to end-to-end latency is largest, because end-to-end wall-clock time is the objective rather than per-task speedup in isolation.
The task scheduler's motivation is that a uniform-budget baseline (equal time per subgraph) wastes effort on already-optimal or low-contribution subgraphs; the scheduler exists to fix this.
The task scheduler is a runtime scheduler that decides which kernel to launch at inference time; it has nothing to do with autotuning search budget.
The task scheduler enforces that every task must receive at least 10% of the tuning budget so that no task is ever under-tuned.

questions.explanation: The Ansor paper's §5 explicitly introduces the task scheduler to redirect tuning budget toward subgraphs whose end-to-end impact is largest (A), and argues against uniform allocation as a baseline (B). C confuses tuning-time scheduling with runtime execution scheduling. D fabricates a floor rule not present in the paper.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: non-uniform allocation driven by marginal impact on end-to-end time.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: the paper motivates the scheduler by the failings of uniform baselines.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: the task scheduler operates during autotuning, not at inference.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: no such fixed floor rule is described.

assumptions: Familiarity with Ansor paper §5.
'Task' means a subgraph carved out for scheduling in Ansor.
nonImplications: Does not imply Ansor's specific speedup numbers generalize across workloads and hardware.
Does not imply the scheduler ignores per-task convergence; plateau detection is part of the marginal-improvement estimate.

sourceRefs.locator: §5 task scheduler design and comparison to uniform baseline

questions.subtopic: FlashAttention: IO-awareness, exactness, scope of speedup
questions.learningObjective: Explain FlashAttention's core IO-aware optimization, the mechanism (tiling + online softmax + recomputation), and identify when the speedup is largest.

hardwareContext.architecture: GPU with on-chip SRAM (e.g. A100, H100)
requiredFeatures: large enough SRAM per SM to hold attention block tiles

questions.stem: Which THREE of the following statements about FlashAttention (v1) are correct, per the paper?

options.text: The speedup versus a naive attention kernel is largest in the memory-bound regime (long sequences where HBM traffic dominates) and can be smaller for very short sequences where the naive kernel is compute-bound on the SM.
FlashAttention's backward pass reuses the N×N attention matrix stored during the forward pass; storing this matrix is what makes the backward efficient.

FlashAttention computes attention block-by-block in on-chip SRAM using an online (numerically stable) softmax and never materializes the full N×N attention matrix in HBM; total HBM traffic drops from Θ(N²) to Θ(N²·d/M), where M is the SRAM budget.
FlashAttention produces exact attention outputs (up to floating-point ordering); it does not approximate the softmax or drop entries.

questions.explanation: A, B, C are the core claims of the FlashAttention paper. A: IO-aware tiling + online softmax. B: exact attention (no approximation). C: speedup scales with the memory-bound regime — long N is where naive attention's Θ(N²) HBM traffic dominates, so FlashAttention gains most; for very short sequences the naive kernel may already be compute-bound and FlashAttention's tiling overhead can eat into gains. D is wrong: FlashAttention deliberately does NOT store the N×N matrix; the backward recomputes intermediates from stored per-row softmax statistics.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: speedup is shape-dependent; largest in the memory-bound regime.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: the N×N matrix is not stored; recomputation from statistics is used.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: IO-aware tiling + online softmax + Θ(N²·d/M) HBM traffic.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: exact attention.

assumptions: Familiarity with FlashAttention paper §3–§5.
SRAM refers to on-chip shared memory / L1 that holds a tile of Q/K/V and running statistics.
nonImplications: Does not imply the paper's specific speedup numbers (e.g. 2–4×) apply to arbitrary hardware or shapes; they are measurements on specific GPUs.
Does not imply that FlashAttention beats every attention kernel; for short N some hand-tuned baselines can match it.

performanceClaim.scope: Attention on GPU with sequence length N and head dim d; comparison against a naive unfused attention baseline

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish peak (best-case) speedup from geometric-mean speedup and understand the scope-limits of reported paper numbers such as those in GSPMD.
questions.stem: A colleague summarizes GSPMD as 'partitioning gives 2× speedup end-to-end', citing a peak result from one model in the paper. Which TWO statements about interpreting such paper speedups are correct?

options.text: Any speedup reported in a systems paper is a property of the technique alone and is independent of the baseline; comparing against an older framework version is equivalent to comparing against its current version.

A paper's 'peak' speedup is the best-case observation on one (workload, hardware) pair; the geometric-mean speedup across the paper's full workload suite is typically smaller, so summarizing the paper by the peak overstates typical benefits.

Reported speedups are conditioned on that paper's hardware, software stack, workload set and baseline; treating them as a general property of the technique that transfers to arbitrary settings requires additional justification.
Peak and geometric-mean speedup are the same metric computed differently and can be used interchangeably as long as the workload set is identical.

questions.explanation: A: peak is by definition the max, typically strictly larger than the geomean summary across a suite; using peak as a general claim overstates. B: paper speedups are conditioned on hardware, software stack, workload and baseline; the paper's numbers require restatement of conditions when generalized. C confuses two distinct statistics. D ignores that baselines evolve — comparing against an outdated baseline is not the same as comparing against a current one.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: baselines matter and evolve.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: peak-vs-geomean semantics and the overstatement risk.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: paper numbers are conditioned on the paper's setup.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: peak and geomean are different summaries.

assumptions: The reader understands geometric mean as (∏ speedup_i)^(1/N).
The comparison is across a multi-workload benchmark suite.
nonImplications: Does not imply peak numbers are useless; they are useful for characterizing best case.
Does not imply a paper's technique fails outside its evaluated setup; it means quantitative claims must be re-supported.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Halide paper separates the algorithm (what to compute) from the schedule (how to compute) and identify the design intent behind this separation.
questions.stem: The Halide paper is best known for separating the algorithm (what to compute) from the schedule (how to compute). Which statement best captures the design intent argued in the paper?

options.text: The separation exists so that the compiler can hide the algorithm behind an opaque API; users interact only with schedules.
The separation is required for correctness: only by moving loop order out of the algorithm can Halide guarantee that per-pixel updates remain race-free on multi-core CPUs.

The separation lets a single, portable algorithm be re-scheduled (tiled, vectorized, parallelized, fused, recomputed) without changing its semantics, so many performance-relevant strategies can be explored on each target without rewriting the pipeline.
The separation is a legacy artifact from Halide's origins as a C++ template library; in modern implementations the two parts are merged and the design contribution is largely obsolete.

questions.explanation: Halide's §1–§3 explicitly argue that the algorithm/schedule split is the central design contribution: the algorithm is a portable, semantics-only description; the schedule expresses per-target loop nesting, tiling, parallelization and storage/recomputation trade-offs. Users can enumerate many schedules cheaply, autotuners can search over them, and the compiler guarantees each legal schedule preserves the algorithm's output.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: the paper argues for exposing schedules to programmers, not hiding algorithms.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: correctness is preserved by dependence analysis, not by the syntactic separation itself.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: matches the paper's stated design intent — portability + tunability without rewriting.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: the separation is Halide's flagship contribution, not a legacy artifact.

assumptions: Familiarity with Halide paper Sections 1–3.
Understanding that a 'schedule' in Halide covers loop order, tiling, storage, parallel/vector directives, and produce-consume relations.
nonImplications: Does not imply that any schedule is beneficial; most are worse than the default.
Does not imply Halide's schedule language is complete for every optimization; some transformations (e.g. arbitrary polyhedral reordering) fall outside its scope.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses dependence analysis with algorithm/schedule separation.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the design intent behind MLIR's multi-level lowering and dialect ecosystem.
questions.stem: The MLIR paper motivates a design with many co-existing dialects at different abstraction levels rather than a single universal IR. Which statement best captures the design intent argued in the paper?

options.text: MLIR argues that a single universal IR is optimal; the multiple dialects are transient artifacts that are collapsed into one representation before any optimization runs.
MLIR's design goal is to be a runtime system that dispatches operations across hardware at execution time; the dialects correspond to different runtimes.

MLIR is designed so each optimization can be expressed at the abstraction level where it is most natural (e.g. tensor-level fusion at a high dialect, tiling at Linalg, code emission at LLVM), with progressive lowering between dialects; the payoff is shared compiler infrastructure reused across domains.
MLIR replaces LLVM as the compilation backend; projects using MLIR no longer emit LLVM IR at any point.

questions.explanation: The MLIR paper's core argument is that different optimizations belong at different abstraction levels, and having a shared infrastructure (parser, type system, pass manager, pattern rewriter) that hosts multiple dialects lets compiler authors share machinery across domains. Progressive lowering between dialects (e.g. TF → Tosa → Linalg → Vector → LLVM) is the standard pipeline pattern. MLIR complements LLVM rather than replacing it.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: reverses the paper's argument — dialects are first-class, not transient.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: MLIR is a compiler infrastructure, not a runtime system.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: multi-level dialects + shared infrastructure + progressive lowering.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: MLIR typically lowers to LLVM IR via the LLVM dialect.

assumptions: Familiarity with MLIR paper §1–§3 and the general pipeline pattern.
nonImplications: Does not imply every project needs many dialects; small pipelines can use one or two.
Does not imply MLIR guarantees better code than existing compilers; the argument is about infrastructure reuse and abstraction.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses multi-dialect design with a monolithic IR.

sourceRefs.locator: §1–§3 motivation for shared multi-level IR infrastructure

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish end-to-end model speedup from kernel-level speedup when interpreting the PyTorch 2 paper's `torch.compile` results.

softwareContext.frameworkVersionScope: PyTorch 2.x as reported in the paper

questions.stem: The PyTorch 2 paper reports end-to-end speedups under `torch.compile` on TorchBench-style benchmarks. A reader sees an Inductor-generated Triton kernel that is 3× faster than the eager kernel and infers 'the whole model runs 3× faster'. Which statement most accurately characterizes the reasoning error?

options.text: The reader's error is that Triton kernels never provide speedup over eager on GPUs; the observed 3× must be a measurement artifact and should be discarded.
The reader correctly identifies end-to-end speedup; kernel-level speedup and model-level speedup are always identical when the same benchmark suite is used.

The reader conflates kernel-level and end-to-end speedup. Amdahl's law limits the end-to-end benefit to the fraction of runtime spent in the accelerated kernel; host-side overhead, graph breaks, and non-compiled subgraphs cap the observable end-to-end speedup below the per-kernel factor.
The reader confuses forward and backward pass; end-to-end speedup is defined only for backward-pass time, not the whole model.

questions.explanation: Kernel-level speedup does not equal end-to-end speedup: by Amdahl's law, end-to-end improvement is bounded by the fraction of time the accelerated kernel occupies. In `torch.compile` workloads that fraction is further reduced by host-side Python overhead, graph breaks that force eager fallback, and non-compiled subgraphs. The other options mis-characterize either the relationship (B), the empirical fact (C), or the scope of the metric (D).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: Triton kernels can and do provide speedups; the error is generalization, not measurement.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: kernel and end-to-end speedups are not equal in general.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: Amdahl-bound argument for kernel vs end-to-end speedup.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: end-to-end speedup covers full-model time, not backward-only.

assumptions: Familiarity with the PyTorch 2 paper's evaluation methodology.
Amdahl's law understanding.
nonImplications: Does not imply Triton kernels are ineffective; they can substantially accelerate certain kernels.
Does not imply that the paper's numbers apply to arbitrary hardware/models.

sourceRefs.locator: § evaluation methodology and end-to-end speedup reporting
torch.compile behavior: graph breaks, eager fallback

questions.subtopic: Scope limits of single-paper quantization claims
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the scope limits and common overclaims around single-paper quantization results (SmoothQuant, GPTQ, AWQ).
questions.stem: A colleague summarizes recent quantization work by combining results from SmoothQuant, GPTQ and AWQ into universal claims. Which THREE of the following statements about interpreting these papers are correct?

options.text: An ablation study (e.g. SmoothQuant's migration-factor α) supports the specific mechanism it isolates but does not by itself establish head-to-head superiority over other quantization methods at every setting.

Because all three papers report memory footprint reductions when quantizing to 4-bit, one can conclude that 4-bit quantization always yields ≥3× end-to-end latency speedup regardless of hardware and kernel implementation.

The papers' accuracy results are conditioned on specific model families, sizes, tasks and calibration sets; extending them to 'LLMs in general' (including smaller models, code/math tasks and long-tail benchmarks) requires additional evaluation.

Reported wall-clock speedups depend on the availability of an efficient dequantized-GEMM kernel for the given precision/granularity on the target hardware; the same scheme can be faster on one GPU generation and no faster (or slower) on another.

questions.explanation: A, B, C reflect careful reading of the papers' scopes. D confuses memory footprint (largely arithmetic, hardware-independent) with wall-clock latency (kernel- and hardware-dependent). Memory savings do not automatically translate to speedup; a specific dequantized-GEMM kernel must exist for the target hardware, or the operation may run slower due to overhead.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: ablations isolate mechanism, not head-to-head verdicts.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: memory reduction ⇏ latency speedup.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: paper-scope discipline on model/task/calibration conditioning.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: latency depends on kernel availability, not just bit width.

assumptions: Familiarity with SmoothQuant, GPTQ, AWQ evaluation sections.
Distinction between memory footprint and wall-clock latency.
nonImplications: Does not imply the techniques never generalize; they often do, subject to re-evaluation.
Does not imply that ablations are useless — they characterize mechanism.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses memory footprint with latency speedup.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Triton paper introduces a tile-level IR, positioned between CUDA-thread and pure tensor abstractions.
questions.stem: The Triton paper positions its programming abstraction at the 'tile' (block-of-elements) level rather than at the CUDA thread level. What is the primary design intent argued in the paper?

options.text: Triton targets CPUs and TPUs but not GPUs; the tile IR was designed to hide vendor-specific GPU details that the paper explicitly declines to support.
Triton is a strict superset of CUDA where every CUDA program is also a valid Triton program; the tile abstraction only adds convenience macros without changing what the programmer must reason about.
Triton is a runtime library that dispatches PyTorch operators to hand-written CUDA kernels; the 'tile' terminology refers to caching policies inside the dispatcher.

Programmers write kernels over blocks of elements; the compiler translates tile-level ops into per-thread PTX with coalescing, shared-memory staging and register tiling handled automatically, so users focus on block shapes and memory access patterns rather than per-thread indexing.

questions.explanation: The Triton paper's tile-level abstraction is the key design decision: users express computation over blocks/tiles of elements; the compiler is responsible for translating those tile ops into per-thread PTX, handling coalescing, shared-memory staging and register tiling. This is a middle abstraction between raw CUDA thread programming and high-level tensor libraries, aimed at competitive performance with much less per-thread bookkeeping.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: Triton primarily targets NVIDIA GPUs.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: Triton is not a superset of CUDA; the user does not write per-thread code.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: Triton is a compiler for kernels, not a dispatcher over hand-written CUDA.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: tile-level abstraction with compiler-emitted per-thread code.

assumptions: Familiarity with Triton paper §2–§3.
nonImplications: Does not imply Triton beats hand-tuned CUDA on every kernel.
Does not imply users can ignore memory access patterns; block shapes and offsets remain user-facing.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses tile-level abstraction with a CUDA extension.

questions.subtopic: TVM: real measurement vs analytical cost model
questions.learningObjective: Explain why TVM (and its Ansor/AutoTVM descendants) rely on real hardware measurement rather than a pure analytical cost model to select schedules.
questions.stem: TVM's schedule search relies on on-device measurement (feeding a learned cost model) rather than a pure analytical performance model. Which statement best captures the design rationale argued in the TVM paper?

options.text: Analytical models cannot express any form of loop tiling, so measurement is the only way to compare tiled schedules; without measurement TVM would be forced to emit only untiled code.

On modern accelerators, effective performance depends on hard-to-model factors (cache/coalescing, register pressure, instruction mix, compiler back-end choices) that closed-form models fail to rank reliably at fine granularity, so a measurement-driven (and learned) cost model is used to guide the search.
Measurement is used purely for reproducibility: since analytical models depend on constants that vary by driver version, TVM re-measures every kernel on every deployment to remove that dependency.
The paper argues that a sufficiently detailed analytical model is always superior; measurement is included only as a compatibility path for hardware without a published architecture manual.

questions.explanation: TVM (and Ansor) argue that closed-form analytical models miss important microarchitectural effects. A learned cost model trained on measurements ranks candidates cheaply; a subset is then measured on-device to refine the model. The design accepts autotuning wall-clock time as a trade-off for high-quality schedules across many targets.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: analytical models can express tiling; the objection is about ranking accuracy, not expressibility.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: matches the paper's stated argument for measurement-based (learned) cost.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: reproducibility is not the stated motivation.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: the paper does not claim analytical models are always superior.

assumptions: Familiarity with the TVM paper's autotuning pipeline.
nonImplications: Does not imply autotuning is free; TVM explicitly accepts autotuning time as a trade-off.
Does not imply analytical models are removed; a learned cost model on top of measurements is analytical in a broad sense.

sourceRefs.locator: §4–§5 schedule search + learned cost model motivation

questions.learningObjective: Explain vLLM's PagedAttention design intent: the KV-cache memory-fragmentation problem it targets.
questions.stem: The vLLM paper introduces PagedAttention. What problem, as stated in the paper, is PagedAttention primarily designed to solve?

options.text: It targets KV-cache memory inefficiency: reserving one contiguous buffer per sequence sized to a worst-case length causes internal fragmentation (unused reserved slots) and external fragmentation (holes between sequences); paging KV in fixed-size blocks with a page table lets the serving system fit more concurrent sequences on the same GPU.
It reduces attention FLOPs by paging out cold key/value entries and reloading them only when needed, cutting per-token compute for long sequences.
It eliminates the KV cache entirely by recomputing K and V on demand each decode step, trading extra compute for HBM savings.
It replaces attention with a paged Mixture-of-Experts routing scheme in which each expert operates on one memory page at a time.

questions.explanation: The vLLM paper's central problem statement is KV-cache memory waste from worst-case contiguous reservation. PagedAttention stores KV in fixed-size blocks addressed via a per-sequence page table, dramatically reducing internal and external fragmentation and letting the server fit more concurrent sequences (larger effective batch), which raises throughput. It does not change attention FLOPs, eliminate KV cache, or introduce MoE routing.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: internal+external fragmentation of KV cache is the target.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: no compute reduction is claimed; the mechanism is memory management.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: KV cache is preserved, just paged.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: unrelated to MoE.

assumptions: Familiarity with vLLM paper §3.
Reader understands 'internal fragmentation' (unused slots inside a reservation) vs 'external fragmentation' (gaps between reservations).
nonImplications: Does not imply PagedAttention speedup comes from a faster attention kernel; it comes from a larger feasible batch size.
Does not imply the paper's specific throughput numbers apply to arbitrary hardware / workloads.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses memory management with compute reduction.
distractorRationales.C: Denies the existence of the KV cache.

sourceRefs.locator: §3 KV cache fragmentation problem and PagedAttention design
